issues.title: Proposal: Add `computer` Tool for Agentic UI Automation

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

issues.body:
## Summary

Integrate [Cua's computer-server](https://github.com/trycua/cua/tree/main/libs/python/computer-server) into Clawdbot to enable desktop/screen control across all ExecHost types.

## Motivation

### Current Capabilities

Clawdbot agents can today:
- Run shell commands (in sandbox or gateway)
- Control browsers via CDP
- Read/write files
- Search the web
- Send messages

### What's Missing

Agents **cannot**:
- Take screenshots of the desktop
- Click at screen coordinates
- Type outside of browser contexts
- Control native applications
- See what's on screen (beyond browser)

This limits agents to CLI and browser workflows. With computer-use, agents could automate any GUI application.

## Proposed Solution

Add a `computer` tool that delegates to [cua-computer-server](https://pypi.org/project/cua-computer-server/), which provides 40+ desktop automation commands via WebSocket, HTTP, and MCP interfaces.

### How It Fits with ExecHost Types

| ExecHost | Current | With computer-server |
|----------|---------|---------------------|
| **Sandbox** | Docker container, shell + files | + desktop control via `cua-xfce`/`cua-ubuntu` images |
| **Node** | Companion app (iOS/Android/macOS) | + device screen control via embedded server |
| **Gateway** | Host shell + files | Not recommended (controls your actual screen) |

> **Note**: Computer-use on Gateway is discouraged since it gives agents control of your actual desktop. Use Sandbox (isolated container) or Node (separate device) instead.

### Architecture

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                      Clawdbot Agent                         │
│  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │                   Computer Tool                        │  │
│  │            (calls computer-server MCP/API)             │  │
│  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                              │
              ┌───────────────┴───────────────┐
              ▼                               ▼
       ┌─────────────┐                 ┌─────────────┐
       │   Sandbox   │                 │    Node     │
       │  (Docker)   │                 │  (Device)   │
       │             │                 │             │
       │ cua-xfce or │                 │ computer-   │
       │ cua-ubuntu  │                 │ server      │
       │ (built-in)  │                 │ (embedded)  │
       └─────────────┘                 └─────────────┘
```

### End-User Setup

#### Sandbox Mode (recommended)

Just use Cua's desktop container images - no extra setup:

```bash
# In clawdbot config, set sandbox image to cua-xfce or cua-ubuntu
clawdbot configure
# → agents.defaults.sandbox.docker.image = "ghcr.io/trycua/cua-xfce:latest"
```

These images include computer-server running as a daemon with a virtual display.

#### Node Mode (companion devices)

Computer-server is embedded in the companion apps. Pair your device and agents can control it.

**Limitations:**
- **iOS**: Requires device to be on the same LAN as Clawdbot
- **Android**: May require ad-hoc setup (ADB, accessibility permissions)

### Available Sandboxes

All include computer-server pre-installed. See [Cua Desktop Sandboxes](https://cua.ai/docs/cua/guide/get-started/what-is-desktop-sandbox#docker-sandboxes) for details.

| Sandbox | OS | Description |
|---------|-----|-------------|
| `cua-xfce` | Linux | Docker + XFCE desktop |
| `cua-ubuntu` | Linux | Docker + Kasm desktop |
| `cua-qemu-linux` | Linux | QEMU/KVM VM (Ubuntu 22.04) |
| `cua-qemu-windows` | Windows | QEMU/KVM VM (Windows 11) |
| `cua-qemu-android` | Android | QEMU/KVM emulator |
| Lume | macOS | Native VM (Apple Silicon) |

### Computer Tool Actions

```typescript
interface ComputerToolInput {
  action:
    | 'screenshot'
    | 'click' | 'double_click' | 'right_click'
    | 'type' | 'key' | 'hotkey'
    | 'scroll' | 'move_mouse' | 'drag'
    | 'get_accessibility_tree'
    | 'get_screen_size';

  coordinate?: [number, number];
  text?: string;
  key?: string;
  keys?: string[];
  direction?: 'up' | 'down';
  amount?: number;
}
```

### Security Model

Follows Clawdbot's existing security patterns:

| ExecHost | Security | Approval |
|----------|----------|----------|
| **Sandbox** | Full access (isolated container) | None needed |
| **Node** | Device screen access | Per-device policy |

## Integration Approach

Since computer-server exposes an **MCP interface**, integration could be as simple as:

1. Connect to computer-server's MCP endpoint (`http://localhost:8000/mcp`)
2. Expose its tools as Clawdbot tools
3. Route based on ExecHost type

## Open Questions

1. **Tool exposure**: Single `computer` tool with action parameter, or separate tools?

2. **MCP vs custom**: Use computer-server's MCP directly, or build a custom adapter?

## Related

- [cua-computer-server](https://github.com/trycua/cua/tree/main/libs/python/computer-server) - Desktop automation server
- [Cua Desktop Sandboxes](https://cua.ai/docs/cua/guide/get-started/what-is-desktop-sandbox) - Pre-built sandbox images
- [Lume](https://github.com/trycua/cua/tree/main/libs/lume) - macOS VM management

---

**Feedback welcome!**

issues.title: Timeout paths produce wrong output, not absent output: duplicate sends, a fabricated user turn, and a non-clearing restart loop

issues.body:
## Summary

Three distinct defects on the timeout paths, found in one day of forensics on a
self-hosted deployment (three Telegram-bridged agents, local Ollama provider).
They share a theme: **when a run or an ingress times out, the system produces
output that is wrong rather than absent** — a duplicate message, a fabricated
user turn, or a claim of work that never happened.

Version: `2026.7.1-2`. Evidence below is from gateway logs, the audit SQLite
store, and session transcripts; identifiers are redacted.

---

## 1. A run-budget timeout emits exactly two messages

Every duplicate message observed was a run-budget timeout notice, sent twice
~0.75s apart.

The correlation is total **in both directions**: all 5 `run_timed_out` rows in
the entire `audit_events` table map 1:1 onto all 5 back-to-back send pairs in the
entire gateway log. All 17 non-timeout sends in the same log are singletons.

```
run_timed_out (agent A) -> msgId N   @T+0.000, msgId N+1 @T+0.788
run_timed_out (agent A) -> msgId M   @T+0.000, msgId M+1 @T+0.718
run_timed_out (agent B) -> msgId P   @T+0.000, msgId P+1 @T+0.756
```

Each pair fires **exactly 600s after its prompt** (600.674s, 600.711s measured),
matching the run budget. Both sends log `chunkCount=1`, so this is not message
splitting.

Ruled out with evidence:
- **Two pollers** — zero `409` / `Conflict` / `terminated by other getUpdates` /
  `429` / `retry_after` lines anywhere in the log.
- **Spool redelivery** — that handler's timeout is 300s, not 600s, and produced
  zero sends.

Corroborating: for one such run the trajectory records
`{"aborted":true,"timedOut":true,"timedOutByRunBudget":true,"promptError":"request timed out","usage":{"output":701}}`
and the session's final assistant message is literally `[]` — the model's 701
output tokens were discarded, yet two messages still went out.

**Expected:** one timeout notice per timed-out run.

---

## 2. An ingress timeout substitutes a fabricated user turn

This is the serious one: a user message was dropped **and replaced with text the
user never wrote**, which the model then answered and quoted back.

`channel_ingress_events` shows the drop:

```
event <id-A>  failed_reason=handler-timeout  attempts=0  completed_at=NULL   (after 300.2s)
event <id-B>  failed_reason=handler-timeout  attempts=0  completed_at=NULL   (after 300.5s)
```

Note `attempts=0` — the queue never retried.

The work actually **finished** and the result was orphaned:

```
spooled update <id-A> completed after buffered processing but could not tombstone
its claimed spool row: ... lost claim ownership before completion
```

That timestamp coincides exactly with an `audit_events` row
`status=cancelled error_code=run_cancelled` — a watchdog cancelled a run whose
output already existed.

**The substitution.** The inbound message was **116 characters** per the gateway
log. The transcript's corresponding user turn reads:

```
Continue the OpenClaw runtime event.
```

— 36 characters, not what the user sent. The same synthetic turn appears a second
time ~7 minutes later. The user's real (34-char) message reaches the transcript
2m54s late. The model then referenced the fabricated text back to the user.

**Expected:** a failed ingress should surface as an error or a retry, never as
invented user content. An agent's record of what the human said must not be
synthesised. This is a correctness problem well beyond a dropped message: the
model acted on text the user never wrote.

---

## 3. Bots restart-loop with a reason that never clears

Twenty restarts across four channel accounts in 40 minutes, five rounds exactly
ten minutes apart:

```
T+00  [health-monitor] [telegram:<acct>] restarting (reason: stale-socket)
T+10  [health-monitor] [telegram:<acct>] restarting (reason: disconnected)
T+20 / T+30 / T+40   (reason: disconnected)  + "auto-restart attempt 1/10 in 5s"
```

The reason never cleared — the restarts were not fixing the condition — and it
ended only because the host was shut down. The same shape appears on one earlier
date in the same log (also 20 restarts).

Two observations that may help:
- `auto-restart attempt 1/10` — the counter reads 1/10 on every round, so the
  backoff/escalation never advances past the first attempt.
- The health monitor's own restart lines keep the gateway log "fresh", which
  defeats any external liveness check based on log recency.

**Expected:** either the restart escalates/backs off past attempt 1, or a
persistently-unclearing reason surfaces as a hard failure rather than an
indefinite ten-minute loop.

---

## Why these are grouped

All three make a timeout produce *incorrect output* rather than *no output*:
duplicate delivery (1), invented user text (2), and an unbounded "recovery" that
never recovers (3). A deployment cannot mitigate any of them locally — (2) in
particular means transcripts cannot be trusted as a record of what the user said.

Happy to supply fuller log extracts or run instrumented builds against the
reproduction; the deployment reproduces (1) reliably by letting any run exceed the
600s budget.

issues.body:
### Summary

On 2026.7.2-beta.7, every `sessions_spawn` call from our router agent is blocked before
dispatch with `error_code=tool_blocked`. The tool is built, offered to the model, and
permitted by every config knob we can find — it simply never executes. The same agent
successfully used the predecessor tool `collab.spawnAgent` on 2026-07-25 (beta.4 era),
so this looks like a regression introduced with the rename in the beta.5–beta.7 line.

Net effect: the agent cannot delegate to **any** sub-agent. All agent-to-agent
delegation from that agent is dead.

### Environment

- openclaw `2026.7.2-beta.7`
- macOS (Apple Silicon), gateway supervised externally by launchd
  (`OPENCLAW_SUPERVISOR_MODE=external`)
- Provider/model for the calling agent: anthropic / claude-opus-5
- Calling agent tools profile: `messaging`

### Diagnostic signature (the key detail)

From the gateway's own `audit_events` table. `sessions_spawn` emits
`tool.action.finished` with `status=blocked` and **never emits `tool.action.started`** —
i.e. it is rejected pre-dispatch. Every other tool from the same agent emits both.

```
-- sessions_spawn: 6 events, ALL blocked, ZERO started
ts                   agent_id     tool_name       action                 status   error_code
2026-08-12 20:25:45  core-router  sessions_spawn  tool.action.finished   blocked  tool_blocked
2026-08-13 16:45:28  core-router  sessions_spawn  tool.action.finished   blocked  tool_blocked
2026-08-13 16:45:33  core-router  sessions_spawn  tool.action.finished   blocked  tool_blocked
2026-08-13 16:50:07  core-router  sessions_spawn  tool.action.finished   blocked  tool_blocked
2026-08-13 16:50:11  core-router  sessions_spawn  tool.action.finished   blocked  tool_blocked
2026-08-14 14:45:11  core-router  sessions_spawn  tool.action.finished   blocked  tool_blocked

-- collab.spawnAgent (predecessor tool, same agent): dispatches normally
2026-07-25 10:50:54  collab.spawnAgent  tool.action.started    started
2026-07-25 10:50:54  collab.spawnAgent  tool.action.finished   succeeded

-- web_fetch (same agent, unrelated tool): dispatches normally
2026-08-08 22:19:41  web_fetch  tool.action.started   started
2026-08-08 22:19:42  web_fetch  tool.action.finished  failed
```

The 2026-08-12 occurrence is organic production traffic, not a synthetic probe.

### What we ruled out

All verified against the live config and the shipped `dist/`:

1. **Permission / allowlist.** `tools.agentToAgent = {enabled: true, allow: [main,
   core-router, personal-engine]}`; `tools.sessions.visibility = "all"`; the agent's
   `tools.alsoAllow` includes `sessions_spawn`, `sessions_send`, `sessions_yield`,
   `subagents`; `tools.deny` does not include it; `subagents.allowAgents` lists the
   intended target. Spawn depth is 0 against a default `maxSpawnDepth` of 1.
   `sessions_spawn` is not in `GATEWAY_OWNER_ONLY_CORE_TOOLS`, and the caller is the
   owner regardless.
2. **Tool availability.** `includeSubagentSpawnTool = !embedded ||
   options?.allowGatewaySubagentBinding === true`, and the gateway conversation path
   passes `allowGatewaySubagentBinding: true`, so the tool *is* built. The tool-policy
   availability predicate (`coreTools.has(tool)`) is satisfied — this is not the
   "shipped core tools but unavailable in the current runtime/provider/model/config"
   path (which we do see separately for a codex-runtime agent, as expected).
3. **Approvals.** The denial is not in the approval family. Per
   `agent-tools.before-tool-call-*.js`, specific reasons are
   `client-voice-confirmation`, `tool-loop`, and `plugin-approval`, with
   `plugin-before-tool-call` as the *default* fallback (`deniedReason ??
   "plugin-before-tool-call"`). No approvals/admission config gates `sessions_spawn`;
   the only approvals config present is an unrelated channel exec-approvals block.

### The observability gap (secondary ask)

We could not recover the actual denial reason anywhere:

- `audit_events` records `status`/`error_code` but no reason payload.
- `diagnostic_events` did not persist the tool-block payload; `capture_events` empty.
- Nothing in the gateway logs.

Because the reason is unavailable, the calling model *invents* one. Ours consistently
narrated a confident, entirely fabricated `deniedReason: "plugin-before-tool-call"` with
a reason string belonging to a completely different (shell/exec) policy — a string that
exists nowhere in the shipped code. That cost us significant debugging time chasing a
non-existent hook.

**Request:** persist `deniedReason` (and the blocking hook/plugin identity) on the
`tool.execution.blocked` audit row, or surface it in the tool result returned to the
model. A pre-dispatch block that is invisible to both operator and model is very hard
to diagnose.

### Regression window

- 2026-07-25: `collab.spawnAgent` **succeeds** (newest published build at that point was
  `2026.7.2-beta.4`, 2026-07-24).
- 2026-08-12 onward, on `2026.7.2-beta.7` (published 2026-08-02): `sessions_spawn`
  **always blocked**.

So the regression landed in beta.5 (2026-07-28), beta.6 (2026-08-01), or beta.7. The
2026.7.2 release highlights an approvals/admission gate, which seems like a plausible
neighbourhood, though we could not confirm it is the cause.

### Impact

Agent-to-agent delegation is completely unavailable from the affected agent. In a
router/specialist topology where the front-line agent intentionally holds a reduced
toolset and delegates everything else, this silently degrades the whole system to
"whatever the router can do alone" — and because the block is invisible, the model
apologises with a fabricated explanation instead of surfacing a real error.

### Questions

1. What sets `deniedReason` for a pre-dispatch `tool_blocked` on `sessions_spawn`, and
   what config (if any) is expected to permit it beyond `tools.agentToAgent` +
   `subagents.allowAgents`?
2. Was the `collab.spawnAgent` → `sessions_spawn` migration expected to require a config
   change that we've missed?
3. Is this fixed in `2026.8.1-beta.2`? (We could not adopt it to test: 8.1 moves the
   iMessage channel out of core into `@openclaw/imessage`, which is a larger migration
   than we can take right now on a production gateway whose primary channel is iMessage.)

issues.body:
### Summary

Allow agents to probabilistically ignore incoming messages using a configurable `replyRate` parameter to feel more human.

### Problem to solve

Currently, when an agent is running on a personal account (WhatsApp, iMessage) and a sender is in the `allowFrom` list, the agent responds to 100% of their messages instantly. In a real human relationship, people read texts and sometimes don't reply right away, or they expect the user to handle it. 100% response rates are a dead giveaway that it's a bot and can monopolize a conversation.


### Proposed solution

Introduce a replyRate configuration option (0.0 to 1.0) in the channel configurations (e.g., `whatsapp`). When an incoming message passes the allowlist, the access-control module evaluates `Math.random() < replyRate;` if it fails, the message is silently dropped before being queued for an agent turn. The default should be `1.0` (100% backward compatible).

### Alternatives considered

The only current alternative is completely removing the sender from the `allowFrom` list, which entirely disables the AI for that person. Trying to use prompt engineering ("don't reply sometimes") fails because the system still queues a turn and expects a response object. This must be handled at the gateway/access-control level.

### Impact

Affected users: Anyone running relationship automations or personal AI clones.
Severity: High utility for realism.
Frequency: Always.
Consequence: Agents feel drastically more authentic and less overwhelmingly responsive.

### Evidence/examples

I have already built a proof of concept for the WhatsApp extension and updated the Zod schema locally. It intercepts the message in extensions/whatsapp/src/inbound/access-control.ts right after hasTargetAccess().

### Do you plan to open a PR for this?

Yes, I plan to implement this myself

### Additional information

 I already have the code written and tested locally. It is 100% backward compatible since the default rate is 1. I will link the PR to this issue once created.

### Summary

When a command that takes an argument (registered with `acceptsArgs: true` or an `args:[{captureRemaining:true}]` spec, e.g. the built-in `/btw` and `/steer`) is tapped from the Telegram "/" command menu, Telegram sends the bare command immediately with no argument. The command handler then returns its usage string (`Usage: /btw [side question]` / `Usage: /steer <message>`). The user has to notice the hint, then re-type the command plus the argument.

### Proposal

On external channels that support it (Telegram in particular), when an args-requiring command is received with an empty/missing argument, reply with a Telegram **ForceReply** keyboard:

```json
{ "reply_markup": { "force_reply": true, "input_field_placeholder": "e.g. what changed in the last run?" } }
```

ForceReply opens the compose box pre-focused (and, in a group, replying to the bot), so the user just types the argument and sends. This turns a menu tap into a single guided flow instead of a usage hint followed by a manual re-type.

### Notes

- `force_reply` / `ForceReply` does not currently appear anywhere in the Telegram send path, so this is a net-new capability rather than a tweak.
- Ideally opt-in per command (a flag on the command definition, e.g. `promptForMissingArgs: true`) so commands that are meaningful with no argument keep their current behavior.
- TUI/other surfaces are unaffected; this is a Telegram-surface enhancement gated on the channel supporting ForceReply.
- Tested against openclaw 2026.6.10.

issues.title: [Feature]: Hive of Minds - Real-Time Cognitive Orchestration Toward Gestalt Intelligence

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

labels.name: P3
labels.description: Low-priority cleanup, docs, polish, ergonomics, or speculative work.

issues.body:
### Summary

I propose evolving OpenClaw beyond traditional multi-agent task orchestration toward Hive of Minds, a unified cognitive runtime inspired by my broader research architecture, Gestalt Intelligence.

The fundamental distinction:

Instead of one agent assigning tasks to multiple independent agents, one persistent cognitive mind should be able to directly operate, redirect, interrupt, and coordinate multiple active cognitive units as extensions of itself.

This is not another multi-agent workflow framework. It is a proposal for a different software execution paradigm.

Swarm Intelligence → Hive of Minds → Gestalt Intelligence → Systemic Superintelligence

OpenClaw already has many of the underlying execution capabilities. The missing abstraction is a shared cognitive control plane that turns those capabilities into one continuously coordinated system.

### Problem to solve

The Problem: Swarms Execute Tasks, Not Unified Cognition

Most multi-agent systems follow a similar pattern:

A primary agent delegates tasks.

Subagents independently execute them.

Each agent maintains its own context and reasoning process.

Results are eventually returned and aggregated.

The primary agent decides what happens next.

Existing session messaging, steering, and cancellation mechanisms help, but they do not automatically create continuous shared cognition.

Even eight agents running simultaneously are still eight largely independent workers.

Parallel task execution is not the same as one mind operating through eight cognitive capabilities.

Imagine how a human works: while programming, the brain continuously coordinates vision, memory, reasoning, decision-making, and physical actions.

The hands do not receive an independent assignment and return a result after five minutes.

They operate as parts of a continuously coordinated system.

That is the architectural direction I propose.

### Proposed solution

### Introduce a Hive Cognitive Runtime

I propose an optional cognitive execution layer within OpenClaw, allowing one primary intelligence to operate multiple specialized agents as continuously controlled cognitive extensions rather than independent task workers.

**The fundamental architectural change:**

Current approach:

`Primary Agent → Task Delegation → Independent Execution → Result Aggregation`

Proposed approach:

`Unified Cognitive Core ⇄ Shared Cognitive State ⇄ Active Cognitive Units ⇄ Continuous Feedback`

The central intelligence should not need to wait for an agent to finish a task before responding to new information or changing its behavior.

It should maintain continuous awareness of active operations and dynamically control them while they execute.

This is closer to how a human brain coordinates cognitive and physical capabilities than to how conventional multi-agent systems distribute work.

### Core Architecture

**Persistent Cognitive Core**

A continuously operating central intelligence that maintains shared objectives, situational awareness, active reasoning, attention allocation, and operational decisions.

The core should be capable of controlling several active cognitive processes without repeatedly reconstructing the entire workflow after each completed task.

**Live Cognitive Control**

Enable the central intelligence to dynamically:

- Activate specialized agents or models.
- Interrupt, pause, resume, or terminate ongoing operations.
- Redirect an agent while it is actively reasoning or executing.
- Reassign resources and change priorities.
- Transfer discoveries between active experts.
- React to emerging conflicts without waiting for task completion.
- Coordinate multiple active operations as one continuous cognitive process.

OpenClaw already supports several individual agent lifecycle operations. The proposal is to integrate them into a persistent, coordinated cognitive runtime.

**Shared Cognitive State and Memory Fabric**

Introduce a structured shared state containing active goals, working memory, world-state representations, observations, hypotheses, and operational decisions.

All participating cognitive units should contribute to and receive relevant state updates continuously.

This must go beyond ordinary session history, shared documents, or message forwarding.

The system should support event-driven updates, selective context synchronization, versioned state changes, and conflict resolution.

**Continuous Cognitive Feedback**

Implement bidirectional communication between the central intelligence and active cognitive units.

An important discovery by one expert should immediately become available to the central cognitive process and potentially influence other experts.

Instead of isolated task-completion cycles, the architecture should support continuous:

`Observe → Reason → Act → Evaluate → Adapt`

**Dynamic Cognitive Routing**

The central intelligence should select and activate experts based on evolving cognitive requirements.

Routing should not be limited to predefined task decomposition. Experts may participate temporarily, continuously, or in response to changes in the shared cognitive state.

The system should remain compatible with different LLM providers, inference backends, and distributed infrastructure.

### Practical Example: One Mind Controlling Eight Agents

Imagine eight active OpenClaw specialists working on software development, security, infrastructure, databases, testing, architecture, research, and monitoring.

In a conventional swarm, each specialist receives a task, performs independent work, and eventually reports back.

In Hive mode, they operate within one continuous cognitive process.

While a coding specialist modifies an application, the security specialist detects a vulnerability.

The central intelligence immediately changes the coding specialist's direction, updates the testing strategy, requests infrastructure analysis, and pauses an affected deployment.

Other specialists continue operating while incorporating the updated shared state.

**The primary intelligence does not simply collect eight answers. It continuously operates eight cognitive capabilities.**

This is the essential distinction between task orchestration and cognitive orchestration.

### Long-Term Architecture: Gestalt Intelligence

Hive of Minds is the practical software foundation for a larger architecture I call **Gestalt Intelligence**.

The proposed long-term system consists of a general cognitive core connected to hundreds of specialized models through a hierarchical, cloud-native Mixture-of-Experts architecture.

A possible large-scale configuration includes:

- 200–300 specialized models distributed across cloud infrastructure.
- Models with approximately 100 billion parameters each.
- Hierarchical expert routing and sparse activation.
- Individual models containing hundreds of internal MoE experts.
- Persistent shared memory and coordinated reasoning.
- Continuous integration of specialized capabilities into one unified cognitive process.

For example, eight active models containing 512 internal experts each expose 4,096 potential expert components. Actual simultaneous activation depends on the underlying MoE architecture and routing strategy.

This distinction is important: internal MoE experts are not equivalent to independently executing software agents.

The ultimate goal is to investigate whether distributed specialized intelligence can be integrated into a unified general cognitive system with capabilities exceeding those of its individual components.

My research hypothesis is that the transition from independent swarms to integrated cognitive systems may provide an architectural path toward AGI and eventually systemic superintelligence.

**Gestalt is not intended to be another orchestrator supervising hundreds of workers. It is intended to be the unified cognitive intelligence operating through hundreds of specialized capabilities.**

### Suggested OpenClaw MVP

The immediate implementation does not require the complete Gestalt architecture.

I propose starting with an experimental `Hive Runtime` supporting:

- One persistent cognitive controller.
- Eight real, concurrently operating agents.
- A shared, versioned cognitive state.
- Bidirectional cognitive event streaming.
- Runtime interruption and redirection.
- Dynamic activation and deactivation of agents.
- Continuous feedback between experts and the central intelligence.
- Resource and attention management.
- Observable cognitive-state transitions.
- Existing permission boundaries, authorization, and execution safeguards.

This could be implemented incrementally above OpenClaw's existing agent and session infrastructure.

The first milestone should demonstrate that a central intelligence can continuously influence active agents, that discoveries propagate during execution, and that coordinated behavior remains consistent without waiting for independently completed tasks.

Testing should use real models, real tools, and real concurrent execution in a production-localfork environment.

Mocked agents, synthetic shared state, helper-only tests, and regtests should not be accepted as proof of end-to-end cognitive integration.

Success should be measured through control latency, intervention accuracy, shared-state consistency, conflict resolution, recovery behavior, and improvements over conventional multi-agent orchestration using comparable computational resources.

**The objective is not simply to scale from eight agents to eight hundred. It is to fundamentally change how those agents participate in one intelligence.**

This would establish the software foundation for Hive of Minds and create a practical development path toward Gestalt Intelligence.

### Alternatives considered

_No response_

### Impact

**Affected users:** OpenClaw developers, advanced multi-agent users, autonomous-system researchers, enterprise operators, and developers building persistent, long-running cognitive applications.

**Current limitation:** Existing multi-agent workflows primarily optimize task distribution and parallel execution. As agent counts increase, coordination overhead, context fragmentation, inconsistent decisions, redundant operations, and delayed intervention become increasingly important architectural challenges.

**Expected impact:**

- **Unified cognitive execution:** Multiple agents function as continuously controlled extensions of one primary intelligence rather than isolated task workers.
- **Real-time adaptability:** The central intelligence can redirect ongoing operations immediately when new information becomes available.
- **Reduced coordination overhead:** Shared cognitive state and continuous feedback reduce repeated task delegation and result-reconstruction cycles.
- **Better cross-domain reasoning:** Specialized models can contribute to one evolving reasoning process instead of producing disconnected outputs.
- **Greater operational coherence:** Centralized cognitive direction, combined with enforced execution boundaries, improves coordination and conflict management.
- **Scalability:** Establishes software foundations for hierarchical, cloud-native expert systems involving hundreds of specialized models and potentially thousands of internal MoE experts.
- **Research opportunities:** Enables measurable experimentation with unified cognitive architectures, persistent intelligence, distributed reasoning, and future Gestalt-style systems.

**Why this matters for OpenClaw:**

OpenClaw already provides much of the infrastructure required for agent execution. A Hive Cognitive Runtime could extend that foundation beyond traditional automation into a new category of continuously integrated cognitive systems.

This would represent a significant architectural direction rather than another incremental agent-management feature.

**The long-term opportunity is to evolve OpenClaw from a platform that runs autonomous agents into a platform capable of supporting a unified intelligence operating through distributed cognitive capabilities.**

The potential impact extends beyond software development to scientific research, cybersecurity, infrastructure management, robotics, enterprise systems, and other environments requiring continuous coordinated intelligence.

**From Swarm to Hive. From Hive to Gestalt.**

### Evidence/examples

_No response_

### Do you plan to open a PR for this?

Maybe, with maintainer guidance

### Additional information

_No response_

2. In Telegram for iOS, send `/models`.
3. Choose a provider and then a model from the inline keyboard.
4. Observe the final “Model changed” confirmation in the original picker message.

The final confirmation replaces the picker body completely. Telegram Bot API `editMessageText` supports editing rich messages through its `rich_message` parameter: https://core.telegram.org/bots/api#editmessagetext

### Actual behavior

The final confirmation is rendered over the stale “Select a provider:” rich body, leaving overlapping, unreadable text. The attached screenshot captures the observed result.

2026.7.1 (2d2ddc4)

npm global

mlx/Qwen3.5-122B-A10B-4bit

openclaw -> local MLX OpenAI-compatible endpoint

```shell
2026-08-14T15:45:01.158-07:00 [telegram] sendRichMessage ok chat=<redacted> message=6213
```

Current `main` (`2ce443d9a46bd4c5280a3eac9e419655f945e836`) still routes callback edits through grammY's legacy text signature:

- Initial picker text and channel data: [`commands-models.ts#L579-L591`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/2ce443d9a46bd4c5280a3eac9e419655f945e836/src/auto-reply/reply/commands-models.ts#L579-L591)

![Telegram iOS showing the final model confirmation over stale picker text](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/d61a9377-5730-4fc7-85e6-7b5164727d9e)

issues.body:
## Summary

Codex-backed agents (`@openclaw/codex` plugin) intermittently fail `apply_patch`/`exec` calls with a `bwrap: execvp .../bin/codex: No such file or directory` error, even though the target binary exists on disk and is a valid executable. This has reproduced 4 times in one day on our setup, each time requiring a gateway restart + config change to temporarily work around.

- OpenClaw version: `2026.7.1-2 (0790d9f)`
- `@openclaw/codex` plugin, vendored `codex-cli 0.144.3`
- `appServer.mode: "guardian"`, `approvalsReviewer: "auto_review"`, `sandbox: "danger-full-access"`

## Root causes found (two distinct layers)

**1. Guardian path resolution bug (npm generation suffix)**

The main codex app-server correctly resolves the installed package path including npm's generation suffix (e.g. `.../npm/projects/openclaw-codex-<hash>__openclaw-generation__g-<hash2>/...`). The **guardian subagent** (the risk-review pass that runs before approving a planned action) computes the binary path **without** that suffix, trying `.../npm/projects/openclaw-codex-<hash>/...vendor/.../bin/codex`, which never exists on disk — only the suffixed directory does. This produces an ENOENT that manifests as a `bwrap` failure inside the guardian's read-only sandbox check.

Workaround used: a compatibility symlink from the bare (unsuffixed) project dir to the real suffixed one. Fragile — breaks again if the plugin package is reinstalled/updated (new generation hash).

**2. `network_proxy` triggers an internal bwrap re-exec that fails to resolve `current_exe()`**

Independent of (1): when `plugins.entries.codex.config.appServer.networkProxy.enabled: true` (used to auto-approve loopback-only network access without opening full network), the plugin patches Codex's own `features.network_proxy.enabled: true`. This causes Codex to invoke `bwrap` for network-namespace isolation on tool calls, **even when `sandbox: "danger-full-access"` is set** (which by itself does not use bwrap — `codexSandboxPolicyForTurn` correctly returns "no sandbox" for `dangerFullAccess`). Inside that bwrap network-namespace, Codex's own re-exec of itself (`current_exe()`) fails to resolve the binary path — this matches known upstream Codex CLI issues (openai/codex#17367, #24341) about `current_exe()`/cwd resolution inside bwrap mount namespaces.

Workaround: setting `plugins.entries.codex.config.appServer.networkProxy.enabled: false` + restarting the gateway resolved the failures reliably in our testing (confirmed live with real `apply_patch` create/edit/delete + `exec` round-trips on two separate agents post-restart).

## Suggested fixes

- Guardian's binary path resolver should reuse the same generation-suffix-aware resolver the main app-server loader uses, instead of recomputing the path independently.
- `network_proxy`-driven bwrap invocations should either avoid the internal re-exec entirely (pass an explicit resolved executable path instead of relying on `current_exe()`), or the plugin should document/flag that `networkProxy.enabled: true` can trigger this known upstream Codex bwrap/re-exec failure mode, so it's not silently combined with `sandbox: "danger-full-access"` in a way that looks safe but isn't.

## Environment

- Linux (WSL2), x86_64
- Codex auth: ChatGPT OAuth (not API key)
- Reproduced across two independently configured agents on the same gateway instance

Happy to provide sanitized logs/config on request.

issues.body:
### Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

`openclaw wiki ingest` wraps every input in a ```` ```text ```` fence, so ingesting a Markdown file produces a source page whose entire body renders as one code block, and the file's own frontmatter is left buried inside that block instead of being lifted onto the page.

### Steps to reproduce

````sh
printf -- '---\ntags: [demo]\nurl: https://example.invalid/demo\n---\n\n# Demo heading\n\nBody text with `code`.\n\n```bash\necho hi\n```\n' > /tmp/upstream-repro.md

openclaw wiki ingest /tmp/upstream-repro.md --title "Upstream Repro"
cat <vault>/sources/upstream-repro.md
````

Deterministic: 1/1 on the first attempt, and the same shape has appeared on every `.md` ingest into this vault (6 pages across two separate days).

### Expected behavior

A Markdown source page whose body is Markdown: headings, tables and links render as such, and the ingested file's frontmatter keys (`tags`, `url`, `date`, …) land in the page frontmatter, where `wiki lint` and `wiki compile` can see them.

The grounded reference for "Markdown input should not be treated as opaque text" is the sibling import path in the same file: `unsafe-local` calls `renderMarkdownFence(raw, detectFenceLanguage(...))`, and `detectFenceLanguage` explicitly returns `"markdown"` for `.md`. The `wiki ingest` call site is the outlier — it hardcodes `"text"`.

### Actual behavior

The whole document, frontmatter included, is emitted inside a fence. Verbatim output of the repro above on 2026.7.2-beta.3 (only the local path is redacted):

`````markdown
## Content
````text
---
tags: [demo]
url: https://example.invalid/demo
---

# Demo heading

Body text with `code`.

```bash
echo hi
```

````
`````

Page frontmatter after ingest contains only `pageType`, `id`, `title`, `sourceType`, `sourcePath`, `ingestedAt`, `updatedAt`, `status` — `tags` and `url` from the source file are not lifted.

Source, in `ingestMemoryWikiSourceUnlocked` — read from the shipped bundle (`dist/cli-*.js` in the npm package), whose nearest `//#region` marker is `extensions/memory-wiki/src/ingest.ts`:

```js
body: [
	`# ${title}`,
	"",
	"## Source",
	`- Type: \`local-file\``,
	`- Path: \`${sourcePath}\``,
	`- Bytes: ${buffer.byteLength}`,
	`- Updated: ${timestamp}`,
	"",
	"## Content",
	renderMarkdownFence(content, "text"),   // <-- unconditional, every input type
	...
```

Fence *sizing* is correct — `renderMarkdownFence` widens to 4 backticks so an inner ```` ```bash ```` block survives. The defect is only that Markdown is fenced at all.

### OpenClaw version

2026.7.2-beta.3

### Operating system

Ubuntu (Linux 6.17.0-41-generic)

### Install method

npm global

### Model

Not applicable — the defect is in the `openclaw wiki ingest` CLI path. No model is involved in producing the page; the output above is deterministic file rendering.

### Provider / routing chain

Not applicable — no provider request is made by this code path.

### Additional provider/model setup details

Not applicable.

### Logs

```shell
$ openclaw wiki ingest /tmp/upstream-repro.md --title "Upstream Repro"
Ingested /tmp/upstream-repro.md into sources/upstream-repro.md. Refreshed 3 index files.
```

The command reports success; the defect is in the written page, not in the exit path.

### Impact and severity

- **Affected:** anyone using `openclaw wiki ingest` on Markdown, which is the documented maintenance loop — `skills/wiki-maintainer/SKILL.md` tells agents to use `openclaw wiki ingest` as the default.
- **Severity:** blocks workflow, no data loss. The source text is preserved intact; it just renders as an unreadable code block, and agents reading the page back treat it as opaque.
- **Frequency:** always, for every Markdown input.
- **Consequence:** each ingested Markdown source needs a manual unwrap afterwards — promote the body, move the inner frontmatter out, check that real code blocks survived. In this vault that repair has been done twice, on 5 pages (2026-08-14) and on 1 page (2026-08-15). Between the two repairs, downstream pages cited the affected sources while their content was invisible to `wiki compile`'s link graph.

### Additional information

No evidence of a previously-working version — this looks like original behavior rather than a regression, so "last known good" is `NOT_ENOUGH_INFO`.

Suggested fix, for Markdown input on the `wiki ingest` path only:

1. inline the body instead of fencing it;
2. demote its headings one level so the page keeps a single H1 under `# ${title}`;
3. lift its frontmatter into the page frontmatter, skipping keys the page owns (`pageType`, `id`, `title`, `sourceType`, `sourcePath`, `ingestedAt`, `updatedAt`, `status`);
4. keep the current fence for non-Markdown input.

Two details worth getting right in (2): heading demotion must track open code fences, so a `#` comment inside a ```` ```bash ```` block is not rewritten and a 4-backtick fence containing a 3-backtick one is not mis-closed. And malformed inner frontmatter, or an empty body after stripping it, should fall back to the current fenced rendering rather than throwing.

I am running exactly this as a local patch against 2026.7.2-beta.3 and it holds on the cases above (Markdown with frontmatter, `.txt`, malformed frontmatter, nested fences). Happy to open a PR if the approach looks right — say the word and I'll port it to the TypeScript source.

The `bridge` and `unsafe-local` import paths deliberately were not touched by that patch: they ingest logs and JSONL, where fencing is the correct rendering. Only `wiki ingest` is at issue here.

### Bug type

### Beta release blocker

### Summary

A guest working in a managed project can finish dependency or test-tool preparation and then have the command reported as failed because its downloaded cache is treated as a changed workspace result above the 64 MiB per-file limit.

### Steps to reproduce

In a managed guest project whose sandbox commands use the default workspace HOME, run the repository's declared dependency and test-tool preparation. An observed dependency command was `npm exec --yes --package=pnpm@12.11.1 -- pnpm install --frozen-lockfile`, without HOME, XDG, PNPM_HOME or store-dir overrides. Subsequent commands using `scripts/run-vitest.mjs` and `scripts/run-node-package-bin.mts` reached the same result failure for their tool downloads.

The normal command output is followed by `Cloud workspace result is too large` for a file under one of these roots:

- `.local/share/pnpm/store/`
- `.cache/openclaw/bun/`
- `.cache/ms-playwright/`

### Expected behavior

Derived package and test-tool downloads stay with the runtime that owns them. Ordinary source changes and authored artifacts still reconcile, while genuinely oversized authored results retain the existing rejection. This follows the existing exact-root generated-file policy documented in `docs/gateway/sandboxing/workspace-access.md`.

### Actual behavior

The observed commands were marked failed during result capture. Dependency output had already reported installation progress before the pnpm store file was rejected. Bun and Chromium executable paths produced the same error on subsequent commands. This evidence does not establish that installation itself failed or that user data was lost.

### OpenClaw version

Observed on 69eefd48c800ed575b43949c451c004cc942373c; the relevant environment and result-classification code is unchanged at 172fe5791520c37aa1ff1f9a1f1bc3aa933eb3f3.

### Operating system

Linux sandbox. Exact host distribution: NOT_ENOUGH_INFO.

### Install method

NOT_ENOUGH_INFO

### Model

Not required for the workspace-result failure; isolated regression uses no model.

### Provider / routing chain

Sandbox command finalization enters managed workspace reconciliation. Effective inference/provider identity is not established by this report.

### Logs

```text
Cloud workspace result is too large: .local/share/pnpm/store/v11/files/10/<content-hash>
Cloud workspace result is too large: .cache/openclaw/bun/<pinned-version>/linux-x64/bin/bun
Cloud workspace result is too large: .cache/ms-playwright/chromium-1248/chrome-linux64/chrome
```

### Screenshots, recordings, and evidence

A remote Linux regression at 172fe5791520c37aa1ff1f9a1f1bc3aa933eb3f3 created real cache files of 67,108,865 bytes, captured them through `readActualWorkspaceManifestImpl`, and passed that capture through `parseChangedWorkspaceResult`. It reproduced the Chromium-path error at `workspace-manifest-comparison.ts:118`. This is model-free result-boundary proof; the effective environment of the original live sandbox was not separately probed.

### Impact and severity

This obstructs ordinary guest coding work: dependency installation and test-tool preparation can require manual cache cleanup before command finalization succeeds. All three failures occurred in one normal coding session. Broader frequency and data-loss impact are not established.

### Additional information

`buildSandboxEnv` defaults HOME to the command's container working directory. The Bun and Playwright owners use home-relative cache roots, while `workspace-path-exclusions.ts` omits all three observed roots. `parseChangedWorkspaceResult` therefore treats those downloads as authored result payloads and applies its per-file limit. Configured environment overrides remain possible; the actual effective environment was not separately probed.

issues.body:
### Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

The agent prompt advertises Telegram inline buttons whenever `capabilities.inlineButtons` is any non-`off` scope, without regard for the current chat type, so a group turn under `inlineButtons: "dm"` is told to send buttons that the Telegram send runtime then rejects.

### Steps to reproduce

Source-verifiable on current `main`; no live run required to see the mismatch.

1. Set `channels.telegram.capabilities.inlineButtons: "dm"`.
2. Have the agent take a turn in a Telegram **group**.
3. Read the system prompt's Messaging section for that turn, then attempt a button send.

### Expected behavior

The prompt should advertise inline buttons only when the current target can actually accept them. Per `AGENTS.md`: "Never dead-end the agent: failure text states what to try next; unavailable tools are hidden by gating, not left to fail." A capability the runtime will reject for this target should not be presented as available for this turn.

### Actual behavior

The two sides disagree because only one of them is target-aware.

**Advertisement is scope-only.** `extensions/telegram/src/channel.ts:828` emits the capability for every non-`off` scope:

```ts
...(inlineButtonsScope === "off" ? [] : ["inlineButtons"]),
```

**The prompt gate is a plain boolean.** `src/agents/system-prompt.ts:1069` and `:658`:

```ts
const inlineButtonsEnabled = runtimeCapabilitiesLower.has("inlinebuttons");
```

with no chat-type condition on the line that teaches the button payload.

**The runtime is target-aware and rejects.** `extensions/telegram/src/action-runtime.ts:596-601`:

```ts
if (inlineButtonsScope === "dm" && targetType !== "direct") {
  throw new Error('Telegram inline buttons are limited to DMs when inlineButtons="dm".');
}
```

So under scope `dm` in a group, the model is shown the button shape, follows it, and the send throws. The symmetric case exists for scope `group` in a DM.

### OpenClaw version

Reproduced by reading `main` at `76e4ef68ced11426637a62964a06a54ee1754fa5`

### Operating system

macOS (Darwin 27.0.0)

### Install method

source checkout

### Model

Not model-specific; the mismatch is in prompt construction and capability resolution.

### Provider / routing chain

Not provider-specific.

### Additional provider/model setup details

The capability seam is the constraint. `ChannelAgentPromptAdapter.messageToolCapabilities` (`src/channels/plugins/types.core.ts:659`) receives only `{ cfg, accountId }`, and its caller `resolveChannelPromptCapabilities` (`src/agents/channel-tools.ts:135`) has no chat type either. A channel plugin therefore *cannot* answer "is this capability available for the current target?" even though its own runtime decides exactly that. Any fix likely needs the current chat type threaded to that seam, which is an additive optional field rather than a breaking change.

### Logs

```shell
No runtime logs. This is reported from source on the line references above; the
disagreement is visible without executing a turn.
```

### Screenshots, recordings, and evidence

None; see the cited lines.

### Impact and severity

- **Affected:** Telegram operators using the scoped values `inlineButtons: "dm"` or `"group"`. The `all` and `off` scopes are unaffected, since for those the advertisement and the runtime agree.
- **Severity:** Moderate. The failure is loud (the send throws with a clear message) rather than silent, so it is well below the silent-drop class, but it dead-ends the agent on a path the prompt told it to take.
- **Frequency:** Deterministic for the mismatched scope/target combination.
- **Consequence:** a wasted model turn and a rejected send, on a configuration the operator set deliberately.

### Additional information

Found while addressing review feedback on #120330, which was correct to flag it. Filing separately because it is not introduced by that PR: #120330 touches no `extensions/telegram` files and changes no line of the capability gate, so the mismatch is present identically on `main` today. That PR does make the path easier to reach, by removing prompt wording that had discouraged same-destination `message(action=send)` in groups — which is how the issue surfaced.

Happy to implement the fix, in #120330 or on its own branch, once a maintainer indicates whether threading chat type into `messageToolCapabilities` is the shape they want.

_Filed by an AI agent (Claude) on behalf of the account owner. Every claim above is from the cited source lines._

issues.body:
### Summary

Setting `channels.whatsapp.sendReadReceipts: false` does not just suppress outbound blue ticks — it causes WhatsApp's server to **stop delivering group messages to the linked device**. Direct/1:1 (and self-chat) messages keep flowing, `openclaw channels status` still reports `linked / connected / healthy`, and the gateway log simply shows **zero group inbound**. There is no error and no health signal, so it presents as "group mentions silently do nothing."

WhatsApp mandates read receipts in groups; a linked device that never sends them appears to get its group delivery throttled/cut by the server.

### Reproduction

1. On a config that participates in WhatsApp groups, set `channels.whatsapp.sendReadReceipts: false`.
2. Group inbound goes dead (in my case for ~2 days) — no group message reaches the gateway. 1:1/self-chat still works; `channels status` still reports healthy.
3. A plain channel/gateway restart does **not** recover it (restarted with the flag still `false` → still broken).
4. Flip `sendReadReceipts: true` and restart → group inbound is restored **immediately**.

The only variable changed between the failing restart and the recovering restart was `sendReadReceipts`, which points squarely at the flag rather than the reconnect.

### Docs gap

`docs/gateway/config-channels.md` (~line 134) documents the flag only as:

```
sendReadReceipts: true, // blue ticks (false in self-chat mode)
```

There is no mention of the group-delivery side effect.

### Request

- Document that `sendReadReceipts: false` can break WhatsApp **group** inbound delivery (not just hide blue ticks).
- Ideally, warn (or refuse) when a groups-enabled WhatsApp config sets `sendReadReceipts: false`.

### Environment

- OpenClaw dist ~v2026.7.1-2, macOS, Baileys/WhatsApp Web linked-device.

issues.body:
## Summary

A persistent ACP session spawned into its own thread (via `sessions_spawn({ thread: true })`, e.g. an OpenCode coding thread) never delivers its replies back to that thread. The user sends a message in the thread and the session runs, but no reply appears on the channel.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. From a channel that supports threads, spawn a persistent ACP session with `sessions_spawn({ runtime: "acp", agentId: "opencode", thread: true, mode: "session", cwd: "/path/to/project" })`.
2. A new thread is created and bound to the session.
3. Send a normal message in that thread.

## Expected

The ACP session's reply is delivered in the thread; multi-turn conversation works.

## Actual

No reply is delivered in the thread. The gateway logs:

```
visible channel turn dispatched with no queued reply payloads: channel=... sessionKey=agent:opencode:acp:...
```

The session did produce output (visible in the ACP transcript), but delivery to the user channel was suppressed.

## Root Cause

Delivery suppression is keyed only on session lineage. `resolveAcpSessionInteractionMode` (`packages/acp-core/src/session-interaction-mode.ts`) classifies any ACP session carrying `spawnedBy`/`parentSessionKey` as `parent-owned-background`, and `prepareDispatchDelivery` (`src/auto-reply/reply/dispatch-from-config.prepare-delivery.ts`) suppresses user-channel delivery for that whole class. A thread-bound child carries `spawnedBy` too, even though it is the user-facing owner of its own thread, so its replies are dropped alongside genuine silent background delegations. The conversation binding (`boundAcpDispatchSessionKey`, already resolved in the gather phase) is not consulted.

## Impact

Persistent ACP coding sessions spawned into a thread are effectively unusable: the user cannot converse with them in-thread. Only the operator slash-command spawn path (which does not set `spawnedBy`) delivers replies.

## Environment

- OpenClaw 2026.7.1
- macOS
- Runtime: ACP via acpx (OpenCode harness)

## Proposed Fix

Gate suppression on the conversation binding so a background session bound to the visible conversation it is delivering to still speaks there, while unbound background children stay silent.

issues.body:
## Summary

Add a Telegram-native `/ignore` command that keeps one human-only message out of agent context.

## Problem to solve

Shared Telegram chats often contain side conversations intended for other humans. Today those messages still enter OpenClaw's history and prompt context, which can distract the agent and cause later replies to reference irrelevant chatter.

## Proposed solution

Treat `/ignore <message>` and `/ignore@ThisBot <message>` as Telegram-native commands. After normal sender authorization, drop the update before reply-chain recording, media download/transcription, typing indicators, history compilation, or agent dispatch. Bare `/ignore` returns concise usage help.

The command is exact-token only: `/ignoreme`, inline mentions, and commands addressed to another bot remain ordinary messages. Albums are suppressed as a unit at the existing media-group flush boundary. A deliberate direct reply may reintroduce the replied-to Telegram quote for that turn, while the ignored ancestor is not recursively persisted into ambient history.

No new configuration or storage schema is introduced. Disabling native Telegram commands disables `/ignore` as well.

## Alternatives considered

- `/btw` controls whether the bot replies while retaining the message in context; it solves the opposite half of the workflow.
- A plugin hook runs too late to prevent history ingestion and media processing.
- Per-chat configuration, tombstones, or durable ignore tracking add complexity that is unnecessary for a one-update context-hygiene command.

## Impact

- Affected: people using OpenClaw in active Telegram groups and forum topics.
- Severity: recurring context pollution rather than data loss or a security boundary.
- Frequency: potentially daily in mixed human/agent conversations.
- Consequence: irrelevant agent context, confused follow-ups, and manual correction.

## Evidence/examples

The behavior follows existing Telegram ingress and native-command patterns, including foreign-bot command handling and early media policy checks. Local focused validation covers exact matching, foreign-bot and near-miss negatives, both album arrival orders, native-command disablement, reply-chain persistence, and Telegram bot ingress behavior.

## Do you plan to open a PR for this?

Yes, I plan to implement this myself.

## Additional information

This is context hygiene, not deletion, secrecy, encryption, or message redaction. Telegram retains the original chat message normally.

labels.name: P1

labels.name: clawsweeper:no-new-fix-pr
labels.description: ClawSweeper does not recommend queueing a new automated fix PR for this issue.

issues.body:
### Summary

On an idle-ish 2026.9.6 gateway, SQLite store/read workers are created and torn down about 7 times per minute. Each one boots the full worker runtime (about 2,000 module files, all plugin manifests) with a 512 MB heap limit and exits after 2–25 seconds. The churn alone keeps the four V8 platform threads at roughly 80% CPU each, plus GC pressure on every isolate. The main-thread JS heap does not grow (1027 MB → 1027 MB across two heap snapshots 47 minutes apart), so this is load, not a JS leak.

### Environment

- OpenClaw 2026.9.6 (npm build plus local backports of #158323 and the catalog discovery fix from #159514), Linux x64, 12 cores, Node 24.20.0
- 32 agents, Telegram + Discord, no Control UI or desktop client connected during the measurements

### What was measured (bpftrace on the live gateway)

**Worker entry scripts.** The first file each new `WorkerThread` opens, over 90 seconds:

```
5 × dist/state/openclaw-state-read.worker.js
3 × dist/infra/sqlite-store.worker.js
2 × dist/config/sessions/session-transcript.worker.js
```

**Lifetimes.** Thread start via the entry-script open, thread exit via `sched_process_exit`:

```
13:23:36 START state-read   13:23:41 EXIT
13:23:36 START state-read   13:23:41 EXIT
13:23:36 START sqlite-store 13:23:41 EXIT
13:23:51 START sqlite-store 13:23:53 EXIT
13:24:07 START sqlite-store 13:24:11 EXIT
13:24:13 START session-transcript 13:24:38 EXIT
13:24:36 START state-read   13:24:41 EXIT
13:24:36 START state-read   13:24:41 EXIT
13:24:36 START sqlite-store 13:24:41 EXIT
```

Every minute, at the same second offset from gateway start, one `sqlite-store` worker and two `state-read` workers start together and exit together 5 seconds later. The state-read pool itself uses `SQLITE_IDLE_HANDLE_TTL_MS` (30 min), so these readers appear to be created by the short-lived store worker and die with it.

**SQL run by that per-minute sqlite-store worker** (uprobe on `sqlite3_prepare_v2/v3`):

```
delete from "plugin_state_entries" where (...) in (select ... )
delete from "state_leases" where "scope" = ? and "lease_key" = ? and "expires_at" <= ?
insert into "state_leases" (...)
delete from "secret_store_entries" where "deleted_at_ms" is not null and "deleted_at_ms" < ?
select "links".* from "session_upstream_links" ...
select * from "device_pairing_pending" / "device_pairing_paired"
delete from "device_pair_setup_completions" where "retain_until_ms" <= ?
PRAGMA wal_checkpoint(TRUNCATE);
```

This looks like the per-minute maintenance in `src/gateway/server-maintenance.ts` (`dedupeCleanup` interval → `performDevicePairSetupCompletionGc` and siblings). No `PRAGMA wal_checkpoint(PASSIVE)` from the idle inspection showed up in 150 s, so these workers are not retired by `inspectIdle`. They exit before the 60 s inspection would run. My reading is that the operations run under a maintenance scope, where `scheduleIdleRetirement` returns early, and `closeActor` then retires the empty slot right away. I could not confirm the exact call path without JS stacks.

**Memory churn** from the same process in 7 minutes:

```
mprotect(RW)          WorkerThread  20.4 GB
madvise(DONTNEED)     WorkerThread  20.8 GB
munmap                WorkerThread  33.0 GB
```

Per thread it is about 537 MB committed per short-lived worker, which matches the 512 MB `maxOldGenerationSizeMb` limit.

### Why this matters

- Constant CPU: a gateway with no active chats sits at about 3–4 cores, mostly V8 platform/GC threads.
- Main-thread stalls: each boot competes with the event loop. We see `liveness heartbeat delayed` of 20–80 s when a boot coincides with plugin loading.
- Native RSS drifts upward and then plateaus. This is consistent with glibc arena high-water marks left by about 1,000 worker threads over a few hours.

### What I tried

Keeping empty `sqlite-worker-broker` slots alive for a few minutes and reusing them in `acquireSlot` removes the churn in principle. It breaks 16 of 293 tests in `src/infra/sqlite-worker*.test.ts`, though: WAL-pin release, cleanup-failure propagation and CPU-source registration all rely on immediate retirement. So I don't think the broker is the right layer. The better fix is likely on the caller side. Either run periodic maintenance on the retained shared-state store instead of a fresh maintenance-scoped one, or don't run it at all when there is nothing to prune.

### Expected

Periodic housekeeping that usually finds nothing to delete should not boot one or more worker runtimes every minute.

Reclamation recognizes the current agent-directory layout, cleans expired snapshots, and at most logs unrecognized *entries* individually — without skipping the whole pass.

```
[...] WARN Skipped SQLite snapshot reclamation: Unrecognized snapshot directory
```
Fires every reclamation cycle — observed 6×/43min (~2,700/day pace at this agent density). No snapshots are ever reclaimed. issues.body:
### Bug type
Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)

### Beta release blocker
No

### Summary
On 2026.10.10-beta.1, an auth-triggered prepared-model-runtime publication failed after its fresh-generation retry timed out; subsequent real Telegram/WhatsApp messages repeatedly failed reply dispatch until Gateway restart, despite Gateway health reporting OK.

### Steps to reproduce
NOT_ENOUGH_INFO

We do not have deterministic end-to-end steps to induce the initiating auth mutation/plugin-load timeout. The observed production sequence and a separately labeled isolated installed-code check are below. No claim that the original timeout has been reproduced in isolation.

### Expected behavior
Before the fault and after a Gateway restart, actual incoming Telegram/WhatsApp messages are admitted and replies are sent. Once a transient rebuild failure has settled, affected agents should have bounded, credential-safe recovery or an explicit unhealthy/unavailable diagnostic rather than persistently failing incoming messages behind an OK Gateway health probe. Invalidated credential/runtime generations must not be reused unsafely.

### Actual behavior
- An auth-triggered rebuild exhausted one fresh-generation retry and logged a configured-model-projection timeout.
- Subsequent incoming Telegram and WhatsApp messages reached the Gateway but failed before reply generation with `prepared reply dispatch runtime owner was not published for main` (also observed for other configured agents).
- A cron targeting main produced the same error. Gateway health remained OK while actual inbound dispatch was failing.
- A controlled Gateway restart restored actual outbound replies. The same missing-owner symptom later recurred during uptime; a second restart again restored a WhatsApp reply.
- The second recurrence is not independently attributed to another identical auth timeout: the retained logs contain one explicit auth-refresh exhaustion record for the first post-restart failure chain.

### OpenClaw version
2026.10.10-beta.1 (87175a8)

### Operating system
macOS 26.7.1, arm64; Node v26.5.0

### Install method
npm global; existing system launchd LaunchDaemon

### Model
openai/gpt-6.1-sol on affected direct chat sessions; fault occurs before model response generation

### Provider / routing chain
Telegram/WhatsApp inbound -> local OpenClaw Gateway -> configured agent; successful direct-chat runs use OpenAI via Codex runtime

### Additional provider/model setup details
Multiple configured agents, agents.ownership=explicit. Active Memory disabled. No credential values or private message content included. The auth-related event initiating the rebuild has not been identified: no claim that a token expired, that a specific provider caused it, or that someone edited credentials.

### Logs
Times below are CDT (UTC-05:00), October 16, 2026; payloads and identifiers not needed for diagnosis omitted.

```text
19:22:24.714 main-thread stall: elapsedMs=22180
19:22:54.807 main-thread stall: elapsedMs=18891
19:23:40.205 main-thread stall: elapsedMs=18774
19:24:01.473 auth-triggered model runtime refresh failed: Error: Auth-triggered model runtime refresh failed after 1 fresh-generation retry: prepared model runtime publication (configured model projection; agent main) timed out
19:24:01.661 main-thread stall: elapsedMs=18791
19:24:29 multiple plugins log forced retirement after 5000ms with still-running calls
19:26:40.198 remote model catalog check superseded; deferred to the next check
19:42:35.061 cron: job run returned error status: prepared reply dispatch runtime owner was not published for main
```

Main-thread stall profiles identify `loadRuntimePluginCandidate`, `loadOpenClawPluginsSteps`, `loadOpenClawPluginsCore`, `withPluginCache`, and `acquireAgentRuntimePluginRegistry`. This supports plugin preparation being costly in the interval; it does not prove why it was costly or identify the initial invalidation producer. Plugin forced-retirement warnings follow the terminal timeout and should not be assumed to be its initial cause.

On October 17, real inbound Telegram and WhatsApp messages repeatedly logged the missing-owner failure while the same serving PID continued running and `Gateway Health` returned `OK (10ms)`. After the approved restart, a real WhatsApp outbound send was confirmed.

### Screenshots, recordings, and evidence
Installed bundle `dist/prepared-model-runtime-Cs2DBPx3.mjs`:
- `invalidateForAuthMutation` removes affected configured agents from `replyDispatchPublication` before the auth publication work (around lines 3493–3501).
- Auth publication terminal rejection clears owner pending gates and can leave an owner stale with a recorded refresh error (around lines 2167–2180).
- `ensureGatewayPreparedModelRuntimeReady` returns if the owner has no `catalogRecovery` record (around lines 2546–2556); its retry path is specific to catalog-worker recovery.
- `PreparedReplyDispatchPublicationOwner.load` calls ensureReady, then throws if no publication remains once no replacement/startup wait applies (around lines 3023–3053).

Isolated check executed with the actual installed dispatch class and recovery implementation extracted into a separate Node VM, using stubbed lifecycle/auth/plugin hosts and no production module imports or state access:
1. A ready configured owner + publication admitted successfully.
2. Simulated a terminal auth-refresh failure state: owner stale, publication removed, pending cleared, no catalogRecovery.
3. Three consecutive dispatch demands all threw the exact missing-owner error; the stub publication callback was invoked zero times.
4. Simulated a successful lifecycle republish; admission succeeded again.

This verifies the demand-recovery gap under those explicit preconditions, NOT the initiating timeout. In the installed recovery code, the decisive early return is:

```js
const recovery = owner?.catalogRecovery;
if (!owner || !recovery) return;
```

Public source: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/87175a8/src/agents/prepared-model-runtime.refresh-scope.ts

### Impact and severity
High: ordinary incoming messages cannot receive a reply while the process and channel transport remain alive. Confirmed on Telegram and WhatsApp, including direct and group routing, and a scheduled task. Repeated failed attempts persist until intervention. This report does not establish data loss or a precise overall failure rate.

### Additional information
- #156561 is already included in installed commit 87175a8 (GitHub ancestry comparison verified). The warning records that its one fresh-generation retry was exhausted, not that the repair is missing.
- Closely related symptom/path: #158592 (auth-publication timeout after sleep/wake). This report does not establish a sleep/wake trigger for our failure.
- #157814/#168826 concern startup publication waiting; this observed failure is during uptime.
- #173482 remains open and fixes auth publication inheriting a temporary SQLite read scope. Its `SQLite read-only worker scope closed` trigger has NOT been established here; our logged terminal reason is configured-model-projection timeout. Not claiming that patch fixes this incident.
- Current post-restart host measurements show ample available memory, no swap I/O and ample free disk; this does not reconstruct host pressure at the original timeout. Retained October 16/17 logs have no matching SQLITE_IOERR, SQLITE_FULL, ENOSPC or malformed-index errors in the scoped search.
- No patch, database reset, credential change or plugin disablement was applied to work around this report.

Request: please assess bounded recovery for exhausted auth-publication failures (distinct from catalogRecovery), and operational health visibility for unpublished configured reply runtimes. Avoid weakening auth invalidation/lifetime gates.

issues.body:
### Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

A Code Mode `exec` can return `waiting` while a nested tool is still running, then lose that resumable work when the observing model response or dynamic tool call completes successfully. The next `wait` reports that the run is unavailable, although the parent agent run remains live.

### Steps to reproduce

This was reproduced in isolated source-level scenarios through the actual Code Mode executor, nested file tools, and both harness adapters:

1. Enable Code Mode and run a cell that awaits a small file write followed by a read of that file.
2. Hold the read's backend byte delivery until the cell returns `waiting`. The write has already completed exactly once.
3. Allow the successful observing call to finish: a streamed asynchronous tool call in the built-in harness, or an OpenClaw dynamic tool call in the Codex adapter.
4. Release the read and call `wait` with the returned top-level `runId`.

### Expected behavior

The pending read remains owned by the live cell and the next `wait` continues it. The equivalent direct Code Mode and non-streamed built-in calls both complete in the controls. Parent cancellation, active-call cancellation, catalog disposal, and snapshot expiry should still cancel owned work.

### Actual behavior

The pending read is cancelled after `exec` returns `waiting`. The built-in streamed path records `Model response closed`; the Codex adapter records `OpenClaw dynamic tool call finished.` The next `wait` cannot resume the cell. The parent run signal remains live in both reproductions, and the file write is not repeated.

### OpenClaw version

Executed against source revision 69eefd48c800ed575b43949c451c004cc942373c. The affected cell owner and both cleanup producers are byte-identical at f84d2ca6726ccab0ac72c7898bc09f358b62fa63.

### Operating system

Linux remote test runner; exact distribution was not recorded in the retained scenario output.

### Install method

Source checkout with repository-declared dependencies and native test entrypoints.

### Model

Synthetic model response fixtures; no external model request.

### Provider / routing chain

Built-in streamed tool execution and the OpenClaw Codex dynamic tool adapter, exercised independently without a live provider.

### Screenshots, recordings, and evidence

The shared owner in `src/agents/code-mode-state.ts` binds the observer's abort signal in `createCodeModeRunOwner.bindCall`. That listener remains installed after `storeSuspendedRun` returns and is released only by a later bind or closure. The normal completion cleanup in `packages/agent-core/src/agent-stream-response.ts` and `extensions/codex/src/app-server/dynamic-tool-execution.ts` therefore reaches the parked cell through the completed observer.

### Impact and severity

This blocks continuation of nested work that outlives the observing call. Earlier effects may already have completed, so replaying the whole cell can repeat those effects. Both isolated adapter reproductions failed while their direct/non-streamed controls completed; production frequency is not established by these scenarios.

### Additional information

This report is limited to the demonstrated successful-observer lifetime failure. It does not establish the cause of other nested-tool cancellation errors or propose a larger timeout.

issues.body:
## Summary

When the CLI and native macOS app share one paired cryptographic device identity, the native app can refresh the paired platform to a rich value such as `macOS 26.6.2`. A later `openclaw status --deep` connects as `clientId=cli`, `clientMode=probe`, `platform=darwin`, with no device family. The gateway treats that Mac-platform alias as a metadata mismatch and creates a `metadata-upgrade` pairing request. Repeating the read-only status command creates another request.

This is distinct from a genuine key, scope, or device-family change.

## Reproduction

1. Pair a local CLI identity on macOS.
2. Reuse that identity from the native macOS app so the paired platform is refreshed to a rich `macOS x.y.z` value.
3. Run `openclaw status --deep`.
4. Observe a new pairing request for the same public key with reason `metadata-upgrade`.
5. Reject or clear it and run the command again; another request appears.

The probe handshake reports the same key and roughly this client tuple:

```json
{"id":"cli","mode":"probe","platform":"darwin"}
```

## Expected behavior

The exact local `cli/probe` tuple should receive the same narrow macOS platform-alias treatment as ordinary `cli/cli` on the same paired key. A real pinned device-family mismatch, non-CLI client, wrong mode, or non-macOS platform must still require pairing.

## Narrow fix

In the shared-primary Mac metadata comparison, include `GATEWAY_CLIENT_MODES.PROBE` alongside `GATEWAY_CLIENT_MODES.CLI` for exact `GATEWAY_CLIENT_IDS.CLI`. Keep the independent device-family mismatch check unchanged.

Regression coverage should include both:

- the metadata comparison matrix for `cli/probe` with `darwin` and `macos` aliases; and
- the shared-primary integration sequence with a rich native macOS platform followed by a family-omitted `cli/probe` connection, asserting zero pending pairing requests and unchanged token/scopes.

This is intended as a small upstream fix, not a new pairing or retry mechanism.

issues.body:
### Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

ensureContextWindowCacheLoaded() no longer captures or checks a cache generation. A discovery started before a context-window refresh can therefore finish afterwards and publish its staged token cache unconditionally, replacing the newer metadata that refreshContextWindowCache() just published. The refresh path is used on Gateway config hot reload. The result is that a model added or changed by the reload can lose its context-window value until the next refresh or restart.

### Steps to reproduce

Start from a source checkout of the affected revision.
Begin a context-window discovery by calling ensureContextWindowCacheLoaded() while the model-catalog owner load is still pending. This represents a request-time load started before a reload.
Call refreshContextWindowCache() and let it complete. Its catalog contains new-model with contextWindow: 222000.
Resolve new-model with resolveContextTokensForModel(); it returns 222000.
Now resolve the first, pre-refresh discovery. It contains only old-model with contextWindow: 111000.
Resolve new-model again.

### Expected behavior

A discovery started before a refresh is superseded. It may complete, but it must not publish its staged cache. The refreshed generation must remain authoritative until another refresh begins, so new-model stays at 222000 and old-model is not introduced by the stale load.

### Actual behavior

The pre-refresh discovery calls replaceDiscoveredContextTokenCache() without any generation comparison and replaces the whole discovered cache. Newly published entries disappear, and metadata from the older discovery becomes visible. The condition persists until the next refresh or process restart.

2026.10.4 (main @ 3f9822434)
