issues.body:
### Summary

Request a maintainer-led performance review and explicit latency budgets for the path from receiving a user message to starting the provider request. On one continuously used self-hosted gateway, ordinary turns repeatedly spent 9–16.5 seconds in pre-provider work, while concurrent session/UI activity produced 31–36 second event-loop stalls.

This is a field report from a live system, not a proposed implementation and not a claim that one root cause explains every stall.

### Problem to solve

The visible symptom was initially attributed to an oversized conversation. Stage traces and isolated benchmarks showed a separate problem: most of the measured delay occurred before prompt dispatch, and key portions reproduced without reading conversation history or making an LLM request.

The delay is distributed across runtime preparation, model/catalog resolution, auth materialization, synchronous filesystem/plugin discovery, SQLite/session operations, and duplicate UI RPCs. Individual fixes exist, but their interaction on the single Node.js event loop can make the gateway unusably slow.

### Proposed solution

This is not a code proposal. Please consider a focused performance review that:

1. Defines budgets for input-to-provider latency on cold, warm, and long-running gateways.
2. Treats prepared runtime/plugin/model/auth facts as lifecycle-owned data that hot turns consume without rediscovery.
3. Audits synchronous filesystem, plugin discovery, auth-store, and SQLite work on the gateway event loop.
4. Coalesces identical client RPCs and considers server-side defenses against request herds.
5. Keeps production stage timing from message receipt through provider dispatch so regressions are visible without bespoke instrumentation.

### Alternatives considered

Continue addressing each slow surface independently. That work is useful and already underway, but this live trace crossed runtime preparation, model resolution, auth, state DB access, and UI request behavior in the same user-visible incident. A shared latency budget and end-to-end owner would make the individual fixes additive rather than incidental.

Related work includes:

- #77700 — prepared runtime resolution migration
- #75782 — synchronous embedded-run auth latency
- #77331 — cold coding-tool construction blocking the event loop
- #83672 and draft #118464 — repeated plugin metadata scans
- #119884 — slow session DB operations and event-loop starvation
- #121985 — duplicate agent SQLite open/integrity checks
- Merged #113817, #120809, #121250, and #121687; draft #118465

### Impact

- Affected: one always-on self-hosted gateway under ordinary interactive use.
- Severity: high; the CLI and agent turns felt unusably slow even when provider latency was not involved.
- Frequency: repeated across consecutive normal turns; the duplicate session-RPC bursts also recurred several times.
- Consequence: roughly 10–16.5 seconds before provider dispatch, plus occasional 30+ second event-loop stalls affecting unrelated gateway work.

### Evidence/examples

Environment:

- OpenClaw 2026.8.1, custom build `1e3b418f22cdc30132fc678742fcdf030d20ff7d` based on upstream main from 2026-08-08.
- Ubuntu 26.04 LTS LXC, 12 vCPU, 32 GiB RAM. Memory pressure was not observed.
- OpenAI `gpt-5.6-sol` through the bundled Codex harness.
- Measurements were collected on 2026-08-11. Upstream has moved substantially since this build and has since merged additional performance work, so the exact absolute timings should be rechecked on current main. A source spot-check of current main (`66b92e91365099eb6dd0a8a18d91a13c9c8713ae`) found that the exact prepared plugin-metadata threading and UI branch-request coalescing changes tested locally were not present.

Sanitized consecutive startup-stage traces (run/session identifiers omitted):

| Sample | Total before dispatch | Prepared runtime | Model resolution | Auth |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| A | 10,739 ms | 3,475 ms | 3,677 ms | 3,555 ms |
| B | 10,703 ms | 1,616 ms | 4,462 ms | 4,525 ms |
| C | 16,549 ms | 9,297 ms | 3,553 ms | 3,622 ms |

The remaining measured stages were small: context-engine was 1 ms in each sample and attempt setup/dispatch accounted for the residual time. These are pre-provider timings, not model inference.

An isolated source benchmark of `resolveModelAsync("openai", "gpt-5.6-sol")` took 3.2–4.2 seconds per call without loading a session or issuing a provider request. A CPU profile showed repeated synchronous `lstat`, `realpathSync`, `existsSync`, and plugin-metadata/index work. A local diagnostic change that consistently reused the already prepared plugin generation reduced warm model resolution to 156–165 ms; when auth profile ID and mode were already known, auth materialization was 5.5–6.4 ms. These local changes are not being proposed as the solution here and no PR is planned from this report.

The same gateway log showed request herds from one Control UI connection:

- 127 `sessions.branches.list` responses completed in one approximately one-second burst.
- A later burst contained 98 identical method calls in approximately one second.
- Individual calls took roughly 0.68–0.95 seconds.
- Nearby liveness warnings reported heartbeat delays of 31,110 ms, 35,806 ms, 34,070 ms, and 33,787 ms.

No conversation content, credentials, hostnames, addresses, or request identifiers are included here.

### Do you plan to open a PR for this?

No, proposing the idea only.

### Additional information

I am deliberately filing this as an operational comment rather than another narrowly prescribed fix. The existing issues and recent PRs show that useful performance work is happening, but the live behavior suggests the accumulated hot-path costs need to be reviewed as a system.

Given the breadth across runtime, auth, plugins, state, and UI, @steipete may want to consider whether a coordinated performance review is now overdue.

issues.body:
### Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

In `packages/normalization-core/src/balanced-json.ts`, `extractBalancedJsonPrefix` treats an opening brace inside quoted prose as the start of a JSON object, returning a non-JSON fragment and ignoring a later valid JSON value.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Check out OpenClaw main at commit `d8488a94067c8b935390968d6274dbe6f041432e`.

2. Add the following test as `packages/normalization-core/src/balanced-json.test.ts`:

```ts
import { describe, expect, it } from "vitest";
import { extractBalancedJsonPrefix } from "./balanced-json.js";

describe("extractBalancedJsonPrefix", () => {
  it("skips an opener inside quoted prose", () => {
    const raw =
      'prefix "notjson{here}" middle {"a":[1,{"b":"c"}]} suffix';

    const fragment = extractBalancedJsonPrefix(raw);

    expect(fragment?.json).toBe('{"a":[1,{"b":"c"}]}');
  });
});
```

3. Run:

```shell
pnpm exec vitest run packages/normalization-core/src/balanced-json.test.ts
```

4. Observe that the focused assertion fails.

### Expected behavior

Given the input above, `extractBalancedJsonPrefix` is expected to return the later valid JSON object:

```json
{"a":[1,{"b":"c"}]}
```

The function comment states that it extracts the first balanced JSON object or array from text. The earlier `{here}` substring is enclosed by braces but is not a JSON object, whereas the later substring is a complete value accepted by `JSON.parse`.

### Actual behavior

`extractBalancedJsonPrefix` returns `{here}` instead of the later valid JSON object.

The returned fragment is:

```ts
{
  json: "{here}",
  startIndex: 15,
  endIndex: 20,
}
```

`{here}` is not valid JSON, yet the later valid object is not examined.

### OpenClaw version

main@d8488a94067c8b935390968d6274dbe6f041432e

### Operating system

macOS 15.7.3

### Install method

Source checkout; focused Vitest test launched with pnpm

### Model

Not applicable; reproduced by directly invoking deterministic normalization utility code

### Provider / routing chain

Not applicable; the reproduction does not make a provider or model request

### Additional provider/model setup details

_No response_

### Logs

```shell
FAIL  |unit| ../../packages/normalization-core/src/balanced-json.test.ts > extractBalancedJsonPrefix > skips an opener inside quoted prose
AssertionError: expected '{here}' to be '{"a":[1,{"b":"c"}]}' // Object.is equality

Expected: "{"a":[1,{"b":"c"}]}"
Received: "{here}"

❯ ../../packages/normalization-core/src/balanced-json.test.ts:11:28
     9|     const fragment = extractBalancedJsonPrefix(raw);
    10|
    11|     expect(fragment?.json).toBe('{"a":[1,{"b":"c"}]}');
      |                            ^
    12|   });
    13| });

Test Files  1 failed (1)
Tests       1 failed (1)
```

### Screenshots, recordings, and evidence

The focused assertion fails deterministically on the tested commit. The test is collected and executed normally, with no import, setup, teardown, timeout, or mock error.

`extractBalancedJsonPrefix` is exported through the public `@openclaw/normalization-core` barrel. Its result is also consumed by JSON-processing paths including tool-call argument repair, CLI output parsing, and diagnostic credential redaction.


### Impact and severity

Affected: OpenClaw code paths that use the balanced-JSON helpers to extract structured data from model, tool, CLI, or diagnostic text containing quoted prose before a JSON value.

Severity: Structured-data extraction defect; no crash or state corruption was observed.

Frequency: Deterministic when an opening brace or bracket occurs inside quoted prose before a later valid JSON object or array.

Consequence: A non-JSON fragment can be returned while the actual JSON value is ignored, causing downstream parsing, repair, or normalization to reject otherwise recoverable structured data.

### Additional information

At the tested commit, `extractBalancedJsonPrefix` locates its initial opening delimiter before it starts tracking quoted-string state:

```ts
let start = 0;
while (start < raw.length && !isJsonOpeningDelimiter(raw[start], openers)) {
  start += 1;
}
```

String and escape tracking begins only after `start` has already been selected. For the focused input, the `{` inside `"notjson{here}"` therefore becomes the initial delimiter, and the following `}` completes the returned `{here}` fragment.

One possible fix direction is to make the initial opening-delimiter scan use the same quote and escape handling as the subsequent balancing loop, so braces and brackets inside quoted text are skipped before `start` is selected. Regression coverage should include quoted braces and brackets, escaped quotes, and a later valid object or array.

### Steps to reproduce

The Details panel should respect the account’s existing automation read access. An intentional scope limit should not issue an unauthorized inventory request or appear as a recoverable loading failure. Authorized readers should retain the current inventory and retry behavior.

`ChatSummaryAutomations` unconditionally enters `loadCompactCronJobsPage`, which calls `cron.list`. The Gateway correctly rejects that method for missing `operator.read`; the component presents the rejection as a load failure with Retry. The source path remains present at `30184f85d02ec9d34918c39c1017b9026bc36522`. The Gateway’s existing cron authorization is not the defect; this report concerns the UI’s request admission and presentation.

Source build `69eefd48c800ed575b43949c451c004cc942373c`; current source inspected at `30184f85d02ec9d34918c39c1017b9026bc36522`.

Browser Control UI against a Linux Gateway.

issues.body:
### Problem

When a Slack bot is added to a channel, OpenClaw only records a passive system event (`Slack: <bot> joined #channel.`), which the agent sees on the next heartbeat tick. There is no supported way to have the agent react to the invitation itself:

- Agents with long heartbeat intervals greet minutes or hours after being invited, which reads as unresponsive to the humans who just added them.
- Agents with heartbeat disabled (`every: "0m"`, common for cost control on event-driven deployments) never react at all.
- Operators who want a "introduce yourself and offer help when invited" behavior have no hook: the member-join handler cannot dispatch an agent turn today.

Being added to a channel is an explicit human action directed at the bot — closer to a mention than to ambient room telemetry — but it is currently handled like telemetry.

### Proposed solution

An opt-in Slack account config, default off:

```json5
{
  channels: {
    slack: {
      selfJoinIntro: {
        enabled: true,
        // optional: replaces the default introduction instruction
        prompt: "Read the recent channel history, introduce yourself, and offer up to three concrete ways you can help, in a thread.",
      },
    },
  },
}
```

When enabled and the `member_joined_channel` event is about the bot itself, the members handler dispatches an immediate agent turn through the normal message pipeline (the same lane every real mention uses), attributed to the inviting user, with an explicitly automated instruction text. Joins by other members are untouched. When Slack omits the `inviter` (e.g. the bot joined via API on its own), behavior falls back to today's passive system event.

No new Slack scopes or event subscriptions: `member_joined_channel` is already in the recommended manifest and already handled.

### Alternatives considered

- **Heartbeat wake on self-join** — still couples reaction latency to heartbeat config, and does nothing for deployments that disable the heartbeat.
- **Third-party plugin** — the member-join event is consumed inside the bundled Slack extension's monitor; a plugin cannot intercept it or dispatch into the account's message pipeline.
- **Leaving it to operators via external automation** (Events API sidecar posting a message) — requires a second Slack app or socket consumer per workspace just to simulate what the extension already observes natively.

### Impact

Operators can make agents respond to channel invitations the way human teammates expect — greet, introduce capabilities, offer to help — within seconds. Default off, so existing deployments see zero behavior change.

### Prior art

Slack's own agent surfaces (e.g. Claude's Slack app) greet and post a capabilities briefing immediately on being added to a channel. The mechanism (synthetic inbound turn attributed to the inviter) has been running in production on a 2026.7.1 deployment as a local extension patch since 2026-08-10.

issues.body:
### Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

A run can overwrite one file indefinitely with different successful `write` bodies: each call has a unique argument hash and returns `changed: true`, so current tool-loop detection treats every rewrite as progress even when the run never produces a final answer.

### Steps to reproduce

Production reproduction:

1. Start OpenClaw `2026.7.2-beta.7` with `tools.loopDetection.enabled: true`.
2. Run a normal embedded-agent turn using MiniMax M3 through the Anthropic Messages transport.
3. Have the model draft a document using the built-in `write` tool and enter a refinement loop that repeatedly replaces the same target with a newly generated body.
4. Observe that every write succeeds, the target path stays constant, every body/argument hash differs, and the run remains active without producing a final answer.

Deterministic source-level reproduction on current `main` (`30131a572b0c0c56ec1151451bbe43ce314b5799`):

1. Exercise the production wrapped built-in `write` tool repeatedly in one run.
2. Keep `path` constant and provide a different valid `content` string on every call.
3. Each result reports `details.changed === true`.
4. Call `detectToolCallLoop` before each execution with loop detection enabled.
5. No same-target mutation-churn warning or critical verdict is produced: every `argsHash` is unique, successful changed writes have no `noProgress` marker, and the current argument-churn classifier requires stable `noProgress` outcomes.

No private document content, target path, session identifier, chat identifier, or user/agent name is included in this report.

### Expected behavior

After a bounded number or duration of consecutive successful `write` calls to one target without intervening read/verification, target change, or user-visible/final model progress, OpenClaw should classify the sequence as mutation churn and provide bounded recovery. Legitimate iterative edits must remain possible; the guard should use same-target continuity plus absence of higher-level progress rather than treating every changed write as an immediate no-op.

### Actual behavior

One observed turn issued 323 successful `write` calls over 88.63 minutes:

- target paths: 1 unique target
- bodies: 323 unique bodies
- body size: 3,776–9,254 characters (median 5,472)
- median interval between writes: 16.21 seconds
- final answer during the looping turn: none
- loop warning/block for this sequence: none

A non-aborting steer instruction reached the active turn but was followed by five more writes. Operator-approved interruption of only the active turn stopped the rewrites; a same-session continuation then completed in 12 seconds with zero tool calls and one final response. The file and session were preserved.

### OpenClaw version

2026.7.2-beta.7

### Operating system

Ubuntu 26.04, x86_64

### Install method

npm global, systemd user gateway

### Model

MiniMax-M3

### Provider / routing chain

openclaw embedded runtime -> MiniMax via Anthropic Messages transport

### Additional provider/model setup details

The provider remained responsive; every write tool call completed successfully. This was not a provider timeout, Hindsight failure, database corruption, or gateway restart loop. Loop detection was enabled. Credentials and private routing identifiers are intentionally omitted.

### Logs

```shell
Sanitized aggregate transcript evidence:

write_calls=323
unique_target_paths=1
unique_body_hashes=323
first_to_last_write_minutes=88.63
median_interval_seconds=16.21
body_characters_min=3776
body_characters_median=5472
body_characters_max=9254
final_answer_before_interruption=0

All body hashes were computed locally and are not published because the hashes are unnecessary for reproduction and could become identifiers for private content.
```

### Screenshots, recordings, and evidence

No private transcript or document is attached.

Current-main source boundary:

- `src/agents/tool-loop-detection.ts`: tool-call identity hashes the complete arguments; only `sessions_send` receives semantic argument normalization.
- `src/agents/tool-loop-write-outcome.ts`: a write contributes semantic no-progress evidence only when `details.changed === false`.
- `src/agents/tool-loop-argument-churn.ts`: argument churn requires repeated stable variants whose outcomes are marked `noProgress` and share a result hash.
- `src/agents/tool-loop-no-progress.ts`: non-`exec` streaks remain keyed to the exact argument hash.

Related but distinct:

- #79301 was closed after generic exact-argument loop detection landed; changing full document bodies keep arguments non-identical.
- #112479 / #112620 handle stable no-progress argument churn and identical-content built-in writes (`changed: false`). The maintainer resolution explicitly preserves successful content-changing writes as progress.

### Impact and severity

Affected: embedded-agent runs allowed to mutate files, across any channel/model capable of entering this behavior.

Severity: High for the affected turn. The run silently consumed model calls for 88.63 minutes, repeatedly destroyed the immediately preceding revision of important work, blocked a final reply, and required operator intervention.

Frequency: one fully evidenced production incident; broader frequency is not established.

Consequence: token/resource waste, prolonged unresponsiveness, repeated loss of prior file revisions, and no user-visible final answer.

### Additional information

The safe repair should not label every successful rewrite as no-progress. A conservative direction is a separate, warning-first same-target mutation-churn signal owned by run liveness:

- same mutation tool and canonical target path;
- many consecutive `changed: true` outcomes;
- changing content/argument hashes;
- no target escape, readback/verification step, final/model progress, or other higher-level progress;
- warning at a bounded threshold, then owner-bound recovery if churn remains continuous until the existing stale-run boundary.

Compatibility controls should prove that ordinary iterative editing, multi-file generation, write-then-read verification, and short rewrite sequences remain allowed.

issues.body:
## Summary
Official @openclaw/codex 2026.9.4 prepares a user prompt and fingerprints that prepared message for annotateCurrentUserTurn, while the host validates the exact persisted admission content. Divergence causes best-effort prompt mirroring to be skipped. Observed on Linux with OpenClaw 2026.9.4; the affected scheduled run completed successfully, so this is not a report of execution failure or confirmed transcript loss.

## Evidence and reproduction limits
Installed official producer: dist/transcript-mirror-C5CKgNy6.js around line 184 (source counterpart: extensions/codex/src/app-server/transcript-mirror.ts). It checks persisted admission visibility but hashes userPromptMessage. Host dist/selection-BUvT8BOT.mjs lines 109–145 validates admittedMessage.content before anchored rewriting.

Five isolated cases executed against the extracted, unchanged installed producer with mocked host fingerprint validation and I/O: identical string/block cases accepted; string-versus-block, trailing-newline difference, and synthetic write-time redaction rejected and caught before mirror invocation. These reproduce the mechanism, not a full host integration test or the exact production transformation. The original incident log rotated; no claim of exact raw admission reconstruction.

Minimal synthetic mismatch: persisted content is `hello`, prepared content is `hello\n`; their exact-content fingerprints differ. Also cover a string versus its text-block representation. The host must continue rejecting mismatched evidence.

## Expected repair boundary
Derive annotation evidence from the authoritative persisted admission through supported ownership capabilities; preserve active writer/anchor, visibility, redaction, unchanged-content, and provenance conflict checks. Do not merely relax the validator or substitute a hash without checking subsequent mirror behavior.

Acceptance coverage: prepared/persisted divergence, hidden admission, missing capability/receipt, stale writer/anchor, conflicting provenance, redaction refusal, idempotence, and no duplicate admitted row.

The documented annotateCurrentUserTurn API is live-only and cannot repair historical admissions. No production state or vendor code was changed for this investigation.

Related but distinct: #143335 (redaction refusal) and #141233 (duplicate unkeyed admissions). Investigation/report preparation was AI-assisted.

issues.body:
### Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

On 2026.9.2, running `openclaw channels login --channel whatsapp` in the gateway container rewrote `~/.openclaw/openclaw.json` and, as the only material change, added `plugins.entries.codex` with `enabled: true`. The `@openclaw/codex` dependencies are not installed on this host, so from then on the plugin sat in an `error` state and every agent run in a channel session logged a missing-binary error. A channel login should not enable an unrelated plugin, and should never enable one whose dependencies are absent.

This is the same silent-codex-enablement family as #97180 (`doctor --fix`) and #95131 (official openai/* model selection), both closed by fixes released in v2026.8.1. Whatever opt-out those added does not cover the `channels login` path on 2026.9.2.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Run 2026.9.2 with the gateway running, an OpenAI route in use (ChatGPT sign-in here), and no `plugins.entries.codex` in the config.
2. Install `@openclaw/whatsapp` and run, inside the gateway container as the gateway's user: `openclaw channels login --channel whatsapp --verbose`.
3. Note the `Config overwrite:` line printed before the QR, and diff the new `openclaw.json` against the `openclaw.json.bak` the command writes.
4. Run `openclaw plugins list`, and watch the gateway log during any channel conversation.

### Expected behavior

A channel login writes only what the login needs — the channel's own credentials and configuration — and leaves the rest of the config as the owner wrote it. In particular it does not enable a plugin the owner never configured, and does not enable any plugin whose required dependencies are not installed. #97180 and #95131 established the same expectation for the `doctor --fix` and model-selection paths, and both were fixed.

### Actual behavior

The command printed, before the QR:

`Config overwrite: /home/node/.openclaw/openclaw.json (sha256 … -> …, backup=/home/node/.openclaw/openclaw.json.bak, changedPaths=54)`

Diffing the backup against the new file, exactly one material change: a new entry

`"codex": { "enabled": true, "config": { "codexDynamicToolsLoading": "searchable", "codexDynamicToolsExclude": [] } }`

under `plugins.entries`, which nothing in the session asked for. The `changedPaths=54` count against one real change suggests the write is a full re-serialisation of the config rather than a targeted patch.

From then on `openclaw plugins list` showed Codex in an `error` state — `Plugin "codex" cannot load because required dependencies are missing: @openai/codex, smol-toml` — and every agent run in a channel session logged, from `gateway/session-observer`, `Managed Codex app-server binary was not found for @openai/codex. Reinstall or update OpenClaw…`. Replies still went through; the error was constant background noise with no owner-visible cause.

`openclaw config unset plugins.entries.codex` and a restart put the plugin back to plainly disabled.

### OpenClaw version

2026.9.2 (official Docker image ghcr.io/openclaw/openclaw:2026.9.2-browser)

### Operating system

the image's Debian, in Docker on an Ubuntu 24.04 host

### Install method

Docker Compose; onboarding by `openclaw onboard --non-interactive`

### Model

openai/gpt-5.6-sol through the ChatGPT subscription sign-in

### Provider / routing chain

OpenAI (ChatGPT sign-in) -> openai/gpt-5.6-sol, no fallbacks configured

### Additional provider/model setup details

_No response_

### Logs

```shell
Config overwrite: /home/node/.openclaw/openclaw.json (sha256 … -> …, backup=/home/node/.openclaw/openclaw.json.bak, changedPaths=54)

plugins list: │ Codex │ codex │ openclaw │ error │ stock:codex/index.js │ 2026.9.2 │ Plugin "codex" cannot load because required dependencies are missing: @openai/codex, smol-toml

gateway/session-observer: {"sessionKey":"agent:main:<channel>:…","error":"Managed Codex app-server binary was not found for @openai/codex. Reinstall or update OpenClaw, …"}
```

### Screenshots, recordings, and evidence

_No response_

### Impact and severity

Affected: any install on an OpenAI route where the owner runs `channels login` and does not have the Codex dependencies installed.
Severity: moderate. Nothing stops working — replies continued — but a clean install starts logging a plugin error on every conversation, and the config has an entry the owner did not write.
Frequency: once per `channels login` run; the error then repeats on every agent run until the entry is removed.
Consequence: an owner who does not diff the config against the backup cannot tell where the error came from, and the natural reading of "Managed Codex app-server binary was not found. Reinstall or update OpenClaw" is that their install is broken.

### Additional information

Observed on 2026.9.2, official `-browser` image, Docker Compose on Ubuntu 24.04. The login itself succeeded; this is a side effect of it.

Possible fixes, for whoever owns this to weigh: have `channels login` write only the keys it needs, or nothing at all when the link is completed through the running gateway's store; and gate any automatic plugin enablement on the plugin's `requires` actually being installed.

No

### Summary

On 2026.9.2, running `openclaw channels login --channel whatsapp` in the gateway container rewrote `~/.openclaw/openclaw.json` and, as the only material change, added `plugins.entries.codex` with `enabled: true`. The `@openclaw/codex` dependencies are not installed on this host, so from then on the plugin sat in an `error` state and every agent run in a channel session logged a missing-binary error. A channel login should not enable an unrelated plugin, and should never enable one whose dependencies are absent.

This is the same silent-codex-enablement family as #97180 (`doctor --fix`) and #95131 (official openai/* model selection), both closed by fixes released in v2026.8.1. Whatever opt-out those added does not cover the `channels login` path on 2026.9.2.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Run 2026.9.2 with the gateway running, an OpenAI route in use (ChatGPT sign-in here), and no `plugins.entries.codex` in the config.
2. Install `@openclaw/whatsapp` and run, inside the gateway container as the gateway's user: `openclaw channels login --channel whatsapp --verbose`.
3. Note the `Config overwrite:` line printed before the QR, and diff the new `openclaw.json` against the `openclaw.json.bak` the command writes.
4. Run `openclaw plugins list`, and watch the gateway log during any channel conversation.

### Expected behavior

A channel login writes only what the login needs — the channel's own credentials and configuration — and leaves the rest of the config as the owner wrote it. In particular it does not enable a plugin the owner never configured, and does not enable any plugin whose required dependencies are not installed. #97180 and #95131 established the same expectation for the `doctor --fix` and model-selection paths, and both were fixed.

### Actual behavior

The command printed, before the QR:

`Config overwrite: /home/node/.openclaw/openclaw.json (sha256 … -> …, backup=/home/node/.openclaw/openclaw.json.bak, changedPaths=54)`

Diffing the backup against the new file, exactly one material change: a new entry

`"codex": { "enabled": true, "config": { "codexDynamicToolsLoading": "searchable", "codexDynamicToolsExclude": [] } }`

under `plugins.entries`, which nothing in the session asked for. The `changedPaths=54` count against one real change suggests the write is a full re-serialisation of the config rather than a targeted patch.

From then on `openclaw plugins list` showed Codex in an `error` state — `Plugin "codex" cannot load because required dependencies are missing: @openai/codex, smol-toml` — and every agent run in a channel session logged, from `gateway/session-observer`, `Managed Codex app-server binary was not found for @openai/codex. Reinstall or update OpenClaw…`. Replies still went through; the error was constant background noise with no owner-visible cause.

`openclaw config unset plugins.entries.codex` and a restart put the plugin back to plainly disabled.

### OpenClaw version

2026.9.2 (official Docker image ghcr.io/openclaw/openclaw:2026.9.2-browser)

### Operating system

the image's Debian, in Docker on an Ubuntu 24.04 host

### Install method

Docker Compose; onboarding by `openclaw onboard --non-interactive`

### Model

openai/gpt-5.6-sol through the ChatGPT subscription sign-in

### Provider / routing chain

OpenAI (ChatGPT sign-in) -> openai/gpt-5.6-sol, no fallbacks configured

### Additional provider/model setup details

_No response_

### Logs

```shell
Config overwrite: /home/node/.openclaw/openclaw.json (sha256 … -> …, backup=/home/node/.openclaw/openclaw.json.bak, changedPaths=54)

plugins list: │ Codex │ codex │ openclaw │ error │ stock:codex/index.js │ 2026.9.2 │ Plugin "codex" cannot load because required dependencies are missing: @openai/codex, smol-toml

gateway/session-observer: {"sessionKey":"agent:main:<channel>:…","error":"Managed Codex app-server binary was not found for @openai/codex. Reinstall or update OpenClaw, …"}
```

### Screenshots, recordings, and evidence

_No response_

### Impact and severity

Affected: any install on an OpenAI route where the owner runs `channels login` and does not have the Codex dependencies installed.
Severity: moderate. Nothing stops working — replies continued — but a clean install starts logging a plugin error on every conversation, and the config has an entry the owner did not write.
Frequency: once per `channels login` run; the error then repeats on every agent run until the entry is removed.
Consequence: an owner who does not diff the config against the backup cannot tell where the error came from, and the natural reading of "Managed Codex app-server binary was not found. Reinstall or update OpenClaw" is that their install is broken.

### Additional information

Observed on 2026.9.2, official `-browser` image, Docker Compose on Ubuntu 24.04. The login itself succeeded; this is a side effect of it.

Possible fixes, for whoever owns this to weigh: have `channels login` write only the keys it needs, or nothing at all when the link is completed through the running gateway's store; and gate any automatic plugin enablement on the plugin's `requires` actually being installed.

### Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

With managed proxy routing enabled (proxy.proxyUrl), the realtime Talk gateway-relay WebSocket to api.openai.com does not use the proxy, so Talk fails with "Realtime provider error" on hosts without direct egress.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Run the Gateway (2026.10.3, Docker) in a container with no direct internet egress; only a forward proxy (squid) is reachable.
2. Set proxy.proxyUrl: http://<proxy>:3128 (log shows "routing process HTTP traffic through external proxy").
3. Configure talk.realtime: provider openai, model gpt-live-1, transport gateway-relay (talk.catalog reports realtime.ready = true).
4. Start Talk from the Android app and speak one sentence.

### Expected behavior

Per docs/security/network-proxy.md, managed proxy routing covers runtime HTTP and WebSocket egress, so the realtime provider WebSocket should open via HTTP CONNECT through the proxy and the Talk session should proceed. A manual CONNECT through the same proxy to wss://api.openai.com/v1/realtime?model=gpt-live-1 returns 101 Switching Protocols.

### Actual behavior

Every attempt: talk event turn.started -> ~2 s -> session.error -> session.closed. The app shows "Talk failed: Realtime provider error." The proxy access log shows no connection attempt to api.openai.com from the Gateway during Talk (other egress such as Discord and model calls is logged normally). Inside the Gateway container, the bundled `ws` without an agent fails with ENETUNREACH.

### OpenClaw version

2026.10.3 (same bridge code in 2026.10.4, 2026.10.5-beta.4, 2026.10.10-beta.1)

### Operating system

Ubuntu 24.04 host, Gateway in rootless Docker (Node 24.21.0)

### Install method

docker

### Model

openai/gpt-live-1 (talk.realtime)

### Provider / routing chain

Android app -> Gateway (talk.realtime gateway-relay bridge, ws) -> expected: managed proxy (squid) -> api.openai.com; actual: direct connect (no egress) -> ENETUNREACH

### Additional provider/model setup details

Android app -> Gateway (talk.realtime gateway-relay bridge, `ws`) -> expected: managed proxy (squid) -> api.openai.com; actual: direct connect attempt (no egress) -> ENETUNREACH

### Logs

```shell
info  proxy  routing process HTTP traffic through external proxy http://<proxy>:3128
info  talk   talk event turn.started
warn  talk   talk event session.error
info  talk   talk event session.closed
info  gateway/ws  res ✗ talk.session.appendAudio errorCode=UNAVAILABLE errorMessage=Error: Unknown Talk session
(session.error raw payload contains only talkEventType/talkMode/talkTransport/talkProvider; no underlying error)
```

### Screenshots, recordings, and evidence

dist/realtime-voice-bridge-*.mjs:
  const proxyAgent = this.runtime.createDebugProxyWebSocketAgent(debugProxy)
  const ws = new WebSocket$1(resolvedConnection.url, { ...proxyAgent ? { agent: proxyAgent } : {} })
-> an agent is attached only for the debug proxy. Without an agent, ws uses its own tlsConnect (createConnection), which is not routed by managed proxy routing.

Checks inside the Gateway container:
- ws, no agent -> wss://api.openai.com/v1/realtime -> ENETUNREACH
- HTTP CONNECT via proxy + WS upgrade -> 101 Switching Protocols
- POST /v1/realtime/client_secrets via proxy -> 200

### Impact and severity

Affected: any egress-restricted / proxy-only deployment using realtime Talk.
Severity: blocks the feature (Talk unusable).
Frequency: always (6/6 observed attempts).
Consequence: no voice sessions; only the opaque "Realtime provider error" is shown, the root error is not logged.

### Additional information

Related: with transport webrtc, createOpenAIRealtimeClientSecret uses fetchWithSsrFGuard in STRICT mode and also bypasses the proxy.
Workaround: a local TCP relay forwarding api.openai.com:443 via HTTP CONNECT through the proxy, plus --add-host api.openai.com:<relay IP> on the Gateway container.
Suggestion: log the underlying provider error at warn level.

issues.body:
## Problem

Supported Codex cloud-worker chats cannot start or resume OpenClaw Goals through core admission, even though their execution placement is managed by the existing remote-exec owners. Core Goal tools are also filtered out when native tools are enabled, despite Codex’s separate autonomous Goal engine being disabled. Settled automatic Goal turns do not consistently update continuationTurns, including the completing turn.

## Expected behavior

Existing idle supported Codex worker sessions should use the core Goal ID, operation receipt, transcript binding, budgets, and follow-up queue. Worker setup must admit the exact input before the Goal and user turn commit and before success acknowledgment. Setup failure or revoked authority must leave no Goal or transcript turn.

Core get_goal/create_goal/update_goal should remain directly callable with native execution, subject to normal deny/custom policy and the existing sandbox policy owner. Each settled automatic continuation should count exactly once, including completion, while human Start/Resume should not count. Replaced/cleared Goals must not be modified by old completion accounting.

## Evidence and scope

Production-host regressions reproduce missing Goal controls with native tools enabled. Core RPC, queue, SQLite actor/restart, and host construction/completion tests provide the accompanying fix’s proof. Busy Resume refusal retirement is already implemented on main and should remain intact. The general solution uses existing owners and does not require a provider-specific broker, new authentication protocol, alternate scheduler, or native autonomous Goal engine.

issues.body:
## Summary

`openclaw sessions list --json` reads the session store locally but does not project `archivedAt`, and it treats an unlocked historical `agentHarnessId` as the current runtime. The authoritative Gateway `sessions.list` projection reports both lifecycle state and the runtime that would handle the next turn.

This creates an operator-visible split brain: after a successful stock `sessions archive`, the CLI list still looks active; after changing the configured runtime, old unlocked sessions still look pinned to the historical harness even though the Gateway will use current policy.

## Reproduction

With current policy selecting `codex`, use an existing unlocked session that contains historical `agentHarnessId: openclaw`, then archive it:

```text
openclaw sessions archive <key> --json
# status: archived

openclaw sessions list --all-agents --limit all --json
# no archived field
# agentRuntime: { id: openclaw, source: session }

openclaw gateway call sessions.list --json \
  --params {limit:500,archived:all,includeGlobal:true,includeUnknown:true}
# archived: true
# agentRuntime: { id: codex, source: implicit }
```

Observed on the signed `2026.8.1-beta.2` build and confirmed by current-main source:

- `src/commands/sessions-table.ts` omits `archivedAt` from `SessionDisplayRow`.
- `src/commands/sessions.ts` passes the whole entry to `resolveModelAgentRuntimeMetadata`, which calls `resolvePersistedSessionRuntimeId` and treats historical `agentHarnessId` as current intent.
- the Gateway projection uses `resolveSessionRuntimeOverrideForProvider`; unlocked `agentHarnessId` is history, while only a compatible explicit override or locked transcript owns future runtime.

## Expected

The stock CLI inventory should expose archive state and report the same effective runtime semantics as the authoritative Gateway. Historical harness provenance should not be presented as an active pin for unlocked sessions.

## Why this matters

Operators use `sessions list` to choose lifecycle targets and diagnose routing drift. A false active/runtime inventory encourages unnecessary config changes and makes successful cleanup impossible to verify.

## Proposed minimal fix

Keep the local read-only list, but:

1. project `archived`/`archivedAt` from the existing entry;
2. resolve effective runtime with the same compatibility rule used by the Gateway: configured policy unless a compatible explicit override or locked transcript owns the session;
3. add parity regressions for archived rows, unlocked historical harnesses, explicit overrides, and locked ownership.

No new persistence, migration, background reconciliation, or configuration is required.

issues.body:
## Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)

## Summary

When an agent session times out (or is otherwise terminated), any background `exec` processes spawned by that session's tool calls are not killed or cleaned up. They continue running as orphaned processes, holding resources (PTY sessions, file handles, memory) until the OpenClaw process eventually reaps them or they complete naturally.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Start an agent session.
2. In the session, call `exec` with a command that takes >15s to complete (e.g., a large build, a long-running test, or a pipeline script).
3. The `exec` tool returns with a status indicating the command is still running in the background (via the `process` tool infrastructure).
4. Allow the parent session to time out (e.g., hit `agents.defaults.timeoutSeconds`).
5. Observe that the background process remains alive after the session ends. The process is visible in `ps` with a parent PID of 1 (init) or the OpenClaw gateway, not the terminated session.

## Expected behavior

On session termination (timeout, abort, or normal close), the gateway should:

1. Enumerate all background `exec` processes spawned by the session
2. Send SIGTERM to each, followed by SIGKILL after a grace period
3. Close PTY sessions and file descriptors
4. Log the cleanup actions for observability

## Actual behavior

The session termination path cleans up the model call and the session record, but does not walk the tree of spawned child processes. The transcript records the background process's existence, but nothing acts on it at session end.

Evidence from a session transcript:

```json
{
  "type": "message",
  "role": "toolResult",
  "toolName": "exec",
  "content": "Command still running (session <process-session-name>, pid <pid>). Use process (list/poll/log/write/send-keys/submit/paste/kill/clear/remove) for follow-up."
}
```

This tool result appears at the end of the session's transcript. The session status was `"timeout"` and `endedAt` was set, but the referenced process remained alive after the session record was closed.

Evidence from the gateway source: the `buildTimeoutAbortSignal` function creates an abort signal for the model call timeout, but the signal is scoped to the model invocation only. There is no cleanup path that walks spawned `exec` children:

```javascript
const { signal, cleanup } = buildTimeoutAbortSignal({
  // ...
});
// ... model call ...
cleanup();
```

No equivalent cleanup for background exec processes spawned via the `exec` tool during the session.

## OpenClaw version

2026.7.1-2 (0790d9f)

## Operating system

Linux 6.8.0-137-generic (x86_64)

## Install method

npm global

## Model

zai/glm-5.2 (primary), minimax/MiniMax-M3 (fallback)

## Provider / routing chain

openclaw → z.ai API (openai-completions compatible)

## Additional provider/model setup details

The `exec` tool's behavior when a command exceeds the default timeout is to return a "still running" message and assign a `process` session (auto-generated short name) and PID. These process sessions persist in the OpenClaw process table until explicitly cleaned up.

## Logs

Transcript evidence (last tool result before session timeout):

```
{"type":"toolResult","toolName":"exec","content":"Command still running (session <process-session-name>, pid <pid>). Use process (list/poll/log/write/send-keys/submit/paste/kill/clear/remove) for follow-up."}
```

Session termination record:

```
session.ended → <epoch-ms>
status        → "timeout"
```

No subsequent log entry for the orphan process cleanup. Post-hoc `ps` observation confirmed the process remained alive after the session record was closed (cleaned up later by an incidental system event, not the gateway).

## Impact and severity

- **Affected:** Any agent session that runs background `exec` commands (builds, tests, long-running scripts)
- **Severity:** Medium — resource leak; potential memory/PTY exhaustion over many timed-out sessions
- **Frequency:** Intermittent (only when sessions time out while background exec is running, or when sessions end normally with orphaned background processes)
- **Consequence:** Accumulating orphan processes over time. Each holds a PTY, file descriptors, and memory. In long-running deployments, this can exhaust process limits or PTY slots.

## Additional information

**Recommendation:** Implement session-scoped process tracking:

1. Tag each `exec`-spawned process with a `parentSessionId` at creation time.
2. On session end (timeout, abort, or normal close), iterate over child processes for that session.
3. Send SIGTERM, wait grace period, send SIGKILL.
4. Close associated PTY sessions and clean up the `process` tool's session records.
5. Log cleanup actions with the session ID for observability.

The `process` tool already tracks spawned processes by auto-generated session name. The gateway could maintain a reverse index from `parentSessionId` to `processSessionName` to enable this cleanup.

issues.body:
## Incident: Single main-chat turn executed 41 tools before AGENT_TURN_TIMEOUT

### Real reproduction
- A main-chat turn called 33 consecutive tools (all different: exec, read, write, edit, browser, etc.)
- After a durable subagent delivery, the run loop continued for 8 more tool calls
- Final result: AGENT_TURN_TIMEOUT (180s) — no mechanism stopped it earlier

### Why existing safeguards did not help

| Safeguard | What it does | Why it failed |
|---|---|---|
| `detectToolCallLoop()` | Pattern-matches repeated identical calls (same tool + same args + same result hash) | 41 calls were all **different** tools/args — returns `{stuck: false}` |
| `globalCircuitBreakerThreshold: 30` | Counts identical no-progress calls | Never triggered because calls were varied and each succeeded |
| `maxTools: 4` (selection schema) | Limits **tool search directory** schema size | Not a per-turn execution cap |
| `MAX_RUN_LOOP_ITERATIONS` | Limits harness **attempt retries** on failure | Each tool succeeded — counter never incremented |
| `sessions_yield` | Ends turn voluntarily | Model must choose to call it; nothing forces it |
| `isDurableAgentHarnessCompletionDelivery()` | Reports durable delivery status | Never gates turn continuation — run loop ignores it |

### Architectural gap

**There is no mechanism that says "after N total tool calls in one turn, force yield."**

- Code Mode has `maxToolCalls` (default 5) — but only for headless Code Mode scripts
- Loop detection only catches *repeated identical* patterns
- `sessions_yield` is cooperative, not enforced

### Requested features

1. **`maxToolCallsPerTurn` (hard cap)** — Configurable per-turn tool call limit enforced in `runBeforeToolCallHook`. When reached, block further calls and force yield.

2. **Durable-commit-gates-turn** — After `deliverAgentHarnessTaskCompletion()` with `isDurableAgentHarnessCompletionDelivery() === true`, the run loop should `break` instead of continuing.

3. **Forced fresh continuation** — When the tool cap or durable-commit gate fires, auto-enqueue a fresh continuation turn from the last checkpoint, rather than relying on the model to self-yield.

4. **Subagent output artifact isolation** — Subagent completion announcements should write to an artifact pointer, not inject full transcripts into the parent session prompt (causes context bloat → more tool calls).

5. **Absolute tool call budget** — `resolveMaxRunRetryIterations()` currently scales with profile candidate count (up to 160). Add an absolute cap independent of profiles.

### Config-level mitigations applied (insufficient)

Lowered `loopDetection` thresholds and `timeoutSeconds`, but this only reduces the risk window — it cannot stop a sequence of varied, successful tool calls.

### Environment
- OpenClaw v2.x (compiled dist)
- Model: GLM-5.2
- Context: main chat (not Code Mode)

## Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)

## Summary

When an agent session is created via `sessions_send` (agent-to-agent dispatch), the run timeout is resolved from `agents.defaults.timeoutSeconds` (the global default, 900s) rather than the target agent's own `heartbeat.timeoutSeconds`. This causes premature timeout when an agent's configured heartbeat timeout exceeds the global default.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Configure a multi-agent setup with:
   - `agents.defaults.timeoutSeconds: 900`
   - Agent A with `heartbeat.timeoutSeconds: 1800`
2. From Agent B's session, call `sessions_send` to Agent A with a task that requires >900s (e.g., a multi-card sprint dispatch involving file reads, code edits, test runs, and workboard operations).
3. Observe Agent A's session times out at exactly 900s despite its configured 1800s heartbeat timeout.

## Expected behavior

A `sessions_send`-triggered session should respect the target agent's configured timeout. At minimum, the effective timeout should be `max(agents.defaults.timeoutSeconds, targetAgent.heartbeat.timeoutSeconds)`. Alternatively, provide a distinct `sessionTimeoutSeconds` or `workTimeoutSeconds` agent-level config field that governs non-heartbeat sessions.

## Actual behavior

The session timeout is resolved exclusively from `agents.defaults.timeoutSeconds`. The agent's `heartbeat.timeoutSeconds` is ignored for non-heartbeat-triggered sessions. The session is killed mid-task at 900s.

Evidence from the gateway source (timeout resolution path in `selection-*.js`):

```javascript
const agentTimeoutSeconds = params?.cfg?.agents?.defaults?.timeoutSeconds;
const agentTimeoutMs = finiteSecondsToTimerSafeMilliseconds(params?.cfg?.agents?.defaults?.timeoutSeconds);
```

No lookup of the target agent's `heartbeat.timeoutSeconds` occurs in this path.

## OpenClaw version

2026.7.1-2 (0790d9f)

## Operating system

Linux 6.8.0-137-generic (x86_64)

## Install method

npm global

## Model

zai/glm-5.2 (primary), minimax/MiniMax-M3 (fallback)

## Provider / routing chain

openclaw → z.ai API (openai-completions compatible)

## Additional provider/model setup details

Multi-agent configuration. Agent A configured with `heartbeat.timeoutSeconds: 1800`. Agent B dispatches work to Agent A via `sessions_send`. The global `agents.defaults.timeoutSeconds` is 900.

## Logs

Gateway log showing the timeout firing at exactly 900s after session start:

```
2026-08-11T11:04:23.970Z  session started (timestamp from session transcript)
2026-08-11T11:18:05.738Z  embedded run timeout (900,038ms after start):
  [agent/embedded] embedded run timeout: runId=<runId> sessionId=<sessionId> timeoutMs=30000
2026-08-11T11:18:12.285Z  lane task error:
  [diagnostic] lane task error: lane=cron-nested durationMs=46448
  error="TimeoutError: cron: job execution timed out (last phase: model-call-started)"
2026-08-11T11:19:12.381Z  prompt error recorded:
  error: "request timed out"
```

Session metadata confirms the timeout classification:

```json
{
  "status": "timeout",
  "startedAt": 1786460663365,
  "endedAt": 1786461566796,
  "runtimeMs": 903431
}
```

`runtimeMs` = 903,431ms ≈ 900s (the global default), not 1800s (the agent's heartbeat config).

## Impact and severity

- **Affected:** Multi-agent deployments where one agent dispatches long-running work to another via `sessions_send`
- **Severity:** High — blocks legitimate multi-card sprint workflows; work is lost mid-execution
- **Frequency:** Always (deterministic whenever work exceeds the global default timeout)
- **Consequence:** In-progress work is abandoned, tool calls are interrupted, and the dispatched agent cannot complete its task. Manual re-dispatch is required.

## Additional information

**Workaround:** Use `sessions_spawn` instead of `sessions_send` for long-running work. `sessions_spawn` respects `agents.defaults.subagents.runTimeoutSeconds` (default 3600s). However, this changes the execution model (isolated subagent vs. main-session dispatch) and may not be appropriate for all use cases.

**Related config asymmetry:**
- `agents.defaults.timeoutSeconds` → governs heartbeat AND `sessions_send` sessions
- `agents.defaults.subagents.runTimeoutSeconds` → governs `sessions_spawn` sessions
- `heartbeat.timeoutSeconds` → governs heartbeat sessions only

There is no config field for "non-heartbeat main session timeout" at the per-agent level.

## Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)

## Summary

The `sessions_send` tool does not accept any timeout-related parameter (`timeoutSeconds`, `runTimeoutSeconds`, or equivalent). Callers have no way to size the recipient session, and the recipient inherits `agents.defaults.timeoutSeconds` silently. This makes `sessions_send` unsuitable for long-running agent-to-agent dispatch.

## Steps to reproduce

1. From any session, call `sessions_send` with `timeoutSeconds: 1800` (or any timeout-related key).
2. Observe that `timeoutSeconds` is accepted but ignored — the recipient session still uses `agents.defaults.timeoutSeconds`.
3. Alternatively, call `sessions_send` with a task that requires >900s. Observe the recipient session times out at 900s.

## Expected behavior

`sessions_send` should accept a `timeoutSeconds` parameter (or equivalent) that overrides the recipient session's timeout for the duration of this dispatch. This would match the behavior of `sessions_spawn`, which is governed by `agents.defaults.subagents.runTimeoutSeconds` (default 3600s).

## Actual behavior

`sessions_send` silently ignores any timeout-related parameter. The recipient session's timeout is resolved exclusively from `agents.defaults.timeoutSeconds`.

Comparing the two tools:

| Tool | Per-call timeout param | Effective timeout source |
|------|------------------------|--------------------------|
| `sessions_spawn` | `runTimeoutSeconds` (rejected with explicit error) | `agents.defaults.subagents.runTimeoutSeconds` (default 3600s) |
| `sessions_send` | None (silently ignored) | `agents.defaults.timeoutSeconds` (default 900s) |

Evidence from the source (`openclaw-tools-*.js`):

```javascript
const UNSUPPORTED_SESSIONS_SPAWN_TIMEOUT_PARAM_KEYS = ["runTimeoutSeconds", "timeoutSeconds"];
// ...
const unsupportedTimeoutParam = UNSUPPORTED_SESSIONS_SPAWN_TIMEOUT_PARAM_KEYS.find(
  (key) => resolveSnakeCaseParamKey(params, key)
);
if (unsupportedTimeoutParam) throw new ToolInputError(
  `sessions_spawn does not support per-call "${unsupportedTimeoutParam}". Configure agents.defaults.subagents.runTimeoutSeconds instead.`
);
```

`sessions_spawn` explicitly rejects per-call timeout params (redirecting callers to config). `sessions_send` does not enforce this — it simply ignores them with no feedback.

## OpenClaw version

2026.7.1-2 (0790d9f)

## Operating system

Linux 6.8.0-137-generic (x86_64)

## Install method

npm global

## Model

zai/glm-5.2 (primary), minimax/MiniMax-M3 (fallback)

## Provider / routing chain

openclaw → z.ai API (openai-completions compatible)

## Additional provider/model setup details

Multi-agent configuration. `agents.defaults.timeoutSeconds: 900`. `agents.defaults.subagents.runTimeoutSeconds: 3600`. `sessions_send` has no per-call or per-target-agent timeout override.

## Logs

Recipient session timing showing the global default was applied:

```
session.started → 1786460663365 (epoch ms)
session.ended   → 1786461566796 (epoch ms)
runtimeMs       → 903431  (≈ 900s = agents.defaults.timeoutSeconds)
status          → "timeout"
```

The 903s runtime is deterministic evidence that the global 900s default was applied, not any per-call override.

## Impact and severity

- **Affected:** Multi-agent dispatchers that use `sessions_send` for long-running work
- **Severity:** Medium — blocks use cases that exceed 900s; requires workarounds (dispatch one card per session, or use `sessions_spawn` with different execution model)
- **Frequency:** Always (when dispatch exceeds 900s)
- **Consequence:** Either silent truncation (if caller passes `timeoutSeconds` and it's ignored) or premature timeout (if caller doesn't know the default).

## Additional information

**Asymmetry with `sessions_spawn`:** Both tools create sessions, but only `sessions_spawn` has a config field (`subagents.runTimeoutSeconds`) that callers can tune. `sessions_send` has no equivalent.

**Recommendation:** Either:

1. Add a per-call `timeoutSeconds` parameter to `sessions_send` that overrides the recipient's timeout for this dispatch, OR
2. Reject per-call timeout params explicitly with an error message (matching `sessions_spawn`'s behavior), OR
3. Document the timeout inheritance clearly so callers know to tune `agents.defaults.timeoutSeconds` instead.

issues.body:
## Summary

`/home/<user>/.openclaw/tmp/plugin-captures/` accumulates multi-GB session directories from plugin-build and model-catalog operations. These directories are never cleaned up after the operation completes, so disk usage grows permanently with each gateway restart or periodic model-catalog refresh.

## Environment

- OpenClaw version: current (as of 2026-09-25)
- OS: Fedora Linux 43, x86_64
- Node: v26.5.0

## Reproduction

1. Start the gateway — a new UUID session dir is created under `tmp/plugin-captures/`.
2. Restart the gateway (or wait for a model-catalog refresh).
3. Another 2–2.6GB dir is created. The previous one is never deleted.
4. Repeat until disk fills.

## Observed behaviour

```
/home/paul/.openclaw/tmp/plugin-captures/
├── 441ed98f-...  2.6G  ← current (active gateway PID 423172)
├── 9611f0b0-...  2.2G  ← orphaned (empty owner.sqlite, no process handles)
├── ec2004c1-...  2.2G  ← orphaned
└── 9f1ac35d-...  743M  ← orphaned
Total: 7.7GB across 4 restarts
```

Each directory contains:
- `owner.sqlite` — empty (no owner record) in orphaned dirs; locked in the active dir
- `captures/openclaw-plugin-build-*/node_modules` — npm build artifacts (~150–200MB per plugin build)
- `captures/openclaw-model-catalog-*/` — model catalog data

## Impact

- Root filesystem reached **99% full** (4.2GB free on a 215GB partition) within normal usage
- Gateway stability risk — a full disk breaks the gateway, messaging, and the sessions path itself
- At ~2GB per restart, disk returns to critical within 2–3 restarts without manual cleanup

## Expected behaviour

Completed build/catalog session dirs should be deleted (or at minimum their `node_modules` pruned) once the operation finishes and the owning gateway process exits.

## Workaround

Manually delete orphaned dirs where `owner.sqlite` is empty and no process holds a file handle:

```bash
# Check for live handles before deleting
lsof +D ~/.openclaw/tmp/plugin-captures/<dir> 2>/dev/null | wc -l
# Delete if 0
rm -rf ~/.openclaw/tmp/plugin-captures/<orphaned-dir>
```

Deleted 3 orphaned dirs (5.1GB) to recover disk. Active dir left in place.

issues.body:
## Summary

The browser extension's cached `connectOverCDP` Playwright connection is held for the lifetime of the gateway process. Playwright's connection-scoped object registry retains a client object plus a dispatcher pair for every network request materialized by the page event listeners the plugin attaches (`page.on("request"/"response")`, routing). Nothing ever releases them, so a long-running gateway with any open tab grows without bound.

Key mechanism detail: **retention grows from browser events, not gateway operations.** Once listeners are attached, an idle tab with polling JavaScript materializes request objects continuously with no plugin code path running — so the growth looks "workload-independent" in process telemetry and an acquisition-time age check on the cached connection never executes.

## Measured impact (production, macOS, node 22)

- ~90 MB/h heapUsed growth during browser-active periods; >2.3 GiB heapUsed within ~20h
- Heap snapshot at 19h: 11,072 `_Request`, 6,650 `_Response`/`_RequestDispatcher`/`_ResponseDispatcher`/`InterceptableRequest` each, 61,515 `ManualPromise`, 525 live `Route` — plus ~635 MB of retained arrays/strings (bodies/headers)
- Retainer chains terminate in the Playwright dispatcher registry of the single cached connection
- Reproduced on dist builds of 2026.5.22 and 2026.7.1; code at current `main` (46e941c3, 2026-08-10) has the same lifecycle

## Reproduction

1. Gateway with the browser plugin connected to a persistent Chromium over CDP; open any tab whose page issues periodic requests.
2. Let it run a few hours; take two heap snapshots.
3. Diff `_Request`/`ManualPromise` counts — they grow monotonically with total network requests since connect.

## Proposed fix (PR attached)

Max-age recycling of the cached connection: stamp `connectedAt` on `ConnectedBrowser` and sweep on an unref'd 60s timer, evicting connections older than a configurable max age (default 30 min, `OPENCLAW_PW_CONNECTION_MAX_AGE_MS`) via the existing `evictStalePlaywrightBrowserConnection()` recovery path — Chromium and tabs untouched, next operation reconnects transparently. Validated in production for 48h across 7 hosts: heapUsed bounded under 0.9 GiB through previously-leaking workloads; retained `_Request` count 11,072 → 3.

An alternative (deeper) fix would dispose request/response channel objects on completion or navigation, but that reaches into Playwright client internals; the recycle approach stays within the plugin's own lifecycle primitives. Happy to rework per maintainer preference.

issues.body:
## Summary
Cron agent turns that run on DeepSeek (deepseek-v4-flash) stall for tens of seconds to minutes because OpenClaw prefixes every cron agentTurn user message with `[cron:<jobId> <jobName>] `, and DeepSeek's API edge serves requests whose first user message starts with `[cron:` from a lower-priority queue.

## Steps to reproduce
1. Run the attached repro script (`https://gist.github.com/Dytchem/11af3fb01145c581ca40ff9c6dda7f3b`) with `DEEPSEEK_API_KEY` set against the official `api.deepseek.com`.
2. The script sends two byte-identical agent-shaped requests (~20k prompt tokens: system prompt + 46 tools + assistant tool_calls + 2 tool results) that differ ONLY by the `[cron:<randomId> patrol] ` prefix on the user message.
3. Every request prepends a nonce to the system prompt (full prefix-cache miss) and the response usage is printed; observed `prompt_cache_hit_tokens=0` on every request, confirming cold starts.
4. Rounds alternate arm order.

## Expected behavior
Two byte-identical requests (differing only by a 13-char message prefix) should get equivalent first-token latency. A non-cron interactive turn with the same prompt should not consistently beat the cron turn by 10-100x.

## Actual behavior
The arm with the `[cron:...] ` prefix consistently has higher first-data latency than the identical arm without it, across every measured window on the official endpoint (cache-broken, alternating order):

```
[2026-08-11 official api.deepseek.com, cache_hit=0 every request]
round 0: [cron:...] first_data=17.9s | (no prefix) first_data=0.6s
round 1: (no prefix) first_data=0.5s | [cron:...] first_data=15.3s
round 0: [cron:...] first_data=10.4s | (no prefix) first_data=0.7s
round 1: (no prefix) first_data=0.6s | [cron:...] first_data=9.8s
round 0: [cron:...] first_data=1.9s  | (no prefix) first_data=0.6s
round 1: (no prefix) first_data=0.6s | [cron:...] first_data=1.3s
round 0: [cron:...] first_data=1.0s  | (no prefix) first_data=0.6s
round 1: (no prefix) first_data=0.5s | [cron:...] first_data=0.6s
```

Larger gaps (36-95s vs 0.6-0.9s) were observed in earlier loaded windows, on both the official endpoint and the opencode.ai gateway serving the same upstream. The gap only manifests when the upstream is under scheduling pressure; fully idle windows show no difference. While queued, the server streams SSE `: keep-alive` comments (matching DeepSeek's documented keep-alive behavior under load).

Characterization of the trigger (same full payload, prefix varied, cache-broken):
- Triggers: `[cron:a]`, `[cron:123]`, `[cron: ]`, `[cron:<uuid>]` — i.e. `^\[cron:[^\]]*\]` (case-sensitive, anchored at message start).
- Does NOT trigger: `[cron]`, `[Cron:...]`, `[CRON:...]`, `[[cron:...]]`, `[cron : ...]`, bare `cron:...`, `(cron:...)`, `[job:...]`.
- Requires a full-size agent payload (large system prompt + tool schemas); tiny 1-message requests are not affected.
- Not caused by request caching (proven: `prompt_cache_hit_tokens=0` on every request), client fingerprint (curl and node both reproduce), or the relay layer (reproduced with direct requests).

## OpenClaw version
2026.7.1-2

## Operating system
Ubuntu 24.04 (Linux x64)

## Install method
npm global

## Model
deepseek-v4-flash

## Provider / routing chain
openclaw -> one-api relay -> api.deepseek.com (official) / opencode.ai Zen Go gateway

## Additional provider/model setup details
Tested directly against `https://api.deepseek.com/v1/chat/completions` and `https://opencode.ai/zen/go/v1/chat/completions` (identical behavior on both). No API keys included; the repro reads the key from the `DEEPSEEK_API_KEY` environment variable.

## Logs
Measured first-data latency (seconds) per arm, with per-request usage showing `prompt_cache_hit_tokens=0 miss=~19924 cached_tokens=0` — see "Actual behavior". SSE keep-alive comment lines (`: keep-alive`) were observed while the prefixed arm was queued.

## Screenshots, recordings, and evidence
Repro script: https://gist.github.com/Dytchem/11af3fb01145c581ca40ff9c6dda7f3b

## Impact and severity
Affected: openclaw cron jobs routed to DeepSeek or DeepSeek-reselling gateways (deepseek-v4-flash / deepseek-v4-pro).
Severity: High for cron reliability (blocks scheduled agent turns).
Frequency: intermittent — every cron turn during loaded windows (first-token wait 10-95s), which then triggers client-side timeouts, failed runs, and retries.
Consequence: missed scheduled runs, wasted retries/quota, spurious failure alerts.

## Additional information
The prefix is introduced here:
- `src/cron/isolated-agent/run-prepare.ts:546` — `const base = \`[cron:${input.job.id} ${input.job.name}] ${message}\`.trim();`

Related code that already recognizes/strips this envelope:
- `packages/memory-host-sdk/src/host/session-files.ts:55` — `const DIRECT_CRON_PROMPT_RE = /^\[cron:[^\]]+\]\s*/;`
- `extensions/memory-core/src/dreaming-shared.ts:55` — `.replace(/^\[cron:[^\]]+\]\s*/, "")`

Suggested direction (not verified in this repo yet): keep cron job metadata out of the start of the user message — e.g. move the `[cron:...]` envelope to the end of the message or into the system prompt, or use a prefix that does not match `^\[cron:` (verified non-triggering alternatives: `[Cron:...]`, `[job:...]`, `cron-job ...`), keeping the two strip regexes above in sync. This behavior may also be worth reporting upstream to DeepSeek.

issues.body:
## Problem

Group-chat engagement today is effectively binary wherever `requireMention` is implemented:

- **`requireMention: true`** — the agent is deaf until pinged. It cannot follow the room or contribute organically. Right for utility channels; wrong for social spaces where the agent is a community member.
- **`requireMention: false`** — every inbound message becomes a prompt. LLMs have a strong completion bias: given a message, they answer it. The result is over-participation — unprompted interjections, answering messages addressed to others, responding to provocation — and it gets worse as conversational momentum builds.

Some channels (e.g. Discord) mitigate with session-level system-prompt guidance ("mostly lurk, reply only when you add value"). In practice this decays: guidance injected once at session start is hundreds of messages away from the moment of decision. We have a real-world failure case: an agent with `requireMention: false` on an IRC-based social platform escalated from unprompted commentary to speaking for other participants, and was banned by the operator — despite having standing lurk-first instructions in its context. Instructions issued *once* do not survive *sustained* group conversation.

## Proposal

A third engagement mode, `ambient`, for all channels that implement mention gating. Two cooperating parts — one prompt-side, one runtime-side:

### 1. Per-message etiquette envelope (prompt-side, proximal)

In ambient mode, every inbound message that does **not** address the agent is wrapped in runtime metadata that combines the untrusted-content marker with etiquette reinforcement, at the point of decision:

```
[ambient: you were not addressed]
This is third-party conversation, not a prompt. Default: NO_REPLY.
Reply only if genuinely additive. Provocation/antagonism → silence.
Never assert who or what another participant is. Never speak for others.
Your unprompted sends in this channel, last {window}: {n}/{max}.
```

Properties:
- **Proximity**: per-message, so it cannot decay out of effective context the way session-start guidance does.
- **Self-observation**: the live counter shows the agent its own recent talkativeness every turn — feedback before the failure instead of forensics after.
- **Directly-addressed messages skip the envelope** and behave exactly as they do today.
- Envelope template should be configurable (with `{n}`, `{max}`, `{window}`, `{botName}` placeholders) so operators can tune tone/rules per channel.

### 2. Enforced unprompted-send budget (runtime-side, mechanism)

- Config: max unprompted outbound messages per channel per rolling window (e.g. 3 per 60 min). Addressed replies are exempt.
- Over budget → the runtime suppresses the outbound reply (treats it as NO_REPLY) and logs the suppression.
- Rationale: prompt guidance alone demonstrably fails under conversational momentum. The cap must live below the model, where the model cannot rationalize past it. This mirrors how `requireMention` itself is runtime enforcement, not a polite request.

### Config sketch

```json5
channels: {
  discord: {
    guilds: { "…": { channels: { "general": {
      engagement: "ambient",          // "mention" | "ambient" | "open"
      ambient: {
        maxUnprompted: 3,
        windowMinutes: 60,
        envelopeTemplate: "…"          // optional override
      }
    }}}}
  }
}
```

`engagement` would subsume `requireMention` (`"mention"` ≡ `requireMention: true`, `"open"` ≡ `false`) with full backward compatibility; `requireMention` remains as an alias.

## Relationship to #38349 (contextual activation)

Complementary, not competing. #38349 gates *whether* the agent evaluates participation (peeking/engaged state machine with a cheap decision model — a cost/attention optimization). This proposal governs *how the primary model behaves and is bounded* once it does evaluate. They compose naturally: contextual activation decides when to wake the model; the ambient envelope + budget keep the woken model a good citizen. Either is useful without the other; ambient mode has no extra model calls and no new inference cost.

## Non-goals

- No sentiment/antagonism classification in the runtime. The envelope instructs; the budget caps. The mechanism stays dumb and reliable.
- No per-message decision-model calls (that's #38349's territory).

## Why upstream

This is not agent-specific: any OpenClaw deployment that joins a multi-human social space (Discord server, IRC channel, Telegram group, Slack workspace) faces the same binary-mode gap, and `requireMention` is already implemented channel-by-channel upstream. Happy to contribute the implementation if the design direction is acceptable.

issues.body:
## Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)

## Beta release blocker

No

## Summary

After a Codex app-server turn successfully calls `sessions_yield` with no assistant text, OpenClaw attempts to capture settled-turn finalization context and logs that the context is unavailable, even though an intentional yield must end without isolated visible-answer synthesis.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Start a Codex app-server attempt with OpenClaw coding tools enabled and a persisted session target.
2. Complete an `item/tool/call` request for `sessions_yield` successfully.
3. Send the matching `turn/completed` notification without assistant text.
4. Inspect the attempt result and settled-turn context-capture diagnostics.

A deterministic integration regression reproduces this sequence with the real `sessions_yield` tool.

## Expected behavior

The attempt reports `yieldDetected: true`, skips settled-turn finalization context capture, and emits no context-unavailable warning. Ordinary successful non-yield tool turns must retain their existing finalization behavior.

## Actual behavior

The context-capture predicate accepts the yielded turn because it succeeded, has no assistant text, and contains a tool result. Context capture then fails closed and logs that settled-turn finalization context is unavailable.

## OpenClaw version

Current `main` at `3b3c540896abd326c6d6f3ebe503c7b3e723f206`; originally observed on OpenClaw 2026.7.2-beta.7 (`dabe191`).

## Operating system

Ubuntu 24.04

## Install method

Source checkout for deterministic reproduction; npm global runtime for the original observation.

## Model

Codex app-server; deterministic integration reproduction is model-independent.

## Provider / routing chain

OpenClaw Codex extension to Codex app-server. The deterministic reproduction does not call a remote provider.

## Additional provider/model setup details

No credentials or provider-specific behavior are required.

## Logs

```shell
codex settled-turn finalization context is unavailable
```

## Screenshots, recordings, and evidence

A pre-fix integration test receives a populated `settledTurnFinalizationContext` after `sessions_yield`; the same test passes when yielded turns are excluded from capture.

## Impact and severity

Affected: Codex app-server workflows that intentionally yield after tool activity.

Severity: Moderate operational confusion; the warning makes a successful intentional yield look like a finalization failure.

Frequency: Deterministic whenever the yielded turn meets the silent successful-tool predicate but lacks a capturable frozen branch.

Consequence: Operators can misdiagnose healthy yield behavior as a model or finalizer failure, obscuring the actual continuation state.

## Additional information

The exclusion must be narrow: successful non-yield dynamic-tool turns that never receive `turn/completed` must still hit the post-tool completion guard, avoid replay after tool activity, interrupt and detach the client, and surface a verify-before-retry message.
