prs.title: fix(slack): keep progress updating after native streams expire
prs.body:
<details>
<summary>Additional instructions</summary>

Keep **Allow edits from maintainers** enabled.

</details>

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users watching a Slack native progress card see frozen or failed-looking progress after Slack expires the stream, even though the agent continues working. Later text can fail or arrive in a separate reply.

## Why This Change Was Made

Keep a bounded projection of the streamed message and use `chat.update` on the same timestamp after an explicit `message_not_in_streaming_state` rejection. Subsequent progress, final text, and final metadata use that same message, following [Slack SDK recovery guidance](https://github.com/slackapi/node-slack-sdk/pull/2611).

The existing scoped writer and user Stop handling remain in control. Ambiguous writes are not replayed. If the full message cannot be reconstructed within the limits, or an update definitively rejects pending text, only the undelivered tail uses normal chunked delivery. This includes `edit_window_closed` and `cant_update_message`, so workspace editing restrictions do not discard an otherwise deliverable final reply. Once ordinary delivery succeeds, its retained recovery projection is retired, so native cleanup cannot replay that delivered tail onto the original card.

A stream started with a custom agent name or avatar retains the established identity-aware route: because `chat.update` cannot preserve custom authorship, explicit expiry retires that stream and sends only its unacknowledged tail through ordinary delivery with the same custom identity. The acknowledged prefix is not replayed.

## User Impact

Progress and eligible final replies continue on the existing card after stream expiry. Task state, source links, narration order, and accumulated detail/output text are retained. Recovered task details and outputs use plain rich text, so embedded Markdown syntax is not interpreted. Customized agent authorship is preserved by using ordinary tail delivery instead of editing the customized message.

## Evidence

- Before the fix, a real-SDK regression failed on the first expired append with `SlackStreamNotDeliveredError`.
- On final head `e09af9ae6480498f819843e034ac86da2fde372f`, **155/155** focused tests passed across streaming, real-SDK delivery traces, and preview fallback. These include same-message recovery, edit-restriction fallback, cleanup non-replay, and the custom-identity expiry regression proving no `chat.update`, no acknowledged-prefix replay, and identity-aware ordinary delivery of only the pending tail.
- Extension production and test typechecks passed. Type-aware lint on the five touched Slack files reported 0 warnings/errors; formatting and `git diff --check` passed.
- Fresh AutoReview completed at P0-P2. Its sole P1 concern claimed the initial stream payload was absent from the projection; source and passing recovery assertions show `startSlackStream` installs the projection before invoking `appendSlackStream`, which records the initial text/chunks. No code change was made for that false positive.
- Slack `blocks.validate` previously accepted synthetic plan and timeline projections, including rich-text details/output and source elements.

### Real Slack recovery proof

Executed the actual compiled `streaming.ts`, `streaming-projection.ts`, and their client modules from measured revision `2fec06eb352ffb4fc89178b5130aa594c7c1a4d0` with the real Slack SDK **8.0.0** and installed public OpenClaw SDK modules. API responses were not mocked. A separate `chat.stopStream` call closed only each synthetic test stream on Slack, leaving the SDK stream object active, so the next real append exercised `message_not_in_streaming_state`.

```text
Baseline owner (4d7a33874):
  chat.startStream -> ok
  chat.stopStream  -> ok (test-induced server closure)
  chat.appendStream -> message_not_in_streaming_state
  readback: rejected tail absent; no recovery update

Candidate owner (2fec06eb):
  chat.startStream -> ok
  chat.stopStream  -> ok (test-induced server closure)
  chat.appendStream -> message_not_in_streaming_state
  chat.update -> ok; readback: same message, task in_progress, working text present
  chat.update -> ok; final answer and complete task appended
  chat.update -> ok; final metadata acknowledged

Independent native-CLI readback:
  expected bot identity: true
  same message: true
  all tasks complete: true
  acknowledged prefix occurrences: 1
  final answer occurrences: 1
  final metadata preserved: true
```

Task details, output, and source links also survived the recovery. The executed bundle hashes matched after the run. The custom-identity repair does not change the measured default-identity `chat.update` path; it keeps customized messages on the ordinary identity-aware route. Only synthetic content was used; identifiers and private environment details are omitted here.

This proves the real server-closed-stream recovery contract and Slack message readback. It does not measure Slack's undocumented natural expiry duration or claim screenshot-based rendering verification. The installed production plugin and Gateway were not replaced or restarted.

## Current-main refresh (2026-10-18)

Current head: `e09af9ae6480498f819843e034ac86da2fde372f`. Non-destructively merged main `7aab596ad005c15824143c482e9d6da732c6f102`; the prior PR head remains an ancestor. No force push.

The merge preserves current main's serialized-HTTP progress fixture and its refactored delivery-trace harness while retaining the PR's expiry/fallback/Stop traces. The reviewed custom-identity defect is repaired at the stream owner and covered at both the production stream boundary and ordinary dispatch boundary.

Live Slack was not rerun for the custom-identity branch because the supported API contract is deterministic: stream start accepts identity overrides while `chat.update` does not. The earlier live recovery measurement remains historical evidence for the unchanged default-identity recovery path. Full-suite and full-build proof were not run locally; canonical PR CI owns broad validation. Production plugin, Gateway, Slack channel, and auth configuration were not changed.

prs.title: refactor(browser): centralize action and act-kind facts
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The browser plugin repeats the same action and act-kind inventories across schema capability filtering, tab binding, lifecycle dispatch, selector admission, timeout policy, and Lightpanda support.

## User Impact

No visible behavior or text changes. Normal and tab-bound action ordering stay distinct and unchanged. `insertText` remains API-only; `clickCoords` accepts explicit timeouts but does not gain a default timeout.

## What Changed

Two dependency-light, plugin-owned tables now hold tool-action and act-kind facts. Their consumers read declared capability, lifecycle, selector, path, timeout, and engine-support facts instead of maintaining parallel ladders and sets. The retired route-local kind inventory is deleted. Authentication, navigation policy, admission checks, and runtime dispatch effects remain at their existing owners.

This is a bounded area slice of widely consumed browser action owners, keeping schema, policy, route, and engine attribution together rather than mixing unrelated cleanup into a larger PR.

## Best-effort tradeoffs accepted

None. This removes duplicate static facts, not guards, authorization checks, supported failure handling, or features. No config, schema shape, protocol, dependency, or persisted-data changes.

## Evidence

prs.title: feat(telegram): support copy-text presentation buttons
prs.body:
## Merge Brief

- **Problem:** plugins cannot express a portable copy-to-clipboard control through message presentation.
- **Demand:** continues the missing capability first explored in #36105; current `main` still has no equivalent portable action or Telegram encoder.
- **Value:** Telegram gets a native `CopyTextButton`; channels without native support keep a safe, readable manual-copy fallback.
- **Smallest complete fix:** add one capability-gated shared action, Telegram encoding, and fallback behavior at every affected channel boundary.
- **Scope:** presentation payloads, shared limits, Telegram, and existing Discord/Slack/Feishu fallback owners; no raw Telegram button input.
- **Risk:** public additive SDK surface and message-delivery behavior; exact-value privacy, select budgets, mentions, locations, and edits are regression-covered.
- **Proof:** exact-head focused suites pass **127/127**; core and extension production/test typechecks, changed-file format/lint, assertion ratchet, and merge simulation pass.
- **Gap:** native Telegram Test Server send → tap → clipboard proof remains externally blocked on authenticated broker access.
- **Non-goals:** no callback reinterpretation, provider-keyboard takeover, Gateway/config change, or production activation.
- **Maintainer ask:** accept the additive portable `copy-text` contract and review the repaired exact head.

## What Problem This Solves

Add a portable typed `copy-text` presentation action. Telegram renders it as a
native Bot API `CopyTextButton`; channels without native support keep a readable,
safe manual-copy fallback.

This updates the existing contribution first explored in #36105. It does not
reintroduce the retired raw Telegram button input.

## Current maintenance head

- **Exact head:** `d3c9ca87eb7ce42243ff9f65796f474f8e8c6007`
- **Frozen base:** `cd57bc91d991ba1350009e935caaf21e70c09c89`
- **Shape:** one signed semantic commit, 45 files, +2,636/-343.
- **Merge simulation:** clean against the frozen base.

The frozen base has no equivalent portable `copy-text` presentation action or
Telegram `copy_text` encoder. Existing inline-code tap-to-copy behavior is a
separate rendering path and does not expose this capability to plugins.

## Behavior

- The message tool schema exposes a typed `copy-text` action with a required
  string value.
- The shared presentation adapter preserves the action only when a channel
  declares `copyTextButtons`; unsupported channels render readable manual-copy
  fallback while callback payload values remain private.
- Telegram emits `InlineKeyboardButton.copy_text` only for values satisfying
  the Bot API's 1–256-character contract. Values that cannot be encoded safely
  remain visible as escaped fallback instead of being silently rewritten.
- Native controls share Telegram's existing 100-action budget, including every
  option in a select that Telegram renders as an individual button. Every
  native select row is reserved before Discord-sized button selection.
- Direct Telegram sends retain authored select prompts while excluding native
  copy values from visible text.
- Standalone location sends never receive a synthetic text anchor.
- Provider-owned and usable legacy keyboards retain precedence; unusable legacy
  controls do not falsely displace a valid presentation keyboard.
- Drop-time copy identity keeps duplicate labels paired with the correct value
  when an action falls back after planning.
- Markup-only edits do not synthesize replacement body text. If a rejected,
  over-budget, or shadowed copy control needs readable fallback, the action
  returns a recoverable result requiring explicit content or caption.
- Discord long-copy fallback uses a complete collision-safe fence in every
  independently rendered fragment. Mention suppression derives from the exact
  rendered fallback text, including enabled and disabled labels.

## Evidence

Exact-head focused behavior suites pass **127/127** across the 14 changed test
files:

- shared payload, message-tool visibility, and presentation limits: **13**
- Discord delivery/fallback/mention boundaries: **93**
- Telegram native/fallback/direct-action paths: **19**
- Slack fallback: **1**
- Feishu fallback: **1**

The PR-wrapper runtime-closure suite also passes **19/19** after adding the new
payload fallback helper to the wrapper's explicit trusted inventory. This
repairs the only branch-owned failure found by the first hosted run.

Exact-head static gates:

- core production typecheck: pass
- core test typecheck shards: pass
- extension production typecheck: pass
- extension test typecheck: pass
- changed core/extension/script lint: pass
- changed-file Oxfmt and `git diff --check`: pass
- assertion-safety ratchet: pass; the branch shrinks the
  `outbound-components.ts` baseline from two assertions to one
- merge tree against the frozen base: clean

The canonical changed-check also reports two full-tree failures already present
unchanged in the frozen base: three pre-existing UI `max-lines` suppressions are
absent from their baseline, and the database-first guard flags two pre-existing
retired-runtime migration files. This PR does not touch those files. Hosted PR
CI is the authoritative broad gate for the published head.

The isolated worktree was hydrated with the frozen lockfile to run the pinned
toolchain. No lockfile or dependency declaration changed; no Gateway, runtime
configuration, credential, or production state was touched.

## Live proof state

No exact-head live Telegram send/tap/clipboard claim is made. Historical branch
proof is not used as a substitute for current-head evidence. Remaining live
proof requires an authenticated Telegram Test Server/broker route to send the
native button, tap it in a Telegram client, verify exact clipboard bytes, and
exercise invalid-value/edit fallback. That route is currently unavailable to
the contributor environment.

## Maintainer decision

This intentionally keeps `copy-text` as a portable, capability-gated
presentation action rather than a Telegram-local input. Maintainer acceptance
of that public SDK surface remains the upstream product gate.

Closes #112747

AI-assisted: implemented and verified with Codex.

## What Problem This Solves

Arcee setup through OpenRouter should keep provider configuration, model references, and the stored OpenRouter credential under the same provider owner. The original July onboarding preset wrote an `arcee/...` route while storing the credential as `openrouter:default`, causing the first agent request to fail. Current main also has legacy auth-alias support; this PR makes new OpenRouter setup canonical and repairs previously persisted configuration.

The previous PR head had two compatibility defects: Doctor removed the old provider without migrating every agent model scope, and re-onboarding overwrote an existing shared OpenRouter endpoint/API mode.

## Why This Change Was Made

- New OpenRouter-backed Arcee setup selects `openrouter/arcee-ai/trinity-large-thinking` and owns its provider configuration under `models.providers.openrouter`.
- Doctor migrates defaults, keyed agent entries, legacy agent lists, primary/fallback references, model aliases, nested subagent/heartbeat/compaction/media selections, and explicit model-policy references before removing the old OpenRouter-backed Arcee catalog.
- Existing canonical model settings win on collisions. Migration is immutable and idempotent; direct Arcee configuration is unchanged.
- Both registered onboarding and the public catalog helper preserve an existing OpenRouter `baseUrl` and `api`, seeding defaults only when absent.
- Integration with current main preserves connection-only setup in merge mode and catalog seeding in replace mode, plus the eager public catalog helper. The Doctor repair is declared in the plugin manifest and uses the current lightweight migration SDK.

## User Impact

Fresh OpenRouter setup has matching credential and model ownership. Existing installations retain their proxy transport and authored model settings. Older OpenRouter-backed Arcee configuration can be repaired with `openclaw doctor --fix`; direct Arcee setup is unaffected.

prs.title: fix(telegram): isolate private DM topic inbound buffers by thread id
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Messages in distinct private Telegram topics share one inbound debounce identity. Work waiting in one topic blocks another topic, and a text `/stop` in one topic discards buffered input from another.

## Why This Change Was Made

The shared conversation serializer intentionally has no `scope: "dm"` case, so private bot topics fall back to the bare chat id. That same id is what session bindings look up. Changing it would stop existing private-chat bindings from matching, and a new delivery-target marker would not be honored by outbound thread selection.

Enqueue and cancellation both take their identity from the inbound debounce key. This change leaves shared peer ids and delivery targets alone, and adds a positive DM thread id only when building that key. A non-topic private DM (`scope: "dm"` with no positive thread id) still uses the bare chat id, so those messages stay one buffer.

## User Impact

Distinct private DM topics no longer block or cancel each other's buffered text. Ordinary private DMs without a topic keep the previous single-buffer behavior. Existing private-chat session bindings and outbound targets are unchanged.

## Evidence

Live run of `createTelegramInboundProcessing` (the real inbound debounce path) at `5d6eb9ad436030aac2eca7a7cb21bb93f5cbd0c4`. The debounce clock is advanced with Vitest fake timers, not a wall-clock sleep.

Two private DM topics in chat 7 were buffered separately and flushed as their own batches. Two messages in the same topic coalesced. A non-topic DM in the same chat still coalesced onto the bare chat id and did not mix with either topic.

```
HEAD 5d6eb9ad436030aac2eca7a7cb21bb93f5cbd0c4

DM_TOPIC_DEBOUNCE_PROOF {
  "keys": {
    "topic100": "7:dm-topic:100",
    "topic200": "7:dm-topic:200",
    "nonTopicDm": "7"
  },
  "dispositions": [
    { "kind": "buffered", "buffer": "debounce" },
    { "kind": "buffered", "buffer": "debounce" },
    { "kind": "buffered", "buffer": "debounce" },
    { "kind": "buffered", "buffer": "debounce" },
    { "kind": "buffered", "buffer": "debounce" }
  ],
  "flushed": [
    { "text": "beta", "thread": { "id": 200, "scope": "dm" } },
    { "text": "alpha-1\nalpha-2", "thread": { "id": 100, "scope": "dm" } },
    { "text": "plain-1\nplain-2", "thread": { "scope": "dm" } }
  ]
}

Test Files  1 passed (1)

```

prs.title: fix(process): stdout.pause() is ignored on a spawn broker command after ready()
prs.body:
Closes #162135

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: `stdout.pause()` is ignored on a broker-launched command when it is called right after `await child.ready()`.

## User Impact

User impact: a caller that pauses a command's output gets it paused, so it can apply backpressure instead of receiving data it asked to hold.

## Why This Change Was Made

While the pipe is held, the broker now records the caller's last `pause()` or `resume()` and replays it after Node's own release-time resume. Before, it replayed only a past `resume` event and Node then resumed the stream anyway.

## Evidence

Test from the issue, on current `main`: `2 failed | 10 passed`. With the fix: `12 passed`. Both cases fail on `isPaused()`.

`pipe.test.ts` covers a `pause` or `resume` made right after release, which a first version of this fix got wrong (found in review, fails if the wrappers are restored early).

prs.title: feat(subagents): show how long a continuable yielded leaf has been paused
prs.body:
Related #165685 This covers part 2 of #165685 only (pause age) and does not close it. The continuation stage vocabulary (never enqueued, enqueued, accepted, applied) is not included, and `agents_wait` is unchanged. There is no expiry, and nothing about when a run settles, sweeps, restores or wakes changes. ## What Problem This Solves A parked leaf that waits for a message shows no pause age, so an operator cannot tell a leaf paused a minute ago from one paused two days ago. On a real isolated Gateway, `subagents list` for a leaf paused about 1.8 days earlier reports only `waiting for external continuation`. The entry carries the wait kind, `deliveryStatus`, runtime and `endedAt`, but no age. ## User Impact `subagents list` entries and the native `subagents action=wait` run snapshots gain an optional `pausedForMs` for a yielded leaf that only an external continuation can resume. The list line reads `waiting for external continuation, paused 1d 19h`. Nothing else in either output changes, and the field is absent for every other run. No config, schema, migration or prompt change. The tool schema and description are unchanged, so no prompt or tool-schema snapshot moves. ## Why This Change Was Made The review of the issue asked for additive fields derived from registry-owned facts, and said pause age alone cannot establish a continuation stage. This change ships only the age. - The yield records its pause time as `execution.endedAt`. `markSubagentRunPausedAfterYield` also sets `pauseReason`, makes the execution terminal, and clears the outcome, `endedReason`, archive deadline, cleanup state, delivery state and captured result; `endedAt` is the one of those writes that the age reads, so no new persisted field is needed. - `resolveYieldedLeafPausedForMs(entry, observation, now)` (`subagent-execution-observation.ts`) returns `now - endedAt` only when the existing observation reports a `waiting` / `external` wait, the run is terminal, it is not a collector, and `endedAt` is a finite number. A parent waiting on announced children observes `kind: "children"` and gets nothing. - `subagents list` calls it with the observation it already computed and the list context's `now`, and appends `, paused ` with the existing `formatDurationCompact` (spaced). - `subagents action=wait` calls it with an observation built from full run rows that include the announced children of each yielded run. Both paths hand `observeSubagentExecution` full rows from `prepareSubagentRunReadSnapshot`, so a parent whose children exist only in persisted rows is classified the same way in both. The wait snapshot is handed only the selected runs, so `prepareSubagentRunsSnapshotForRunIds` takes a `yieldedChildren` option (set by the wait only): the read scope and selection add the children of selected yielded runs, and the consumed map carries them for observation only. Waits that select no yielded run read exactly what they read before. - The wait `attention` check still observes with no children (existing behavior); a code comment says so. `docs/tools/subagents/tool-reference.md` documents the field next to the list and wait output. Tests: one SQLite-backed tool test covers both outputs and the persisted-only parent; one unit test covers the guard cases. An earlier revision also had an in-memory list test; every mutation it caught is caught by these two, so it was removed. ### Is `endedAt` stable while a run stays paused? Two callers mark the same row for one yield: `subagent-registry-requester-yield.ts` (`Date.now()` at its commit) and `subagent-registry-completion-runtime.ts` (`terminal.endedAt` from the lifecycle end event). When both run, the second write replaces `endedAt` if the values differ. Calling the real function twice with timestamps 4000 ms apart gives `endedAt` 50000000, then 50004000, and a third call with the same value does not mutate. The age can therefore shift by the delay between those two events of one turn end. That is a bounded imprecision, not a drift: it is the gap between two events of the same turn, small next to the hours and days this field exists to show. That gap was not measured on a live yield. Paths read for any rewrite of `endedAt` on a row that is still paused: - Settle: the completion path in `subagent-registry-lifecycle-completion.ts` returns early for a yielded row unless the reason is killed (the `pauseReason === "sessions_yield"` guard comes before any write). Interrupted recovery is refused for a yielded row in the same file and in `subagent-registry-restart-recovery.ts` / `-helpers.ts`. - Kill: a killed completion clears `pauseReason`, so the row is no longer listed as a paused leaf (`isYieldedSubagentRun` also excludes kill intent, kill reconciliation and killed end reasons). - Restore: `subagent-registry-restore.ts` only resumes rows; its writes touch `suppressSessionEffects` and queued collectors, never `endedAt`. - Sweeper: `subagent-registry-sweeper.ts` sets `endedAt` only for rows that have none; session cleanup is deferred for yielded rows (`isSessionCleanupDeferred`); the orphan path reuses the existing `endedAt` and goes through the settle path above. - Adoption of a paused row by its continuation (`subagent-registry-run-recovery.ts`) replaces it with a new run id, so the paused row is superseded rather than rewritten. - Collector rows write `endedAt` in `swarm-collector.ts` and are excluded by the `collect` guard. - Startup settlement of requester continuations without a saved operator source (#175033) writes `delivery`, `suppressCompletionDelivery` and `cleanupHandled` on a paused row (and drops an orchestrator's `wakeOnDescendantSettle`) and leaves `execution.endedAt` and `pauseReason` alone (checked field by field on the seeded rows in both Gateway arms). I found no path other than the two yield callers that rewrites `endedAt` on a still-paused row. A later yield of the same resumed run restarts the age, which is the intended reading. ## Contract choices 1. Age only. `pausedForMs` is the only new vocabulary, and no continuation stage is reported. The registry holds no field that records an authoritative enqueued, accepted or applied fact (`requesterSettleWake.pauseNotice` records a wait registration, and `delivery.status` is cleared by the pause), so a stage would need a new recorded fact. Reporting a stage from the age alone would claim something the registry does not know. 2. A future `endedAt` (clock skew) gives `pausedForMs: 0`. The field's presence means "this is a continuable yielded leaf", and that is true regardless of clocks, so it is not dropped when the clocks disagree. The list line shows no age only when the value is exactly `0`, because `formatDurationCompact` renders nothing for `0`. The observation test asserts the `0`. 3. Open question for the owner: main lists a yielded row whose completion delivery it has marked `failed` (`permanent_failure`, no saved operator source) as `waiting for external continuation`, so this change gives it a `pausedForMs` too. That follows main's observation rather than adding a delivery guard here; whether such a row should show an age is part of the same direction decision as the field itself. ## Contract table | Case | `pausedForMs` | List line | |---|---|---| | Yielded leaf, terminal, no pending announced children | `now - execution.endedAt` | `waiting for external continuation, paused 1d 19h` | | Parent yielded while an announced child is pending (in memory or only in persisted rows) | absent | `waiting on 1 child` | | Collector row carrying a yield | absent | unchanged | | Running run | absent | unchanged | | Ordinary finished run | absent | unchanged | | Yielded row marked killed | absent (not listed active) | unchanged | | Yield row with no `endedAt` | absent | unchanged | | `endedAt` in the future | `0` | the line omits the age | ## Evidence All of the following ran on one machine (Mac Studio) after merging main `09cf9282b8f` into this branch as merge commit `4b2a9973805`. The merge resolved two conflicts with #170998, which moved the read-scope merge into `mergeSubagentRunReadScope`: the `yieldedChildren` expansion now sits in that function's `runIds` branch, byte-identical apart from one indent level, and the registry test sits after the test #170998 added. `git diff 09cf9282b8f...4b2a9973805` is the same 8 files, +225 / -16, as before the merge. The merge commit's tree is `e9933d7baf0297245e91dc66b35bbfd4e4ad6673` (`git rev-parse 4b2a9973805^{tree}`); the evidence was produced on the unsigned commit `f68a4d3331d` with that same tree, before signing. Every section below was rerun on that tree; BEFORE is a clean build of `09cf9282b8f`. The expansion inside `mergeSubagentRunReadScope` runs only for the wait's `runIds` scope and only when a selected run is yielded; every other scope of that function returns the same output as on main. ### Real built Gateway, before and after Each arm is its own checkout with `pnpm install` and `pnpm build`, started as `node openclaw.mjs gateway run --port

--bind loopback --auth token --token x --allow-unconfigured` with `HOME`, `OPENCLAW_HOME`, `OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR` and `OPENCLAW_CONFIG_PATH` pointing at an isolated state directory. No model provider is configured, because neither read runs a model. The state was seeded once with main `09cf9282b8f`, through the production registry persistence path (`persistRegistryFixture` into a real SQLite database), and each arm starts on a byte-identical `cp -a` copy restored to the same path. The rows are a parked leaf paused 43h12m before seeding, an orchestrator paused 50h with one announced child that was still running when seeded, and a collector row carrying a yield. `subagents list` and `subagents action=wait` are read through `POST /tools/invoke` with `sessionKey: "agent:main:main"`. BEFORE is `09cf9282b8f`, AFTER is `4b2a9973805`. On this base, startup recovery settles what a seeded row cannot keep (main #175033 settles requester continuations whose original operator source was not saved, without inventing one): it marks the announced child interrupted by the restart, and sets `delivery.status: failed` with "The original operator source was not saved for this requester continuation" on the leaf and the orchestrator. It does not touch `pauseReason`, the terminal status or `execution.endedAt` of either yielded row, it does the same in both arms, and both arms still list the leaf as `waiting for external continuation` and the orchestrator as `waiting on 1 child`, because the child's completion announcement is still pending. Persisted `subagent_runs` rows, SHA-256 of `SELECT * FROM subagent_runs ORDER BY run_id` (4 rows each time): | Point | BEFORE | AFTER | |---|---|---| | Restored copy | `242774eb1d7d` | `242774eb1d7d` | | After Gateway start (startup recovery writes) | `e064e6d9715b` | `6635846e9823` | | After both reads | `e064e6d9715b` | `6635846e9823` | | After Gateway stop | `e064e6d9715b` | `6635846e9823` | The two arms differ after start only in the timestamps startup recovery writes for the announced child (`execution.endedAt`, outcome, delivery timestamps), which are wall clock at each start. Every yielded row is identical between the arms. The reads write nothing in either arm. Both arms log the same two warnings, both about the seeded running child that has no process behind it: `subagent completion authority was not restored runId=run-announced-child` ("Subagent restart recovery lacks its original operator source") and `Subagent announce flow failed during cleanup for run run-announced-child: Error: Subagent completion authority is no longer active`. BEFORE, `subagents list` text: ``` active subagents: 1. restart-recoverable work (model n/a, 1m) waiting for external continuation 2. restart-recoverable work (model n/a, 1m) waiting for external continuation 3. restart-recoverable work (model n/a, 1m) waiting on 1 child recent (last 60m): (none) ``` AFTER, `subagents list` text: ``` active subagents: 1. restart-recoverable work (model n/a, 1m) waiting for external continuation 2. restart-recoverable work (model n/a, 1m) waiting for external continuation, paused 1d 19h 3. restart-recoverable work (model n/a, 1m) waiting on 1 child recent (last 60m): (none) ``` Line 1 is the collector row, line 2 the parked leaf (`endedAt` 1792126057701), line 3 the orchestrator. List entries and wait runs, extracted from the two JSON responses of each arm: ``` BEFORE list run-collector status="waiting for external continuation" pausedForMs=(absent) BEFORE list run-parked-leaf status="waiting for external continuation" pausedForMs=(absent) BEFORE list run-awaiting-orchestrator status="waiting on 1 child" pausedForMs=(absent) BEFORE wait reason=attention BEFORE wait run-parked-leaf status=waiting endedAt=1792126057701 pausedForMs=(absent) BEFORE wait run-awaiting-orchestrator status=waiting endedAt=1792101577701 pausedForMs=(absent) BEFORE wait run-collector status=waiting endedAt=1792274377701 pausedForMs=(absent) AFTER list run-collector status="waiting for external continuation" pausedForMs=(absent) AFTER list run-parked-leaf status="waiting for external continuation" pausedForMs=156026931 AFTER list run-awaiting-orchestrator status="waiting on 1 child" pausedForMs=(absent) AFTER wait reason=attention AFTER wait run-parked-leaf status=waiting endedAt=1792126057701 pausedForMs=156026963 AFTER wait run-awaiting-orchestrator status=waiting endedAt=1792101577701 pausedForMs=(absent) AFTER wait run-collector status=waiting endedAt=1792274377701 pausedForMs=(absent) ``` `156026963` ms is 43.34 hours: the 43h12m seeded pause plus the time between seeding and the read. The wall clock taken right after the AFTER reads was 1792282084708, which minus `endedAt` is 156027007, 44 ms after the wait value. List and wait agree for every shape here: the leaf has an age in both, the orchestrator and the collector have none in either. The persisted-only parent cannot be constructed against a live Gateway. A Gateway restores every persisted row into its in-memory registry at start, so the orchestrator's announced child above is also in memory. That case is proven in the registry test below, on a real SQLite registry whose in-memory registry is empty. ### Tests At `4b2a9973805`, one `pnpm test` run over the two changed test files plus `subagent-list.test.ts` (3 Vitest shards), 15 passed, 0 failed: | File | Result | |---|---| | `subagent-execution-observation.test.ts` | 4 passed | | `subagent-list.test.ts` (not changed by this PR; main now has 8 tests here) | 8 passed | | `subagents-tool.registry.test.ts` | 3 passed (main's 2, including the 5,000-run control-scope bound from #170998, plus this PR's 1) | Owning directories at `4b2a9973805`, `pnpm test src/agents/subagents/registry/ src/agents/tools/` (6 Vitest shards). The runner stops at the first failing shard and the command did not go green in one run on this machine, so it was run three times and shard 6's three files were then run on their own: ``` Test Files 34 passed (34) Tests 302 passed (302) Test Files 2 passed (2) Tests 42 passed (42) Test Files 45 passed (45) Tests 805 passed (805) Test Files 54 passed | 1 skipped (55) Tests 750 passed | 1 skipped (751) Test Files 1 failed | 125 passed | 1 skipped (127) Tests 1 failed | 1941 passed | 1 skipped (1943) Test Files 3 passed (3) Tests 90 passed (90) ``` That is 3930 passed, 2 skipped and 1 failed. The failure is `web-fetch.sandbox.test.ts` ("stages readable output without granting guest writes in a read-only workspace"), which calls GNU `stat -c` and fails on macOS `stat` (`stat: illegal option -- c`); it fails the same way alone on main `09cf9282b8f`. Shard 3 failed in two of the four full runs on `swarm-tools.integration.test.ts` (see below) and passed in the other two. `swarm-tools.integration.test.ts` "spawns text and structured collectors ... drains them in completion order" fails intermittently with `expected [ 3, 1 ] to deeply equal [ 1, 3 ]`. The assertion records which collector launch finishes its structured-output call first; launch 1 builds the child tool set cold and launch 3 warm, so they race. It fails on main `09cf9282b8f` too. Counted runs on this machine (load average 25 to 68): main's production code failed 4 of 19 (2 of 13 in a separate main checkout, 2 of 6 in this branch's checkout with main's versions of the five production files), this branch failed 13 of 23 (7 of 13 alone, 4 of 6 in the same in-place comparison, 2 of 4 full lane runs). The assertion fires before any `subagents` wait runs, and this change adds no import and only constant-time work on the spawn path, so I found no mechanism for the higher rate on the branch; it is reported here rather than called noise. The registry test persists a leaf and an orchestrator with an announced child into a real SQLite registry and reads both `subagents list` and the native wait snapshot through the tool, with nothing seeded into the in-memory registry. The orchestrator's announced child therefore exists only in persisted rows, and the test asserts the orchestrator gets no `pausedForMs` in either output. It fixes `Date` with `vi.useFakeTimers({ toFake: ["Date"] })` and `vi.setSystemTime` and asserts exact ages. The observation test passes `now` explicitly and needs no timers. Ordinary finished, running, killed and collector runs are covered once, in the observation test, because they all fail the same guard in `resolveYieldedLeafPausedForMs`; the list and wait outputs only forward its result. ### Regression proof Each production behavior was mutated in place at `4b2a9973805`, the two new test files were each run on their own, and the tree was restored (`git status` clean afterwards). Every failure is an assertion failure; the first one in each failing file is quoted. | Mutation | `subagent-execution-observation.test.ts` | `subagents-tool.registry.test.ts` | |---|---|---| | drop the collector guard | fails: `expected 90000000 to be undefined` | passes | | drop the `external` wait-kind guard | fails: `expected 90000000 to be undefined` | fails: `expected { runId: 'waiting-orchestrator', …(8) } to not have property "pausedForMs"` | | drop the terminal-status guard | fails: `expected 90000000 to be undefined` | passes | | measure from `createdAt` instead of `endedAt` | fails: `expected 207717711911 to be 90000000 // Object.is equality` | fails: `expected +0 to be 155520000 // Object.is equality` | | list entry omits the field | passes | fails: `expected undefined to be 155520000 // Object.is equality` | | list line omits `, paused ` | passes | fails: `expected 'active subagents:\n1. parked-leaf (mo…' to contain 'waiting for external continuation, pa…'` | | wait run omits the field | passes | fails: `expected undefined to be 155520000 // Object.is equality` | | wait observes with no children | passes | fails: `expected { runId: 'waiting-orchestrator', …(8) } to not have property "pausedForMs"` | | wait does not read yielded children into its snapshot (`yieldedChildren: false`) | passes | fails: `expected { runId: 'waiting-orchestrator', …(8) } to not have property "pausedForMs"` | | wait observes in-memory children only (`subagentRuns.values()`) | passes | fails: `expected { runId: 'waiting-orchestrator', …(8) } to not have property "pausedForMs"` | | the merged read scope skips the yielded-children expansion (`const yielded = false`, in `mergeSubagentRunReadScope`) | passes | fails: `expected { runId: 'waiting-orchestrator', …(8) } to not have property "pausedForMs"` | Every mutation is caught by at least one of the two files. The last three are the persisted-only parent; the eleventh mutates the conflict-resolved code itself: with either mutation the orchestrator whose announced child exists only in persisted rows gets an age. On main `09cf9282b8f` with these two test files copied in, both fail (`resolveYieldedLeafPausedForMs is not a function`; `expected undefined to be 155520000 // Object.is equality`). With the production code restored, both pass. ### Measured test cost Measured at `62da7f32daa`, before the merge, and not rerun after it: the two test files are unchanged by the merge apart from main's own registry test, which this PR does not own. Method: `pnpm test --maxWorkers=1`, three runs per file, wall time from `/usr/bin/time -p`. The Mac Studio was carrying unrelated load from other sessions (1-minute load average 37 to 51 during these runs), so these are upper-end numbers. No CI run exists yet for this commit; a changed file runs again in every CI run that selects its lane. | File (lane) | Tests | Vitest duration, runs 1 / 2 / 3 | Wall, runs 1 / 2 / 3 | This PR's test, runs 1 / 2 / 3 | |---|---|---|---|---| | `subagent-execution-observation.test.ts` (unit-fast) | 4 | 2.82 / 2.00 / 1.10 s | 8.29 / 5.86 / 4.63 s | 0 / 0 / 0 ms | | `subagents-tool.registry.test.ts` (agents-tools) | 2 | 42.05 / 24.50 / 28.12 s | 52.06 / 29.92 / 33.88 s | 1154 / 673 / 575 ms | The registry file exceeds the 5 s target because of its existing transform and import cost (transform plus import is 90% to 92% of its duration); this PR adds one test of about 0.6 to 1.2 s. It boots one real `withOpenClawTestState` SQLite state, the same fixture the file already uses. The contract is that the wait path reads announced children from persisted rows, which no cheaper layer exercises, because the in-memory registry is exactly what a cheaper test would seed. `subagent-list.test.ts` is no longer changed by this PR. ### Other checks | Check | Result | |---|---| | `OPENCLAW_CHECK_CHANGED_SKIP_DEADCODE=1 pnpm check:changed --base 09cf9282b8f` | exit 1 on two steps, both reproduced unchanged on a clean `09cf9282b8f` worktree and both about files this PR does not touch: `max-lines suppression ratchet` (new suppressions in `ui/src/pages/chat/components/chat-message.test.tsx`, `ui/src/pages/config/config-page-state.ts`, `ui/src/pages/sessions/sessions-page-state.ts`) and `core tsgo graph boundary` (`gateway-root: 728` and `infra: 741` test roots over the 720 limit). The other 32 steps pass, including line-cap growth ratchet, SQLite worker, SQLite dialect, test timeout race and first-party mock export ratchets, format changed files, typecheck core, typecheck core tests, lint core changed files (0 warnings, 0 errors) | | `node --import tsx scripts/check-deadcode-exports.mts` (the step skipped above) | exit 1 on 30 entries, the same 30 on main `09cf9282b8f`; none is in a file this PR touches | | `git diff --check 09cf9282b8f...4b2a9973805` and `oxfmt --check` on the 8 changed files | exit 0 | ## Gaps - The age is a fact about when the yield was recorded. It does not say whether a continuation was sent, accepted or applied. - `endedAt` can be rewritten by a few seconds when both yield callers mark the same row (see above); that gap was not measured live. - Wall clock skew between the host that wrote `endedAt` and the host that reads it shows up directly in the age. A future `endedAt` reads as `0`. - Real-Gateway coverage uses a copied, seeded state directory, not a leaf yielded live by a model turn. The seed goes through the production registry persistence path. - The persisted-only parent is covered by the SQLite-backed registry test, not by the live Gateway run, for the reason given under Evidence. - On the new base, startup recovery marks the seeded yielded rows' completion delivery failed, because a seeded row has no operator source a real Gateway can restore. prs.title: fix: generated tool files block guest commands
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Guest coding commands can finish installing dependencies or preparing a test runtime and then report `Cloud workspace result is too large` when finalization captures a downloaded executable or package-store object. The observed failures involved pnpm's store, the pinned Bun fork, and Playwright Chromium. Compiled Vitest worker files could also enter a pending result and then disappear during their normal cleanup, leaving reconciliation blocked. The sandbox's normal command environment uses the working directory as HOME, so these tool downloads can live inside the managed checkout.

Fixes #175956.

## User Impact

Workspace reconciliation now leaves the four observed generated roots with their owning runtime: `.local/share/pnpm/store/`, `.cache/openclaw/bun/`, `.cache/ms-playwright/`, and `.artifacts/vitest-workers/`. Source edits and ordinary authored artifacts can settle without treating those downloads as result payloads. The existing per-file and aggregate result limits remain unchanged.

The exclusion matches only those checkout-relative roots. Neighboring `.local`, `.cache`, and `.artifacts` files, nested project fixtures, and owned staged inputs retain their existing handling. Environment defaults, sandbox permissions, dependency versions, and publication behavior are unchanged.

## Why This Change Was Made

The result-size and source-conflict guards were correctly rejecting mismatched inputs, but the shared derived-path inventory did not recognize these tool-owned roots. Adding them to the existing inventory keeps local and standalone capture, rsync, manifest comparison, apply, and recovery consistent. Recovery also recognizes the roots in older retained results without changing authenticated receipt bytes.

The existing capture/transfer and legacy-result fixtures now include these downloads, removed compiler outputs, and adjacent user content. Canonical workspace-access and cloud-session lifecycle docs describe the exact boundary.

## Evidence

On the unchanged production base 172fe5791520c37aa1ff1f9a1f1bc3aa933eb3f3, a remote Linux regression created real cache files of 67,108,865 bytes and passed their filesystem capture through the result owner. It reproduced the exact Chromium-path error at `workspace-manifest-comparison.ts:118`. The baseline test stage took 31.92 seconds, including 22.92 seconds of cold worker preparation.

The four-root candidate passed changed-file formatting/lint and the owning production/test type graphs. Complete consumer type checks passed on the prior three-root candidate and remain applicable: the final addition changes only fixed paths and fixture data, with unchanged imports and public types.

The repository test runner ran the generated-path capture/transfer, local projection recovery, managed-skill, staged resource-transfer, and reconciliation-authority files: **80 passed, one optional Podman case skipped**. The test stage took **103.24 seconds** (98.02 seconds in Vitest), including the existing process/SQLite recovery fixtures; no new process boots or timers were added. The fourth-root baseline separately showed the compiler's 18-byte module marker incorrectly entering the captured result. The final controls preserve neighboring/nested user files and staged inputs, reject an oversized authored artifact, recover older cache-bearing receipts after compiler cleanup, and retain real source conflicts.

Exact-head [hosted CI](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/39085452599) passed in 501 seconds of workflow wall time, and independent review is clean. This change does not claim deployment to the originally observed server; the live sandbox's effective environment was not separately probed.

prs.title: feat(slack): delay typing indicators for short turns
prs.body:
Closes #123746

## What Problem This Solves

Slack observers can finish an ambient channel turn with `NO_REPLY` while briefly showing a typing reaction. In busy channels, that reaction makes a silent observer look noisy or indecisive; suppressing ambient indicators entirely instead hides useful feedback during genuinely long tool-driven turns.

## Why This Change Was Made

This adds an opt-in Slack `typingIndicatorDelayMs` setting at the channel or account level. The existing typing lifecycle starts only after that delay, cancels the pending start when a short turn finishes first, and otherwise keeps the existing reaction, Slack typing-status, timeout, and cleanup behavior. The unset and zero-delay defaults remain unchanged.

## User Impact

Operators can keep ambient Slack participation enabled without flashing a reaction on ordinary silent turns. Long-running turns still become visibly active after the configured delay.

## Evidence

### Before

On the live Slack observer, the desktop reaction appeared immediately on a message whose turn completed with `NO_REPLY` after 11.497 seconds. Across 27 recent exact `NO_REPLY` turns, the mean was 11.42 seconds, p95 was 15.31 seconds, and none exceeded 16 seconds.

<image elided>

### After

The patched build was deployed to the same observer with `typingIndicatorDelayMs: 16000` and `typingReaction: "desktop_computer"`:

- A short ambient turn completed with exact `NO_REPLY` 11.978 seconds after ingress and showed no reaction.
- A deliberately long ambient turn showed no reaction before the threshold, then showed the desktop reaction while work continued.

<image elided>

### Tests

- Red test: applying the new timing test to unpatched `f5c46de8ac5` failed because `start()` was called immediately instead of remaining pending.
- Green core lifecycle suite: `26 passed`.
- Green Slack schema and dispatch suites: `196 passed`.
- Bundled channel metadata check: passed.
- Full `pnpm check` passed before the final rebase. After rebasing onto `3289e08c300`, it reaches a pre-existing `OPENCLAW_*` count gate: untouched current `main` and this branch both contain the same 504 names against a budget of 502; this patch adds none.
- Post-rebase autoreview: no accepted or actionable findings; confidence 0.83.

AI-assisted: Codex implemented and tested this change under human direction. A human operator selected the behavior and delay, observed both live Slack cases, and reviewed the evidence above.

prs.title: refactor(agents): consume prepared adapter facts
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Agent adapters repeat checks of already-typed internal facts, rebuild an MCP canonical representation already prepared by the caller, and duplicate shared scope/block predicates. Consume the existing owner facts and helper contracts instead. Raw MCP/guest/config input validation and actual effect authority remain at their boundaries; this is not a measured performance claim.

## User Impact

No user-visible behavior change is intended. Raw input validation, credential and execution authority, and accepted work settlement remain unchanged; no configuration or migration is required.

## Why This Change Was Made

Consume prepared internal facts and existing shared predicates rather than revalidating, recopying, or rebuilding them in adapters.

## Best-effort tradeoffs accepted

- Code Mode bridge/replay consumes typed request arrays after guest JSON ingress validation; config readers consume canonical typed config while retaining actual unknown option/limit and payload validation.
- Message discovery/execution, workspace provisioning and worktree ownership drop only nullish-to-undefined no-ops on optional typed strings/records. Captured sandbox read sources still receive their full current-source assertion whenever present.

- Tool display reads its argument record once and reuses it; accessor-driven mutation between repeated internal option reads is not supported.
- MCP App reads return a new root projection with shared nested host facts rather than a deep copy; ingress validation, ingress snapshot, exact-view lease/revocation, model metadata stripping and custody remain.
- MCP result projection supplies its already-computed canonical JSON to the existing mirror matcher; raw result parsing, deep-value handled failure, distinct text retention and guest/model result separation remain.

- External CLI scope detection lives in the existing profile-reference leaf shared by external-auth and store-read, avoiding an eager external-auth import. Empty arrays/Sets remain explicit scopes; resolveExternalCliOverlayOptions omits falsey string inputs before this call.

prs.title: fix: session lists stall while the gateway republishes an unchanged config
prs.body:
## Maintainer verification (2026-10-01)

Reporter and original fix: @azuretek; all contributor commits are retained. Merged `origin/main` at `d0f06ee8554dd6afad688f1be8be37c05ec2a787` only to resolve an actual conflict in the runtime publisher. The resolution retains both the equivalence guard and main's `prepareRuntimePluginsConfig(config)` publication side effect. Verified head: `f764c03929e139d15b96984968ef50c92b2297e8`.

Built and ran two isolated Linux arm64 Gateways in secretless Docker, with separate explicit profiles/state/config paths and loopback ports. Each Gateway had 400 sessions created through `sessions.create`. The same WebSocket harness performed `config.get`, value-identical `config.apply` (alternating JSON whitespace, with parsed equality asserted), then `sessions.list`; a real `agents.defaults.model` change was the control. Eight samples per phase, 2.2 seconds apart; all lists returned 100 of 400 sessions.

| First sessions.list p50 | main baseline | candidate |
|---|---:|---:|
| No config write | 4.06 ms | 4.20 ms |
| Value-identical config.apply | 100.51 ms | 8.72 ms |
| Changed config.apply | 55.25 ms | 71.35 ms |

The immediate second list after identical writes measured 4.94 ms on main and 3.72 ms on the candidate. Real config changes retain their rebuild cost. This measures repeated per-write stalls, not a sustained multi-minute concurrent drain.

The contributor's projection regression was applied to the frozen main proof copy and failed at `dirtyRowCount`: expected 0, received 4. On the candidate, `session-row-projection.invalidation.test.ts` passed all 18 tests (58.04 s including cold worker compilation), including no-op preservation and changed-value/provenance controls; `runtime-snapshot.preparation.test.ts` passed all 30 (1.55 s). Combined wrapper wall time: 65.58 s. The first baseline test setup lacked built plugin assets; after building the supported CLI, the test executed and failed for the intended assertion.

No projection storage, schema, or protocol change. No overlap with Pash/Sarah changes.

---

Fixes #157798.

Related: #154124.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: `sessions.list` calls that take minutes, and a gateway that stops answering, when a config republish resolves to a runtime snapshot whose values have not changed. The trigger is the config write path: a byte-identical file rewrite produces no republish, so this is not a file-watcher effect.

## User Impact

A value-identical config write no longer invalidates every projected session row. Operators who rewrite an unchanged config on a schedule stop paying a full row rematerialization for each write, and concurrent session list reads return instead of landing together after a drain that never converges.

## Why This Change Was Made

`publishRuntimeConfigSnapshot` emitted an unconditional `all`/`config` session change, so a publication that resolved to the values already on the runtime still invalidated every row, moved the projection epoch and started a drain the next publication abandoned.

A value-identical `config.apply` only restamps the file's `meta`, so the gateway takes its effective-config-unchanged branch: the runtime object stays and only its source advances, through `setRuntimeConfigSourceSnapshotIfCurrent`. That is a same-object publication, which must keep invalidating in general because it can follow an in-place edit or carry changed resolution provenance. Session rows read only the runtime object, never the source snapshot, so a source-only republish can change them only in those two ways. The setter now checks both, comparing the object's hash with the fingerprint recorded at its last publication and the serialized resolution facts before and after the copy, and withholds the session change only when neither moved. Each publication records its serialized resolution facts beside the value fingerprint its metadata already keeps. A distinct object is withheld only when its fingerprint and facts equal that record, never by comparing with the live previous object, which may have been edited in place after it was published. Every other publication still invalidates.

Scope classification reads the same record. The publication that follows one whose live object no longer matches the previous publication's record in either its value fingerprint or its serialized resolution facts selects the broad `config` scope, because that object was edited in place and cannot classify the change. Checking the value hash alone missed a provenance-only in-place edit: the edited object still hashed to its recorded fingerprint, so comparing its edited facts with a distinct next object carrying those same facts selected a presentation-only scope and left rows built from the earlier publication stale. The previous-publication check now compares the recorded resolution facts too.

### How refresh is validated

This keeps the broad-refresh rule's check and changes how it is made. The rule exists because a same-object publication may follow an in-place edit or carry changed provenance, and comparing an object with itself cannot see either, so it refreshed every row. The publication record can see both: the runtime metadata already records a value fingerprint at every publication, and this PR records the serialized resolution facts beside it. A publication is withheld only when the object hashes to the recorded fingerprint and its facts equal the recorded facts; any difference refreshes rows as before. The scope classifier consults that same record, so an in-place edit of either the values or the resolution provenance cannot select a narrow scope.

This is the validation pattern the config owner already uses. `preparationFingerprint` decides whether a prepared snapshot is still current by hashing config and resolution facts rather than preparing it again, and identity-scope-only snapshots already retain unchanged session facts. The guide line in `src/gateway/AGENTS.md` is updated to describe refresh in these terms rather than as an exception.

It implements the fingerprint-skip principle of #154124 for the config emitter; it does not change the catalog emitter, refresh phases, worker generation caching or `sessions.catalog.changed`.

## Evidence

### Live gateway A/B

Matched arms on one host, run back to back: stock `main` at `80db3393e6c`, and this head (`f5ff36a38b9`), which is that same commit merged into the branch, so the arms differ only in the files this PR changes. Both were built from source and run as real gateways (`node openclaw.mjs gateway run`, loopback) on an 8-core arm64 macOS host, Node v26.7.0, each from a fresh copy of one seeded state directory with 3,000 session rows. Runs alternated stock, head, head, stock, with a new gateway process per run.

Each run took, in order, 40 baseline samples (`config.get`, then `sessions.list`), 40 value-identical samples (`config.get` for `baseHash`, then `config.apply` with `{ raw, baseHash }` alternating two byte-different configs whose parsed values are asserted equal, then `sessions.list`), and 20 changed samples (`config.apply` alternating a config that changes `agents.defaults.model`). Samples were paced 2.2 s apart to stay under the control-plane write limit. `sessions.list` was called through the gateway's own client, so process startup is not in the timing. Every call succeeded and every listing returned 100 of 3,000 rows. Pooled over both runs per arm, first `sessions.list` after the step, in ms:

| phase | n per arm | stock p50 | stock p95 | stock max | head p50 | head p95 | head max |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| baseline | 80 | 35.1 | 38.9 | 39.4 | 34.8 | 38.6 | 47.5 |
| value-identical `config.apply` | 80 | 355.3 | 424.8 | 449.8 | 15.4 | 26.3 | 461.1 |
| changed `config.apply` | 40 | 460.8 | 617.7 | 695.2 | 475.8 | 625.7 | 664.6 |

Per run, value-identical p50: stock 354.9 and 356.0, head 15.5 and 15.1. A second `sessions.list` straight after the first takes about 15 ms in every phase and arm, so the first-list cost is the full row rematerialization the stock arm pays on every identical apply and the head arm now skips. Median `config.apply` itself: 97.5 ms stock, 86.7 ms head.

The head max of 461.1 ms is the first identical apply of each run (437.8 and 461.1 ms, sample 0 in both), the only head samples above 35 ms in that phase; the first apply after startup still invalidates. The changed phase and baseline match between arms, which is the control: a real config change still pays the rebuild.

The same harness on the previous revision of this PR, where the guard withheld only distinct equivalent objects, showed no difference (value-identical p50 376.4 stock, 385.0 head), because `config.apply` on current `main` reaches the rows through the same-object source-only path. That measurement is why the guard was narrowed to that path, and it replaces an earlier 8-sample A/B in this body that was taken before the same-object safeguard existed. The same A/B on `f7dcf65f4b4`, before the recorded-publication change, gave value-identical p50 358.5 stock and 15.6 head, so that change did not alter the result.

Limits: one host and one seed; two runs per arm; the 2.2 s pacing means this measures the per-write rebuild, not the concurrent-drain stall at high write rates.

### Tests

New and extended cases, each shown failing without the change it covers.

Config owner, `src/config/runtime-snapshot.preparation.test.ts`:

- A table of republishes after the same first publication: a distinct object with equal values and equal fresh provenance is withheld; the published object republished without an edit, equal bytes whose provenance changed, equal bytes that lost their provenance, and a distinct object matching values or provenance changed in place on the published one each invalidate. Every emitting case asserts the change it emits is broad `config` scope, never a presentation-only refresh.
- A source-only republish is withheld when it only restamps `meta`, and invalidates when it carries changed provenance, follows an in-place edit of the published object, or follows a provenance change made in place on it.

Projected rows, `src/gateway/session-row-projection.invalidation.test.ts`:

- New: `keeps projected rows clean when config.apply rewrites a value-identical config` drives `setSecretsRuntimeSourceSnapshotIfCurrent`, the effective-config-unchanged path `config.apply` takes, and asserts no row is dirtied.
- New: `invalidates projected rows when a distinct config matches an in-place edit of the published one` publishes a mutable config, edits its default model in place, then publishes a distinct object carrying the edited values, and asserts rows are dirtied.

prs.title: fix: rate-limit Retry-After past maxRetryDelayMs sleeps the turn instead of failing over
prs.body:
Related: #143274 (canonical), #145719. Filed from #148558, which ClawSweeper closed into #143274 as a duplicate; this PR is the implementation of that report's proposal.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: an agent run sleeps a `429` `Retry-After` of hours inside the turn instead of failing over, when the provider's message matches no usage-window keyword. Anthropic session-window exhaustion is this shape ("Please try again later." with a `Retry-After` equal to the window reset), so every scheduled job that hits it dies at its own timeout with `cron: job execution timed out (last phase: model-call-started)` while the configured fallback chain is never tried.

## User Impact

User impact: with a fallback configured, a rate-limit floor longer than the saved `retry.provider.maxRetryDelayMs` (default 60 s) now fails over to the next auth profile or model immediately, so scheduled jobs complete on the fallback instead of timing out and interactive turns do not hang for hours. Short throttles inside the cap keep retrying on the same model. Nothing changes when no fallback is configured (the floor is honoured in full), when `maxRetryDelayMs: 0` (cap disabled), or after a replay-unsafe tool action (the attempt keeps waiting and continuing the transcript, since neither rotation nor fallback can run there).

## Why This Change Was Made

`retry.provider.maxRetryDelayMs` is documented as the longest server-requested wait before "the request fails immediately ... allowing higher-level retry logic to handle it". The SDK honours that and returns control, but only `maxRetries` was wired into the embedded run's failover controller, so `maybeRetryTransient` then slept the same delay the setting had just refused. This carries `maxRetryDelayMs` from the prepared session settings onto the attempt and into `maybeRetryTransient` next to the floor it caps, and treats a rate-limit floor above the cap as long-window evidence when a fallback exists and the attempt can still fail over. No new constant and no new setting; the threshold is the one the operator already configured.

How this relates to the two open PRs on the same lines:

- #145720 declines the wait past a fixed 60 s (`MAX_SHORT_WINDOW_RETRY_AFTER_SECONDS`) when a fallback or a remaining auth profile exists. This PR uses the operator's `maxRetryDelayMs` instead of a constant, and adds the replay-safety gate that ClawSweeper's P1 on #145720 asks for: without it, a long floor after an exec or write returns `false`, `recoverEmbeddedRunAttempt` exits at its replay-safety gate and `handleEmbeddedAssistantFailure` refuses fallback, so a turn that used to wait and continue now terminates. That case is covered by a recovery-level test here. #145720's remaining-auth-profile signal is complementary and not taken here; `run-loop.ts` sits at the 700-line `max-lines` ceiling on `main`, so wiring a new controller input needs a small refactor that deserves its own evidence.
- #145348 bounds the wait by the run's remaining deadline. Independent criterion, same lines; both can land. With the default 48 h agent timeout the deadline bound alone does not reach an interactive turn, which is why the cap matters.

The docs sentence in `docs/concepts/retry.md` that described the old behaviour as intended is updated to describe the cap.

## Evidence

The prepared head `1207422ed4a` is a patch-identical rebase onto repaired `main` at `2ba076dc630`; the stable patch ID and touched-file set are unchanged, so the prior exact-patch proof remains applicable. Cloudflare Crabbox passed `git diff --check`, changed-scope guards through core production typecheck, the root/shard contract (24 tests), the focused controller and recovery suites (124 tests), and the embedded fault-sequence e2e (10 tests). Full core-test typechecking was not completed on the 12 GiB runner after 31 minutes without diagnostics; hosted CI remains required.

Regression tests fail on `main` at the branch's previous base (`3d21b1dce`) and pass with the change, with the source patch stashed and the tests kept:

```
src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/run/failover-retry-controller.test.ts
 × rate-limit floor past retry.provider.maxRetryDelayMs > fails over instead of sleeping when a fallback is configured
   → expected true to be false
      Tests  1 failed | 33 passed (34)

src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/run/attempt-recovery.test.ts
 × recoverEmbeddedRunAttempt > fails over past the saved maxRetryDelayMs when a fallback exists
   → expected 'retry' to be 'proceed'
      Tests  1 failed | 64 passed (65)
```

The replay-safety gate has its own failing-then-passing pair. With the `failoverEligible` check removed from the shortcut and everything else in place:

```
 × recoverEmbeddedRunAttempt > keeps waiting past the cap when tool activity made the attempt replay-unsafe
   → expected 'proceed' to be 'retry'
 × createEmbeddedRunFailoverRetryController > ... > still sleeps the floor when the attempt cannot fail over
   → expected false to be true
```

`'proceed'` there is the terminated turn ClawSweeper described on #145720; with the gate the attempt returns `'retry'` and sleeps the floor as before.

The controller test uses the measured Anthropic body and a `retry-after: 9897` header (`resolveRetryAfterMs` gives 9,897,000 ms) with `maxRetryDelayMs: 30000`. Control cases that must keep their current behaviour pass in both states: the same floor with no fallback still sleeps 9,897,000 ms; cap `0` and cap `undefined` still sleep; a 20 s floor inside the cap still retries on the same model; a `server_error` floor is still governed by the transient time window rather than this cap. The existing 120 s and 30-day floor tests are unchanged (they run without a fallback).

### After-fix real behavior through the embedded runner (injected transport fault)

The fault-sequences e2e drives the real `runEmbeddedAgent` and injects a 429 whose assistant error text matches no usage-window keyword and carries the reset only in `errorBody.headers["retry-after"]` (9897 s), with the operator's `retry.provider.maxRetryDelayMs: 30000` on the attempt. This is the real path `buildAssistantFailoverSignal` -> `resolveRetryAfterMs` -> `maybeRetryTransient`, not a controller mock; a single openai profile and a `groq/mock-2` fallback are configured.

The test asserts the observed provider attempts. Reverting the four source files to `upstream/main` and keeping the test, the second attempt is the same model, proving the runner slept the floor and retried instead of failing over:

```
 × fails over a header-only multi-hour 429 past retry.provider.maxRetryDelayMs instead of sleeping it
   → expected [ [ 'openai', 'mock-1' ], [ 'groq', 'mock-2' ] ]
              to deeply equal [ [ 'openai', 'mock-1' ], [ 'openai', 'mock-1' ] ]
```

With the fix the second attempt is the `groq` fallback, the run completes on it, and `sleepWithAbort` is never called with the 9,897,000 ms floor. This is the after-fix runtime evidence the review asked for: an injected transport fault standing in for an on-demand session-window 429, exercised end to end through the production runner.

With the change: `src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/run/` 54 files, 599 tests pass; the retry-related e2e files (`model-fallback.run-embedded`, `run-embedded-agent.auth-profile-rotation`, `run-embedded-agent.fault-sequences`) 3 files, 63 tests pass under `test/vitest/vitest.e2e.config.ts`. `oxlint` and `oxfmt --check` clean on the changed files.

`run-loop.ts` is deliberately untouched: it sits exactly at the 700-line `max-lines` ceiling on `main`, which is why the cap rides the existing `maybeRetryTransient` call in `attempt-recovery.ts` rather than a second `setTransientRetryBudget` argument.

Live shape this fixes, from the gateway log on 2026.9.4 (host clock Pacific):

```
12:00:01.196 [agent/embedded] transient same-model retry 1/3 for anthropic/claude-fable-5-1 reason=rate_limit: delayMs=7198000
12:40:00.292 [diagnostic] message processed: channel=cron ... outcome=error duration=2400016ms error="cron: job execution timed out (last phase: model-call-started)"
```

This is a library-level fix with no container to A/B; the failing-then-passing tests, including the embedded-runner e2e above, are the validation, and the deploy is the next release. An organic session-window 429 cannot be provoked on demand, which is why the e2e injects the exact transport shape rather than waiting for one; if the account's window closes again while this is open, the patched gateway log will be added here.

### Contract decision

Adopted: `retry.provider.maxRetryDelayMs` also bounds fallback timing for an existing replay-safe run, so an install with a positive or default cap and a configured fallback switches account or model sooner rather than sleeping a multi-hour floor. Unchanged elsewhere: with no fallback configured the floor is honoured in full, `maxRetryDelayMs: 0` leaves the cap disabled, and a replay-unsafe attempt still waits and continues the transcript, since neither rotation nor fallback can run there. The `docs/concepts/retry.md` sentence that described the previous behaviour as intended is updated to describe the cap.

prs.title: fix(memory-lancedb): refresh the table version so recall observes external writes
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Closes #137805. A running Memory LanceDB reader can miss memories committed by another process until it writes or restarts. The same stale snapshot also prevents deletion of externally committed rows.

## Why This Change Was Made

Refresh the existing table handle through LanceDB's supported `checkoutLatest()` before reusing it. The refresh stays at the shared database owner, so recall, search, count, list, query, store, and delete use the same boundary. Agent predicates, stored rows, connection settings, and snapshot rules remain unchanged.

## User Impact

External ingestion becomes visible to an already-running reader without a reader-side write, plugin reload, or Gateway restart. Each operation observes a complete snapshot at its refresh boundary; this does not promise a transaction across later concurrent commits. Refresh errors propagate instead of silently returning stale data.

## Evidence

- A real source Gateway with the bundled plugin and deterministic local embeddings completed two public `tools.invoke` calls for `memory_recall`. A separate process committed between the calls. Baseline still returned zero memories while a fresh reader saw the row; the candidate returned that exact row in the same Gateway lifetime.
- Independent stale-reader controls cover search, count, list, query, and delete, plus agent isolation before ranking, limits, score filtering, ordering, projections, later commits, and close/reopen.
- Twenty external two-row commits overlapped four readers per wave. Every result matched one complete committed version, and each post-commit read saw the latest version. A same-handle write remained durable after close/reopen.
- Focused regression and sibling tests pass, including refresh-error propagation and concurrent initialization. The corrected regression assertions fail on baseline. Formatting and scoped lint pass.
- A local-path benchmark retained 21 versions and 100 samples per operation. Direct refresh took about 0.022 ms median. End-to-end count/list/search timing includes their own work; these measurements do not establish object-storage cost or latency.

The contributor's original separate-process proof and review history are preserved. This repair adds no schema, configuration, poller, retry, lock, or new dependency.

prs.title: test(gateway): drain the chat run instead of a 1s agent.wait in the verboseLevel case
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The Gateway WebSocket test `chat.send does not persist verboseLevel for operator.write callers` intermittently fails with `expected 'timeout' to be 'ok'` because it asks `agent.wait` to finish within one second immediately after `chat.send`.

Fixes #161760. Report and fix by @azuretek; contributor commit is preserved.

## User Impact

Test-only change. No production behavior, permissions, persistence, or compatibility changes.

## Why This Change Was Made

Use the existing `waitForAgentRunDrained(runId)` helper, as the sibling thinking-metadata case does. It joins request execution, detached execution, and tracked effects, asserts root work is drained, then checks terminal `agent.wait` status with a zero timeout. The write-scoped client still sends `/verbose full`, and the session-store assertion still requires `verboseLevel` to be undefined. No sleep or timeout was increased.

No overlap with Pash/Sarah changes.

## Evidence

Verified head: `8c82989bf3d4801ee232cdd5938918fe9fff4c42`.

### Baseline failure in hosted CI

Both downloaded job logs contain the named operator.write verboseLevel case, `Expected: "ok"`, `Received: "timeout"`, and `src/gateway/server.chat.gateway-server-chat.test.ts:1683:41`:

- [PR #161304, checks-node-changed-compact-large-40-2](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/36606460839/job/109537913443): failure annotation at 2026-09-29 17:52:42 UTC. [Attribution](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/161304#issuecomment-5904011717).
- [PR #161155, checks-node-changed-compact-large-24-1](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/36559737708/job/109378142882): failure annotation at 2026-09-29 11:20:34 UTC. [Attribution](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/161155#issuecomment-5906341488).
- The linked issue also records the same failure on two consecutive #152205 heads, and full-file failures on main `0303f2250` and unrelated head `b3e6f721a8` with byte-identical test source.

The local parent-baseline comparison (`754453157b15c02d535670cf2ddf4df4639222fc`) passed both attempts under the pressure setup below. Those passes do not invalidate the captured original-shard failures; local reproduction of the timeout is not claimed.

### Candidate: 20/20 under CPU pressure

Secretless Docker, `node:24-bookworm`, container limited to two CPUs, with a continuously busy Node process alongside every run. Executed the entire file 20 times:

```sh
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run --config test/vitest/vitest.gateway-server.config.ts \
  src/gateway/server.chat.gateway-server-chat.test.ts --maxWorkers=1
```

All 20 runs passed all 41 tests (820 case executions), including the sibling thinking-metadata and chat lifecycle tests. Wall times: first cold run 151 seconds; subsequent runs 75–82 seconds. Existing exact-head hosted `checks-node-changed-compact-large-40` also passed (167-second job), and `openclaw/ci-gate` passed. No hosted job was rerun.

### Negative control

In the disposable Docker source copy only, deliberately persisted `{ verboseLevel: "full" }` through `updateSessionEntry({ sessionKey, storePath }, ...)` immediately after `handleChatSendWithOptions` resolves its prepared session. Ran the unchanged candidate case with `-t "chat.send does not persist verboseLevel for operator.write callers"`.

It failed at the actual session-store assertion, not at run completion:

```text
AssertionError: expected 'full' to be undefined
src/gateway/server.chat.gateway-server-chat.test.ts:1687:11
Tests 1 failed | 40 skipped (41)
```

The mutation was removed afterward and is not in the PR. An earlier permission-helper mutation and a write in a later durable-turn-only branch did not affect this mocked slash-command flow; neither is claimed as negative proof.

### Original multi-file shards and sibling-file coverage

Replayed both original failing shard selections in secretless Docker on the same unchanged head. Decoded each hosted job's `OPENCLAW_NODE_TEST_GROUPS_GZIP_BASE64`, preserving its exact file lists, configs, group environment and Vitest arguments (`[]`), then ran the same entry point:

```sh
CI=true node --import tsx scripts/ci-run-node-test-shard.mts
```

The container had a three-CPU quota. Preserved `NODE_OPTIONS=--max-old-space-size=8192`, worker cache enabled, plan concurrency 1, continue-on-failure 1, and the original group worker limits of 2. The outer worker limits were 2 for run 36606460839 and 3 for run 36559737708. No sleeps, timeout increases, test filters, source changes, or omitted files were used.
