prs.title: improve(memory): faster repeated memory keyword searches
prs.body:
Related: #114777, #149793

## What Problem This Solves

Repeated memory keyword searches recompile their SQL on every search, so the statement cache added in #114777 saves nothing for them.

Keyword search runs four statements per request on the memory search worker's retained read-only connection, which has the bounded statement cache enabled. Two things make SQLite recompile them on every run:

- Each search calls `db.function(...)` again for `openclaw_memory_normalized_contains` and `openclaw_memory_exact_path_specificity` (3 calls per search on these stores). Replacing an existing SQL function expires every prepared statement on the connection, including FTS5's own cached statements.
- The statements bind a bare `LIMIT ?` (all four) and `LIKE ? ESCAPE '\'` (the exact-path statement). Since SQLite 3.47, a bare bound LIMIT value or LIKE pattern is marked as plan-relevant (`select.c:2538` and `whereexpr.c:208-215` in 3.53.4), and `node:sqlite` clears bindings before every run, so a cached handle with such a parameter is recompiled on each run.

Through a real `gateway run`, 30 `memory.search` requests on base registered the two functions 90 times and recompiled the four search statements on every request, although the cache had stopped calling `prepare` after the second request.

## User Impact

User impact: memory keyword searches, including the keyword half of hybrid searches (both run the same worker query), spend less CPU per request on the memory search worker; results are identical.

| Measure | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| `db.function` calls, 30 Gateway `memory.search` requests | 90 (3 per request) | 2 (first request only) |
| Search statement recompiles, Gateway requests 3 to 30 | 4 per request | 0 |
| SQLite authorizer callbacks per Gateway request (3 to 30) | 147 | 5 |
| Time per search, real store with 6,012 chunks (quiet host) | 1173.3 us | 1001.9 us (171.4 us, 14.6 percent less) |
| Time per search, real store with 43,634 chunks (quiet host) | 3656.7 us | 3515.6 us (141.2 us, 3.9 percent less) |

The saving is a fixed amount of compile work per search, so its share shrinks as query execution grows with the index. It is CPU on the worker thread; the Gateway's own millisecond-resolution `memory.search` latency (about 22 to 24 ms per request in these runs) cannot resolve it. Nothing an operator configures or stores changes, and no config key, schema, migration or stored byte changes.

## Why This Change Was Made

The statement cache (#114777, raised to 64 entries in #149793) exists so hot synchronous statements are compiled once and reused. Memory keyword search is one of the hottest read paths on the agent database, and both causes above defeat that cache for it. Either cause alone keeps the four statements recompiling on every search, so this change removes both; builds with only one half are measured in Evidence.

## The change in one sentence

Register the two memory search SQL functions once per connection and let each search swap the state they read, and bind the search LIMIT values and LIKE patterns as `LIMIT +?` and `LIKE (? || '')` so SQLite no longer treats them as plan inputs.

Diff: 3 files, 132 insertions, 20 deletions. Production: `extensions/memory-core/src/memory/manager-search.ts` (+43/-16, including 9 new comment lines). Tests: `manager-search.test.ts` (+84, one new `describe`) and `manager-search-worker.sqlite.test.ts` (+5/-4, the four pinned keyword statement hashes and one comment line, see Tests).

- Registration: a module-level `WeakMap<DatabaseSync, state>` holds the substring matchers and the exact-path matcher. The first search on a connection registers both functions with the same names, argument counts, `deterministic: true` flag and return values; later searches assign the state. This follows the per-connection memo `loadedExtensions` in `manager-publication.worker.ts` in the same directory. `searchKeyword` and `searchPathKeyword` run their statements synchronously after setting the state, so no other search can interleave on the connection.
- SQL: `LIMIT ?` becomes `LIMIT +?` in the four search statements and `LIKE ? ESCAPE '\'` becomes `LIKE (? || '') ESCAPE '\'` in the exact-path statement. A unary plus or a concatenation is not a bare variable, so SQLite does not mark it; the bound values and results are the same. A comment at the top of the module cites the SQLite source lines so a later cleanup does not revert it.

| Input case | Expected outcome |
|---|---|
| Body search with substring terms (trigram, non-ASCII) | Same rows, scores and order; matchers set before the statement runs |
| Path search, exact and lexical partitions | Same rows; exact-path specificity read from the current query's matcher |
| Searches with different queries on one connection, sequential or interleaved at their `await` points | Each statement uses its own search's matchers (the test compares every sequential and repeated result with a fresh connection, and the interleaved results with the sequential ones) |
| `matchAny` retry and MATCH failure fallback | Unchanged; they set the state through the same call before running |
| First search on a new connection | Registers both functions once (2 calls), as before it registered them on first use |
| Connection closed and reopened as a new `DatabaseSync` | New object, new registration |
| PostgreSQL | Not on this path (`searchPostgresMemoryKeyword`) |
| Query plans | Identical for every executed statement shape (below) |

Unchanged: function names, arity, `deterministic`, return values, statement count and order per search, the statement cache policy (capacity, second-use admission), schema, config, stored data, the vector and KNN statements, and the dialect construct counts (`SQLite dialect design (changed files): 1 -> 1.`).

## Evidence

All of the following ran on one machine (Mac Studio Mac15,14, macOS 27.0.1 arm64, Node v24.21.0, SQLite 3.53.4 from `node:sqlite`) against base `a7e31844f2e` and this branch. The measured AFTER build was made from an earlier commit of this branch whose production code differs from the final commit only in comments; the final commit rebuilt is byte-identical in every built JavaScript chunk; only files that embed the commit and build time differ (`gates-final/tree-identity.out`, `gates-final/dist-rebuild-diff.out`). Scripts and raw outputs: https://github.com/etzelm/openclaw/tree/e9a04b920c5a4711a40c0e7d416044a7eb4702a1

### Build

`pnpm build` succeeded for both arms (`build/`):

```
[build-all] phase timings: total 4m 15.5s; slowest write-unified-entry-dts 2m 7.6s; tsdown-packages 26.9s; tsdown 26.3s; ui:build 14.6s; runtime-postbuild 13.9s; check-cli-bootstrap-imports 9.81s; external-plugins:local-dist 9.65s; tsdown-ai 6.89s; write-cli-startup-metadata 5.61s; plugins:assets:build 5.23s; plugins:assets:copy 4.45s; check-plugin-sdk-exports 1.30s; build-stamp 263ms; write-build-info 142ms; runtime-postbuild-stamp 85ms; native-protocol 79ms
[build-all] phase timings: total 4m 14.5s; slowest write-unified-entry-dts 2m 7.8s; tsdown-packages 26.9s; tsdown 26.3s; ui:build 14.5s; runtime-postbuild 13.6s; check-cli-bootstrap-imports 9.95s; external-plugins:local-dist 8.95s; tsdown-ai 6.86s; write-cli-startup-metadata 5.49s; plugins:assets:build 5.22s; plugins:assets:copy 4.29s; check-plugin-sdk-exports 1.50s; build-stamp 313ms; write-build-info 118ms; runtime-postbuild-stamp 87ms; native-protocol 80ms
```

The first line is BEFORE, the second AFTER. In the built search chunk the only differences are the registration code and the SQL text (`prod/dist-diff.out`):

```
-      ORDER BY rank ${rankOrder} LIMIT ?`;
+      ORDER BY rank ${rankOrder} LIMIT +?`;
...
-	params.db.function(EXACT_PATH_SPECIFICITY_SQL_FUNCTION, { deterministic: true }, (candidatePath) => typeof candidatePath === "string" ? matchExactPath(candidatePath) : 0);
+	db.function(EXACT_PATH_SPECIFICITY_SQL_FUNCTION, { deterministic: true }, (candidatePath) => typeof candidatePath === "string" ? state.matchExactPath(candidatePath) : 0);
```

### Behavior through the shipped Gateway and CLI

Both builds ran through their shipped entry point, `node openclaw.mjs`, with their own `HOME` and `OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR`, a clean environment and `memory.search.provider: "none"` (keyword only, no network). A seeded generator wrote the same synthetic workspace in both arms (manifest sha256 equal), and `memory index --force --agent main --verbose` built a store of 401 files and 3,626 chunks in each (`proof/`).

The code logs nothing about statement compilation, so a read-only preload loaded with `NODE_OPTIONS=--import=...` (`proof/tools/observe-search-prepare.mjs`) wraps `DatabaseSync.prototype.prepare`, `function` and the statement run methods, and installs a counting authorizer through the prototype `setAuthorizer` before the first search statement (the instance wrapper would disable the statement cache). An authorizer callback fires only while SQLite compiles a statement, so callbacks that read `memory_index_chunks` during a run are a recompile. It changes no OpenClaw source; timing runs used a variant without the authorizer.

`gateway run --port <port> --bind loopback --auth token --token <test-token> --allow-unconfigured`, then 30 `gateway call memory.search` requests cycling five queries, observed in the Gateway process and its worker threads (`proof/summary.md`, `proof/gateway/<arm>/c1/`):

| Arm | `db.function` calls | Search statement `prepare` calls, requests 1 / 2 / 3 to 30 | Recompiles, requests 1 / 2 / 3 to 30 | Authorizer callbacks per request, 3 to 30 | Total callbacks, 30 requests |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| base | 3 per request, 90 total | 4 / 4 / 0 | 8 / 8 / 4 each | 147 | 4644 |
| patched | 2 on request 1, 2 total | 4 / 4 / 0 | 4 / 4 / 0 | 5 | 409 |

Both arms prepare the statements on the first two requests (the cache admits a statement on its second use) and never again. On base the cached handles still recompile on every request; on this branch they do not. The 5 callbacks left per request are FTS5's own sorter statement, which FTS5 prepares for every `ORDER BY rank` query: a parameterless FTS5 control query shows the same `SELECT 1, FUNCTION 1, READ 3` callbacks on every run, and none without `ORDER BY rank` (`fts5/fts5-sorter-control.out`).

Summed search statement time per request, timing observer without the authorizer, median of requests 11 to 30, runs in the order base, patched, patched, base with a Gateway restart each (`proof/summary.md`, section D): base 4047.6 and 4085.7 us, patched 3922.1 and 3772.8 us. The host was busy during these runs (1-minute load average 21.40 to 30.85), so the production-path timings below are the better measure of size.

`memory search "<query>" --json --agent main --max-results 25` from the CLI, five queries, each a new process: exit 0 and 25 results in every run. A one-shot process runs each statement once, so reuse across searches cannot show there, but the recompile on first run still does: per process, base 3 `db.function` calls, 8 compiles and 270 authorizer callbacks; patched 2, 4 and 153.

Search results are identical between arms for all five queries, through the CLI and all six Gateway runs (sha256 of `[path, startLine, endLine, score]` in result order, `proof/parity.md`), and `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN` is identical for every statement shape (`proof/plans.md`).

### Behavior through the production search function on real stores

The built `searchKeywordWithFallback` of each arm was called as `executeMemorySearchWorkerQuery` calls it, with the request the manager builds by default (`limit` 24, `exactPathLimit` 200, `snippetMaxChars` 700, source `memory`, `unicode61`, `boostFallbackRanking`; derivation with file and line in `prod/params.md`). The stores are two private agent databases taken with `openclaw backup sqlite create`; the agent read-only opener refuses these schema 24 snapshots, so both arms opened them with the built `openSqliteReadOnlyDatabase` (the layer that opener uses) and the built `enableNodeSqliteKyselyStatementCache`, as the retained reader does. The inputs are 8 common words and 12 file-name stems drawn from each store; only counts, hashes, timings and plans are published.

Per search, first 10 searches on one connection, counting authorizer installed before the first search (`prod/compiles-dev.out`, `prod/compiles-main.out`, the same on both stores):

```
reads of memory_index_chunks while compiling   BEFORE 86 86 43 43 43 43 43 43 43 43   AFTER 43 43 0 0 0 0 0 0 0 0
db.function calls                              BEFORE  3  3  3  3  3  3  3  3  3  3   AFTER  2  0 0 0 0 0 0 0 0 0
```

Over a later 60-search run on each store, base had 2,580 such reads and 180 `db.function` calls; this branch had 0 and 0.

Warm timing in one process: 2 warm-up passes over the 20 inputs, then 5 reps of N searches each (400 on the 6,012-chunk store, 200 on the 43,634-chunk store), mean per search per rep, fresh process per run. Two interleaved rounds (base, patched, patched, base) ran at 1-minute load averages of 7.2 to 10.7; 8 more runs in the order base, patched, patched, base, base, patched, patched, base ran at 3.4 to 3.6 (`prod/timing-dev.out`, `prod/timing-main.out`, raw rep means included):

| Store | Runs | Base, median us per search | Patched | Saving |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 6,012 chunks | rounds 1 / 2 | 1198.4 / 1311.6 | 1126.0 / 1096.2 | 6.0 / 16.4 percent |
| 6,012 chunks | 8 quiet runs, 20 rep means per arm | 1173.3 | 1001.9 | 171.4 us, 14.6 percent |
| 43,634 chunks | rounds 1 / 2 | 4068.1 / 3872.1 | 3553.7 / 3702.0 | 12.6 / 4.4 percent |
| 43,634 chunks | 8 quiet runs, 20 rep means per arm | 3656.7 | 3515.6 | 141.2 us, 3.9 percent |

Over both loaded rounds, the medians of all 10 rep means per arm are 1239.9 to 1111.4 us (10.4 percent) and 3950.9 to 3618.8 us (8.4 percent); over all 30 rep means per arm, 14.1 and 4.4 percent. Single loaded rounds swing by more than the effect, so User Impact quotes the quiet runs.

Results: the sha256 of the full result object (`body` and `path` rows with scores and errors) is identical for 20 of 20 inputs on both stores (`prod/parity-dev.out`, `prod/parity-main.out`; 227 body and 49 path rows on the smaller store, 408 and 148 on the larger, no errors).

Plans: every executed statement was explained with its own bound values on the same connection, in both arms. 80 of 80 identical on each store, four statement shapes (`prod/plans-dev.out`, `prod/plans-main.out`). For example the exact-path statement on both arms:

```
MATERIALIZE exact_paths
MATERIALIZE scored_paths
MATERIALIZE pattern_candidates
MATERIALIZE candidates
SCAN memory_index_paths_fts VIRTUAL TABLE INDEX 0:M2
SCAN candidates
SCAN pattern_candidates
SCAN scored_paths
SEARCH live EXISTS USING COVERING INDEX idx_memory_index_chunks_path_source (path=? AND source=?)
USE TEMP B-TREE FOR ORDER BY
SCAN exact_paths
SEARCH c USING INDEX sqlite_autoindex_memory_index_chunks_1 (id=?)
CORRELATED SCALAR SUBQUERY 6
SEARCH candidate USING INDEX idx_memory_index_chunks_path_source (path=? AND source=?)
USE TEMP B-TREE FOR ORDER BY
```

The `LIKE` patterns are applied to the path FTS table or to a materialized CTE, neither of which can use an index for `LIKE`, which is why rewriting them does not change a plan.

Either half alone, measured the same way with two more builds of this branch (one with the SQL text reverted to bare `LIMIT ?` and `LIKE ?`, one that registers the functions on every call against the shared state), per steady-state search (search 10) and over a 60-search run on each store (`halves/tables-dev.out`, `halves/tables-main.out`, `halves/compiles-<store>.out`):

| Build | Reads of `memory_index_chunks` while compiling, per search | `db.function` calls per search | FTS5 shadow-table and `PRAGMA data_version` callbacks per search (6,012 / 43,634 chunks) | Total callbacks per search (6,012 / 43,634 chunks) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| base | 43 | 3 | 26 / 36 | 147 / 160 (147 to 160 by input on the smaller store) |
| registration once, bare `LIMIT ?` and `LIKE ?` | 43 | 0 after the first search | 0 / 0 | 116 / 116 |
| `LIMIT +?` and `LIKE (? || '')`, functions registered on every call | 43 | 6 | 26 / 36 | 147 / 160 (147 to 160 by input on the smaller store) |
| this change | 0 | 0 after the first search | 0 / 0 | 5 / 5 |

Registering once stops the expiry of FTS5's own cached statements (the shadow-table reads) but the bound `LIMIT` and `LIKE` still recompile the four search statements; the rewrite alone is undone by the next registration. Results were identical across all four builds, 20 of 20 inputs on each store (`halves/parity-dev.out`, `halves/parity-main.out`).

Two synthetic stores (3,030 chunks over about 300 paths, including non-ASCII and NFD names) cover what the real stores lack, the `trigram` tokenizer and the pattern-only exact-path statement used for non-ASCII queries: results identical 20 of 20 on each, plans identical on 101 of 101 statements (12 shapes, `unicode61`) and 90 of 90 (18 shapes, `trigram`), the same compile pattern, and 236.2 us (9.6 percent) and 143.8 us (4.1 percent) saved per search (`prod/synthetic-unicode61.out`, `prod/synthetic-trigram.out`).

### Tests

`pnpm test extensions/memory-core/src/memory/manager-search.test.ts extensions/memory-core/src/memory/manager-search-worker.sqlite.test.ts`:

```
 Test Files  2 passed (2)
      Tests  12 passed (12)
```

Owning directory, `pnpm test extensions/memory-core/src/memory`:

```
 Test Files  99 passed | 4 skipped (103)
      Tests  911 passed | 23 skipped (934)
```

Consumers outside the directory and the search entry tests, `pnpm test` with `manager-search-orchestration.test.ts`, `manager-search-path.test.ts`, `manager-search-worker.test.ts`, `manager-search.unicode-query.test.ts`, `doctor-contract-api.test.ts`, `memory-forget.test.ts`, `manager-search-worker.sqlite.test.ts` and `manager-search.postgres.test.ts` (the PostgreSQL file skips without a server):

```
 Test Files  7 passed | 1 skipped (8)
      Tests  135 passed | 6 skipped (141)
```

`manager-search-worker.sqlite.test.ts` pins the sha256 of each statement's exact SQL bytes. Its four keyword hashes change because the SQL text changes; the vector fallback and KNN hashes do not. Recomputed from both built trees, each new hash is the sha256 of the base statement with only `LIMIT ?` to `LIMIT +?` and `LIKE ? ESCAPE` to `LIKE (? || '') ESCAPE` applied (`gates-final/baseline-hashes.out`; its fifth line repeats statement 1 because the empty store triggers the relaxed body retry):

```
statement 1: before 4ef955cb... | rewrite(before) 0d8edb57... | after 0d8edb57... | rewrite(before) === after: true | LIMIT ? 1 -> 0, LIKE ? 0 -> 0
statement 2: before e0eb673f... | rewrite(before) d21b7990... | after d21b7990... | rewrite(before) === after: true | LIMIT ? 1 -> 0, LIKE ? 4 -> 0
statement 3: before fa8fb140... | rewrite(before) 0452ff06... | after 0452ff06... | rewrite(before) === after: true | LIMIT ? 1 -> 0, LIKE ? 0 -> 0
statement 4: before 60ff181c... | rewrite(before) 6e57716a... | after 6e57716a... | rewrite(before) === after: true | LIMIT ? 1 -> 0, LIKE ? 0 -> 0
```

### Regression proof (red/green)

The new test (`searchKeywordWithFallback statement reuse`, for `unicode61` and `trigram`) runs three different queries (body terms, an exact file name, a non-ASCII name) on one in-memory connection, first one after another plus a repeat, then all three at once with `Promise.all` (each search awaits between its body and path statements, so they interleave), and spies `db.function` and `db.prepare`. It asserts that each function is registered exactly once, that no search statement contains a bare `LIMIT ?` or `LIKE ?`, that the exact-path and lexical path statements ran, and that the sequential, repeated and interleaved results all equal the same search on a fresh connection. The two guards are soft assertions so a failure reports both causes. The interleaved phase guards later edits: each statement run sets its search's state immediately before it, so neither base nor any build of this change fails that assertion today. A spy cannot see SQLite's internal re-prepare (`node:sqlite` exposes no reprepare counter), so the test guards the two causes rather than the recompile itself; the Evidence above shows the recompile.

On base with only the new test file added (`gates-final/red.out`):

```
 FAIL  |extension-database-workers| extensions/memory-core/src/memory/manager-search.test.ts > searchKeywordWithFallback statement reuse > keeps unicode61 search statements reusable across searches on one connection
 FAIL  |extension-database-workers| extensions/memory-core/src/memory/manager-search.test.ts > searchKeywordWithFallback statement reuse > keeps trigram search statements reusable across searches on one connection
AssertionError: expected [ …(25) ] to deeply equal [ …(2) ]
...
 FAIL  |extension-database-workers| extensions/memory-core/src/memory/manager-search.test.ts > searchKeywordWithFallback statement reuse > keeps unicode61 search statements reusable across searches on one connection
AssertionError: expected [ Array(94) ] to deeply equal []
...
 FAIL  |extension-database-workers| extensions/memory-core/src/memory/manager-search.test.ts > searchKeywordWithFallback statement reuse > keeps trigram search statements reusable across searches on one connection
AssertionError: expected [ Array(90) ] to deeply equal []
...
 Test Files  1 failed (1)
      Tests  2 failed | 7 passed (9)
```

On this branch (`gates-final/green.out`):

```
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  9 passed (9)
```

Each half is guarded separately. With only the registration change (SQL text reverted), the test fails only on the SQL assertion (`expected [ Array(94) ] to deeply equal []` and `Array(90)`); with only the SQL rewrite (functions registered on every call against the shared state), it fails only on the registration count (`expected [ …(50) ] to deeply equal [ …(2) ]`) (`mutants/mutant-M1.out`, `mutants/mutant-M2.out`).

### Other checks

`pnpm check:changed --base a7e31844f2edcc6a0a783549f1f5c1394ec83fb8`, lanes `extensions, extensionTests`:

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| typecheck extensions / extension tests | ok |
| lint extension changed files | ok |
| format changed files | ok |
| SQLite dialect ratchet | ok (`SQLite dialect design (changed files): 1 -> 1.`; `SQLite dialect ratchet OK: no construct-group growth against a7e31844f2edcc6a0a783549f1f5c1394ec83fb8.`) |
| SQLite worker ratchet | ok (`SQLite worker ratchet OK: no T1 call-count growth against a7e31844f2edcc6a0a783549f1f5c1394ec83fb8.`) |
| line-cap growth ratchet | ok (`Line-cap ratchet OK: 3 changed source files; no new violations or over-cap growth.`) |
| mock export, assertion SAFETY, test timeout race ratchets; plugin boundaries; import cycles; database-first legacy-store guard | ok |
| `git diff --check` | clean |
| max-lines suppression ratchet | failed on `ui/src/pages/chat/components/chat-message.test.tsx`, `ui/src/pages/config/config-page-state.ts`, `ui/src/pages/sessions/sessions-page-state.ts`; none are in this diff, and the same check fails on the same three files in a clean checkout of `a7e31844f2e` (`gates-final/base-checks.out`) |
| dead export scan | failed on 8 production and 7 full-tree exports (for example `src/agents/model-auth-env-vars.ts: listKnownProviderEnvApiKeyNames`); none are in this diff, and the same scan lists the same 15 exports in a clean checkout of `a7e31844f2e` (`gates-final/base-checks.out`) |

### Measured test cost

`pnpm test extensions/memory-core/src/memory/manager-search.test.ts --maxWorkers=1`, arms interleaved, each tree warmed once first (`gates-final/cost/`):

| Run | Arm | 1-minute load before | Wall | Shard | Tests | New cases |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | base | 47.03 | 18.54 s | 16.93 s | 7 | |
| 2 | this branch | 43.94 | 26.13 s | 25.22 s | 9 | 18 ms, 16 ms |
| 3 | this branch | 45.42 | 59.82 s | 57.53 s | 9 | 70 ms, 16 ms |
| 4 | base | 53.21 | 75.99 s | 72.67 s | 7 | |

Owning directory, `pnpm test extensions/memory-core/src/memory`: 405.93 s wall (shard 403.83 s), 911 passed, 23 skipped, at a 1-minute load of 56.96 (`gates-final/cost/owning-dir.out`).

The host was shared with unrelated builds during these runs. Transform is 95 to 97 percent of each file's duration and the wall time of the same arm varies by up to 4 times, so the file walls do not separate the arms; the new cases themselves take 16 to 70 ms. Each new case opens four in-memory databases with three rows each and runs ten searches. CI seconds are not available before the PR runs.

## Gaps, stated plainly

- `pnpm changed:lanes --json` returns `extensions: true, extensionTests: true` and every other lane false. The owning directory and the out-of-directory consumers of the search worker ran anyway. Unrelated suites were not run.
- The two `check:changed` failures are in files outside this diff and reproduce on a clean checkout of the base.
- The real stores went through the built production search function with the built reader layer and statement cache, not through the Gateway: the Gateway and agent opener refuse these schema 24 snapshots without `doctor --fix`. The Gateway and CLI runs used the synthetic store. The counts match across both routes (4 recompiles and 3 registrations per search before, 0 after admission).
- The re-prepare itself is observed through authorizer callbacks during compilation, from a preload; `node:sqlite` exposes no reprepare counter. The Gateway timing ran on a busy host and is supporting evidence only.
- A `DatabaseSync` object that is closed and then reopened with `open()` would keep its registry entry without the functions. A repository search finds no production caller of `open()` on a connection object other than the reopen wrapper that `openNodeSqliteDatabase` installs; the existing per-connection `loadedExtensions` memo makes the same assumption. In production code the two SQL function names appear only in `manager-search.ts` (`gates-final/grep-checks.out`).
- One host, macOS only. Real stores use `unicode61`; `trigram` is covered by a synthetic store and the existing tests.
- Out of scope: other statements that bind a bare `LIMIT ?`, including Kysely `.limit(n)`, which compiles to `limit ?`. They re-prepare on every run for the same reason and would need their own change at the statement owner.

prs.title: feat(ui): show the Gateway connection state in the sidebar footer
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: connection state is effectively invisible on desktop and jumps the layout on mobile when the Control UI loses its Gateway.

On desktop the identity card lives in the 52px persistent rail, which clipped the status text to 1×1 px, so the only visible signal of "Reconnecting…" or "Disconnected" was a 1 px amber outline around the avatar. When the navigation surface was hidden, a status row was inserted into the shell grid on every blip (layout shift), and on mobile it appeared under the top bar. Settings replaced its save indicator with the connection label, hiding pending/failed save feedback exactly while reconnecting.

## User Impact

User impact: the connection state is readable at the bottom left again, next to your avatar, and nothing in the page moves when the link drops.

- **Sidebar open:** while unhealthy, a status row appears in the sidebar footer slot, on the same line as the avatar: `Reconnecting… · 2 queued` with Retry and the redacted last error on hover. After recovery it shows "Connected" for about 2 seconds, then disappears. Community moves up inside the sidebar; the content area never moves.
- **Sidebar collapsed:** the avatar's presence dot (green / amber / red) carries the state. On each transition a small flag slides out beside the avatar for about 4 seconds, and hovering or focusing the avatar reopens it with Retry. It only opens when it clears the visible composer or sticky save bar; otherwise the dot and tooltip carry the state.
- **Mobile:** the header's small breadcrumb line becomes the status line (tap to retry) and the menu button gets the same dot. No new element, no layout shift.
- Settings keeps its save indicator. Native embeds are unchanged (their host chrome owns status); the initial-connection suppression and the 2 s offline grace are unchanged.

## Why This Change Was Made

`resolveGatewayStatus` stays the single status resolver and the existing outbox total supplies the queued count. The footer row, the collapsed flag and the mobile line are presentations of one shell projection. Exactly one always-mounted polite live region at the shell level (outside the inert mobile drawer) announces each transition once; none of the visible surfaces are live regions.

An earlier iteration of this PR used a floating chip anchored above the composer; it was replaced with this sidebar-footer design after review because it had to dodge every composer and sticky bar. Also fixes a timing-dependent mobile overflow found by the theme E2E: the lobster pet's invisible motion wrapper spanned the composer and was translated while walking.

First PR of the offline-first series (retained presentation through blips, offline boot/asset recovery, draft/data retention, opportunistic sends).

## Evidence

- Unit/browser and E2E coverage for the footer row, collapsed flag (transition timing, hover/keyboard reopen, clearance against writing surfaces, no tooltip duplication), mobile header line and menu dot, content-frame stability, queued count, Settings save indicator, native-embed exclusion, recovery flash and error redaction.
- Before (main, isolated Gateway behind a fault proxy, connection cut): only a thin outline at the avatar.

  ![before](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/b9e26cc8-dedc-4158-809f-1834ec8cca72)

- After (synthetic E2E captures):

| Sidebar open | Sidebar collapsed | Mobile |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ![footer row](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/fd0e3da7-e161-4e51-b8f8-f902cf542090) | ![collapsed flag](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/be002daf-5b8f-413d-b92a-94d70e5ce103) | ![mobile header](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/7c9b11aa-5383-475d-a54a-c7f56a43b499) |

- Live offline behavior of the series (drafts kept, offline send queued and delivered on reconnect) is shown in #174044 and #174043.

## Landing conflict repair

Merged main at `64a52842a1a` into the branch as `0e6933b9c4c`. The repair preserves main's shared chat-pane input registration and registers `gatewayStatus` there, keeping the footer, collapsed rail, mobile header, live region, Settings save indicator, lazy Settings preparation, and lobster motion origin unchanged. The English catalog retains the queued-count label and main's removal of obsolete reconnect copy.

The five repair files pass formatting, targeted lint, and whitespace checks. Focused local proof passed 83 tests across the chat-pane header, native bridge, and pane suites with one worker. Fresh independent Codex P2 autoreview was scoped-clean. The already-inspected screenshots remain above; this conflict repair does not change their visual contract.

Prior preparation also passed 14 E2E and 75 unit tests after the header/footer repair. The subsequent lazy Settings preparation measured startup JavaScript at 339,044 bytes against the 339,379-byte limit, with Chat boot below main. Those E2E and performance results are prior-head evidence, not a fresh run on this merge commit. Current-head required checks remain enforced by GitHub auto-merge.

Full CI on `0e6933b9c4c` found a Settings lazy-wrapper type-import cycle and a redundant `Boolean(canAdmin)` conversion. Commit `2f80ed3742d` fixes both by deriving wrapper props from the existing lazy renderer contract and passing the already-boolean value directly. The exact failing Madge check now reports zero cycles, targeted lint with the failing core config passes, formatting/whitespace pass, and fresh independent Codex P2 autoreview is scoped-clean. No runtime import, budget, assertion, timeout, or suppression was added. Required CI must pass on this new head.

The final merge repair, `476867091d7`, incorporates main `104dc5af562` and retains its newer speech-bubble and sidebar fixture helpers. The compact-menu assertion still follows opening the parked menu, and footer tests retain the branch's avatar-dot, accessible-name, recovery, and shell-announcement contracts. Formatting, whitespace, targeted lint, and fresh independent P2 autoreview pass. The sidebar suite passed 75/75 tests (268.42 seconds; 296.05 seconds including runner overhead), and the two focused production-bundle E2E files passed 4/4 tests (423.98 seconds including setup).

CI on the preceding head had one GitHub-panel heading timeout among 462 E2E cases. The exact test passed on scheduled main run `39075221970` (job `117521062834`, 1.6 seconds) and in the single local replay (8.78 seconds), without changing its source, assertions, or timeout. This is intermittent-failure evidence, not a claimed code repair. No hosted CI rerun was requested; the final pushed head must satisfy its own required checks.

prs.title: fix(logging): preserve UUID-shaped account IDs in Telegram token redaction
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The shared Telegram token matcher accepts any six-or-more digit id followed by twenty token characters, which also matches Atlassian Cloud account IDs (`<digits>:<uuid>`). Because finalized tool-result text is redacted before it enters model context, the Atlassian Rovo tool result `lookupJiraAccountId` reaches the model as `123456…e8f9`; Jira only accepts the full account ID for `assignee`, so agents cannot assign issues or mention users.

Closes #164109. Reproduced against `origin/main` at `063685e96d00ce25a9a7b4ac5e00a40dda32d488`:

```js
redactSensitiveText('{"accountId":"123456:0a1b2c3d-4e5f-6071-8293-a4b5c6d7e8f9"}')
// current main:  '{"accountId":"123456…e8f9"}'
// exact head:    '{"accountId":"123456:0a1b2c3d-4e5f-6071-8293-a4b5c6d7e8f9"}'
```

Precedent: #128258 (`5355a7ad855`, `fix(logging): preserve UUID token fragments`) — the same shape one pattern over: a vendor token matcher consumed a UUID fragment, and the repair narrowed the matcher and added the regression next to it. This PR only moves that shape onto the two Telegram matchers.

## Why This Change Was Made

The owner is the shared matcher table in `src/logging/redact-patterns.ts`. Both Telegram matchers (`TELEGRAM_TOKEN_REDACT_PATTERN` and the `bot`-prefixed sibling) now exclude a UUID-shaped suffix with one negative lookahead placed immediately after the `:` separator; both keep their previous `\d{6,}` id, `[A-Za-z0-9_-]{20,}` secret class, `\b` boundaries, list position, and chunk-unsafe classification.

The exclusion cannot reduce credential coverage: a Telegram token secret is 35 characters, while a UUID-shaped suffix is 36 characters, so no Telegram secret can be UUID-shaped. Every non-UUID match — bare tokens, `bot`-prefixed tokens, and registered-secret masking — behaves exactly as before. The UUID-shaped suffix is deliberately excluded with a lookahead instead of a fixed `\d{8,10}:[A-Za-z0-9_-]{35}` token length, because the supported Telegram token format contract is not established from source and fixed lengths could silently stop masking a real token.

No validator, option, config key, fallback, allowlist, or persistence surface is added. The shared prefilter triggers (`redact-prefilter.ts`) already accept these strings and stay deliberately broader than the matcher table, so the fast path is unchanged and no pattern becomes unreachable.

Production LOC: `+6/-2` (net `+4`; the delta is the single shared exclusion constant plus the three-line invariant comment). The absorbing refactor would be inlining the lookahead into both matchers, which duplicates the shape and removes the stated reason the exclusion is safe; deviating from the reviewed shape is worse than the four lines.

Classification: `behavior-preserving` (removes a measured false positive; no legitimate match changes).

## User Impact

Agents on an Atlassian/Rovo MCP server receive the full account ID again and can assign or mention Jira users. Real Telegram bot tokens — bare and `bot`-prefixed — are still masked in logs and in model-visible tool results, and custom `logging.redactPatterns` behavior is untouched.

## Evidence

### Exact-head proof receipt

- Product head SHA: `4bd260e0caeb65a1882b46b24ec3863bc1273832`
- Current-main base SHA: `063685e96d00ce25a9a7b4ac5e00a40dda32d488`
- Production entry: the real modules, no test double — `redactToolPayloadTextWithConfig(payload, undefined)` (the model-visible tool-result boundary) and `redactSensitiveText(text, { mode: "tools" })`, driven with `node --import ./scripts/tsx.mjs <probe>.mts` on Node `v24.18.0`.
- Canonical owner exercised: `TELEGRAM_TOKEN_REDACT_PATTERN` / `TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN_REDACT_PATTERN` in `src/logging/redact-patterns.ts:360` (head).
- Decision surface: the two Telegram entries of `DEFAULT_REDACT_PATTERNS` and `TOOL_PAYLOAD_REDACT_PATTERNS`.
- Recorder/readback boundary: the returned string from the two exported production functions (masked `first-6…last-4` vs verbatim).
- Cleanup: probe files live in `/tmp`; the worktree is a detached `origin/main` checkout with an isolated `TMPDIR`. No production Gateway, session, token, or config was touched.

### Inspectable RED -> GREEN terminal trace

RED, with `src/logging/redact-patterns.ts` restored byte-for-byte from `origin/main` (identical probe, same Node):

```text
$ node --import ./scripts/tsx.mjs /tmp/probe-redact4.mts
tool-payload accountId : {"accountId":"123456…e8f9"}
tools-mode bare token  : 110201…Dsaw
tools-mode bot  token  : bot110201…Dsaw
```

GREEN, exact head `4bd260e0cae`:

```text
$ node --import ./scripts/tsx.mjs /tmp/probe-redact4.mts
tool-payload accountId : {"accountId":"123456:0a1b2c3d-4e5f-6071-8293-a4b5c6d7e8f9"}
tools-mode bare token  : 110201…Dsaw
tools-mode bot  token  : bot110201…Dsaw
```

The last two lines are the legal control: both Telegram token shapes still mask, on both revisions, so the change is a false-positive exclusion and not an under-redaction.

### Regression test (fails before, passes after)

prs.title: fix(config): align dry-run preview with the commit's roster guard
prs.body:
> **Update 2026-10-15 — rebased onto current main (`7845ca07c`); new head `802831df3bc`** > > Main refactored `src/cli/config-cli-runner.ts` after the reviewed head, so the preview persistence probe was re-applied onto the new structure instead of replayed: same behavior (include routing on the pre-topology authored candidate, then `resolvePersistCandidateForWrite` for root-owned writes), with the 2026-10-02 review's classification `ConfigMutationConflictError ? "conflict" : "schema"`. The regression now lives in main's existing `src/cli/config-cli.roster.integration.test.ts` (the reviewed head's separate `config-cli.roster-preview.integration.test.ts` does not exist on main); the five cases are unchanged in intent. > > Evidence for this head: > - `run-vitest run src/cli/config-cli.roster.integration.test.ts --maxWorkers=1` → **27 passed** on `802831df3bc`. With main's runner restored (no probe) the #133895 case is red: `promise resolved "undefined" instead of rejecting`. > - Sibling config-CLI suites (`config-cli.integration.test.ts`, `config-cli.test.ts`, `config-cli-runner.supplied-intent.test.ts`, `config-cli.secrets.integration.test.ts`, `config-cli.reference-values.integration.test.ts`) → **131 passed**. > - Shipped CLI, isolated `OPENCLAW_CONFIG_PATH`, fixture `{"agents":{"entries":{"main":{}}}}`, `node dist/index.js`: > - base (current main): `--dry-run --json` → `{"ok": true, …, "checks": {"schema": true, …}}`, exit 0; the committing command → `Config write would drop agent roster entries without an explicit deletion: main.`, exit 1 — the #133895 mismatch. > - this head: `--dry-run --json` → `{"ok": false, "operations": 1, "inputModes": ["json"], "checks": {"schema": true, …}, "errors": [{"kind": "schema", "message": "Config write would drop agent roster entries without an explicit deletion: main."}]}`, exit 1; text preview exit 1 with the same diagnostic; commit exit 1; config sha256 unchanged before/after. > - include-owned edit preview (`logging.level` behind `$include`) → `ok: true`, exit 0; committing it routes to the include and leaves the root file byte-identical. > - `tsgo:core` clean; `oxfmt --check` clean on both changed files. > > The transcripts below describe the earlier heads (`6091c72e1cc` vs `9658ea8d8af`) and are kept for the design rationale. Fixes #133895 ## What Problem This Solves `openclaw config set agents.entries '{}' --replace --strict-json --dry-run` reports `Dry run successful` (exit 0) while the equivalent committing write is rejected with `Config write would drop agent roster entries without an explicit deletion: main.` (exit 1). A preview that claims a write will succeed, when the same write is refused, misleads scripts and operators into trusting a change that cannot be persisted. Maintainer-flagged follow-up: #133895 was explicitly left open by #133920 (merged) — "Two named follow-ups remain. #133895 tracks an empty-roster preview that accepts a request the root writer rejects." ## Why This Change Was Made The dry-run branch (`src/cli/config-cli-runner.ts`) ran only the write-topology projection (`prepareConfigWriteTopology`) before validation, so the committing writer's roster-retention guard (`assertCanonicalAgentRosterRetainsEntries` inside `resolvePersistCandidateForWrite`) was never armed for previews. This change adds a preview-only persistence probe that mirrors the commit exactly: 1. **Same routing order** — the probe consults the commit owner's include-write decision (`resolveConfigIncludeWriteBoundary`, the same candidacy the committing `tryWriteIncludeOwnedConfigMutation` uses) on the **pre-topology** candidate with the same normalized explicit paths the committing write receives, because the commit selects the include writer before root topology preparation. An edit owned by an authored `$include` skips the root writer's projection, exactly like the commit. 2. **Same routing inputs** — the probe passes the committing write's `persistCanonicalAgentRoster` write option to the routing decision, not the topology-derived flag. Topology preparation derives `persistCanonicalAgentRoster` from roster shape (e.g. an `ownership: "explicit"` agents include gaining a second entry), but the committing CLI never supplies that derived value when it selects the include writer — feeding it into routing made preview refuse an agents-include roster expansion that commit accepts. 3. **Same guard, root-owned writes only** — root-owned previews run the shared persistence projection (`resolvePersistCandidateForWrite`), arming the roster-retention guard — reusing the existing owner's guard instead of adding an empty-roster special case or weakening commit protection (the direction #133895's body specifies). 4. **Same invocation order** — the probe runs after `validateConfigMutation`, matching the commit (validation errors surface before persistence checks). This also keeps pathological inputs on the schema-error path: validation rejects them before any persistence projection runs. 5. **Same no-op short circuit** — the committing command reports `No change` before persistence, so no-op previews skip the probe instead of rejecting an include-owned explicit set. Classification: `behavior-completing` — preview now reports the same refusal the commit already enforced, without refusing edits the commit accepts. ## User Impact - `--dry-run` on a guarded roster removal now fails with the same `Config write would drop agent roster entries...` error and exit 1 as the committing write, instead of falsely reporting success. - `--dry-run` on an edit owned by an authored `$include` previews successfully — including edits that topology preparation reshapes at the root (e.g. `session.store` beside `agents.defaults.sessionStore.agentId`), roster expansion into an explicit-ownership `agents` include, and no-op assignments — exactly matching the committing write. - Genuinely allowed root mutations still preview successfully; the existing preview assertions still pass. ## Evidence ### Real CLI proof (packaged `dist` binaries, exact head `6091c72e1cc` vs base `9658ea8d8af`) Refreshed 2026-10-08 with the admission-valid fixture. Current main rejects legacy `agents.entries.*.default` markers at config admission (`Legacy agents.entries default markers need explicit surface owners`), so the 2026-09-22 transcript's `default:true` fixture no longer reaches the changed owner. Every scenario below uses `{"agents":{"entries":{"main":{}}}}` (or no root roster), which passes admission on both builds. Environment: Node v24.18.0 on the remote docker runner (`lexiflow-all`), `dist` built from each tree with `build-all.mts` on 2026-10-08 (both report `OpenClaw 2026.9.8`; the in-container `.buildstamp` records `head: null` because the build host has no git — the trees were synced from the exact SHAs above). Each scenario uses an isolated `OPENCLAW_CONFIG_PATH`, one real CLI process per invocation (`node dist/index.js config ...`), no mocks or output/exit interception. `OPENCLAW_FS_SAFE_NATIVE_MODE=off` because the host kernel (3.10) predates `openat2` — fs-safe's documented JavaScript fallback, as in earlier rounds. (The `ui:build` phase fails on this host over a stale `ui/node_modules` missing `jsonc-parser`; the CLI dist is complete, and the failing phase is unrelated to the config CLI.) **A. Empty-roster replace on the admission-valid `main:{}` fixture — RED on base, GREEN on this head** config: `{"agents":{"entries":{"main":{}}}}`, root config sha256 `a2dbb0aa4ecc…f8134` before every run ```text base (9658ea8d8af): $ openclaw config set agents.entries '{}' --replace --strict-json --dry-run Dry run successful: 1 update(s) validated against …/openclaw.json. exit=0 <- preview claims the write is fine $ openclaw config set agents.entries '{}' --replace --strict-json --dry-run --json { "ok": true, "operations": 1, "inputModes": ["json"], "checks": { "schema": true, "resolvability": true, "resolvabilityComplete": true }, "refsChecked": 0, "skippedExecRefs": 0 } exit=0 <- JSON preview also reports success $ openclaw config set agents.entries '{}' --replace --strict-json Config write would drop agent roster entries without an explicit deletion: main. exit=1 <- commit refuses: preview/commit mismatch BYTES-UNCHANGED: yes this head (6091c72e1cc): $ openclaw config set agents.entries '{}' --replace --strict-json --dry-run Config write would drop agent roster entries without an explicit deletion: main. exit=1 <- preview refuses with the guard's own diagnostic $ openclaw config set agents.entries '{}' --replace --strict-json --dry-run --json { "ok": false, "operations": 1, "inputModes": ["json"], "checks": { "schema": true, "resolvability": true, "resolvabilityComplete": true }, "refsChecked": 0, "skippedExecRefs": 0, "errors": [ { "kind": "schema", "message": "Config write would drop agent roster entries without an explicit deletion: main." } ] } exit=1 <- completed validation summary preserved (operations 1, schema check true); the retention refusal is appended classified "schema" (not "conflict") $ openclaw config set agents.entries '{}' --replace --strict-json Config write would drop agent roster entries without an explicit deletion: main. exit=1 BYTES-UNCHANGED: yes (root config sha256 identical before/after every run) ``` **G. Agents-include roster expansion under explicit ownership — accepted on both, no false refusal** root config `{"agents":{"$include":"agents.json"}}`, include `{"ownership":"explicit","entries":{"main":{"name":"before"}}}` — identical on base and this head: ```text $ openclaw config set agents.entries.work '{"name":"worker"}' --strict-json --dry-run Dry run successful: 1 update(s) validated against …/openclaw.json. exit=0 root unchanged: YES include unchanged: YES $ openclaw config set agents.entries.work '{"name":"worker"}' --strict-json Updated agents.entries.work. Change will apply without restarting the gateway. exit=0 root unchanged: YES include now holds both "main" and "work" ``` **I1. Include-owned scalar edit — identical on both builds** root `{"agents":{"entries":{"main":{}}},"logging":{"$include":"logging.json"}}`, include `{"level":"info"}`: ```text $ openclaw config set logging.level '"debug"' --strict-json --dry-run Dry run successful: 1 update(s) validated against …/openclaw.json. exit=0 root unchanged: YES include unchanged: YES $ openclaw config set logging.level '"debug"' --strict-json Updated logging.level. No gateway restart needed. exit=0 root unchanged: YES include now { "level": "debug" } ``` **N. No-op include-owned assignment — identical on both builds** ```text $ openclaw config set logging.level '"info"' --strict-json --dry-run # include already says "info" Dry run successful: 1 update(s) validated against …/openclaw.json. exit=0 include unchanged: YES $ openclaw config set logging.level '"info"' --strict-json No change exit=0 include unchanged: YES ``` Environmental noise, identical in both dists: a best-effort `Config health-state write failed: ENOENT … openclaw-state.worker.mjs` warning (the health-state sidecar resolves its directory from the process cwd rather than `OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR`; both builds behave identically), and — only in the base dist's include scenario — a whatsapp `persistedAuthState` module warning caused by the renamed `dist-r6-main` directory confusing a `dist-runtime` fallback path. Neither touches config write routing.
Historical transcript (2026-09-22, head 094424f8aa vs main 43247c9b2, legacy default:true fixture — superseded by the run above because current admission rejects that fixture before the changed owner runs) The 2026-09-22 run demonstrated the same preview/commit parity with `{"agents":{"entries":{"main":{"default":true}}}}` on the September trees: preview RED on main (`Dry run successful`, exit 0, `ok: true`), GREEN on the PR head (refusal with the guard's diagnostic, `ok: false` + appended `kind: "schema"` error), bytes unchanged, and the same G/I1/N controls. The scenario logic is unchanged; only the fixture's admission validity moved with main.
### Regression tests (exact head, remote docker runner) `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs` on Node v24.18.0, `lexiflow-all:latest`, `OPENCLAW_FS_SAFE_NATIVE_MODE=off` (same kernel reason): ```text src/cli/config-cli.roster.integration.test.ts + config-cli.roster-preview.integration.test.ts 61 passed (2 files) — the five preview/commit parity tests moved verbatim into the sibling file (the roster file sat exactly at the 1000 counted-line cap): ✓ rejects emptying the roster in preview just like the commit (#133895) ✓ previews an include-owned edit without tripping the root persistence guard ✓ previews an include-owned edit that topology preparation reshapes at the root ✓ previews a no-op include-owned assignment without persistence rejection ✓ previews an agents-include roster expansion under explicit ownership src/cli/config-cli.test.ts + config-cli.integration.test.ts 245 passed (245), including: ✓ reports schema errors for deeply nested replacement values without an engine failure ``` Rebased head `6091c72e1cc` (2026-10-08): the four preview fixtures moved from the legacy `{ main: { default: true } }` form to the admission-valid `{ main: {} }`, because current main rejects legacy `default` markers at config admission and the old fixtures never reached the roster guard. Scenario intent is unchanged; the strengthened empty-roster regression also asserts the appended error category `{ kind: "schema" }`. Re-verified on the rebased head (bare vitest, `vitest.cli.config.ts`, `--maxWorkers=1`, remote docker runner, 2026-10-08): **27 passed (2 files)** in 64.9 s. Full CI on `6091c72e1cc` is green (all `checks-node-*`, `checks-ui-e2e`, and security lanes SUCCESS). RED check: the new parity tests fail on the previous heads and pass on this head — the agents-include expansion test fails on `fa9351daeda` (routing fed the topology-derived flag) with a preview-only `Config write would flatten $include-owned config at agents...` refusal while the commit accepts; the deeply nested schema test fails with `Maximum call stack size exceeded` on every earlier revision of this branch (projection ran pre-validation). - tsgo core lane: no errors in the changed files. - `git diff --check` — clean. ### Test cost After the line-cap split, the changed test surface is two files (`config-cli.roster.integration.test.ts` restored to its grandfathered base content, plus the new `config-cli.roster-preview.integration.test.ts` holding the five preview tests). Measured with the policy command on one worker, exact head `094424f8aa`: | Where | Command / environment | Wall | Vitest | | --- | --- | ---: | ---: | | Remote docker runner (`lexiflow-all`, Node v24.18.0, `OPENCLAW_FS_SAFE_NATIVE_MODE=off`) | `run-vitest run src/cli/config-cli.roster-preview.integration.test.ts src/cli/config-cli.roster.integration.test.ts --maxWorkers=1` | **139.2 s** | 129.40 s (shard 136.70 s) | Result: **61 passed (2 files)**, exit 0 (2026-09-22). Test content is identical to the pre-split single file, so the per-file cost shape is unchanged; CI seconds for the new head will be recorded from its run (previous head: `agentic-cli` shard, 386 files in 728.59 s, this file's span 54.2 s, [job 106342251486](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/35602512957/job/106342251486)). ### Scope and risk - Production: `src/cli/config-cli-runner.ts` — dry-run branch only; committing behavior untouched. - Tests: `src/cli/config-cli.roster-preview.integration.test.ts` (new sibling holding the preview/commit parity tests) — `config-cli.roster.integration.test.ts` is byte-identical to main. - Existing-solutions preflight: reuses the commit owner's `resolveConfigIncludeWriteBoundary` routing decision and the existing `resolvePersistCandidateForWrite` projection — no new validator, option, config key, or persistence policy. - Config/default, protocol/schema, authorization, storage, migration, upgrade impact: none. prs.title: fix: offer publication on the first managed conversation turn
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

A new managed conversation could edit a repository but lack the publication tool for its entire first turn. Its first lookup started background GitHub discovery and immediately captured the unavailable result; completing discovery later did not update that turn's tool catalog. A subsequent turn or the dashboard's Publish PR action could publish the same work without any account change.

Fixes #175910.

## User Impact

Managed Gateway conversations can request publication from the first turn through the existing `github_publish` tool. The Gateway still qualifies the current workspace, requesting person, and selected credential when the operation is invoked. Unsupported workspaces and unavailable credentials produce the existing refusal or recovery guidance; offering the tool does not grant repository access or supply credentials to the agent.

Explicit tool denies, restrictive allowlists, and standalone, detached, or disabled-tool exclusions remain effective. The worker's separate credential-launch envelope keeps its existing discovery and revocation checks. No configuration or migration is required.

## Why This Change Was Made

Publication is a brokered request, so constructing its tool should not depend on whether a background credential lookup has finished. The shared local-turn preparation and worker tool-construction paths now offer that request capability directly. Credential discovery remains asynchronous for worker launch, and actual publication continues through the existing authority and identity owners.

The change removes obsolete mocks that made continuation tests appear publication-ready, adds a focused cold-turn/exclusion test, and extends the worker-launch fixture to distinguish tool availability from credential delivery. The GitHub identity documentation now explains this distinction and the existing recovery behavior.

## Evidence

The original production composition reproduced the failure: the first catalog contained only `github_identity_status`; after background discovery, the same session also contained `github_publish`. The expected first-turn assertion failed while all 11 existing discovery lifecycle cases passed.

The candidate passes formatting/source lint, all 38 selected compiler graphs, and 156 cases across 11 targeted files. Coverage includes the cold first turn, standalone/detached/disabled-tool exclusions, explicit and inherited denials, real Gateway continuations, and worker launch with unavailable or revoked credentials. An existing worker assertion was updated for the approved request capability; its restrictive-allowlist control remains.

The original 11-file test batch took 216.10 seconds. After that assertion correction, `pnpm test src/gateway/worker-environments/worker-turn-execution.test.ts` passed all 29 cases through the native targeted recipe in 83.51 seconds; unchanged passes were reused. All validation ran on Linux with the locked dependencies. Hosted [CI](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/39080503689) completed successfully: 51 successful jobs and 26 skipped jobs, with 9,433 summed job seconds (not billing or wall time). Independent review is clean. [Automated review](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/175932#issuecomment-6243530613) found no actionable findings, with Gold proof confidence and Platinum patch quality. Its live shipped-Gateway proof limit is retained below.

This is tool-construction and broker-boundary proof, not a live GitHub write. This PR does not deploy a Gateway or claim a live Team-server recheck.

prs.title: fix(agents): detect sustained same-target write churn
prs.body:
Related: #122577

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where an agent can repeatedly overwrite one file with different successful contents while never producing a final response. Because every write has different arguments and reports `changed: true`, current loop detection treats the sequence as ordinary progress indefinitely.

This PR proposes a conservative behavioral boundary for maintainer review. The issue is currently marked as requiring a product decision; this PR does not claim that decision has already been made.

## Why This Change Was Made

The change keeps successful writes classified as real mutations and adds a separate, warning-first run-liveness signal for a contiguous tail of content-changing writes to one resolved target. Target identity excludes document content and is stored only as a hash.

The existing loop warning threshold is reused. The warned write remains allowed. Continuity clears when the run changes tools (including read/verification), changes targets, repeats an earlier argument variant, or completes/replaces its lifecycle. If churn remains continuous through the existing stale-run boundary, owner-bound recovery can abort only that run whether or not follow-up work is queued.

The behavior is limited to the built-in `write` result contract (`details.changed === true`). It is not tied to a provider, model, transport, channel, or reported private document. No new configuration or default surface is added.

## Batch and Liveness Semantics

A whole assistant batch is admitted before its calls have outcomes. This revision therefore keeps warning and liveness behavior aligned at both lifecycle boundaries:

- successful write-mutation liveness stays inactive below the shared warning threshold;
- a sequential batch emits the same run-scoped warning before the threshold-crossing write implementation starts;
- a post-outcome fallback covers parallel or out-of-order batch completions;
- the shared warning bucket prevents duplicate pre- and post-outcome warnings;
- the existing stable no-progress classifier still includes the just-recorded outcome and activates on its original boundary.

## Scope

The write-churn changes remain in the agent loop owner. A separate memory-core test commit stabilizes the unrelated provenance-repair assertion that failed hosted CI: it holds the detached repair open while asserting that automatic candidates remain hidden, then releases and verifies the repaired result. The test moved into the existing candidate-repair suite to satisfy the line-cap ratchet. No memory-core production behavior changed.

A subsequent agent fix resets the reverse write-variant scan at the newer occurrence of a repeated variant, retaining only post-repeat writes. A replacement regression uses actual `changed: true` outcomes at the shared warning threshold and verifies that a fresh post-repeat streak can warn again.

## User Impact

Runaway same-file rewrite sequences become bounded without immediately blocking normal edits. Short rewrite sequences, multi-file work, write/read/write verification, repeated identical content, and successful writes outside the sustained same-target pattern retain their existing behavior. The latest file state and session remain available after recovery.

## Policy Status

ClawSweeper marked #122577 as requiring a maintainer product decision and disabled automated fix-PR queueing. This PR implements one conservative proposal for review; it does not claim that maintainers have approved the warning, escape, or recovery boundary. It is ready for maintainer review of that decision, but does not claim approval or merge readiness.

## Evidence

Behavioral incident baseline: `v2026.7.2-beta.7` (`dabe1915362e20c25704af91612a32a8f4c96e83`). The beta is provenance only; the patch and tests are bound to the recorded branch head and integrated base below, not an unqualified current-main merge.

Negative controls observed before their fixes:

```text
same-target detector: expected warning, received { stuck: false }
below-threshold liveness: active=true after the second distinct changed write
embedded sequential batch: 11 successful writes, warning event list empty
stable no-progress boundary: sixth completed outcome still reported active=false
default-parallel batch: warning emitted, first churn lease remained absent
loop detection omitted/disabled: changed-write churn emitted a warning
CI dependency scan: three internal helpers were exported but unused
```

## Current revision and verification

Head: `f72242e6faf82f8608abd704b16d868d8a034ada`. The branch's integrated main merge-base remains `d45155d6c51169ac10890445418a9144395d1697`; it has not been integrated with current main.

- Revision 34's staged-write-target lifecycle P2 is fixed in the shared wrapper settlement `finally`, with run-scoped cleanup on success, errors, late cancellation, source-guard refusal and disposal. Batch final-target precedence is retained. The follow-up adds three production lines and +132 net test lines across two files.
- Five regressions failed on the preceding wrapper and passed after the fix. At this exact clean head, the focused detector, warning, write-target, admission and real-Agent sequential/default-parallel suites passed 169 distinct tests across five files. This is native wrapper/Agent lifecycle evidence, not a current-head Gateway recovery proof.
- Production `tsgo:core`, the canonical `core-test-agents-root` compiler graph, focused type-aware lint, formatting, line-cap ratchet and whitespace checks passed. The changed-graph selector stopped on the pre-existing 721-root/advisory-720 budget check; no config or test inventory changed, and the named graph was compiled separately. No full all-graph check claim.
- Independent read-only review found no actionable defect in the lifecycle fix. The full branch surface against its integrated base is source +475 and tests +1503 across 23 files; the added production state remains limited to target-aware detection, batch reconciliation and existing liveness ownership.
- Prior-head hosted CI failed one subagent-registry shard at `subagent-registry.test.ts:5160`, with dependent failure/cancellations; this unrelated failure was not repaired. Local passes are not a new-head hosted-CI pass.
- A merge-tree against main `3f12395208355949832da16c882e83cc5726c560` reports ten conflicting paths. Integration remains explicitly unqualified.

[The final follow-up comment](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/122631#issuecomment-5974613163) contains the exact commands, checked-in proof links and captured terminal excerpts. No new isolated-Gateway result is claimed.

### Historical isolated Gateway proof (`27b24258c8`)

The real gateway, authenticated loopback agent RPC, embedded runner, built-in write/read tools, diagnostic heartbeat, and owner-bound recovery were exercised using a deterministic loopback model transport. No outbound-channel delivery or live-provider claim.

```text

This trace is historical: subsequent target-hash, repeat-continuity and staging-cleanup changes have not been qualified through the isolated Gateway at the current head. No rerun is in progress or claimed; final Gateway qualification is deferred until a maintainer chooses the policy and the branch is integrated. The synthetic harness at the proof head selected the latest marked prompt because runtime context could follow it as another user-role message; no production timing constants were changed for that historical proof.

The [historical proof comment](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/122631#issuecomment-5746076190) contains the sanitized event evidence and artifact digests. Raw logs, runtime identifiers, local paths, credentials, and provider configuration are intentionally not published.

## Remaining decisions

Maintainer acceptance of owner-bound abort for sustained successful writes versus warning-only remains required, including the effect for existing `loopDetection.enabled: true` installations. A maintainer must own the current-main conflicts and final hosted CI/Gateway validation, provide a bounded acceptance path, or reject the proposal. This final cleanup does not select the policy, waive checks, or claim merge readiness. Further contributor-side rebase/build/Gateway-proof cycles are paused again.

prs.title: fix(agents): preserve ACP lifecycle ownership
prs.body:
## Summary

- keep spawned ACP runs under their canonical `acp` task owner while retaining a topology/control observer in the subagent registry
- stop ACP observer rows from creating duplicate `subagent` task projections, terminal delivery obligations, or child-session cleanup authority
- upgrade persisted legacy ACP mirrors during normalization and use the active ACP turn or canonical durable task as observer liveness
- emit a specific ACP owner-loss reason and preserve one-shot session state until a later corroborating maintenance pass

Fixes [GEN-6353](https://linear.app/genhealth/issue/GEN-6353/openclaw-loses-active-shrimp-acp-backing-sessions-after-the-legacy).

## What Problem This Solves

An ACP spawn created the canonical `runtime=acp` task, then the shared spawn pipeline registered the same run as a native subagent. The mirror's sweeper checked `getAgentRunContext`, which never represented external ACP liveness, so it false-failed after the stale grace and ran session-scoped cleanup. Task maintenance later treated only the process-local ACP turn marker as backing evidence, marked the canonical task lost after its grace, and could close the one-shot session in that same pass.

The observed production intervals match those two grace periods plus sweep cadence.

## Design

Patterns found and retained:

- the shared spawn registry remains the source for child topology, admission caps, status, and control
- the ACP manager/task registry remains the canonical lifecycle, progress, delivery, and cleanup owner
- observer ownership is persisted in the existing forward-compatible payload JSON; no SQLite schema change is required
- legacy ACP rows are recognized by their canonical ACP session key and normalized into observer-only state

Patterns intentionally not used:

- native subagent restart recovery and native `AgentRunContext` liveness, because Codex/ACP has a separate durable thread/session identity and resume contract
- deleting ACP rows from the subagent registry, which would regress topology and child controls
- immediate session deletion after declaring loss; cleanup now requires a later pass and rechecks the active turn

## Evidence

- `pnpm test src/agents/subagents/registry/subagent-delivery-state.test.ts src/agents/subagents/registry/subagent-registry-run-launch.test.ts src/agents/subagents/registry/subagent-registry-sweeper-recovery.test.ts src/agents/subagents/registry/subagent-run-liveness.test.ts src/agents/subagents/spawn/acp-spawn.test.ts src/tasks/task-registry.test.ts`
  - 239 tests passed across 3 Vitest shards
- `pnpm tsgo`
- `pnpm tsgo:test`
- scoped `oxlint` and `oxfmt --check`

`pnpm check:changed` could not run because the local Crabbox binary failed its built-in version/help sanity check; the equivalent scoped formatting, lint, type, and focused test checks above passed.

AI-assisted: yes. I reviewed the implementation and validation results.

## What Problem This Solves

Explicit Matrix room delivery could not derive a session under the default DM scope. A canonical room target was marked non-exact, so delivery failed unless the caller supplied `--session-key`, even though Matrix already had an exact room identity.

## Why This Change Was Made

The Matrix plugin owns whether a normalized target is authoritative. This change treats `!`-prefixed room IDs as exact independently of the DM-only session scope while keeping room aliases (`#…`) non-authoritative. Generic delivery and binding ownership remain unchanged.

## User Impact

Commands targeting either legacy `!room:server` IDs or modern server-less room IDs can resolve their room session without a manually supplied session key. Alias and DM routing behavior is preserved.

prs.title: fix(sessions): preserve requester identity at execution admission
prs.body:
Related: #150705.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes delegated work losing the original requester’s identity and applicable permissions across later execution and recovery.

## User Impact

New executions resolve current applicable destination policy for the authenticated requester and retain that prepared policy for their lifetime. Accepted asynchronous work survives normal source completion. Intentional delegation to a more capable agent remains supported, and conversation history remains shared.

`messages.queue.allowCollaborativeSteering` defaults to **false**. Operators can explicitly enable it with `true`. When enabled, admitted human input in the same conversation may join Alice’s active turn under Alice’s unchanged identity and prepared permissions. Bob may influence actions using permissions Alice has that Bob does not: this is an accepted product tradeoff. Bob remains the message author. Permissions are not combined, execution identity does not switch, and no causal attribution machinery is added. New delegations still resolve current destination policy for the original requester.

**With the setting omitted or false, cross-human steering is refused without queueing.** The runtime generates this exact notice without invoking the model:

> Someone else’s turn is still running, and collaborative steering is disabled. Your message wasn’t queued. Resend it as `/followup <message>` to run it afterward.
>
> Admins can enable collaborative steering with messages.queue.allowCollaborativeSteering: true.

The refusal settles pending-input and ingress custody through the existing owners. It cannot drain later or be revived by retry/recovery; history need not be deleted. The prepared admission decision survives detached Gateway preparation and is not retried as ordinary work.

**`/followup <message>` requests one new execution.** Busy sessions use the existing followup queue; idle sessions use ordinary admission while respecting already-queued work. The submitter’s authenticated identity is preserved and current policy is resolved at execution admission. The persistent queue mode stays unchanged. Runtime notices distinguish actual queue acceptance, execution start, and rejection. Native/text commands consume the prefix once, and literal `/queue` or `/stop` inside its message cannot mutate persistent settings or cancel active work. The local embedded TUI uses its existing queue and lifecycle events.

Same-requester compatibility/current-owner checks, normal followup/collect/interrupt modes, backend-unavailable fallback, approvals and explicit cancellation keep their existing contracts. This also applies to local `/steer`/`/tell` where supported. Explicit cross-session `sessions_send(mode="steer")` still refuses incompatible steering with followup guidance. A queued or injected natural-language “stop” is never a cancellation acknowledgment. No new storage, authority manager, confirmation state, or per-tool work is added.

## Why This Change Was Made

The existing admission, queue, execution-authority and recovery owners carry authenticated requester facts separately from calculated policy. A new admission resolves policy; continuing work retains its prepared authority while still checking cancellation and current ownership. Existing channel, worker and transport adapters carry that decision to the actual effect. Registered transport-boundary tests and failure-phase diagnostics support that cutover. The latest fix sends the explicit followup start notice from the actual start callback before streamed output, using the existing delivery and completion owners.

### Configuration and updates

Initial configuration creation writes the default explicitly. Candidate `doctor --fix` creates missing parents and persists absent `allowCollaborativeSteering: false` through the existing backed-up, include-aware writer. Explicit true/false, including values in includes, are preserved; repair is idempotent. Ordinary reads and Gateway startup remain read-only. A supported singly owned nested include receives its repair; ambiguous/shared/external/root-level layouts keep existing refusal and owning-file guidance.

Managed package/source updates invoke candidate Doctor. Older drivers’ read-only phases cannot persist the setting there. Direct package-manager/manual/container replacement can bypass Doctor: the runtime default works immediately, and the next `openclaw doctor --fix` persists it. Existing backup, attribution, and rollback owners remain responsible for restoration.

Historical default-on evidence: the published v2026.10.3 updater against retained ab119 passed absent-default and include-false cells with backups, idempotence, readiness, and history. **Rollback remains unproven:** the injected-failure cell refused with `state-migrated-no-rollback` under the unknown-writer guard. Include-false also changes database generations without changing queue bytes, so queue persistence is not necessary for that condition; persisting the default can still introduce writes that trigger the guard. No bypass or rollback-success claim is made. That package proof is historical after the b76, 2f228 and 8d4e rebases and predates the default-off change. The current increment changes the missing-setting value and its existing include-write staging, while retaining the writer and rollback owners; it does not establish a new published-driver or rollback result. [Installed-updater evidence](https://crabbox.openclaw.ai/portal/runs/run_b02abdb216f1d22dc54f37031a983a66).

Older accepted records lacking requester/delivery ownership remain inspectable but do not automatically replay; recovery records failure/resubmission guidance. Missing or revoked authority requires a fresh request. No schema, backfill, hash format, or retention change is introduced.

## Evidence

**October 17 test cleanup (`91b677ede681`):** Nine test/support files, +111/−218: **107 fewer net lines**, with no cases or production code deleted. Reuses existing HTTP helpers, consolidates duplicated notice/setup code, and removes unused captured data and redundant checks. Distinct identity, cancellation, recovery, ordering, notice, and compaction-policy assertions remain. Fresh scoped review is clean through P2.

**Cleanup proof:** **387 distinct tests passed across six files**; the final correction replay repeats 21 of them. Two type graphs initially rejected passing optional session-entry fields directly to the required compaction guard shape. Restoring the original four explicit snapshots fixes that error. All three affected type graphs, scoped lint, formatting, diff checks, and the increment's size ratchet pass. The final tested tree matches the commit. Existing whole-PR size/conflict gaps below remain. [Six-file proof](https://crabbox.openclaw.ai/portal/runs/run_d438499747e758d52219b2641186a7e1), [final correction proof](https://crabbox.openclaw.ai/portal/runs/run_ddaee817a890572c71081f11a1a6097b).
