prs.title: feat(plugin-sdk): expose bounded status projections from command-status
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Closes #76759. Plugin authors building status integrations had no public types for the gateway `/status` payload: an external plugin (`lossless-claw#516`) guessed the session-row shape from formatted output and navigated fields that do not exist (`sessions.byAgent[].entries[].usage.*` instead of `sessions.byAgent[].recent[]`), so its number extraction returned `null` on every field. Without a public type, this drift recurs for every status-consuming plugin.

## Why This Change Was Made

The previous revision re-exported the host `StatusSummary`/`SessionStatus`/`HeartbeatStatus` types verbatim. ClawSweeper's review correctly rejected that: `StatusSummary` is a mutable host aggregate with transitive gateway, channel, task, audit, plugin, and degraded-secret details, and freezing it into the public SDK would make evolving host-owned nested shapes an implicit compatibility commitment (the old test even had to cast `tasks`/`taskAudit` through `unknown` to compile).

This revision defines **bounded SDK-owned projections** in `openclaw/plugin-sdk/command-status` instead — the smallest shape status-consuming plugins actually need:

- `StatusSessionRow` — one session row: identity (`agentId`, `key`, `sessionId`, `updatedAt`) plus token usage (`inputTokens`, `outputTokens`, `totalTokens`, `remainingTokens`, `percentUsed`, `contextTokens`, `model`, `flags`).
- `StatusSessionsProjection` — the session portion of a `/status` payload (`count`, `recent[]`, `byAgent[]`).
- `StatusHeartbeat` — per-agent heartbeat schedule state.

Drift protection runs in the other direction now: `src/plugin-sdk/command-status.types.test.ts` compiles projection functions from the real host types (`SessionStatus → StatusSessionRow`, `StatusSummary["sessions"] → StatusSessionsProjection`, `HeartbeatStatus → StatusHeartbeat`), so renaming a projected field on the host side breaks the build loudly — with zero `unknown` casts. Host-only fields stay free to evolve.

## User Impact

Third-party plugins can `import type { StatusSessionRow, StatusSessionsProjection, StatusHeartbeat } from "openclaw/plugin-sdk/command-status"` and bind the exact session/heartbeat data the `/status` RPC exposes, without copying host internals or acquiring an implicit contract over unrelated host aggregates. Types only — no runtime surface, no startup cost.

## Evidence

- `pnpm test src/plugin-sdk/command-status.types.test.ts` — green; the test is a compile-time assignability contract from real host types plus behavioral assertions on projected values.
- Plugin SDK surface gate `scripts/plugin-sdk-surface-report.mts --check` — green with the `+3` budget entry ("SDK-owned command-status projection types for plugin status consumers").
- `node scripts/check-changed.mjs` — green (format, oxlint, tsgo core + test shards, `api-baseline` test 22/22, boundary guards).
- Real consumer proof against the built package (fresh `pnpm build` on this head `e06332c90de`): a standalone strict `nodenext` TypeScript project outside the repo resolving `openclaw/plugin-sdk/command-status` binds all three projections and compiles with **exit 0**:

  ```ts
  import type { StatusHeartbeat, StatusSessionRow, StatusSessionsProjection } from "openclaw/plugin-sdk/command-status";
  export function summarizeStatus(sessions: StatusSessionsProjection): string {
    const rows: StatusSessionRow[] = sessions.recent;
    return `${sessions.count} sessions\n` + rows.map((r) => `${r.key}: ${r.totalTokens ?? "?"} tokens`).join("\n");
  }
  ```

  Runtime probe of the built subpath: `import("dist/plugin-sdk/command-status.js")` exposes exactly `buildCommandsMessage`, `buildCommandsMessagePaginated`, `buildHelpMessage` — the projections are type-only and correctly absent at runtime.
- Branch was rebased onto current `main` (post pnpm-12 bump) and squashed to one commit carrying the projection design.

prs.title: feat(tts-local-cli): declare and select voices for the local CLI provider
prs.body:
Related: #165598 (staged delivery: this PR covers voice listing/selection for `tts-local-cli`; `talk.catalog` / `tts.providers` payloads stay out of scope, see below).

## What Problem This Solves

`tts-local-cli` users cannot see or switch voices: `/voice list` and `/voice set` (`/talkvoice` on Discord) fail with `speech provider tts-local-cli does not support voice listing`, so changing the voice of a multi-voice local engine (Kokoro, Piper, anything with a `--voice` flag) means hardcoding it into `command` and reloading.

## User Impact

Operators declare the voices their command accepts once, under `tts.providers.tts-local-cli`, and pass the active one with `{{VoiceId}}`:

```jsonc
// tts.providers.tts-local-cli
{
  "command": "/usr/local/bin/my-tts --voice {{VoiceId}}",
  "args": ["{{OutputPath}}"],
  "outputFormat": "wav",
  "voices": ["af_jessica", "af_bella", "am_michael"],
  "voiceId": "af_jessica"
}
```

`/voice list` shows those voices, `/voice set <voice>` switches Talk playback without a config edit, and TTS replies keep using `voiceId`. No migration: both keys are optional, and a command without `{{VoiceId}}` behaves exactly as before (the voice list is simply empty).

## Why This Change Was Made

The command owns its voice catalog, so the provider config declares it; the plugin adds `listVoices`, a `{{VoiceId}}` template key, and a `resolveTalkConfig` hook. Three rules keep the Talk path correct:

- **Talk selection wins.** `resolveTalkConfig` applies the Talk record over TTS defaults, then drops speaker aliases (`speakerVoiceId`, `speakerVoice`, `voice`, `voiceName`) inherited from the TTS record. Core normalization ranks `speakerVoiceId` above `voiceId`, so before this an inherited alias silently replaced the `/voice set` choice with the TTS default. The CLI only reads `voiceId`; core re-derives the aliases from the merged value.
- **One catalog.** `voices` is read from the TTS provider block only. `/voice list` receives that record and Talk synthesis merges over it, so both see the same list; a `voices` list under `talk.providers` is ignored rather than consulted as a second source. A Talk record may carry just the selection (`voiceId`, as written by `/voice set`) or its own executable settings.
- **Independent commands stay independent.** When Talk supplies its own nonblank `command`, it inherits only the TTS voice defaults, not another executable's arguments, working directory, environment, output format, or timeout. Selection-only and blank-command records still inherit the TTS executable settings. This preserves existing self-contained Talk wrappers when both TTS and Talk are configured.

Out of scope: `talk.catalog` / `tts.providers` payloads read the static `provider.voices` field and do not expose this provider's configured voice catalog; consulting `listVoices` would require asynchronous catalog resolution.

## Evidence

### Follow-up verification (current head `61e6708bb89d3cef0fef1f7fba6b6b04d9bc24c0`)

The follow-up fixes execution-setting leakage when TTS and Talk both define different CLI commands. Two new regressions use the production resolver and real subprocess I/O to verify independent argv, stdin, cwd, environment, and WAV/MP3 defaults; the selection-only path remains covered.

- Before the fix, both new regressions failed on `6bf157f0dfa4ac05af570f5685bc1ae7c6becb2b`: the Talk command inherited TTS arguments/cwd/environment, and an MP3 wrapper inherited WAV output settings.
- After the fix, `pnpm test extensions/tts-local-cli/ --maxWorkers=1`: **48/48 tests passed, 2 files, 48.19s wall time** including compilation, in secretless isolation (Node 24.21.0, pnpm 12.9.0). [Focused proof run](https://crabbox.openclaw.ai/portal/runs/run_67353cd8ee775fc13c898e7d471c7a13). The published source matches the tested bytes.
- Scoped `tsgo`, type-aware lint, formatting, and `git diff --check` passed. Fresh scoped review found no actionable P0–P2 issues.
- New-head hosted test CI: [CI run 38576480132](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/38576480132) is in progress at publication and is attached to the full head above. Hosted CI duration/result is pending. Older-head green checks are not claimed as proof for this commit.
- Live Gateway proof for the mixed-command scenario and a v2026.10.3 upgrade trace are in the next section. Still no real speech-engine or Telegram run for this follow-up.

### Live Gateway on head `61e6708b`: independent Talk command + upgrade from stable 2026.10.3

Isolated Gateway in WSL (Node 24, `pnpm build` of the PR, own state dir, port 19789, `OPENCLAW_SKIP_CHANNELS=1`). Two stub CLIs each write a valid WAV and log argv, cwd, and an env marker. `tts.providers.tts-local-cli` = tts-stub with `--voice {{VoiceId}} --speed 1.0`, its own cwd, `STUB_MARK=tts`, `voices=[af_jessica,af_bella,am_michael]`, `voiceId=af_jessica`. `talk.providers.tts-local-cli` = a separate full command: talk-stub with `--voice {{VoiceId}} --talk-only-flag`, its own cwd, `STUB_MARK=talk`, no `voices`/`voiceId`.

| # | Step | Result |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `health` | `ok: true` |
| 2 | `talk.speak` | talk-stub, `--voice af_jessica --talk-only-flag`, no `--speed`; talk cwd, `STUB_MARK=talk` (voice default inherited from TTS) |
| 3 | `tts.convert` | tts-stub, `--voice af_jessica --speed 1.0`; tts cwd, `STUB_MARK=tts` |
| 4 | `/voice list` (via `chat.send`) | `tts-local-cli voices: 3` |
| 5 | `/voice set af_bella` (operator.admin client) | Talk record gains only `voiceId: "af_bella"`; its command/args/cwd/env/outputFormat unchanged; TTS `voiceId` stays `af_jessica` |
| 6 | `talk.speak`, `tts.convert` | talk-stub `--voice af_bella --talk-only-flag` with talk cwd/env; tts-stub still `af_jessica --speed 1.0` with tts cwd/env |
| 7 | Talk record → `{}` (hot reload), then restored | `{}`: tts-stub with tts args/cwd/env (selection-only inherits TTS). Restored: talk-stub again |

Upgrade: npm `latest` = `openclaw@2026.10.3` (`59cb447`), then this PR on the same state dir. Config shaped like today's users: no `voices`, `voiceId` or `{{VoiceId}}`; TTS `--voice af_jessica`, Talk an independent full command with `--voice am_michael` and its own cwd/env.

| Check | stable 2026.10.3 | PR `61e6708b` (after `doctor --fix`) |
|---|---|---|
| `talk.speak` | talk-stub `--voice am_michael --talk-only-flag`, talk cwd/env | identical |
| `tts.convert` | tts-stub `--voice af_jessica --speed 1.0`, tts cwd/env | identical |
| `/voice list` | `does not support voice listing` | `tts-local-cli voices: 0`, no error |
| config sha256 across the gateway run | unchanged | unchanged |
| `tts`, `talk`, `gateway` subtrees after `doctor --fix` | n/a | content-identical (doctor only added top-level `agents`, `plugins`, `wizard`, `meta`, `skills`) |
| `chat.history` of a session created on stable | 2 messages | same 2 messages still returned |

`doctor --fix` was run before starting the PR gateway (stable-created state needs it on current main; seen in the earlier 2026.10.2 trace as a schema-v24 refusal), so this does not show the PR gateway starting on unmigrated state. The `/voice set` step used a scratch client calling the repo's `callGateway({ method: "chat.send", scopes: ["operator.admin"] })`, since `openclaw gateway call` connects with `operator.write`.

### Live Gateway, real `/voice` command path (head `f431a9ec`)

Isolated Gateway in WSL (Node 24, own state dir and port, `OPENCLAW_SKIP_CHANNELS=1`), `tts.providers.tts-local-cli` as above with a stub voice CLI that writes a valid WAV containing `{"voice": <--voice arg>}` and logs each call. `talk.provider = tts-local-cli`, `talk.providers.tts-local-cli = {}`. Commands go through `chat.send` (plugin command dispatch), replies read from `chat.history`.

```text
## /voice list
$ openclaw gateway call chat.send --params {"sessionKey":"agent:main:main","message":"/voice list"}
tts-local-cli voices: 3
- af_jessica   id: af_jessica
- af_bella     id: af_bella
- am_michael   id: am_michael

## talk.speak before set
$ openclaw gateway call talk.speak --params {"text":"hello"}
{ "provider": "tts-local-cli", "outputFormat": "wav", "mimeType": "audio/wav", ... }
stub log: voice=af_jessica

## /voice set af_bella (operator.write client)
⚠️ /voice set requires operator.admin.          <- existing admin gate, unchanged

## /voice set af_bella (operator.admin client)
✅ tts-local-cli Talk voice set to af_bella
config: "talk": { "provider": "tts-local-cli", "providers": { "tts-local-cli": { "voiceId": "af_bella" } } }

## talk.speak after set
stub log: voice=af_jessica
          voice=af_bella                        <- Talk selection beats the TTS voiceId default (P1)

## add talk.providers.tts-local-cli.voices = ["talk-only"], then /voice list
tts-local-cli voices: 3 (af_jessica, af_bella, am_michael)   <- TTS catalog only (P2)
```

`openclaw gateway call` connects with `operator.write`, so the admin `/voice set` used a small scratch client calling the repo's `callGateway({ method: "chat.send", scopes: ["operator.admin"] })` against the same Gateway and token.

### Real engine (earlier head; provider behavior for these inputs unchanged)

Kokoro ONNX behind a `--voice` wrapper, `openclaw infer tts voices` / `infer tts convert --local` from a clean `pnpm build`:

```text
voices: af_jessica, af_bella, am_michael    (main: "does not support voice listing")
voiceId=af_jessica   bytes=139756 sha256=d327338d29a98ce2
voiceId=af_bella     bytes=141804 sha256=946f88c260afc60a
voiceId=am_michael   bytes=147948 sha256=4ee50265dfd9ea62
```

Three voices produce three distinct WAVs, so `{{VoiceId}}` reaches the engine.

### Tests and checks (WSL, Node 24, head `6bf157f0`)

```text
pnpm test extensions/tts-local-cli/speech-provider.test.ts --maxWorkers=1
  -> 39 passed; 37.2s wall
node scripts/run-oxlint.mjs --tsconfig extensions/tsconfig.json extensions/tts-local-cli
  -> 0 warnings, 0 errors
oxfmt --check (4 touched files)  -> clean
git diff --check                 -> clean
pnpm build                       -> ok (needed to run the Gateway above)
```

New regressions: a TTS record carrying core-normalized `speakerVoiceId: af_jessica` plus Talk `voiceId: af_bella` resolves without the alias and synthesizes `--voice af_bella`; a Talk-declared `voices` list is ignored and list/synthesis agree; `listVoices` does not read other config scopes.

Base-failure runs (same test file, provider swapped):

| Provider source | Result |
|---|---|
| this PR | 39/39 pass |
| previous head `1688d278` | 36 pass, **exactly the 3 new regressions fail** (Talk selection vs inherited `speakerVoiceId`; Talk-declared `voices` ignored; no cross-scope reads) |
| `main` | 13 fail: all voice tests, plus the full-Talk-record compat test (main has no `resolveTalkConfig`) |

New compat test: a pre-existing Talk record that carries its own `command`/`args`/`outputFormat` (required before Talk merging existed) resolves unchanged when TTS has no CLI block.

### Upgrade trace: stable `2026.10.2` → this PR, same state dir and config

Config shaped like today's users: no `voices`, `voiceId` or `{{VoiceId}}`; `tts.providers.tts-local-cli` passes `--voice af_jessica`, and `talk.providers.tts-local-cli` is a full executable record passing `--voice am_michael`.

| Step | stable 2026.10.2 | this PR (`f431a9ec`, after `doctor --fix`) |
|---|---|---|
| `talk.speak` | stub argv `--voice am_michael` | stub argv `--voice am_michael` (saved Talk record preserved) |
| `tts.convert` | `--voice af_jessica` | `--voice af_jessica` |
| `/voice list` | `does not support voice listing` | `tts-local-cli voices: 0` (empty, no error) |
| config sha256 across the gateway run | unchanged | unchanged (PR gateway does not rewrite config) |

The upgrade itself needed `openclaw doctor --fix`: the current-main checkout refuses the stable-created agent DB (schema v24, exit 78) until doctor migrates it. Doctor rewrote `openclaw.json` formatting and added unrelated keys (`agents`, `plugins.entries`, `wizard`, `meta`), but the `tts` and `talk` subtrees were content-identical before and after. That migration comes from `main`, not this PR. `/voice set` on the upgraded state was not re-run here; the live trace above covers it.

### Not covered

Telegram Test Server userbot proof (`proof: telegram-e2e`): that lane needs Convex-leased QA credentials that are not available to contributors. The live Gateway run above exercises the same plugin command handler and `talk.speak` path the channel uses; a maintainer-run Telegram lane would be appreciated if still required.

Needs an owner call: the new optional `voices` / `voiceId` keys on `tts.providers.tts-local-cli`, and accepting this as a partial step toward #165598.

Note for triage: the branch now touches only `extensions/tts-local-cli/**` and `docs/tools/tts/field-reference.md`; the `plugin: azure-speech` and `extensions: fish-audio` labels look left over from an earlier bad merge that has since been rebuilt.

Kept current conversation-turn-capture, channel-alias-migration, heartbeat-wake, and the already-replayed commands/agent-session-compaction files when later cleanup conflicted with new main coverage. Preserved both TTS imports; kept both owner-contention cases and write-failure cleanup in file-lock (renamed two shadowed local paths); retained existing filesystem predicate assertions in fs-safe-compat. Other CI repairs retain the readiness wait before reading the node-host promise, preserve absent-property assertions in cron persistence, give a callback no return value, retain tuple/literal types, remove redundant default type arguments, and explain changed host-isolating module mocks.

prs.title: feat(mcp): per-request header provider for volatile turn attribution on OpenClaw-owned HTTP transports
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Per-turn MCP attribution currently has to enter declarative server headers or the connection resolver. Declarative header changes invalidate the catalog; the reported Reef production measurement was **221 re-catalogs across 222 runs**. The existing connection resolver caches requester credentials for five minutes, and changed resolved headers rotate the connection. Neither path can provide fresh turn attribution while retaining a transport and its catalog.

This adds a separate plugin request-header provider for OpenClaw-owned MCP HTTP transports. Upstream main was checked at `7aaef70932b30f4d7410ae00aa65b07089de2ce0`; no equivalent provider existed.

**Deployment consumer.** The Reef embedder plugin (the same production deployment behind the measurement above) adopts this provider on release adoption: it moves `traceparent` and signed per-turn context headers off declarative server configuration and onto this seam, which retires the measured per-run re-catalog. Requester authentication stays entirely on the existing connection-resolver contract — this consumer sends attribution and turn-scoped credentials only, and its stable credentials are unchanged.

## User Impact

Plugins can attach `traceparent`, signed turn credentials, and optional direct-request credentials to individual MCP requests without rebuilding the catalog or connection. Stable authentication remains in static server configuration or the existing connection resolver.

The SDK infrastructure documentation includes registration and embedded-runtime usage. This contract covers OpenClaw-owned HTTP transports; external harness-native MCP clients need OpenClaw materialized tools to use it.

## Design

- Add `api.registerMcpServerRequestHeaderProvider({ serverName, resolve })`, following connection-resolver registration conventions. Resolver and header-provider registrations share per-server plugin ownership, and the connection resolver is authoritative regardless of registration order: a foreign provider is rejected when the resolver already exists and displaced (removed, error diagnostic on the provider's plugin) when the resolver registers later. Registry state is identical in both orders, so a declared server with a resolver is never partitioned as static.
- Only the host binds run identity. The embedded backend binds MCP attribution to the admitted run's actual `sessionId`/`sessionKey`/`runId` (internal `bindMcpRequestRun`), and the binding is revoked when that run settles. A context the host did not issue (forged) or whose run has settled (stale/reassigned) is dropped: the provider is not called and no volatile headers are sent. The public export from `openclaw/plugin-sdk/agent-harness-runtime` is `runWithMcpRequestMetadata(metadata, callback)` — caller tracing metadata only (e.g. `traceparent`), never identity.
- Capture only MCP attribution when materializing tools. Each retained tool/resource/prompt executor opens its own operation scope, preserving attribution under overlapping acquisitions and calls without capturing unrelated cancellation or runtime authority.
- Resolve volatile headers immediately before actual guarded HTTP fetches, including same-origin redirects and authentication/RPC retries. Streamable HTTP and SSE POST/EventSource paths share this boundary. Header values never enter server configuration, catalog identity, or the resolver rotation digest.
- Keep configured headers, authentication, and MCP protocol fields authoritative. Scope provider headers to the configured origin; register returned values and bare bearer tokens for secret redaction. Bound provider resolution to ten seconds and report provider failures without exposing plugin error contents.

## Correctness

Each operation owns an immutable context. Missing context explicitly clears inherited attribution and skips the provider. No transport stores a mutable latest-turn header map. Provider results are freshly merged into a new request header object and are not retained for redirect replay.

Initial SSE discovery can carry its discovery context. Shared streamable notification GETs and legacy SSE reconnects carry no volatile attribution. The streamable initialized-notification send has a short-lived scope so its shared stream parser and reconnect timers cannot retain the opening turn, including reconnects with `Last-Event-ID`. Resumable RPC streams retain their own still-active operation context. Completed scopes cannot supply headers to background callbacks.

Static authentication, requester credential revalidation/rotation, genuine configuration invalidation, `tools/list_changed`, and transport-close recovery retain their existing owners and behavior.

## Evidence

### Guarded caller-authority revalidation (Rev 24 P1, head `34a4b55ad`)

**Defect (ClawSweeper Rev 24).** `fetchWithSsrFGuard` asserts the captured guarded caller authority (`captureGuardedFetchRequestAuthority`, e.g. a live cron-root claim) *before* invoking the transport `fetchImpl`. The header wrapper is that `fetchImpl` and awaits `provider.resolve()`, so authority revoked during resolution was not re-checked before stable credentials and volatile headers reached the server.

**Fix.** `withMcpRequestHeaders` captures the guarded assertion on entry and re-asserts it immediately before dispatch, alongside the existing abort and run-context checks. A revoked caller gets the assertion's own error, and no request is sent.

**Final-effect proof.** The real-runtime e2e adds a call under `withGuardedFetchRequestAuthority` whose MCP run stays active. Caller authority is revoked while the provider is resolving. The call is rejected, and the recording loopback server's request count is unchanged (no request for `revoked_authority_operation`). **Regression-before-repair:** with the re-assertion removed, the same scenario fails with `promise resolved "{ content: [ ... ] }" instead of rejecting`, meaning the real server received and answered the revoked call. A matching unit case (`mcp-request-headers.test.ts`) fails without the fix and passes with it.

Redacted terminal capture (`OPENCLAW_E2E_SKIP_BUILD=1 OPENCLAW_E2E_VERBOSE=1 pnpm vitest run --config test/vitest/vitest.e2e.config.ts test/pr154043-real-runtime-proof.e2e.test.ts`):

```text
[pr154043-proof] allowed: real tools/call arrived with volatile header present
[pr154043-proof] canceled: rejected before I/O, server request count unchanged; pending send settled
[pr154043-proof] shared transport: subsequent attributed tools/call succeeded
[pr154043-proof] foreign: forged and SDK-asserted identity reached the server unsigned; provider never saw victim-run
[pr154043-proof] reassigned: settled run's captured context reached the server unsigned; provider never saw it
[pr154043-proof] revoked authority: provider resolved, caller authority revoked mid-resolution; rejected before I/O, server request count unchanged
 ✓ test/pr154043-real-runtime-proof.e2e.test.ts > PR #154043 real runtime proof > dispatches attributed calls and rejects canceled calls before HTTP I/O
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  1 passed (1)
```

At this head: focused suites 8 files / 156 tests passed; core `tsgo` passed; timeout-race ratchet clean for PR files; formatting and lint clean.

### Run-identity authority + final-I/O proof (Rev 22 security item, head `a6194b291`)

**Concern (ClawSweeper Rev 22).** The public `runWithMcpRequestContext` accepted caller-supplied `sessionId`/`runId`, and the documented provider signs those IDs, so a caller could assert a foreign run and obtain a signed header at final HTTP I/O. A captured context also stayed usable after its run settled.

**Fix — bind signed identity to admitted runs (the recommended option).**
- Identity is issued only by the host: `runEmbeddedAttemptWithBackend` calls the internal `bindMcpRequestRun` with the admitted run's identity, keeping enclosing caller metadata.
- Each issued context carries run authority that is revoked when the run settles. `getMcpRequestContext()` returns nothing for a revoked or never-issued context, so the provider is never invoked for it. A run that settles while headers resolve is refused before dispatch by the existing `MCP request context expired` check.
- The public SDK export narrows to `runWithMcpRequestMetadata` (metadata only). Plugins and embedded callers can no longer name a session or run.

**Final-effect proof.** `test/pr154043-real-runtime-proof.e2e.test.ts` now also drives, on the same real MCP SDK client + guarded streamable-HTTP transport + recording loopback server:
- **Foreign:** a forged frozen context `{ runId: "victim-run" }` and the public SDK helper each reach the server with **no** attribution header; the provider never sees `victim-run`.
- **Reassigned/settled:** a context captured inside a run that has since settled reaches the server with **no** attribution header; the provider never sees it.

**Regression-before-repair.** With the old trust semantics temporarily restored (any context accepted, no revocation), the proof fails at final I/O. The server received a signed header for the forged run:

```text
- Expected
+ Received
  {
-   "attribution": undefined,
+   "attribution": "synthetic-victim-run",
    "rpcMethod": "tools/call",
  }
 ❯ test/pr154043-real-runtime-proof.e2e.test.ts:193:75
```

Redacted terminal capture after the fix (`OPENCLAW_E2E_SKIP_BUILD=1 OPENCLAW_E2E_VERBOSE=1 pnpm vitest run --config test/vitest/vitest.e2e.config.ts test/pr154043-real-runtime-proof.e2e.test.ts`):

```text
[pr154043-proof] allowed: real tools/call arrived with volatile header present
[pr154043-proof] canceled: rejected before I/O, server request count unchanged; pending send settled
[pr154043-proof] shared transport: subsequent attributed tools/call succeeded
[pr154043-proof] foreign: forged and SDK-asserted identity reached the server unsigned; provider never saw victim-run
[pr154043-proof] reassigned: settled run's captured context reached the server unsigned; provider never saw it
 ✓ test/pr154043-real-runtime-proof.e2e.test.ts > PR #154043 real runtime proof > dispatches attributed calls and rejects canceled calls before HTTP I/O 61ms
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  1 passed (1)
```

Unit coverage (`src/agents/mcp-request-headers.test.ts`) adds: forged identity never resolves headers, captured context revoked after its run settles, and a run settling mid-resolution refuses dispatch. `agent-bundle-mcp-runtime.request-headers.test.ts` now holds each turn open across acquisition and execution, as a host run does, and asserts that a settled turn's executor sends no attribution. On the merged head (current main `3f7689e64`): focused suites (`mcp-request-headers`, `agent-bundle-mcp-runtime{,.request-headers}`, `mcp-transport`, `mcp-http-transport`, `mcp-http-fetch`, `backend`, requester-connect, `registry-registrars-network.mcp-request-headers`) 10 files / 159 tests passed; both PR e2e proofs passed; core `tsgo` passed; `plugin-sdk:surface:check` passed (budget pinned to exactly this PR's two exports); formatting and lint clean. The merge resolved main's `mcp-http-fetch.ts` redirect-policy refactor by applying the provider wrap inside the shared builder.

### Registration-order fix + authority-chain proof (head `2587f4f3`)

**Defect (ClawSweeper P1, Rev 8).** `hasMcpServerOwnerConflict` was first-registration-wins across both seams: a request-header provider registered first by plugin A caused plugin B's later `registerMcpServerConnectionResolver` for the same server to be rejected. `partitionMcpServersByConnectionScope` then found no resolver and classified the declared server as **static**, exposing its configured connection to requesters the resolver would have excluded. The PR's own registrar test pinned that behavior.

**Fix.** The connection resolver is authoritative regardless of order. `registerMcpServerConnectionResolver` still fails closed against a different plugin's resolver; against a different plugin's *provider* it now displaces it — the provider entry is removed and an error diagnostic is reported on the provider's plugin (`MCP server request header provider for "<name>" displaced: connection resolver registered by plugin "<resolver plugin>" owns requester admission`). `registerMcpServerRequestHeaderProvider` is unchanged (rejected when a different plugin owns either seam). Final registry state is identical in both registration orders. `docs/plugins/sdk-overview/infrastructure.md` states the rule.

**Regression proof, unit** (`src/plugins/registry-registrars-network.mcp-request-headers.test.ts`, `it.each(["provider","resolver"])`): with the registrar fix reverted, the provider-first case fails —

```text
AssertionError: expected [ { level: 'error', …(3) } ] to deep equally contain ObjectContaining{…}

- Expected:
ObjectContaining {
  "level": "error",
  "message": StringContaining "displaced",
  "pluginId": "plugin-a",
}

+ Received:
[
  {
    "level": "error",
    "message": "MCP server connection resolver for \"user-mail\" rejected: already registered by plugin \"plugin-a\"",
    "pluginId": "plugin-b",
    "source": "/plugins/plugin-b/index.ts",
  },
]
```

— and passes with the fix (5/5). Both orders additionally assert, under `withPluginRuntimeRegistryScope`, that `partitionMcpServersByConnectionScope` puts `user-mail` in `resolverRequesterServerNames` and `staticServers` is empty.

**Authority-chain proof, real transports** (`test/pr154043-registration-order-proof.e2e.test.ts`, no transport/SDK mocks). plugin-a registers a request-header provider for `user-mail`; plugin-b registers a requester-scoped connection resolver that returns `{ url: <loopback>, headers: { Authorization: "Bearer proof-token" } }` only for `allowed-requester` and `null` otherwise. The declared config is `url: "https://placeholder.invalid/mcp"`; the loopback (`startRequesterScopedMcpProofServer`) 404s without the bearer and records every request. Driven through `materializeRequesterScopedMcpToolsForHarnessRun` from `openclaw/plugin-sdk/agent-harness-runtime`. In **both** orders: `user-mail` partitions as resolver-scoped, never static; the allowed requester materializes tools and executes `requester_probe`, and every loopback request carried the bearer and none carried plugin-a's header; an excluded requester and a run with no `requesterSenderId` get no tools and the loopback request count does not move; plugin-a's provider is never invoked.

With the registrar fix reverted, the provider-first case fails at the static-partition assertion (the exact exposure):

```text
AssertionError: expected { 'user-mail': { …(2) } } to deeply equal {}

- Expected
+ Received

- {}
+ {
+   "user-mail": {
+     "transport": "streamable-http",
+     "url": "https://placeholder.invalid/mcp",
+   },
+ }

 ❯ test/pr154043-registration-order-proof.e2e.test.ts:69
```

Redacted passing capture (`OPENCLAW_E2E_SKIP_BUILD=1 OPENCLAW_E2E_VERBOSE=1 pnpm vitest run --config test/vitest/vitest.e2e.config.ts test/pr154043-registration-order-proof.e2e.test.ts test/pr154043-real-runtime-proof.e2e.test.ts`):

```text

[pr154043-order-proof] provider-first: user-mail partitioned as resolver-scoped
[pr154043-order-proof] provider-first: allowed requester executed requester_probe; loopback served 5 bearer-authorized requests
[pr154043-order-proof] provider-first: excluded + anonymous requesters got no tools; loopback request count unchanged (5); foreign provider never invoked
```

prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

A2A inbound dispatch consumes every exception even though its sole production HTTP caller already owns the same failed-task outcome.

## User Impact

Let the private dispatch helper reject to the existing HTTP task-failure owner. Preserve the original failure message and terminal task state, blocked-request wakeup, reply correlation, deferred outcomes, command refusal, peer/session isolation, validation, authentication and detached admission/settlement. No protocol or public SDK change.

## Why This Change Was Made

Seven net production lines removed (+113/-120) and six test lines removed (+8/-14). Three production lines are formatter compaction of the existing rejection call, not another behavior cut. This is the A2A area of the preserved wide cleanup family, split for bounded CI attribution. No new error carrier, helper, state, retry or public owner.

## Best-effort tradeoffs accepted

- The private helper now rejects rather than recording task failure itself. Its sole awaited production callback reaches the retained HTTP catch, which invokes the same taskStore.fail. Failure recording occurs after detached continuation settlement; accept that extra bookkeeping microtask instead of adding another owner/fence. In-memory tasks are already discarded on restart. Current admitted work and live security authority remain unchanged.
- Original ad1e946c/#130008 introduced both catches together with retained detached work/security/interop support. Full original body and determining source were inspected; no human actual-use incident specifically requiring duplicate total catches was established. The independent HTTP admission catch stays because it also handles failures before the helper starts.

## Evidence

- Complete current inbound, gateway, HTTP and task-store owners, direct public barrels, channel docs and determining webhook/admission frames inspected. The private helper is not SDK-exported. Ordinary callback-reported failure/deferred/terminal outcomes stay at their own owners.
- Existing helper fixture is migrated to exact Error rejection with guaranteed cleanup. The unchanged real HTTP-handler/task-store case still asserts peer-visible FAILED and exact dispatch unavailable text. Existing security, reply correlation, task-reference ownership and response-first rejection coverage remains. No new seam, skip, retry, timeout increase, suppression or baseline expansion.

prs.title: fix(memory-wiki): preserve human notes on OKF concept re-import
prs.body:
Closes #175700

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: Re-importing an OKF bundle (`openclaw wiki okf import`) silently deletes handwritten Notes on imported concept pages.

## User Impact

User impact: Re-running `openclaw wiki okf import` now keeps any human `## Notes` block on concept pages; only generated content is refreshed, matching the documented "human note blocks are preserved across regeneration" invariant and the behavior of source sync and ChatGPT import.

## Why This Change Was Made

`writeOkfConceptPage` replaced the whole page with freshly rendered content, and OKF-rendered pages never carried a `## Notes` + human-marker slot, so there was nothing for a re-import to preserve.

The rendered body now includes the Notes slot (same layout as `renderImportedSourcePage`). Because OKF producer Markdown is unrestricted, preservation is scoped to the local slot anchored at the end of the page:

- The slot is located by its `## Notes` heading plus the closing human marker at the page tail, so:
  - A copied marker example pasted inside the Notes block no longer truncates the preserved range 鈥?the complete outer block (including the example) survives.
  - A legacy fenced producer marker example (from a page produced before the slot existed) is not promoted into the Notes slot; the local slot starts empty.
- The existing page is read through the shared `readExistingWikiPage` recovery owner, so a persistent read failure (e.g. transient EBUSY/EMFILE) aborts the import instead of replacing the page with an empty Notes scaffold.

## Evidence

- Regression tests in `extensions/memory-wiki/src/okf.test.ts` and `wiki-notes-read-retry.test.ts` (14/14 and 16/16 pass locally on the merged head; 30/30 across both files):
  - `preserves human notes on OKF concept pages across re-import` 鈥?fails on `main` (note wiped; `expected ... to contain 'HANDWRITTEN NOTE MUST SURVIVE'`), passes with the fix.
  - `re-imports legacy OKF pages that carry an unmarked producer Notes section` 鈥?covers upgrade compatibility for pages produced by the previous importer (data-model compatibility).
  - `upgrades a pre-Notes OKF concept page to the Notes format on re-import` 鈥?writes a page exactly as the pre-fix importer persisted it (no `## Notes` slot, no human markers), then re-imports and asserts the existing data loads, keeps its body, gains the new slot, and still parses as a concept page (data-model compatibility).
  - `preserves only the local Notes slot when the producer body contains literal human markers` 鈥?covers the scoped-preservation case.
  - `preserves the complete outer Notes block when notes contain a copied marker example` 鈥?covers the outer-boundary finding.
  - `does not promote a legacy fenced producer marker example into the Notes slot` 鈥?covers the legacy-producer-example finding.
  - `leaves OKF concept pages unchanged after a persistent existing-page read failure` 鈥?covers the read-failure finding (page unchanged, import rejects).
- The tests drive the real `importMemoryWikiOkfBundle` through a real vault filesystem.
- `oxfmt` clean on changed files; `git diff --check` clean; `oxlint` clean.
- CI: `openclaw/ci-gate` and related checks are re-running for the merged head (was previously green on the pre-merge head).

## Data-model compatibility

Existing stored vault content is exercised by the regression suite:

- `upgrades a pre-Notes OKF concept page to the Notes format on re-import` writes the exact format the pre-fix importer persisted (frontmatter + producer body, no `## Notes` slot, no human markers), re-imports with the fixed importer, and asserts the existing page loads, keeps its body, gains the new Notes slot, and still parses as a concept page.
- `re-imports legacy OKF pages that carry an unmarked producer Notes section` writes a page exactly as the previous importer produced it (frontmatter + producer body with a plain `## Notes` heading, no human markers), then re-imports and asserts the page loads and is refreshed with the new slot intact.
- `does not promote a legacy fenced producer marker example into the Notes slot` simulates an old page whose producer body contains a fenced marker example and asserts re-import refreshes it without misclassifying the example as human content.
- The OKF import path's real-file read (`readExistingWikiPage` recovery owner) matches the shared owner already used by source sync and ChatGPT import, so upgrade behavior is consistent with those paths.
- Related upstream memory-wiki fixes merged to `main` since this branch started (e.g. #173931, #174573) touch the ChatGPT/ingest/source-sync writers and `wiki-notes-read-retry.test.ts`; this branch was merged with current `main` so the OKF fix composes with them (the OKF writer was not modified by those PRs).

Note: this fix was authored by an agent (CoMind) as part of a bug-hunt on the memory-wiki module. A shipped-CLI terminal capture was not produced in this agent environment: the CLI wrapper's artifact-lock step cannot verify Gateway offline state here (a separate local CoMind agent session holds the workspace lock, and the Windows Scheduled Task service command cannot be inspected), so `openclaw` commands fail before the importer runs. The regression tests instead drive the real production importer (`importMemoryWikiOkfBundle`) against a real vault filesystem, including injected persistent read failures. Root cause, fix, and tests are provided for maintainer review; the CLI evidence item needs a human runner.

prs.title: improve(sessions): faster inbound reply capture on agents with many conversation deliveries
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

When a user replies to an earlier message, OpenClaw first checks whether the reply answers a pending conversation turn. On agents whose database holds many conversation deliveries, that check scans the delivery table instead of using the index built for it, and it runs before the reply is dispatched. A reply that is not an answer to a ledgered turn (a miss) scans the most.

## User Impact

User impact: inbound replies are captured faster on agents whose database holds many conversation deliveries across many conversations, with identical lookup results on every measured input and in a per-status sweep (the one difference is which of two rows tied on `updated_at` is returned, see the contract table). One hit path gets slower on large stores (marked below). Measured through the production lookup on both arms, with and without planner statistics, ms per 200 lookups:

| Store | Case | Phase | Before | After |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| a: 200,000 delivery rows, 50 conversations | miss | with statistics | 6937.923 to 7135.775 | 57.873 to 118.11 |
| a | miss | without statistics | 6196.932 to 6765.907 | 57.814 to 57.898 |
| a | hit on an older `turn` row | with statistics | 6883.977 to 7817.323 | 59.959 to 61.96 |
| a | hit on an older `turn` row | without statistics | 6416.2 to 6806.746 | 58.856 to 60.336 |
| a | hit on the conversation's newest `turn` row | with statistics | 10.024 to 10.696 | 59.674 to 125.585 (slower) |
| a | hit on the conversation's newest `turn` row | without statistics | 9.272 to 10.189 | 58.071 to 58.775 (slower) |
| b: 200,000 delivery rows, 1 conversation | miss | with statistics | 2604.635 to 3327.742 | 2130.611 to 2145.433 |
| b | miss | without statistics | 7661.396 to 8265.693 | 2104.302 to 2167.453 |
| b | hit on the conversation's newest `turn` row | with statistics | 2569.122 to 3343.634 | 2128.977 to 2170.979 |
| b | hit on the conversation's newest `turn` row | without statistics | 9.659 to 11.492 | 2053.875 to 2157.32 (slower) |
| c: 666 delivery rows, 50 conversations | miss | with statistics | 20.934 to 22.531 | 9.075 to 10.832 |
| c | miss | without statistics | 21.532 to 22.441 | 9.004 to 9.264 |
| d: 666 delivery rows, 1 conversation | miss | with statistics | 13.764 to 14.69 | 15.244 to 18.922 (same plan, no gain) |
| d | miss | without statistics | 22.928 to 30.032 | 16.918 to 17.225 |
| e: copy of a real agent store, 18 conversations, 0 delivery rows | miss | as is | 12.475 to 12.601 | 12.33 to 12.73 |

Ranges are the minimum to maximum of the two rounds' medians per arm. Per lookup, the store a miss with statistics is about 34.7 to 35.7 ms before and 0.29 to 0.59 ms after (ms per 200 lookups divided by 200). The 200,000-row stores are synthetic growth cases; the 666-row stores use the status counts reported for one real agent store in #139330 (643 `sent`, 23 `unknown`, no `turn` rows), with a synthetic conversation layout, and differ by a fraction of a millisecond per lookup. The real store copy has no delivery rows, so no real-data gain is claimed.

The same change shows at the shipped seam. A Gateway built from each tree, receiving inbound replies through its bundled QA test channel, runs this lookup on its session read worker with the bound list and the `updated_at` walk on base and with the literal list and the reply index on this branch, for a ledger miss and for a reply to a delivery the Gateway recorded itself. With the store a layout seeded into that Gateway's ledger, the miss took 36305 and 36206 µs on the worker on base and 60 and 69 µs on this branch (Shipped Gateway inbound reply trace below).

Cost: a hit on the newest `turn` row of a conversation gets slower on a many-conversation store (store a: 10.024 to 10.696 before and 59.674 to 125.585 after with statistics; 9.272 to 10.189 before and 58.071 to 58.775 after without). On a single-conversation store without planner statistics the same hit goes from 9.659 to 11.492 before to 2053.875 to 2157.32 after. Before the change, the `updated_at` walk finds the newest row first and stops. After the change, the plan searches the conversation's rows in the reply index and sorts them for `ORDER BY updated_at`. For comparison, the new hit cost stays below the before-change cost of a miss on the same store in every measured cell. The remaining cost is named here as a known edge case (AGENTS.md, Choose good compromises: "Name accepted edge case in comment or PR instead of coding around it"): results are unchanged for every measured input, and the new time stays sub-millisecond per lookup on the many-conversation store.

No schema, index, config key, stored byte, retention, durability, or permission change.

## Why This Change Was Made

The lookup is awaited before ordinary dispatch (`src/auto-reply/reply/dispatch-from-config.prepare-context.ts:468`), and it runs a second time on the parent conversation for a threaded message whose first lookup misses (`src/auto-reply/reply/conversation-turn-capture.ts:161` and `:166`). It is written with a bound status list (`status IN (?, ?, ?)`), so SQLite cannot use the partial index that was created for exactly this lookup, and instead walks `conversation_deliveries` in `updated_at` order across all conversations until it finds a match or runs out of rows. A miss walks the whole table because there is no match to stop at.

`idx_agent_conversation_deliveries_reply` exists for this lookup (`src/state/openclaw-agent-schema.sql:253-255`, `ON conversation_deliveries(conversation_id, platform_message_id, prepared_message_id) WHERE status IN ('queued', 'sent', 'replied')`; the index and this lookup were added together in #109411, commit a2ec3f69046 "refactor: separate external conversations from local sessions (#109411)"), but the lookup never reaches it. SQLite admits a partial index only when a query term provably implies the index's `WHERE`, and that check is an expression comparison (`whereUsablePartialIndex`, SQLite `src/where.c:3699-3727` at tag version-3.53.0, via `sqlite3ExprImpliesExpr`, `src/expr.c:6827-6840`). A top-level bound variable can be matched against an index literal (`src/expr.c:6554-6556`), but an `IN` list is compared through `sqlite3ExprListCompare` (`src/expr.c:6615`), which calls `sqlite3ExprCompare` with no parse context per element (`src/expr.c:6646-6656`), so a bound value inside a list never matches. The same code is present at tag version-3.44.0 (`src/expr.c:5933` and `:6035`), the oldest SQLite line the repo supports (`docs/install/node-compatibility.md:44` requires 3.44.6+ within 3.44.x). A synthetic probe reproduces both halves: a partial index `WHERE s = 'sent'` with a bound `s = ?` plans as `SEARCH t USING INDEX p_eq (a=?)`, while a partial index `WHERE s IN (...)` with a bound `s IN (?, ?, ?)` plans as `SCAN t`. This explanation comes from reading the SQLite source plus that probe; the planner internals were not instrumented. `sql.lit` is a Kysely builder node, not raw SQL, and `pnpm lint:kysely` passes.

Statistics: planner statistics for an agent database come from session maintenance, which runs `PRAGMA analysis_limit = 1000; ANALYZE main;` after a pass that deleted at least 64 session entries (`src/config/sessions/session-accessor.sqlite-maintenance-store.ts:65-80`, `src/config/sessions/session-accessor.sqlite-maintenance.ts:59` and `:124`), so a given agent database may or may not carry them. The copy of a real agent store used below carries one `sqlite_stat1` row for `conversation_deliveries`. Both phases are therefore reported for every store.

Storage-changes checkpoint: `docs/reference/database-schemas/storage-changes.md:2893` says the checkpoint "normally does not apply to a read-only query that preserves existing semantics, a bounded query-plan improvement with no material write/disk tradeoff". This change is a read-only query with no write or disk tradeoff; its results are the rows the existing `ORDER BY updated_at DESC LIMIT 1` admits, and only the choice between rows tied on `updated_at`, which the query does not specify, can differ (contract table).

Alternatives:
- Keep the bound `IN` and write the status test as an OR of bound equalities: SQLite rewrites an OR of equalities on one column into a virtual `IN` term built from the same right-hand operands (`src/whereexpr.c:907-935`), which are still variables. The probe plans `(s = ? OR s = ? OR s = ?)` as `SCAN t`.
- An OR of literal equalities uses the index through the same rewrite, but it is just as order-sensitive (the probe plans a reordered OR as `SCAN t`) and is a larger diff.
- Widen the reply index by dropping its `WHERE`. That removes the dependence on matching text, but it changes an existing index definition and needs a schema version step. It is not in this PR.
- Add a plain `conversation_deliveries(conversation_id)` index. Also a schema change, not in this PR.

## The change in one sentence

Emit the three reply statuses as SQL literals, in the index's own text and order, so SQLite can match the partial index; every other value stays bound.

Diff: 2 files, +53 / -2 (production file +8 / -2, test file +45).

| Input case | Expected outcome |
|---|---|
| Reply to a message that has no ledgered `turn` delivery (miss) | Same `undefined` result; plan uses `idx_agent_conversation_deliveries_reply` instead of the `updated_at` walk |
| Hit on an older `turn` row | Same record; plan uses the reply index |

All of the following ran on one machine (Mac Studio, macOS; the measurements and probes under Node v24.21.0 with node:sqlite SQLite 3.53.4 unless noted) at base `d4d2c3dd1e3` and this branch. The measurements, the consumer and owning-directory test runs, and the builds ran on trees whose production query is identical to this diff; they differ from it only in the wording of the new code comment and, in the new test, one comment line and one statement-count assertion. Script and raw outputs: https://github.com/etzelm/openclaw/tree/e5a3eaa933f7a640426e6297c65845c63c775f61/t3-01-reply-lookup/evidence.

### Method

BEFORE is a checkout of base `d4d2c3dd1e3`; AFTER is this branch; the two trees differ only by this diff's production change and the new test. Each arm's production `readConversationDeliveryInDatabase` and `openOpenClawAgentDatabase` are loaded from that arm's source through tsx, because the dist chunk names are hashed. Fixtures are seeded with plain INSERTs into a file-backed agent database: store a, 200,000 rows over 50 conversations (30,000 `turn` rows); store b, 200,000 rows in 1 conversation (30,000 `turn` rows); store c, 666 rows over 50 conversations and store d, 666 rows in 1 conversation, both using the status counts reported for one real agent store in #139330 (643 `sent`, 23 `unknown`, no `turn` rows) with a synthetic conversation layout. Hit cases use the newest and oldest `turn` row of one conversation. Each cell is the median of 5 samples of 200 lookups after 2 warm-up samples. Each store is measured without statistics and after `ANALYZE`; each arm ran two rounds. The SQL and bound parameters each lookup executes are captured and passed to EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN. The first 16 hex digits of a sha256 over every returned record are equal for BEFORE and AFTER in every case, including both hit cases and the miss (hashes: miss `7598d56576ac2c0d`; store a newest hit `b39b0f0c8588f22c`, oldest hit `b239a888beab8eee`; store b newest hit `00721dde23dd530a`, oldest hit `12a5de9f4a2dc8d9`).

A per-status parity sweep ran on both arms through the same production lookup. For each schema status (created, queued, sent, suppressed, rejected, unknown, replied) it inserts one `turn` row, plus one `send` row with status `sent`, and looks each up by platform message id and by prepared message id. The queued, sent and replied rows are found; the other four statuses and the `send` row are not found; every hash is equal between the arms (queued `adfc07869c3fc5b2`, sent `9382bcd4fb874cdc`, replied `56d50c4d1c742df8`, not found `eb045d78d2731073`), and the two outputs are identical apart from the first line, which names the arm. The lookup results are byte-identical for these inputs. A separate tie-order probe (two eligible rows with equal `updated_at`) is the contract table's tie row.

Store e is a backup copy of a real agent store (18 conversations, 0 delivery rows). The production opener refuses that copy because it needs a schema migration (schema version 24), so the harness opens it directly with node:sqlite and passes it to the production lookup.

Scripts, the proof-build patch, build summary and redacted logs: https://github.com/etzelm/openclaw/tree/f6b19643f95f3ff174a004faa48366105cc62cfc/t3-01-reply-lookup/evidence-gateway (`INDEX.md` describes every file).

What ran. Each arm (base `d4d2c3dd1e3` and this branch) was built with `OPENCLAW_BUILD_PRIVATE_QA=1 pnpm build`, the build mode that bundles the QA test channel `qa-channel`, and started as a real Gateway process, `node dist/index.js gateway run --bind loopback`, by the repo's qa-lab Gateway child harness (`extensions/qa-lab/src/gateway-child-setup.ts:183` and `:330-340`). The harness gives the child an isolated HOME, state directory and config, and its usual QA runtime flags, among them `OPENCLAW_TEST_FAST=1`, `OPENCLAW_SKIP_STARTUP_MODEL_PREWARM=1` and `OPENCLAW_NO_RESPAWN=1` (`extensions/qa-lab/src/gateway-child-env.ts:58-157`). The qa-lab message bus plays the chat platform and the qa-lab mock provider plays the model. Inbound messages are injected on the bus and enter the Gateway through the bundled `qa-channel` plugin and ordinary channel dispatch, which calls `capturePendingConversationTurnReply` (`src/auto-reply/reply/dispatch-from-config.prepare-context.ts:468`). For a reply with a reply-to id, once the session entry is read and no in-process reply waiter claims the reply, that function runs this lookup (`src/auto-reply/reply/conversation-turn-capture.ts:159-161`) on the session read worker. The driver:

1. sends an ordinary DM, which registers the conversation;
2. calls the Gateway RPC `conversations.turn` on that conversation, which records a `turn` delivery and sends a question through `qa-channel`;
3. stops the Gateway and starts it again on the same state, so no in-process reply waiter can remain; in the seeded runs, while the Gateway is stopped, it also inserts the store a layout of the timing measurements into the Gateway's agent database (50 more conversations, 200,000 delivery rows with the same status mix and 30,000 `turn` rows, all older than the Gateway's turn row, no planner statistics);
4. sends a reply whose reply-to id, `qa-reply-target-never-delivered`, was never delivered (ledger miss);
5. sends a reply to the question from step 2 (matching delivery).

Each arm ran twice with only the Gateway's own ledger rows and twice with the seeded ledger, alternating arms, on Node v24.21.0 with SQLite 3.53.4 as printed by the Gateway.

Two additions that are not part of this PR were applied identically to both arms:

- A proof-build patch to `extensions/qa-channel/src/channel.ts` (2 added lines; the patch and `git diff` of each patched tree are published, and the two diffs are byte-identical). `qa-channel` does not implement `prepareConversationTurnMessageId`, the optional outbound hook that opts a channel into `conversations.turn` (`src/channels/plugins/outbound.types.ts:142`); without it the Gateway rejects step 2 with `Channel qa-channel does not support correlated conversation turns; use conversations_send` (`src/gateway/conversation-turn.ts:169`). The only channel that implements the hook is `reef`, which needs a relay and a paired peer. The patch changes no core file and nothing on the lookup path. The QA bus assigns its own message ids, so the sent id differs from the prepared id; the Gateway then keeps the ledger row but cancels its in-process waiter at once, and answers the turn with `"status":"sent"`, `"correlationPersisted":true` and `"error":"Channel delivery did not preserve its prepared message id; reply correlation was disabled."` (`src/gateway/conversation-turn.ts:336-347`). The restart in step 3 removes any waiter in any case.
- A read-only observer (`reply-lookup-observer.mjs`) loaded with `NODE_OPTIONS=--import`, which Node also applies to worker threads. It wraps `node:sqlite` and, for this lookup's statement, appends one JSON record with the thread, the statement text, the bound parameters, the returned rows, the wall time of that one statement call (`statementMicros`), `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN` for that statement and those parameters on the same connection, and the built module names on the stack. It also records inserts and updates on `conversation_deliveries`. It does not change any statement, parameter or result.

What the Gateway did next. After the matching lookup, the capture path calls `markConversationDeliverySent` (`conversation-turn-capture.ts:174-176`), which is allowed only from `created` or `queued` (`src/config/sessions/conversation-delivery-store.ts:230`); the row is already `sent`, so the kernel returns it unchanged (`conversation-delivery-store.kernel.ts:198`) and no further ledger write appears in the observer log. Both replies then went to ordinary dispatch: after each restart the Gateway log shows one `[agent/embedded] [context-diag] pre-prompt` agent run for each of the two replies (three per run, counting the first DM), and the bus shows the Gateway's answer to each reply. A reply that the capture path consumes instead ends at `dispatch-from-config.prepare-context.ts:468-479` with reason `conversation-turn-reply` and starts no agent run.

What this shows: an inbound channel reply, received by a Gateway built from each tree, reaches this lookup on the session read worker exactly once. On this branch the worker executes the statement with the literal status list and SQLite plans it on `idx_agent_conversation_deliveries_reply`; on base it executes the bound list and plans the `updated_at` walk. On a ledger seeded to store a's layout, a miss took 36305 and 36206 µs on the worker on base against 60 and 69 µs on this branch. The miss returns no row; the reply to a delivery the Gateway recorded itself, before a restart, returns that delivery record on both arms; both go on to ordinary dispatch.

What it does not show: a real external channel (`qa-channel` is the repo's QA test channel, messages are injected on the qa-lab bus, and the turn hook comes from the proof-build patch); a ledger built by real traffic (the large ledger is the synthetic store a layout, written into the agent database while the Gateway was stopped); planner statistics on the Gateway's store; the hit path on a `queued` or `replied` row; the slower newest-row hit in a busy conversation; and the second lookup on the parent conversation for a threaded reply (the trace uses a direct message without a thread).

### Tests

`pnpm test src/state/sqlite-query-plan.test.ts` on this branch:

```
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  8 passed (8)
[test] passed 1 Vitest shard in 20.67s
```

The six test files that reach the lookup through its callers (`src/infra/outbound/delivery-queue.recovery.test.ts`, `src/infra/outbound/conversation-delivery.queue-admission.test.ts`, `src/auto-reply/reply/conversation-turn-capture.test.ts`, `src/gateway/conversation-route-ownership.worker.test.ts`, `src/gateway/conversation-turn.test.ts`, `src/gateway/conversation-send.test.ts`):

```
 Test Files  2 passed (2)
      Tests  29 passed (29)
 Test Files  4 passed (4)
      Tests  84 passed (84)
[test] passed 2 Vitest shards in 93.13s
```

Owning directory, `pnpm test src/config/sessions`, run twice. Each run ran two Vitest shards and both runs reported the same two summaries:

```
 Test Files  18 passed (18)
      Tests  221 passed (221)

 Test Files  2 failed | 355 passed | 1 skipped (358)
      Tests  2 failed | 3224 passed | 1 skipped (3227)
```

The wall lines were `[test] failed 2 Vitest shards in 604.64s` and `[test] failed 2 Vitest shards in 728.49s`. The directory includes the two store test files that call the lookup directly through `findConversationTurnDeliveryByReplyTarget`, `src/config/sessions/conversation-delivery-store.test.ts` and `src/config/sessions/conversation-delivery-store.memory.test.ts`; both passed in both runs.

The two failures are the same two cases in both runs, both timeouts under full-directory load: `session-accessor.sqlite-archive-read.test.ts > SQLite transcript archive reads > reads a short final answer beyond the runtime string limit while the caller stays responsive` (`Test timed out in 30000ms`) and `session-accessor.reply-init-concurrency.test.ts > session accessor cross-process concurrency > commits after same-session activity from another process` (`timeout waiting for concurrency worker reply-init`). Neither file references conversation deliveries. Run alone, both files pass:

```
 Test Files  2 passed (2)
      Tests  11 passed (11)
[test] passed 1 Vitest shard in 39.87s
```

### Regression proof (red/green)

The new test drives the production `readConversationDeliveryInDatabase` against an agent database opened by `openOpenClawAgentDatabase`, captures the one `conversation_deliveries` statement it executes together with its bound parameters, runs EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN on exactly that statement and those parameters, and asserts the plan contains `idx_agent_conversation_deliveries_reply` and does not contain `SCAN delivery`. It fails on the original defect and does not mirror the implementation: it asserts the plan, not the SQL text. It runs on an empty store, which has no planner statistics, so the plan depends only on whether the partial index is usable; that keeps the assertion deterministic.

On unchanged base `d4d2c3dd1e3` with only the test file added, it fails on the original behaviour:

```
 FAIL   unit  src/state/sqlite-query-plan.test.ts > sqlite hot query plans > keeps the reply-target delivery lookup on the partial reply index
AssertionError: expected 'SEARCH conversation USING INDEX sqlit…' to contain 'idx_agent_conversation_deliveries_rep…'

- Expected
+ Received

- idx_agent_conversation_deliveries_reply
+ SEARCH conversation USING INDEX sqlite_autoindex_conversations_1 (conversation_id=?)
+ SCAN delivery USING INDEX idx_agent_conversation_deliveries_updated

[test] failed 1 Vitest shard in 8.28s
```

On this branch it passes (output above: 8 passed). With the status list reordered to `["sent", "queued", "replied"]`, narrowed to `["queued", "sent"]`, or replaced by the original bound list, the same test fails each time with `Tests  1 failed | 7 passed (8)`.

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| typecheck core / core tests | ok |
| lint core changed files | ok (0 warnings, 0 errors) |
| format changed files | ok |
| SQLite dialect ratchet | ok (mechanical, design, and engine-maintenance constructs in changed files 0 -> 0) |
| SQLite worker ratchet | ok (T1 live calls 186 -> 186) |
| line-cap growth ratchet, database-first legacy-store guard, runtime import cycles | ok |
| `git diff --check` | clean |
| max-lines suppression ratchet | failed on `ui/src/pages/chat/components/chat-message.test.tsx`, `ui/src/pages/config/config-page-state.ts`, `ui/src/pages/sessions/sessions-page-state.ts`; none are in this diff, and the same check fails on the same three files in a clean checkout of `d4d2c3dd1e3` |
| dead export scan | failed on `src/config/sessions/combined-store-paths.ts` (`discoveryReadOptions`), `src/shared/node-list-types.ts` (`NODE_APPROVAL_STATE_VALUES`), `src/state/user-profiles.types.ts` (`UserProfileAuthority`), plus `extensions/slack/src/monitor/slash.commands.test-harness.ts` (`getFirstActionElementFromCommand`) in the full-tree scan; none are in this diff, and the same scan fails on the same exports in a clean checkout of `d4d2c3dd1e3` |

`pnpm lint:kysely`:

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| Kysely guardrails | ok (`Kysely guardrails OK`, exit 0) |

`pnpm test src/state/sqlite-query-plan.test.ts` with `--maxWorkers=1`, each timed run directly after one untimed warm-up run of the same tree:

| Tree | Tests | File duration | Shard wall | New case |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| base `d4d2c3dd1e3` | 7 | 5.80 s | 7.55 s | none |
| this branch | 8 | 5.87 s | 7.68 s | 94 ms |

The new case adds one file-backed agent database and one EXPLAIN; the file duration is dominated by transform.

## Gaps, stated plainly

- `pnpm changed:lanes --json` for this diff returns `core: true, coreTests: true` and every other lane false, with `extensionImpactFromCore: false`. The six test files above ran anyway because they exercise the lookup. Unrelated suites were not run.
- `src/config/sessions` ran in two shards (358 files and 18 files); 2 cases in the 358-file shard failed by timeout under full-directory load in both runs (cases named above); neither file references conversation deliveries, and both pass alone. They are not addressed here.
- The max-lines ratchet and dead export scan fail on files outside this diff and on a clean base checkout; they are not addressed here.
- The timing tables come from each arm's source loaded through tsx, not from the built artifacts. The Gateway trace runs the built artifacts and times single statements on the worker (two rounds per arm, one lookup per case per round), which confirms the store a miss figure but is not a benchmark.
- The Gateway trace uses the private QA build, the QA test channel `qa-channel` with messages injected on the qa-lab bus, and the qa-lab mock model provider, with a 2-line proof-build patch that gives `qa-channel` the `conversations.turn` hook and a read-only `node:sqlite` observer preload. Neither addition is part of this PR; both are published with the evidence. No external chat platform was used. The large ledger in that trace is the synthetic store a layout written into the stopped Gateway's agent database, not traffic. The private QA build exits 1 on both arms, with and without the proof patch, at the private QA plugin SDK declaration size budget (5449546 bytes against 5340536), a check on generated declarations that this diff does not touch; the two phases that run after that check, `write-cli-startup-metadata` and `write-build-info`, did not run. Both Gateway processes of every run started from the produced `dist/` and processed the run's messages.
- The Gateway trace covers a ledger miss and a hit on a `sent` row in a direct conversation. A hit on a `queued` or `replied` row, the slower newest-row hit in a busy conversation, planner statistics on the Gateway's store, and the second lookup on the parent conversation for a threaded reply were not traced through the Gateway.
- The harness issues a plain `ANALYZE` for the statistics phase; session maintenance issues `PRAGMA analysis_limit = 1000; ANALYZE main;`, which samples each index, so production statistics can differ from the ones measured here.
- The BEFORE second round ran about 25 minutes after the AFTER second round, on a shared host whose load was not controlled. These cells differ by more than 10 percent between rounds: store a after statistics, miss and newest hit, AFTER (104.1 and 110.5 percent) and oldest hit, BEFORE (13.6); store b without statistics, newest hit, BEFORE (19.0); store b after statistics, all three BEFORE cells (27.8, 30.1, 26.5); store c after statistics, AFTER (19.4); store d, no statistics BEFORE (31.0) and after statistics AFTER (24.1). The conclusions above do not rest on those cells alone, but their ranges are wide.
- The real store copy has no delivery rows, so the gain on real data is unmeasured. The 200,000-row stores are synthetic growth cases, and the 666-row stores use the status counts reported in #139330 with a synthetic conversation layout.
- PostgreSQL plans are unmeasured.
- Plans were captured on SQLite 3.53.4 only; the 3.44 line is argued from the source excerpts above.
- The status list is emitted in the index WHERE clause's text and order; a reordered list returns the same rows and loses the index. The new test asserts the plan, on an empty store without planner statistics, and fails with the list reordered or narrowed (output in the evidence). The shipped SQLite schema (`src/state/openclaw-agent-schema.sql`) and the agent schema fixtures of its earlier schema versions (v14, v19, v21, v22, v24, v25, v26, v27 and v2026.9.9) all define the index with `WHERE status IN ('queued', 'sent', 'replied')`, so databases created by earlier schema versions have the same predicate text.
- The mechanism probes (partial-index bound versus literal, order sensitivity, OR forms) ran on a synthetic table under Node v24.20.0 with the same SQLite 3.53.4; the SQLite source excerpts are from the tagged upstream files.
- The only other bound `IN` list against a partial index, the state delivery queue's `status IN ('completed', 'failed')` (`src/infra/delivery-queue-sqlite-bound.ts:37`), plans on a different index with bound values (`idx_delivery_queue_failed` in the probe) and is not changed.

prs.body:
## Proof follow-up

**Tip SHA:** `c6acabd113623d601863ffe6f3b5b6a877bc8601`

### DIRTY rebase

Rebased onto current `main` `16eb38cf9725b073bec2cf89842c28d59509231d` from starting SHA `a947649ada7a98e10f5fddadcd8d51607cba9b02`. Published with `--force-with-lease`.

- **Conflict file:** `packages/ai/src/transports/openai-responses-params-internal.test.ts` (add/add). Kept upstream `buildOpenAIResponsesCompactSystemMessage` coverage and this PR's `reasoning.summary: null` matrix. Imports now use `@openclaw/llm-core`.
- **Production files:** auto-merged. Native ChatGPT builder still distinguishes omitted vs explicit-null summaries and defaults summary-only effort to `medium`. Shared and generic builders keep the same undefined-vs-null contract.

### ClawSweeper findings — this revision

- [x] **[P2] Assert the resolved generic transport effort** — `packages/ai/src/transports/openai-responses-params-internal.test.ts` asserts `{ effort: "high", summary: null }` for the gpt-5.5 summary-only fixture (omitted-effort default is `high`, not `medium`).
- [ ] **[P1] Verify native endpoint acceptance for null summaries** — still blocked: this environment has no OpenAI / ChatGPT-authenticated credentials. Local native tests still capture the request body via `onPayload` and stop before dispatch. Public SDK types allow `summary: null`; that is not `/codex/responses` acceptance proof.

### Before-merge checklist

- [x] Focused Vitest on the three owner test files after rebase (3 files, 142 tests)
- [x] Generic-transport proof text corrected from `medium` to `high`
- [x] oxfmt, oxlint (touched files), `tsgo:core`, and packages test-types
- [ ] Live OpenAI / ChatGPT-authenticated endpoint proof — **not available** (no credentials)

### Focused test transcript (exact head)

```text
[test] starting test/vitest/vitest.unit.config.ts
 ✓ |unit| packages/ai/src/transports/openai-responses-params-internal.test.ts > buildOpenAIResponsesCompactSystemMessage > uses the developer role for reasoning models that support it
 ✓ |unit| packages/ai/src/transports/openai-responses-params-internal.test.ts > buildOpenAIResponsesCompactSystemMessage > falls back to the system role for xAI's native route, which disables the developer role
 ✓ |unit| packages/ai/src/transports/openai-responses-params-internal.test.ts > buildOpenAIResponsesCompactSystemMessage > uses the system role for non-reasoning models
 ✓ |unit| packages/ai/src/transports/openai-responses-params-internal.test.ts > buildOpenAIResponsesParams reasoning summary > preserves null reasoning summary with explicit effort
 ✓ |unit| packages/ai/src/transports/openai-responses-params-internal.test.ts > buildOpenAIResponsesParams reasoning summary > preserves null reasoning summary without explicit effort
 ✓ |unit| packages/ai/src/transports/openai-responses-params-internal.test.ts > buildOpenAIResponsesParams reasoning summary > defaults omitted reasoning summary to auto
 Test Files  3 passed (3)
      Tests  142 passed (142)
[test] passed 1 Vitest shard in 17.25s
```

Command: `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs packages/ai/src/transports/openai-responses-params-internal.test.ts packages/ai/src/providers/openai-responses-shared.test.ts packages/ai/src/providers/openai-chatgpt-responses.test.ts --reporter=verbose`

### Wire payload proof (exact-head, redacted)

Path-local omitted-effort defaults remain intentionally different:

```text
=== exact-head builder proof: reasoning.summary:null without explicit effort ===
HEAD_SHA=c6acabd113623d601863ffe6f3b5b6a877bc8601
transport.buildOpenAIResponsesParams (gpt-5.5 fixture) => {"effort":"high","summary":null}
shared.applyCommonResponsesParams / native ChatGPT builder => {"effort":"medium","summary":null}
LIMIT: no live OpenAI or /codex/responses proof; payload construction is covered locally.
```

---

Closes #121443

## What Problem This Solves

OpenAI Responses payload builders coerced `reasoning.summary: null` to `"auto"`. The OpenAI SDK allows `summary?: 'auto' | 'concise' | 'detailed' | null`, so callers that pass `reasoningSummary: null` to disable summaries silently still requested auto summaries.

### Before (broken)

```ts
{ reasoningEffort: "medium", reasoningSummary: null }
```

became:

```ts
{ reasoning: { effort: "medium", summary: "auto" } }
```

because defaults used `|| "auto"` / `?? "auto"`, both of which treat `null` as missing.

Affected builders:

- `applyCommonResponsesParams` (`openai-responses-shared.ts`)
- Responses params-internal transport builder
- Codex Responses payload assembly (`openai-chatgpt-responses.ts`)

## Why This Change Was Made

Default `"auto"` only when the field is **omitted** (`undefined`):

```ts
summary: options?.reasoningSummary === undefined ? "auto" : options.reasoningSummary
```

Adjacent matrix:

- explicit `null` → `summary: null`
- omitted → `summary: "auto"`
- Codex Responses `onPayload` path preserves `null`

## User Impact

Clients that disable reasoning summaries via `null` now send `summary: null` on the wire instead of accidentally requesting auto summaries (token waste / unwanted reasoning exposure). Omitted summary still defaults to `"auto"`.

## Evidence

### Before vs after (payload projection)

| Case | Before tip | After tip `c6acabd113623d601863ffe6f3b5b6a877bc8601` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `{ reasoningEffort: "medium", reasoningSummary: null }` | `summary: "auto"` | `summary: null` |
| `{ reasoningEffort: "medium" }` (omitted summary) | `summary: "auto"` | `summary: "auto"` (unchanged) |
| Generic transport `{ reasoningSummary: null }` (gpt-5.5, omitted effort) | coerced to `auto` | `effort: "high"`, `summary: null` |
| Shared / native `{ reasoningSummary: null }` (omitted effort) | coerced to `auto` | `effort: "medium"`, `summary: null` |
| Codex Responses `reasoningSummary: null` | coerced to `"auto"` | `summary: null` on captured payload |

```text

command=node scripts/run-vitest.mjs \
  packages/ai/src/transports/openai-responses-params-internal.test.ts \
  packages/ai/src/providers/openai-responses-shared.test.ts \
  packages/ai/src/providers/openai-chatgpt-responses.test.ts \
  --reporter=verbose
result=3 files passed; 142 tests passed
```

### What was not tested

Live OpenAI and ChatGPT-authenticated `/codex/responses` calls with `summary: null` against production endpoints (payload construction covered in unit tests). Native tests still throw from `onPayload` before dispatch.
