prs.title: perf(agent): prepare prompts outside the event loop
prs.body:
Prompt file reads, transcript shaping, and local token estimation currently run on the gateway event loop. A slow read or large replay can delay status handling and cancellation before the next model request.

Move prompt and request preparation into one bounded worker per AgentRunner, carrying the caller's ContextVars. Capture read-only replay inputs from the live JSONL Session on the event loop, and apply prepared request/accepted-history state there. A cancelled caller can return while its physical worker retains the slot until completion. Preserve detached lifecycle hook snapshots, including nonempty cancellation snapshots, and protect the shared tool token cache across worker threads.

Validation:

- `pytest -p no:cacheprovider tests/agent/test_prompt_responsiveness.py tests/agent/test_history_replay.py tests/agent/test_context_governance.py tests/agent/test_runner_core.py tests/agent/test_runner_governance.py tests/agent/test_runner_fallback.py tests/agent/test_runner_hooks.py tests/agent/test_runner_errors.py tests/agent/test_loop_runner_integration.py tests/agent/test_runtime_context.py tests/agent/tools/test_subagent_tools.py tests/utils/test_token_estimation.py tests/utils/test_token_encoding.py tests/utils/test_helpers.py tests/architecture/test_import_boundaries.py tests/llm_usage tests/providers/test_usage_contract.py tests/providers/test_llm_usage_observer.py -q`: 375 passed.
- Eight controlled-provider `process_direct` cases cover JSONL replay, status and heartbeat during blocked prompt/history/budget/usage preparation, cancellation within 0.5 seconds, worker-slot retention after cancellation, absence of subsequent requests from cancelled turns, ContextVar propagation, and detached nested history.
- Two concurrent `process_direct` cases hold the worker slot with a real `AGENTS.md` read and cancel success/finally snapshot waits. Both deliver `on_finally` exactly once with a detached nonempty transcript, `cancelled` and `CancelledError`, then propagate cancellation before the reader is released.

prs.title: fix(webui): hide recovery notice while resumed tasks run
prs.body:
## Why

A continued recovery turn keeps `resuming` metadata until it commits. `RecoveryNotice` only hid that state after clicking Continue on the current component mount, so refreshing or reattaching to an already running task brought back a persistent “Restoring interrupted task…” spinner.

Fixes [NAN-260](https://linear.app/nanobot-ai/issue/NAN-260).

## What changed

- Show recovery notices only for `awaiting_user` and `failed`; use the normal running-turn UI for resumed execution, including after reload.
- Preserve optimistic Continue, rejected-action errors, and renewed decisions after another interruption. Remove the now-unreachable progress-only notice branch.
- Add remount and attached-resuming regressions, including normal Stop dispatch.

## Scope

WebUI presentation only. No changes to recovery confirmation, checkpoints, backend commit timing, persistence, or the client/host protocol. The backend remains `resuming` while the continued turn runs.

## Blast Radius

Only the recovery notice and its tests change. Waiting/failed recovery actions retain their existing alert, buttons, and unavailable-context behavior; normal streaming and Stop controls remain owned by the existing turn lifecycle.

## Verification

- Regression-first: the new remount check failed on the original component, then passed with the fix.
- Focused RecoveryNotice / useNanobotStream / ThreadShell tests: **210 passed**.
- `bun run lint`, `bun run build` (TypeScript + Vite), and `bun run check:imports`: passed. `bun run test:imports`: **38 passed**.
- Real isolated gateway + production WebUI + deterministic loopback SSE model: Continue started execution, full page reload kept the banner hidden and Stop visible, backend recovery state remained `resuming`, and clicking Stop returned `Stopped 1 task(s).`. Final browser run had no console errors/warnings. Screenshot and provenance are recorded in NAN-260. All owned services and ports were cleaned up.
- Full suite is **not locally green**: candidate **2775 passed / 2 failed** (LinearPanel dialog focus and Temporary Chat return-after-refresh). An exact unmodified-base run produced **2767 passed / 7 failed**, including the same Temporary Chat failure. LinearPanel passed on base and a focused rerun; Temporary Chat failures persisted. These unrelated suites are unchanged and were not folded into this fix.

Final-head [GitHub CI](https://github.com/HKUDS/nanobot/actions/runs/38886389536) passed for `d8609596eff963cb7b6fa235be94866c119369f8`: WebUI (including full tests, lint, import checks, and build), Docker, and change detection. Python/TUI jobs were skipped by path filtering.

Browser verification used disposable seeded recovery state and a local deterministic model, not a forced crash or an external provider.

prs.title: fix(channels): retain scheduled results across pre-send outages
prs.body:
## Problem

A scheduled task can finish while its result never leaves the gateway. The outgoing queue is in memory. A channel outage or gateway restart can lose an accepted result.

## Change

- Save scheduled final replies and explicit `message` sends before queue acceptance. Use one bounded, instance-local SQLite queue.
- Retry only when the channel confirms that no part was sent. Recover pending messages after restart without another model call.
- Do not retry uncertain or interrupted sends automatically. Keep each recipient's status separate.
- Apply the pre-send failure contract to all 17 external channel adapters. Keep ordinary chat streaming unchanged.
- Preserve old task bindings and explicit multi-recipient sends. Do not change agent loop code, prompts, or tool definitions.

## Boundaries

This does not diagnose the reported 0.3.5 WebUI-to-WhatsApp case. Instructions do not change a task's saved chat. Recovery cannot create a send that the agent never requested.

External scheduled replies are complete messages, not streamed replies. Pending messages expire after one hour. Uncertain sends need manual verification; this is not an exactly-once or read-receipt guarantee. See [the delivery and backup rules](https://github.com/HKUDS/nanobot/blob/codex/reliable-channel-delivery/docs/automations.md#scheduled-result-delivery).

## Verification

- 2,648 related tests pass; 2 skip. Covers restart recovery, old tasks, separate sends, ordering, expiry, source reset, and delayed attachment access.
- Type, lint, and import-boundary checks pass.
- Serialized model prefix and tool definitions match the base. Recovery makes no model calls.
- Uses controlled model and transport responses. No live accounts were used.

prs.title: feat(recovery): persist completed tool results at execution-batch bou…
prs.body:
## Problem

When a model response contains multiple tool calls, the runtime checkpoint is
only written twice: before execution (`awaiting_tools`, all pending) and after
(`tools_completed`, all completed). If the gateway crashes in the middle of a
tool-execution batch, the durable checkpoint still records every call as
pending. On recovery, completed tools — including side-effecting ones — cannot
be distinguished from work that never ran, so they are marked "interrupted"
and the model may re-run them, repeating external side effects.

## Root cause

`execute_tool_calls` (nanobot/agent/tools/execution.py) runs tool batches
internally with no checkpoint emission between batches, so the only persisted
shapes are "all pending" / "all completed". `_runtime_checkpoint_is_well_formed`
(nanobot/session/recovery.py) mirrors that by accepting only those two shapes,
rejecting legitimate partial state.

## Solution

- **execution.py**: `execute_tool_calls` gains an optional `checkpoint_callback`.
  After each batch (concurrent gather or serial tool) it invokes the callback
  with the cumulative `completed_pairs` in stable result order. The serial
  branch now unpacks the `(result, event)` pair explicitly (behaviour
  unchanged).
- **runner.py**: a closure `_on_tool_batch_completed` normalizes each completed
  tool call into a tool-result row, keeps the remaining calls as pending,
  reuses the existing `_emit_checkpoint` path and writes an intermediate
  checkpoint at the batch boundary (phase stays `awaiting_tools`).
- **recovery.py**: the `awaiting_tools` well-formed check is relaxed from the
  all-or-nothing shape to the partition invariant `completed ∪ pending == all
  calls` and `completed ∩ pending == ∅`. Legacy all-pending checkpoints remain
  valid (`completed = ∅`).

## Tests

- `test_partial_checkpoint_partition_is_well_formed` — intermediate state
  (A completed, B/C pending) and the legacy all-pending shape both pass.
- `test_partial_checkpoint_bad_partition_rejected` (parametrized) — overlapping,
  missing, and duplicated partitions are rejected.
- `test_execute_tool_calls_emits_batch_checkpoint_callback` — one callback per
  batch, `completed_pairs` accumulated in call order.
- `test_execute_tool_calls_serial_mode_emits_callback_per_tool` — serial mode
  emits a callback after each tool.
- `test_execute_tool_calls_without_callback_keeps_previous_behavior` — no
  callback ⇒ identical results/events as before.
- `test_partial_checkpoint_restore_keeps_completed_and_marks_pending_interrupted`
  — integration: completed results are materialized as-is, pending ones become
  explicit interrupted tool results.

Full suite locally: 5973 passed, 19 failed. The 19 failures are pre-existing
baseline failures (verified by a revert-control experiment: reverting the two
source files to HEAD leaves them failing; they also fail on the upstream CI
checkout, e.g. `test_runner_reuses_edit_diff_for_summary_and_progress`), and
are unrelated to this change.

## Summary

Fixes #6192.

`AutoCompact.check_expired` only needs each session's `key` and `updated_at`, but it called `SessionManager.list_sessions()`, which also walks transcript lines to build WebUI previews. On workspaces with thousands of session files that preview work dominated every idle scan (even when the scan interval is already throttled).

This change adds `list_session_activity()` on `JsonlSessionStore` / `SessionManager`: it reads only the metadata line. Idle compact uses that listing. The full `list_sessions()` path used by the WebUI is unchanged.

## Test plan

- Red/green: `tests/session/test_idle_session_activity_listing.py`

labels.name: type/feature
labels.description: New feature or request

labels.name: comp/gateway

issues.body:
## Summary

Hermes currently derives sessions primarily from the messaging source, chat, thread, and participant identity. This provides strong isolation, but it makes long-running project workflows difficult when the same operator uses:

- Multiple Telegram accounts or devices
- A Telegram group
- Telegram topics
- Hermes Desktop
- CLI
- Web interfaces

Each interface can create or resume a different Hermes session even though every message belongs to the same project.

I propose adding an explicit **Project Workspace** abstraction that allows trusted identities and interfaces to route into one canonical project session while preserving security, concurrency control, and complete session history.

All project names and identifiers in this proposal are fictional examples.

## Motivation

A user may operate Hermes through two trusted Telegram accounts and a local computer. With per-user group isolation enabled, messages from the two accounts produce separate session keys:

\`\`\`text
agent:main:telegram:group:-1004827619350:1842057391
agent:main:telegram:group:-1004827619350:7263948105
\`\`\`

The result is two agents with different histories and potentially conflicting interpretations of the same project.

This can cause:

- A clarification response being delivered to a different session
- The original session continuing to wait indefinitely
- Duplicate analysis
- Contradictory semantic decisions
- Concurrent modifications to the same files
- Confusion about which session owns the active task
- Difficulty switching safely between Telegram, Desktop, and CLI

The current choice between globally isolated group sessions and globally shared group sessions is too coarse for this workflow.

## Proposed Abstraction

Introduce a persistent project-level routing object:

\`\`\`text
ProjectWorkspace
├── workspace_id
├── name
├── canonical_session_id
├── allowed_identities
├── allowed_channels
├── active_turn_owner
├── concurrency_policy
└── routing/audit history
\`\`\`

Example:

\`\`\`yaml
workspaces:
  project-atlas:
    canonical_session: "20260815_104233_a7c91e4d"

    identities:
      telegram:
        chat_id: "-1004827619350"
        user_ids:
          - "1842057391"
          - "7263948105"

      desktop:
        profiles:
          - "atlas-primary"

      cli:
        profiles:
          - "atlas-primary"

    concurrency:
      mode: single_writer
\`\`\`

All approved sources would route into the same canonical project context without disabling per-user isolation globally.

## Explicit Binding Commands

Suggested messaging commands:

\`\`\`text
/workspace create project-atlas
/workspace bind-session 20260815_104233_a7c91e4d
/workspace add-identity telegram:-1004827619350:1842057391
/workspace add-identity telegram:-1004827619350:7263948105
/workspace attach project-atlas
/workspace status
/workspace detach
\`\`\`

Equivalent CLI commands could be provided:

\`\`\`bash
hermes workspace create project-atlas
hermes workspace bind-session project-atlas 20260815_104233_a7c91e4d
hermes workspace add-identity project-atlas telegram:-1004827619350:1842057391
hermes workspace add-identity project-atlas telegram:-1004827619350:7263948105
hermes workspace attach project-atlas
hermes workspace status project-atlas
\`\`\`

## Security Model

Cross-channel routing must be explicit and deny-by-default.

Requirements:

- Binding requires authorization from the workspace owner.
- A Telegram identity must include both \`chat_id\` and \`user_id\`.
- Desktop and CLI bindings must use a locally authenticated profile.
- Direct-message sessions must never be merged automatically.
- Sessions must never be joined based only on display names.
- Every identity addition and removal must be recorded.
- Existing session databases must not be rewritten or destructively migrated.
- Removing a binding must not delete the underlying session.
- Cross-user \`/resume\` must remain forbidden unless both identities belong to the same explicitly authorized workspace.
- Workspace membership must not grant access to unrelated sessions.
- Credentials, access tokens, and private configuration values must never appear in routing diagnostics.

## Concurrency Control

A shared project context requires explicit turn ownership.

The recommended default is:

\`\`\`text
single_writer
\`\`\`

Suggested behavior:

1. The first accepted message acquires the workspace turn lease.
2. Other messages are queued while the turn is active.
3. Hermes reports which source currently owns the turn.
4. Duplicate or contradictory commands are not executed concurrently.
5. A lease timeout must not silently discard the active turn.
6. Recovery must preserve the existing session and queued messages.
7. Side-effecting tools must not execute concurrently against the same workspace unless explicitly authorized.
8. A gateway restart must restore the active lease or safely mark it for recovery.

Optional policies could include:

- \`single_writer\` — safest default
- \`queue\` — queue messages in arrival order
- \`clarification_priority\` — route a clarification answer directly to the waiting turn
- \`multi_agent\` — explicit opt-in only

## Clarification Routing

Pending clarification requests should be workspace-scoped rather than tied exclusively to the account or interface that received the prompt.

Example:

\`\`\`text
workspace: project-atlas
session: 20260815_104233_a7c91e4d
clarify_id: <clarify_id>
allowed_responders:
  - telegram:1842057391
  - telegram:7263948105
  - desktop:atlas-primary
\`\`\`

A response from any authorized workspace identity should resolve the same clarification.

Hermes should display an acknowledgement such as:

\`\`\`text
Answer applied to the active clarification in workspace project-atlas.
\`\`\`

If multiple clarifications are pending, Hermes should require an explicit \`clarify_id\` or present a safe selection interface. It should never apply an ambiguous response to an arbitrary session.

## Message Attribution

Messages in a shared workspace must retain their source identity.

Each user message should record:

- Platform
- Chat or channel
- Thread or topic
- User ID
- Display name at the time of submission
- Device or local profile where applicable
- Workspace ID
- Canonical session ID
- Timestamp
- Routing decision

The model may receive a stable attribution prefix:

\`\`\`text
[Telegram / Atlas Team / user:1842057391]
Continue the audit.
\`\`\`

Display names should remain informational only. Authorization must use stable platform identifiers.

## Workspace Visibility and Diagnostics

A \`/workspace status\` command should show:

\`\`\`text
Workspace: project-atlas
Canonical session: 20260815_104233_a7c91e4d
State: waiting_for_clarification
Active source: Telegram group / Project Atlas
Active turn age: 12m 41s
Queued messages: 0
Attached identities: 3
Gateway PID: 48732
\`\`\`

Additional useful fields could include:

- Current model and provider
- Active tool name
- Last successful LLM response
- Last inbound and outbound message
- Pending clarification count
- MCP health summary
- Session lease state
- Recovery status

The status output must not expose tokens, credentials, private prompts, or unrelated user identities.

## Safe Migration from Existing Sessions

When enabling a workspace for an existing project:

1. Select one canonical session.
2. Preserve all other sessions unchanged.
3. Create routing bindings only.
4. Do not merge message rows automatically.
5. Optionally mark secondary sessions as historical.
6. Allow a reversible detach operation.
7. Record the migration in an audit log.
8. Provide an exact rollback command.
9. Verify that the canonical session can still be opened through its original channel.

This avoids destructive database migration and ambiguous message ordering.

An optional import tool could later summarize relevant secondary sessions and propose additions to workspace memory, but it must never silently rewrite the canonical transcript.

## Telegram Topics as a Partial Solution

Shared Telegram topics already provide useful multi-user session semantics when configured with:

\`\`\`yaml
group_sessions_per_user: true
thread_sessions_per_user: false
\`\`\`

However, Telegram topics do not solve:

- Desktop-to-Telegram continuity
- CLI-to-Telegram continuity
- Web-to-Telegram continuity
- Explicit trusted identity management
- Project-level turn ownership
- Clarification routing across authorized channels
- Visibility into which interface owns the active task
- Safe attachment of an existing canonical session

Project Workspaces would generalize this behavior without changing secure defaults for unrelated groups.

## Gateway and Recovery Semantics

Workspace bindings should survive:

- Gateway restart
- Operating-system restart
- Provider timeout
- MCP reconnect
- Messaging-platform reconnect
- Temporary network failure
- Session auto-resume

On recovery, Hermes should determine whether the previous turn:

- Completed
- Failed before execution
- Is safe to retry
- Performed a side effect with an unknown outcome
- Requires user confirmation

Hermes must not automatically repeat a side-effecting tool call when the previous result is unknown.

## Audit Log

Every workspace routing event should be recorded in a structured audit log.

Example:

\`\`\`json
{
  "timestamp": "2026-08-15T10:51:42Z",
  "workspace_id": "project-atlas",
  "source": {
    "platform": "telegram",
    "chat_id": "-1004827619350",
    "user_id": "7263948105"
  },
  "canonical_session_id": "20260815_104233_a7c91e4d",
  "action": "clarification_response_routed",
  "clarify_id": "clarify_example_4821",
  "result": "accepted"
}
\`\`\`

Logs must be secret-redacted and must not contain credentials or unrelated message contents.

## Acceptance Criteria

A successful implementation should demonstrate that:

- Two explicitly authorized Telegram accounts use one canonical project session.
- Desktop or CLI can explicitly attach to the same workspace.
- Unauthorized users remain isolated.
- Direct messages remain private and cannot be merged implicitly.
- A clarification sent through one channel can be answered through another authorized channel.
- Only one side-effecting turn operates at a time.
- Concurrent messages are safely queued or rejected with a clear status.
- Existing sessions and message history remain unchanged.
- Workspace detach restores normal source-based routing.
- Gateway restart preserves workspace bindings and active session state.
- Ambiguous side-effecting operations are not automatically repeated.
- Every routing decision is visible in a structured audit log.
- Complete rollback is possible without deleting any session data.

## Expected Benefits

This feature would provide:

- Reliable continuity across devices and interfaces
- Fewer orphaned clarification requests
- Reduced duplicate analysis
- Fewer conflicting project decisions and file modifications
- Clear project ownership and active-turn visibility
- Secure multi-account operation without globally shared sessions
- Better support for long-running software-development workflows
- A natural integration point for an independent Hermes Guardian
- Improved observability and incident recovery

## Compatibility

Project Workspaces should complement rather than replace the existing source-based session model.

The current behavior should remain the default:

- Direct messages remain private.
- Group sessions remain isolated according to existing configuration.
- Thread-sharing behavior remains configurable.
- No existing session is automatically migrated.
- Workspace routing is enabled only through explicit configuration or commands.

This provides an opt-in, secure, and reversible mechanism for users who need advanced cross-channel project continuity without weakening Hermes' default session isolation.

issues.title: [Bug]: Browserbase-specific warnings shown in local browser mode

labels.name: type/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: tool/browser
labels.description: Browser automation (CDP, Playwright)

labels.name: P3
labels.description: Low — cosmetic, nice to have

issues.body:
### Bug Description

When using a local chromium browser `browser.cloud_provider: none` and `browser.engine: auto` with `agent-browser` installed and the proper environment variables configured to point `agent-browser` to the desired Chromium binary, browse results warn about BrowserBase-specific issues which are irrelevant for such configurations.

## Use case

Users running headless Chromium locally (Alpine musl/ARM64, headless servers, privacy-focused setups, cost avoidance) have zero interaction with Browserbase. Showing them a paid service upsell on every first navigation:

- Creates confusion about which backend is actually in use
- Wastes model context tokens on irrelevant upsell text
- Undermines trust by suggesting the user is on a limited free tier when they're fully local

When running the browser tool in local mode (cloud_provider: local), the browser_navigate tool returns misleading warnings that reference Browserbase-specific features:

```json
{
  "stealth_warning": "Running WITHOUT residential proxies. Bot detection may be more aggressive. Consider upgrading Browserbase plan for proxy support.",
  "stealth_features": ["local"]
}
```

The stealth_features correctly reports `["local"]`, confirming the session is running locally. Yet the `stealth_warning` pushes a Browserbase upsell — a paid cloud proxy service the user isn't using and didn't opt into.


### Steps to Reproduce

1. Install `agent-browser` locally (e.g. `npm install agent-browser` in the Hermes agent directory)
2. Set `AGENT_BROWSER_EXECUTABLE_PATH` to a local Chromium binary
3. Configure `browser.cloud_provider: local` in `config.yaml`
4. Call `browser_navigate` — the first navigation returns `stealth_warning` referencing Browserbase

A similar issue exists for `bot_detection_warning` (line 2477), which suggests `BROWSERBASE_ADVANCED_STEALTH=true` as an option, also Browserbase-specific.

### Expected Behavior

Browse results return only relevant information from the URLs being visited.

### Actual Behavior

Local-only browser setups warn about a free-tier BrowserBase account, causing confusion and undermining trust.

### Affected Component

Tools (terminal, file ops, web, code execution, etc.)

### Messaging Platform (if gateway-related)

N/A (CLI only)

### Debug Report

```shell
Report       https://paste.rs/u05Nd
agent.log    https://paste.rs/iR4IV
gateway.log  https://paste.rs/RQuMS
gui.log      https://paste.rs/YyFsB
```

### Operating System

postmarketOS edge (Alpine)

### Python Version

Python 3.14.3

### Hermes Version

Hermes Agent v0.17.0 (2026.6.19) · upstream 135f2351

### Additional Logs / Traceback (optional)

```shell

```

### Root Cause Analysis (optional)

## Root cause

In `tools/browser_tool.py`, the `_create_local_session()` function returns `{"features": {"local": True}}`. The warning logic at line 2485 checks `if not features.get("proxies")` — which is always True for local sessions (no proxies key exists in `{"local": True}`). The condition doesn't account for local mode at all.

```py
# Line 2482-2490 — browser_tool.py
if is_first_nav and "features" in session_info:
    features = session_info["features"]
    active_features = [k for k, v in features.items() if v]
    if not features.get("proxies"):  # ❌ True for local mode
        response["stealth_warning"] = (
            "Running WITHOUT residential proxies. Bot detection may be more aggressive. "
            "Consider upgrading Browserbase plan for proxy support."
        )
    response["stealth_features"] = active_features
```


### Proposed Fix (optional)


## Proposed fix

Gate both warnings on cloud mode. The features dict already distinguishes local from cloud: local mode sets `{"local": True}`, cloud providers set `{"proxies": bool, ...}`. The fix is minimal — add a local-mode check:

```py
# stealth_warning — only for cloud backends without proxies
if is_first_nav and "features" in session_info:
    features = session_info["features"]
    active_features = [k for k, v in features.items() if v]
    if not features.get("proxies") and not features.get("local"):
        response["stealth_warning"] = (
            "Running WITHOUT residential proxies. Bot detection may be more aggressive. "
            "Consider upgrading Browserbase plan for proxy support."
        )
    response["stealth_features"] = active_features
```

And similarly for `bot_detection_warning` (line 2473-2478), either guard it with `if not features.get("local")` or make the Browserbase-specific option conditional:

```py
if any(pattern in title_lower for pattern in blocked_patterns):
    msg = (
        f"Page title '{title}' suggests bot detection. The site may have blocked this request. "
        "Options: 1) Try adding delays between actions, 2) Access different pages first, "
    )
    if not features.get("local"):
        msg += "3) Enable advanced stealth (BROWSERBASE_ADVANCED_STEALTH=true, requires Scale plan), "
    msg += "4) Some sites have very aggressive bot detection that may be unavoidable."
    response["bot_detection_warning"] = msg
```

## Alternative

Use `_is_local_backend()` (already defined at line 621) to gate the warnings, which covers both local mode and CDP override. This is more robust if new local backends are added.

### Are you willing to submit a PR for this?

- [x] I'd like to fix this myself and submit a PR

issues.body:
## Bug Description

On Windows source installs (PM-managed checkout), any **external** Python entry point launched via the checkout's `venv\Scripts\python.exe` is re-executed by the `hermes_bootstrap` launch-preparation machinery even though it is not a Hermes entry point. The re-exec runs PM's store Python in isolated mode (`-I`) with a bootstrap that only adds the agent repo root to `sys.path`, so the external script loses its own directory **and** the venv's site-packages, and dies on its first local-package import.

The trigger is a consumer merely importing the `hermes_cli` package at module level. The third-party [hermes-webui](https://github.com/nesquena/hermes-webui) does exactly this (`api/config.py` → `from hermes_cli.tools_config import _get_platform_tools`), and its code expects graceful degradation when `hermes_cli` is not installed — instead, importing it re-execs the whole process (after first spawning a PM sync worker).

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Windows, hermes-agent **source install (git)** at `%LOCALAPPDATA%\hermes\hermes-agent`, updated to `main` @ `0b724b178e` (2026.9.24).
2. Consumer: hermes-webui `server.py`, launched with the agent venv python (`venv\Scripts\python.exe`, per its launcher); module-level `from hermes_cli.tools_config import _get_platform_tools` in `api/config.py`.
3. `cd <hermes-webui-repo>` and run `<agent-root>\venv\Scripts\python.exe server.py`.

Observed process chain (WMI capture, 120 ms sampling):

```
venv\Scripts\python.exe  D:\…\hermes-webui\server.py
    # 45,568-byte uv trampoline (SHA256 882CCBF8…); NOT an interpreter copy
    └─ .hermes-runtime\…\cpython-3.11\…\python.exe  D:\…\hermes-webui\server.py
        # 91,648 bytes (SHA256 0D52D7BF…); sys.path carries the venv site-packages
        # (yaml imports fine; editable hermes_agent finder → agent root importable)
        └─ %LOCALAPPDATA%\hermes\installs\<key>\pm-runtime\generations\<gen>\Scripts\python.exe -I -B <agent>\pm\worker.py
            # PM sync worker, ~1 s, spawned on EVERY launch
            └─ <store-python> -I -c "import sys, runpy; sys.path.insert(0, '<agent>'); sys.argv=['D:\…\server.py']; runpy.run_path('D:\…\server.py', run_name='__main__')"
                 → ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'api'   (server.py:102)
```

Control experiments (same checkout, same day):

- **Runtime Python directly** (trampoline's home interpreter, clean site-packages): `import api` succeeds (script dir is on `sys.path`), fails later at `import yaml` — proving the trampoline child in step 3 does carry the venv site-packages, so the re-exec is the only delta in the failing run.
- **Copy of `server.py` into a dir without the sibling `api/` package**: fails at the same line with **no** re-exec — the apparent "exact-path trigger" is actually import-graph difference (in-repo run reaches the `hermes_cli` import; the copy never does).
- **`HERMES_DISABLE_LAZY_INSTALLS=1`** in the environment: the server boots and serves HTTP 200 — the built-in escape hatch works; applied as the local workaround.

## Expected Behavior

`prepare_launch()` exists for Hermes entry points. A consumer process that only imports `hermes_cli` (to read config/toolset data) should run in place with the venv dependencies it was launched with — never be re-executed, never trigger a PM sync.

## Actual Behavior

The process is re-executed under the store Python with `-I`; the bootstrap inserts only the agent repo root, so any non-Hermes entry point is guaranteed to fail (`No module named 'api'`). Additionally, every launch pays for a spurious PM sync worker because `venv_is_current()` reports stale on this machine (root cause 4).

## Affected Component

Other — PM/venv launch preparation (`hermes_bootstrap.py` + `hermes_cli/venv_sync.py`), consumer-visible on Windows source installs.

## Debug Report

Deliberately not attached: `hermes debug share` uploads local config/logs to a third-party paste service. All evidence is inline above; happy to provide more on request.

## Environment

- **OS:** Windows 11 (managed source install under `%LOCALAPPDATA%\hermes\hermes-agent`)
- **Python:** 3.11.15 (venv trampoline's runtime, `.hermes-runtime` cpython-3.11 generation; note: PM's selected environment is tools Python 3.14.7 — see root cause 4)
- **Hermes:** `v git.0b724b1 (2026.9.24)`, install method `git`, `main` @ `0b724b178e`

## Root Cause Analysis

1. `hermes_bootstrap.py:529-543` — at module import time it calls `prepare_launch(_root, sys.argv[1:])` unconditionally (only `pm repair` is exempt) and re-execs the process (`subprocess.call` / `os.execv`) whenever a non-None interpreter is returned.
2. `hermes_cli/venv_sync.py::prepare_launch` — the decision inspects only checkout state (`.git` present, `pyproject.toml` present, install stamp `updateMechanism == "self"`, `pm.venv_is_current()`, store-python identity vs `sys.executable`). It never checks whether the entry point is Hermes-owned, so any external script whose import graph reaches `hermes_cli`/`hermes_bootstrap` (e.g. `hermes_cli.tools_config`) is re-executed.
3. `hermes_cli/venv_sync.py::relaunch_command` — the bootstrap template is `[store_python, …, "-I", "-c", "import sys, runpy; sys.path.insert(0, <agent_root>); sys.argv=[…]; runpy.run_path(<script>, run_name='__main__')"]`: it inserts only the agent repo root and isolates site (`-I`). Correct for in-checkout entry points; for external scripts it drops the script's own directory and the venv site-packages, so `runpy.run_path` on them is guaranteed to fail.
4. Aggravating factor on the reporter's machine: two Python lineages coexist — the repo venv's `pyvenv.cfg` `home` is `.hermes-runtime` cpython-3.11 (uv 0.12.4), while PM's selected environment (`%LOCALAPPDATA%\hermes\installs\<key>\environments\<env>\venv`, recorded in `facts.json`) is tools Python 3.14.7 (uv 0.12.3). `venv_is_current()` (`pm/install.py:545`, facts-stamp comparison) reports stale, so a PM sync worker is spawned on every consumer launch before the re-exec.

## Proposed Fix (any one)

- Gate `prepare_launch` on Hermes-owned entry points (e.g. `argv[0]` resolves inside the project root, or `-m hermes_cli.main` / known console scripts); never re-exec external scripts.
- Or, in `relaunch_command` for script entry points, also insert `str(Path(argv[0]).resolve().parent)` (and preserve the caller's venv site-packages) so external entry points survive the re-exec.
- Or, importing the `hermes_cli` package (including submodules like `tools_config`) should not import `hermes_bootstrap` — a plain import must never re-exec the process. Data consumers of `hermes_cli` (hermes-webui et al.) rely on graceful degradation when `hermes_cli` is absent.

## Workaround (verified)

`HERMES_DISABLE_LAZY_INSTALLS=1` in the consumer's environment (hermes-webui: its `.env` file, loaded by `start.ps1`): `prepare_launch` then returns `None` and the server runs correctly under the venv-trampoline Python (HTTP 200).

issues.title: WhatsApp adapter never marks send failures retryable — cron redelivery unreachable during bridge reconnect

labels.name: type/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: comp/plugins
labels.description: Plugin system and bundled plugins

labels.name: platform/whatsapp
labels.description: WhatsApp Business adapter

labels.name: P2
labels.description: Medium — degraded but workaround exists

issues.body:
## Summary

The WhatsApp adapter never sets the `SendResult.retryable` verdict, so during a bridge reconnect window a failed send is indistinguishable from a logged-out session — and the delivery-ledger redelivery gate (#127187, #127188) never triggers for it. The payload is lost silently.

Surfaced by @dacheah reviewing #127188, with a real incident: cron execution `1b7ff2efde6f430882c9a60324ed4466`, both lanes 503 inside a 4.36 s reconnect window (bridge log 20:47:19.497 → 20:47:23.856 UTC), payload lost. (Refs pinned to `main` @ `ecac27c0af`.)

## Mechanism

- `plugins/platforms/whatsapp/adapter.py`: all 14 `SendResult(...)` constructions omit `retryable`; every `retryable=` in the file is a `_set_fatal_error` argument. So `DeliverySendError.send_retryable` is never set, and the verdict arm of the redelivery gate always reads `None`/`False`.
- The string arm can't catch it either: the reconnect-only set is `{"send_path_degraded"}` (`gateway/delivery_ledger.py:57`), while this adapter's transient failure text is `{"error":"Not connected to WhatsApp"}`.
- Why the adapter can't just start passing `retryable=True` on that string: the bridge's state vocabulary is only `connected`/`disconnected` (`scripts/whatsapp-bridge/bridge.js:379, 430, 451`), and all send gates share one check (`!sock || connectionState !== 'connected'`, e.g. `:842, :882, :916`). A reconnect in progress and a logged-out session produce the identical 503 body — nothing in the response tells the adapter which one it's holding. Setting the verdict on that ambiguity would misclassify a real logout as retryable.

## Scope note

This is edge 5 of the #127187 family, but outside #127188's diff: that PR gates and arms the drain for adapters whose verdict is honest. Making WhatsApp's verdict honest is a bridge-first change.

## Suggested fix (one line)

Bridge exposes a reconnect-pending signal (a `reconnecting` state, or `/health` reporting more than a bare echo of `connectionState`) → adapter maps "503 while reconnect-pending" to `retryable=True`; everything else stays fatal/non-retryable.

labels.name: provider/anthropic
labels.description: Anthropic native Messages API

labels.name: area/auth

labels.name: P2
labels.description: Medium — degraded but workaround exists

labels.description: Sweeper risk: may affect sandboxing, auth, credentials, or sensitive data

issues.body:
### Bug Description

On macOS, when Hermes refreshes a borrowed Claude Code OAuth login, `_mirror_claude_code_credentials_to_keychain()` (added in #115690 for #98334) rewrites the `Claude Code-credentials` login Keychain item. It does this by piping one command line into `security -i`:

```
add-generic-password -U -a "<acct>" -s "Claude Code-credentials" -X <hex of the whole JSON payload>
```

`security -i` reads its input in lines of at most 4095 characters. A longer line is split in two: the first 4095 characters run as one command, and the rest runs as a separate command (`security: unknown command "…"`). So `add-generic-password -U` runs with only the first `4095 - len(prefix)` hex digits and overwrites the item with the start of the JSON, cut off. Claude Code can't parse the item and reports `Not logged in`.

The payload goes over the limit once Claude Code holds MCP OAuth logins. They live in the same item under `mcpOAuth`, and `_merge_keychain_credential_payload()` correctly keeps them. Measured on the item Claude Code re-created after a fresh `claude auth login`:

- the whole item is 11,251 bytes of JSON (33 `mcpOAuth` entries), so the command line is 22,567 characters
- `claudeAiOauth` alone is 509 bytes, which would have made a 1,083-character line

With a 3-character account name the prefix is 65 characters, which leaves room for 4,030 hex digits, or 2,015 bytes. The corrupted item held exactly 2,015 bytes of unparsable JSON. In Claude Code's item `mcpOAuth` comes before `claudeAiOauth`, so a copy cut off at 2,015 bytes holds none of the login. Users with no MCP OAuth entries stay under the limit, which may be why nobody has reported this.

The failure is silent. A non-zero exit from `security -i` is logged only at DEBUG (`Keychain mirror failed (rc=%s)`), and nothing was logged to agent.log or errors.log at INFO or above.

### Steps to Reproduce

This shows the line limit without writing to any Keychain. It runs `show-keychain-info` on a path that doesn't exist:

```python
import subprocess, re
for n in (3000, 5000, 9000):
    path = "/nonexistent-hermes-probe/" + "x" * n
    r = subprocess.run(["security", "-i"], input=f"show-keychain-info {path}\n",
                       capture_output=True, text=True)
    echoed = [len(m) for m in re.findall(r"/nonexistent-hermes-probe/x+", r.stderr)]
    print(len("show-keychain-info ") + len(path), r.returncode, echoed, "unknown command" in r.stderr)
```

Output:

```
3045 50 [3026] False
5045 1 [4076] True
9045 1 [4076] True
```

The path is cut at 4,076 characters, which is 4,095 minus the 19-character `show-keychain-info ` prefix. The rest of the line runs as a separate command.

On the affected machine:

1. Claude Code was logged in on macOS, with MCP servers authenticated through it.
2. `auth.adopt_external_logins` was at its default (true), and Hermes had no Anthropic OAuth login of its own at the time, so the borrowed Claude Code login was the one resolved. A cron script calls `resolve_anthropic_token()` every 10 minutes.
3. The Claude Code access token had expired, so Hermes refreshed it. `~/.claude/.credentials.json` was left valid, and then the Keychain mirror ran.
4. The item's `mdat` is 2026-09-25 15:29:26Z. That cron run wrote its output at 15:29:27Z. From then on, `security find-generic-password -s "Claude Code-credentials" -w` returned 2,015 bytes that `json.loads` rejects, and `claude auth status` reported "Not logged in".

### Expected Behavior

The mirror writes the whole payload. If it can't, it leaves the item untouched and says so. A borrowed login should never be left half-written.

### Actual Behavior

The item is overwritten with the start of the JSON, cut off so it can't be parsed. Claude Code is logged out, and nothing is logged above DEBUG.

### Where

In `agent/anthropic_credentials.py`:

- `_keychain_mirror_command()` builds the single `security -i` line.
- `_mirror_claude_code_credentials_to_keychain()` logs a non-zero exit only at DEBUG.

Both are unchanged on current `main` (903a57c5).

Possible fixes, for maintainers to judge:

- Never send `security -i` a line over 4,095 characters. If the payload doesn't fit and there is no other safe way to write it, skip the mirror and log a WARNING.
- Read the item back after writing and compare, so a partial write is caught.
- The refresh itself spends Claude Code's single-use refresh token. Before refreshing a borrowed login, check whether the mirror can succeed (related: #118199).

Workaround: run `hermes auth add anthropic --type oauth`, set `auth.adopt_external_logins: false`, then run `claude auth login`.

Related: #98334, #115690, #118199

### Environment

- macOS 27.0 (Apple silicon)
- Hermes Agent v0.21.5 (2026.9.24), upstream 3094b5d0. The mirror code is the same on `main` 903a57c5.
- Python 3.12.14
- Claude Code 2.1.222
- Affected component: Agent Core (Anthropic credentials). Any surface that refreshes the borrowed login can trigger it; here it was cron.

### Debug Report

Not attached, because this machine's logs contain private conversations. The relevant facts are above.

issues.title: Dashboard on a non-loopback bind hangs in Chrome: pinned uvicorn 0.41.0 ignores a padded `Connection: close` request header
issues.body:
## Environment

- Hermes Agent v0.22.2 (2026.9.24), stable, git install, macOS 15.8 (Apple silicon)
- Server: `hermes dashboard --host 0.0.0.0 --port 9119` with `HERMES_DASHBOARD_BASIC_AUTH_*` set
- Client: Chrome 155.0.8059.41 on Windows 11 24H2, same LAN
- Relevant dependency: `uvicorn==0.41.0` (exactly pinned in `pyproject.toml`, `web` extra, line 490) with `httptools` 0.8.0

## Symptom

From Windows Chrome, `http://<host-lan-ip>:9119/` is unusable: the login page renders, but its document request never finishes (tab spinner forever) and after submitting the form the POST returns 200 yet the SPA never starts.

Everything else is healthy:

- `curl` from the same Windows box: login page 35 ms, 220 KB asset 49 ms
- Chrome on the Hermes host itself: fine
- Other HTTP servers on the same host (e.g. WordPress on :8080, Vite on :3000): fine in the same Windows browser
- The dashboard's own access log records only the first request of each connection from the Windows client

## Root cause

uvicorn (<= 0.52.0) decides "the client asked to close" with an exact match against the raw header list:

```python
# uvicorn/protocols/http/flow_control.py
CLOSE_HEADER = (b"connection", b"close")

# uvicorn/protocols/http/httptools_impl.py — RequestResponseCycle.send()
if CLOSE_HEADER in self.scope["headers"] and CLOSE_HEADER not in headers:
    headers = headers + [CLOSE_HEADER]
```

Chrome 155 on Windows sends the value padded — captured on the wire with `tcpdump -i <if> -s 0 'tcp port 9119'`:

```
GET / HTTP/1.1
Host: 192.168.0.7:9119
Connection: close␣␣␣␣␣        <- value padded with 5 spaces
...
```

The exact tuple match misses it (`b"close     " != b"close"`), so uvicorn neither adds `connection: close` to the response nor closes the connection. On that connection it then never answers any further request: the next request from Chrome is ACKed by the kernel but never reaches the app, no FIN is sent, and the client waits indefinitely (only the keep-alive timeout eventually closes it). Chrome, having seen no close, reuses the socket for its next request — and hangs.

Per RFC 9110 §7.6.1 `Connection` is a comma-separated list of tokens, whitespace around tokens is allowed, and comparison is case-insensitive, so the padded value is a legal `close`.

## Minimal reproduction (uvicorn alone, no Hermes involved)

```bash
python -m uvicorn tiny_asgi:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port 9199   # any ASGI app
```

Then on a single TCP connection (pseudo-code, any HTTP/1.1 client):

1. send `GET /a HTTP/1.1` + `Host: x` + `Connection: close     ` (5 trailing spaces) and read the response
2. send `GET /b HTTP/1.1` + `Host: x` + `Connection: keep-alive` on the **same** connection

Result on 0.41.0: the second request is never answered; the connection is only closed by the keep-alive timeout.
With `Connection: close` (no padding) the connection is closed immediately after the first response, as expected.
The same hang is reproducible when the second request is sent before the connection is closed by the client's own logic.

## Fix status

Already fixed upstream, no upstream report needed: uvicorn 0.53.0 replaced this logic with the parser's own opinion —

```python
keep_alive=http_version != "1.0" and self.parser.should_keep_alive(),   # httptools/llhttp handles token list + whitespace
```

and `CLOSE_HEADER` is gone. Verified locally against the same reproduction with uvicorn 0.54.0 + httptools 0.9.0: the padded value is honoured, the response carries `connection: close`, the connection is closed after the response, and keep-alive reuse still works. Re-verified against the real dashboard: with `uvicorn==0.54.0`
in the same venv, `hermes dashboard --host 0.0.0.0 --port 9119` answers the padded-close request with
`connection: close` and closes the socket immediately, keep-alive reuse keeps working, and the
basic-auth gate is unaffected.

## Request

Bump the `web` extra pin from `uvicorn==0.41.0` to `uvicorn>=0.53.0,<1` (or at least `>=0.53.0`).

Until then, any Hermes user who exposes the dashboard on a non-loopback address (`hermes dashboard --host 0.0.0.0`, the documented LAN/remote setup) and browses it with Chrome on Windows hits an unusable UI. Chrome is the trigger; the version of uvicorn Hermes pins is the defect.

Local workaround applied for now (lost on the next dependency sync): normalizing the close check in the venv's `uvicorn/protocols/http/{httptools,h11}_impl.py` to tolerate case, surrounding whitespace and comma lists.

issues.title: [Bug]: a running card with an unresolved owner receipt and no worker_bound event is unreclaimable by every dispatcher path
issues.body:
### Bug Description

A `running` card whose worker is killed can become **permanently unreclaimable by every reclaim path**. It holds its profile's `kanban.max_in_progress_per_profile` slot forever, silently: the dispatcher defers every card queued behind it with `has 1 of 1 allowed worker(s) running`, and `hermes kanban diagnostics` reports only those deferred victims — no rule can see a `running` card at all, so the jam is always reported as its consequences, never as its cause.

Measured on one board: a card claimed at 07:48 whose worker (pid 6534) was killed by a restart at 08:59; its claim lock expired at 08:03; no heartbeat, no completion, and **16 hours** later it was still `running` with 15 cards queued behind it, healed only by a human `hermes kanban reclaim`. Board-wide counts from the same period: **76 `owner_admitted` events vs 74 `worker_bound` events** — runs in the shape below — and 4 cards that had needed a manual reclaim.

Exact conditions (all three):

1. the card's current run has an `owner_admitted` event whose receipt is unresolved — e.g. the owning interpreter was killed by a restart, so its session admission is `terminal:interrupted` and/or its recorded pid is gone → `owner_reclaim_paused()` returns True;
2. that run has **no `worker_bound` event** → `bound_interpreter_gone()` returns False, so `_reclaim_dead_workers()`'s only override for the pause cannot fire;
3. the claim lock is expired but non-NULL (so `reconcile_orphaned_running()` does not match) and `detect_stale_running()` is off by default (`dispatch_stale_timeout_seconds = 0`).

Then `release_stale_claims()` (expired lock), `_reclaim_dead_workers()` (dead pid) and `reconcile_orphaned_running()` all skip the card.

### Steps to Reproduce

Reproduced on a scratch board with the incident's own events (hermes-agent `0.21.5`, and unchanged on `main` @ `ccc69563`):

```python
from pathlib import Path
import json, sqlite3, tempfile, time

from hermes_cli import kanban_db as kb
from hermes_cli import kanban_db_dispatch as kbd
from hermes_cli.kanban_db_connect import connect, init_db
from hermes_cli.kanban_owner_recovery import bound_interpreter_gone, owner_reclaim_paused

NOW = int(time.time())
root = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())
board, ledger = root / "kanban.db", root / "state.db"
init_db(board)
conn = connect(board)
with sqlite3.connect(ledger) as L:
    L.execute("CREATE TABLE session_admissions (target_session_id TEXT, request_id TEXT, "
              "status TEXT, outcome TEXT)")

pid = 3_500_000            # provably absent on this host
host = kb._claimer_id().split(":", 1)[0]
lock, expires = f"{host}:{pid}", NOW - 15 * 3600
run = conn.execute(
    "INSERT INTO task_runs (task_id, profile, status, claim_lock, claim_expires, worker_pid, "
    "started_at) VALUES ('t', 'default', 'running', ?, ?, ?, ?)",
    (lock, expires, pid, NOW - 16 * 3600)).lastrowid
conn.execute(
    "INSERT INTO tasks (id, title, assignee, status, created_at, claim_lock, claim_expires, "
    "worker_pid, current_run_id, started_at, priority) "
    "VALUES ('t', 't', 'default', 'running', ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, 5)",
    (NOW - 86400, lock, expires, pid, run, NOW - 16 * 3600))
request_id = 'kanban:["default","t",1]'
for kind, payload in (
    ("claimed", {"source_status": "ready"}),
    ("spawned", {"pid": pid, "started_at": "epoch|start"}),
    ("owner_admitted", {"db": str(ledger), "session_id": "s", "pid": pid,
                        "request_id": request_id}),
):
    conn.execute("INSERT INTO task_events (task_id, run_id, kind, payload, created_at) "
                 "VALUES ('t', ?, ?, ?, ?)", (run, kind, json.dumps(payload), NOW - 15 * 3600))
with sqlite3.connect(ledger) as L:
    L.execute("INSERT INTO session_admissions VALUES ('s', ?, 'terminal', 'interrupted')",
              (request_id,))
conn.commit()

print("owner_reclaim_paused:", owner_reclaim_paused(conn, "t"))
print("bound_interpreter_gone:", bound_interpreter_gone(conn, "t"))
print("release_stale_claims:", kb.release_stale_claims(conn))
print("detect_crashed_workers:", kbd.detect_crashed_workers(conn))
print("reconcile_orphaned_running:", kbd.reconcile_orphaned_running(conn))
print("detect_stale_running:", kbd.detect_stale_running(conn, stale_timeout_seconds=900))
print("status:", conn.execute("SELECT status FROM tasks WHERE id='t'").fetchone()[0])
```

### Expected Behavior

The slot is freed once nothing can still be executing the attempt. That is a different question from "was this attempt's outcome recorded?", and the platform already answers it elsewhere: `hermes kanban reclaim` (operator path) and the dispatcher's own `bound_interpreter_gone()` override both release the claim of an attempt whose interpreter is provably gone. A run that never wrote `worker_bound` should not be excluded from that reasoning.

Liveness evidence the board already keeps, sufficient to release the claim: the receipt's own pid is gone or recycled, every worker pid recorded for the current run (`tasks.worker_pid`, its `spawned` / `worker_bound` events) is dead or recycled, the claim has expired, and no heartbeat arrived inside `DEFAULT_CLAIM_HEARTBEAT_MAX_STALE_SECONDS`. Anything unprovable (a live pid, a missing fingerprint, no recorded pid, another host's lock) should keep the pause.

### Actual Behavior

The card stays `running` forever; the profile's concurrency slot is spent; every card behind it is deferred; `kanban diagnostics` shows `stranded_in_ready` warnings for the deferred cards and no signal about the `running` card holding them there. `release_stale_claims`, `detect_crashed_workers`, `reconcile_orphaned_running` and `detect_stale_running` all decline it.

```text
owner_reclaim_paused: True
bound_interpreter_gone: False
release_stale_claims: 0
detect_crashed_workers: []
reconcile_orphaned_running: []
detect_stale_running: []
status: running
```

### Suggested direction (not prescriptive)

The pause exists so an attempt whose effects may still be in flight is never repeated — that reasoning is about *effects*, and it should not also mean the slot is never freed. Concretely, one of:

- treat "every recorded pid for this run is dead/recycled AND the lock expired AND no heartbeat within `DEFAULT_CLAIM_HEARTBEAT_MAX_STALE_SECONDS`" as sufficient to reclaim even when `owner_reclaim_paused()` is True (today `bound_interpreter_gone()` is the only such override, and it silently depends on a `worker_bound` event that some runs never write); or
- make the missing-`worker_bound` case a first-class signal (`owner_admitted` for the current run + owner pid dead + no `worker_bound` = the owner never bound an interpreter, so nothing can still be running it); or
- add a `kanban diagnostics` rule for a `running` card whose claim expired with no live worker, so the jam itself is visible instead of its victims.

### Environment

- hermes-agent `0.21.5` (installed), and unchanged on `main` @ `ccc69563`
- Linux x86_64, single dispatcher, `max_in_progress_per_profile: 1`
- Reproduced twice on scratch boards seeded with the incident's exact events, and once live on a production board with an injected card of the same shape.

I have a fix with tests for the first and third bullets above and will link it here.

issues.title: Dashboard chat startup waits on unrelated work before opening the terminal
issues.body:
## Problem

Opening the built-in dashboard chat waits on work that does not need to delay the terminal:

1. Fresh plugin manifests keep the chat gate closed until unrelated plugin bundles register, even when no plugin can override `/chat`.
2. ChatPage's lazy/Suspense retry adds approximately 300 ms before its connection effects run.
3. The sidebar RPC WebSocket starts before the terminal WebSocket. In the observed Chromium/HTTPS path, same-endpoint WebSocket handshakes are spaced by roughly 170 ms, putting the terminal last.

These paths were inspected on main `ccc695635094d7615373db267b77f894d978b1a0` in `web/src/plugins/usePlugins.ts`, `web/src/App.tsx`, `web/src/components/ChatSidebar.tsx` and `web/src/pages/ChatPage.tsx`.

## Reproduction

1. Use an authenticated HTTPS dashboard with plugins that do not override chat.
2. Open `/chat?profile=default` in a new tab.
3. Record Network through the first ready frame from `/api/pty`.
4. Inspect the plugin-manifest/ChatPage timing, the gap before the first WS-ticket request, and the order of events, PTY and sidebar RPC connections.

## Observed timings

Measurements used a v0.22.2 deployment with equivalent frontend backports and the earlier same-profile gateway attachment fix. They measure the first PTY ready frame, not the later accessibility-tree update.

| Observation | Before its corresponding change | After |
|---|---:|---:|
| Manifest response → ChatPage request | 406 / 730 ms | 2 / 2 / 2 ms |
| ChatPage request → first WS-ticket request | about 300 ms | 19 / 20 / 22 ms |
| PTY handshake completion, connection-order comparison | 842 / 940 ms | 703 / 688 ms |
| Navigation → ready, connection-order comparison | 1.833 / 1.943 s | 1.668 / 1.657 s |
| Final verification after temporary test terminals were closed | — | 1.609 / 1.467 s |

The full initial frontend baseline was 2.568 / 2.984 s. These are small samples, not a benchmark or a latency guarantee. Changed-asset downloads and accumulated test processes produced slower observations, up to 2.55 s during this follow-up. Both effects are excluded from the paired connection-order comparison, but remain relevant to real opening time.

## Remaining path examined

Authentication/tickets, Caddy, WebSocket acceptance, PTY launch, TUI build freshness, terminal capability detection, gateway attachment, configuration/setup/session RPCs and command discovery were examined. Ticket requests took 4–13 ms in the earlier Caddy sample; arrival-to-backend WebSocket acceptance was about 2 ms. The observed handshake spacing occurred before Caddy.

The TUI command catalog can occupy the RPC queue before session setup. Moving it after create/resume improved two isolated pairs but did not improve the complete browser path consistently. That experiment was removed. The final patch leaves TUI startup and command availability unchanged; the exact cache state of the slower sample was not instrumented.

## Expected behavior

Release the chat gate once manifests rule out a chat override, mount ChatPage when its module resolves, and let the terminal WebSocket start before the sidebar RPC connection. Keep the event subscriber first, preserve independent retries after the initial connection, and release the sidebar even if initial PTY retries are exhausted. Preserve plugin ownership, profile isolation, saved history and lazy loading on other routes.

issues.title: Managed llama-server survives Hermes exit on macOS and keeps the model resident (follow-up to #110561)

labels.name: type/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: comp/cli
labels.description: CLI entry point, hermes_cli/, setup wizard

labels.name: P2
labels.description: Medium — degraded but workaround exists

labels.name: area/local-models
labels.description: Local model inference/runtimes: llama.cpp, Ollama, LM Studio, MLX/vLLM, GGUF, VRAM and offload

issues.body:
## Summary

On macOS, the managed llama.cpp router and its model child stay alive after the Hermes process that started them exits. The model stays resident. Nothing unloads it, because the 15-minute idle sweep runs inside the owner process. #110561 fixed this on Windows with a Job Object. On macOS and Linux, `spawn_server` returns a plain child with no lifetime link to the owner.

## Environment

- macOS 27.2, Apple M5 Pro, 24 GB unified memory
- Hermes git install at `8f21606116c` (2026-09-28)
- Managed runtime `llamacpp-metal-10964`, a 27B GGUF local model, `ctx-size 98304`
- `model.provider: nous` at the time of the report. The local model was used earlier and then the default changed to a cloud model.

## Observed

```
PID    PPID  ELAPSED   FOOTPRINT  COMMAND
4777   1     17:51:00  32 MB      llama-server --port 18434 --models-max 1 --models-autoload ...   (router)
17976  4777  17:37:38  15 GB      llama-server --alias <27B GGUF local model> --ctx-size 98304 ... (model child)
```

- The router's parent is `launchd` (PID 1). `server.json` names `owner_pid 4718`, which no longer exists.
- The model held 15 GB of a 24 GB machine for about 17.5 hours with no requests.
- `SIGTERM` to the router freed the memory at once. The router log shows a clean `unload_all`.

## Cause (from source at `8f21606116c`)

1. `local_runtime/processes.py` `spawn_server()`: on non-Windows it returns the `Popen` object with no containment. Nothing ties the router to the owner's lifetime.
2. `local_runtime/bootstrap.py` `_start_idle_sweeper()`: the idle sweep is a daemon thread in the owner. When the owner exits, the sweep stops, and `IDLE_UNLOAD_S` never applies again.
3. `local_runtime/recovery.py`: the orphan is found only when Hermes next boots the runtime. Until then the model stays resident.
4. No code path unloads the local model when the active provider changes to a cloud provider.

## Proposed changes

1. **Tie the router to its owner on macOS and Linux.** For example, a small reaper that waits for the owner PID to exit (`kqueue` `EVFILT_PROC`/`NOTE_EXIT` on macOS, `pidfd` or `PR_SET_PDEATHSIG` on Linux) and then calls the existing `_terminate_tree()`. This mirrors the Windows Job Object from #110561.
2. **Unload when the provider changes away from local.** When a session or the default model switches to a non-local provider, unload the resident model through `POST /models/unload`. The router stays up, and `--models-autoload` reloads the model if the user switches back.
3. **Expose the idle timeout** as proposed in #119834 (`local_runtime.keep_alive`).

Do not use `--sleep-idle-seconds` for this. #76597 shows that a sleeping endpoint can look like a crash to Hermes.

## Workaround in use

A launchd job runs a short script every 5 minutes and when `~/.hermes/config.yaml` changes. The script reads `server.json`. It stops the router when the owner PID is gone and the server log has been idle for 10 minutes. It calls `POST /models/unload` when the provider is not local and the model has been idle for 5 minutes. It is not a fix, only a stopgap.

Related: #110561, #111154, #119834, #120691, #76597.

issues.title: [Bug]: Local runtime vision capability check loads the whole local model (GET /props?model= under --models-autoload)

labels.name: type/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: comp/cli
labels.description: CLI entry point, hermes_cli/, setup wizard

labels.name: tool/vision
labels.description: Vision analysis and image generation

labels.name: P2
labels.description: Medium — degraded but workaround exists

labels.name: area/local-models
labels.description: Local model inference/runtimes: llama.cpp, Ollama, LM Studio, MLX/vLLM, GGUF, VRAM and offload

issues.body:
### Bug Description

`managed_model_supports_vision()` asks the managed llama.cpp router whether a staged model can see images with `GET /props?model=<id>` and a 3 s timeout (`hermes_cli/local_runtime/capabilities.py:40-52`, `_props_modalities`). The managed router is spawned with `--models-autoload` (`supervisor.py:184`). In router mode, llama.cpp **loads** an unloaded model to answer any `GET ...?model=` request unless the request says `autoload=false` (`tools/server/server-models.cpp`: `proxy_get` → `is_autoload()` → `ensure_model_ready()`; documented in the server README: "you can include `?autoload=true|false` in the query param to control this behavior per-request").

So every time Hermes needs to decide whether to send an image natively (image routing, `vision_analyze`, auxiliary vision auto-detect), it can start a full model load just to answer "can it see?". The 3 s timeout expires long before a multi-GB load finishes, the check falls back to the catalog answer anyway, and the router finishes the load regardless. The model then stays resident until the 15-minute idle sweep, if one is running (see Related below).

`agent/model_metadata.py:_apply_llamacpp_props` already avoids this: it reads `/models` and only probes children whose status is `loaded`/`ready`, because "probing could autoload them". The capability probe has no such guard.

### Steps to Reproduce

With the pinned engine (b10964) and any small GGUF (the 1 MB `tinyllamas/stories260K.gguf` is enough):

```bash
llama-server --host 127.0.0.1 --port 18999 --api-key K --models-dir ./models --models-autoload --no-ui &
H='Authorization: Bearer K'
curl -s -H "$H" http://127.0.0.1:18999/models                                  # status: unloaded
curl -s -H "$H" 'http://127.0.0.1:18999/props?model=stories260K&autoload=false' # 400 "model is not loaded"; still unloaded
curl -s -H "$H" 'http://127.0.0.1:18999/props?model=stories260K'                # the request Hermes sends: 200 ...
curl -s -H "$H" http://127.0.0.1:18999/models                                  # ... and the model is now loaded
```

The router log shows `ensure_model: model name=stories260K is not loaded, loading...` for the bare request only.

Calling Hermes' own `_props_modalities("stories260K")` against that router on `main` returns `False` and leaves the model **loaded**.

### Expected Behavior

A capability lookup never loads a model. For an unloaded model it answers from the catalog plus the on-disk projector (the existing fallback).

### Actual Behavior

Seen on macOS (Apple Silicon) with a ~22 GB 35B-A3B Q4 catalog model plus its mmproj: in one day the managed router loaded the model 8 times while Hermes made 3 chat calls and 2 title-generation calls to it. Most loads were preceded by 1-4 `got exception: request cancelled while waiting for model` lines spaced 3 s apart, which matches the 3 s timeout in `_props_modalities`, and were followed by `Vision auto-detect: using main provider llamacpp` in `agent.log`. Each spurious load kept about 26 GB of unified memory busy until the idle unload.

### Affected Component

Other (local models / managed llama.cpp runtime: `hermes_cli/local_runtime/capabilities.py`)

### Messaging Platform (if gateway-related)

N/A

### Debug Report

```shell
Not attached: this is a code-level bug, reproduced above against a standalone llama-server
with a public 1 MB GGUF. Happy to provide more detail if needed.
```

### Operating System

macOS (Apple Silicon); also reproduced on Linux x86_64 (Ubuntu)

### Python Version

3.14

### Hermes Version

main @ f42f579cf8b

### Root Cause Analysis (optional)

`hermes_cli/local_runtime/capabilities.py:49` sends `/props?model={model_id}` with no `autoload=false`, to a router that runs with `--models-autoload`.

### Proposed Fix (optional)

Send `autoload=false` with the probe (and URL-encode the model id). A loaded child still answers live (the router proxies to it); an unloaded one gets a 400 and the catalog answers. The parameter exists in every router build since the router API was introduced (llama.cpp #17470). PR to follow.

Related:

- #126631: the managed router outlives its owner on macOS, so a load triggered this way can stay resident with no idle sweep.
- #120691: two routers each autoloading their own copy of the same model.
- `agent/model_metadata.py:_llamacpp_context` also sends `/props?model=` for context detection. It is keyless today, so a keyed router answers 401 and nothing loads (#105379). If the route credential is forwarded to local-server probes (#117935), that probe will start autoloading too.

### Are you willing to submit a PR for this?

- [x] I'd like to fix this myself and submit a PR

prs.title: feat(moa): make the advisor tool-result budget configurable per preset
prs.body:
## What & why

The advisory (reference-model) view of a MoA conversation keeps tool **calls** in full but previews
each tool **result** head+tail, because advisor input scales linearly with result size and the
aggregator gets the full transcript anyway. That preview length is a hardcoded module constant:

```python
# agent/moa_loop.py
_REFERENCE_TOOL_RESULT_BUDGET = 4000
```

4000 chars is a reasonable default for shell output and file reads, but it silently guts the
payloads that matter most to an advisor in tool-heavy sessions. Measured on a real repository
(2,638 tool results across 55 sessions):

| tool | avg result size | results truncated at 4000 chars |
|---|---|---|
| `read_file` | 2.9 KB | 22% |
| `patch` | 1.1 KB | 3% |
| `terminal` | 1.6 KB | 9% |
| `web_extract` | 28 KB | 86% |
| MCP doc search (`mcp__…__search`) | 22 KB | **95%** |
| `skill_view` | 15 KB | 72% |

So a MoA advisor in an MCP-heavy or docs-heavy workflow reviews a case file with the substance
removed, while the cost that motivated the cap (advisor input tokens) is exactly the thing a user
may be willing to trade back. There is currently **no way to tune this** — not in `config.yaml`, not
per preset, not via env — while every neighbouring advisory knob (`reference_timeout`,
`reference_temperature`, `reference_max_tokens`, `fanout`, `degraded_reference_policy`) is
configurable.

This PR adds `reference_tool_result_budget` as a per-preset key, defaulting to the existing 4000 so
behaviour is unchanged for every existing config.

```yaml
moa:
  presets:
    default:
      reference_models: [...]
      aggregator: {...}
      reference_tool_result_budget: 8000   # chars per tool result in the advisor view
```

Clamped to `[200, 50000]`: the floor keeps an accidental `1` from erasing the advisory view, the
ceiling keeps a typo from turning every advisor call into a context-window problem. Missing,
blank or non-numeric values fall back to 4000.

## Changes

| file | change |
|---|---|
| `agent/moa_loop.py` | `_reference_messages()` takes a keyword-only `tool_result_budget`; new `_preset_tool_result_budget(preset)` resolves it with the module default as fallback; the facade path passes the preset value, and `aggregate_moa_context()` (one-shot `/moa`) gains a matching parameter. |
| `hermes_cli/moa_config.py` | `DEFAULT_REFERENCE_TOOL_RESULT_BUDGET`, clamps, `_coerce_tool_result_budget()`, wired into `_normalize_preset()` and `_FLAT_PRESET_KEYS` (so the flattened/preset-compat view carries it too). |
| `agent/turn_request_assembly.py` | forwards `moa_config["reference_tool_result_budget"]` to `aggregate_moa_context()`. |
| `hermes_cli/config_defaults.py` | documents the key and its bounds in the shipped default preset. |
| `tests/agent/test_moa_reference_tool_result_budget.py` | 14 new tests. |

## How to test

```bash
# new tests
python -m pytest tests/agent/test_moa_reference_tool_result_budget.py -q
# surrounding MoA suite
python -m pytest tests/agent/test_moa_*.py -q
```

Locally: **14/14 new tests pass**; `tests/agent/test_moa_*.py` → **113 passed** (3 pre-existing
failures in `test_moa_loop_mode.py` / `test_moa_streaming.py` reproduce identically on the
unpatched base commit in the same ad-hoc venv, so they are environment artifacts, not regressions).

Manual check: set `reference_tool_result_budget: 12000` on a preset, run a MoA session that calls a
large-payload tool (an MCP search or `web_extract`), and confirm the `[tool result: …]` block in the
advisor prompt keeps ~12 KB (or inspect the saved turn with `moa.save_traces: true`).

## Behavioural notes

- Default unchanged: absent key → 4000 chars, byte-identical advisory view to today.
- Advisor input (and therefore advisor cost) scales with the value; the aggregator is unaffected.
- The fan-out cache key already hashes the advisory view, so changing the budget mid-session
  invalidates cached guidance correctly — no extra plumbing needed.

## Platforms tested

Linux (gm-pc, Python 3.11). No platform-specific code paths touched — this is string truncation
plus config normalization.

prs.title: feat(moa): make the advisory tool-result budget config-driven per preset
prs.body:
## Summary

MoA reference models (the advisors fanned out to before the aggregator acts)
only ever see a hardcoded 4000-character head+tail preview of each tool
result — `_REFERENCE_TOOL_RESULT_BUDGET` in `agent/moa_loop.py`. For
CJK-heavy or document-analysis workloads (e.g. reviewing a patent PDF via
tool calls), 4000 chars is roughly 2000–3000 effective Chinese characters
once punctuation/ASCII overhead is factored in — often too little for a
reference model to say anything useful about what a tool actually returned.

This PR makes that budget configurable per MoA preset, with a safe
fallback, instead of requiring a source edit that `hermes update` would
overwrite on the next pull.

## What changed

- **`hermes_cli/moa_config.py`**: new `_coerce_reference_tool_result_budget()`
  — normalizes to an int in `[1000, 32000]`; every invalid/missing/non-finite
  input (`None`, `False`/`True`, `0`, negative, `"bad"`, `inf`, `-inf`, `nan`,
  absurdly large numeric strings, fractional values) falls back to `4000`
  rather than raising. Field is added to `_normalize_preset()` and
  `_FLAT_PRESET_KEYS`.
- **`hermes_cli/config_defaults.py`**: `DEFAULT_CONFIG["moa"]["presets"]["default"]`
  declares `reference_tool_result_budget: 4000` so the key is documented and
  recognized out of the box.
- **`agent/moa_loop.py`**:
  - `_reference_messages()` accepts a `tool_result_budget` kwarg (was
    hardcoded via the module constant).
  - New `_preset_tool_result_budget(preset)` helper resolves + clamps the
    preset's value, falling back to the module constant on any failure.
  - `MoAChatCompletions.create()` (the persistent MoA loop) and
    `aggregate_moa_context()` (the one-shot `/moa <prompt>` path) both now
    thread the preset's budget through to `_reference_messages`.
- **`agent/turn_request_assembly.py`**: `_append_moa_context()` passes
  `_preset_tool_result_budget(moa_config)` into `aggregate_moa_context()`.
- **`hermes_cli/config.py`**: `_validate_config_key()` previously only
  recognized sub-keys under the literal `moa.presets.default.*` path — a
  user-named preset (`moa.presets.review.*`) would incorrectly warn as an
  unrecognized key. Added `_DYNAMIC_SCHEMA_TEMPLATES` so any preset name
  under `moa.presets.<name>` is validated against the `default` preset's
  schema, while genuine typos (`reference_tool_result_budge`) are still
  rejected with a suggestion.
- **`hermes_cli/web_models.py`** / **`hermes_cli/web_routers/models.py`**:
  `_MoaReferenceControls` (and therefore both `MoaPresetPayload` and the
  legacy flat `MoaConfigPayload`) declares `reference_tool_result_budget`
  with the same coercion/clamping validator, and it's added to
  `_MOA_PRESET_FIELDS` — so a dashboard `PUT /api/model/moa` round-trip no
  longer silently drops the setting for either named-preset or legacy
  payload shapes.

## Why per-preset config instead of just raising the constant

A hardcoded bump would still be lost on every `hermes update` (git pull)
and requires editing agent internals to tune. This exposes it exactly like
`fanout`, `reference_timeout`, etc. — a normal `moa.presets.<name>.*` knob,
settable via `hermes config set` or the dashboard, without touching source.

## Backward compatibility

- Default/fallback value is unchanged at `4000` — existing configs and
  presets that never set this key behave identically to before.
- This is purely additive: no existing field was renamed or removed.

## Testing

- `tests/agent/test_moa_tool_result_budget.py` (new): budget normalization
  boundaries (missing/bool/zero/negative/huge/string/non-finite/fractional
  inputs), CLI validation for both the default and a custom preset name
  (plus typo rejection), `_reference_messages` truncation at a custom
  budget, and that both the persistent (`MoAChatCompletions.create`) and
  one-shot (`aggregate_moa_context` via `_append_moa_context`) paths
  actually forward the preset's configured value.
- `tests/hermes_cli/test_moa_set_models_preserves_extra_keys.py` (extended):
  PUT round-trip preserves `reference_tool_result_budget` for both a named
  preset payload and the legacy flat payload shape.
- `scripts/run_tests.sh tests/agent/test_moa_tool_result_budget.py tests/hermes_cli/test_moa_config.py tests/hermes_cli/test_moa_set_models_preserves_extra_keys.py tests/hermes_cli/test_set_config_value.py` → **129 passed**
  (re-verified again with `tests/run_agent/test_moa_loop_mode.py` included → **156 passed** on a clean shared clone of this branch).
- `ruff check` on all touched files → clean.
- Two independent review passes (fresh-context code review) run against the
  diff; first pass caught three gaps (custom-preset CLI validation,
  non-finite input crash, API round-trip drop), all fixed and re-verified;
  second pass: no remaining logic or security issues found.

## Not in scope

- No change to the `fanout` modes (`user_turn` / `per_iteration` /
  `every_n:<N>`) themselves — this PR only affects the per-tool-result
  character budget.
- No UI/dashboard form field was added for this setting in this PR (it's
  settable via `hermes config set` and preserved correctly if set via a
  raw API payload, but no new dashboard input control is included).
