prs.title: Add three delivery-verification skills (iOS package gate, native ASC delivery, content language gate)
prs.body:
Three skills extracted from real shipping work on native iOS apps. Each one exists because a specific failure was **measured**, not imagined — and each one is built to distrust itself.

| Skill | What it refuses to let you believe |
|---|---|
| `ios-package-gate` | that `** ARCHIVE SUCCEEDED **` means your app is signed |
| `ios-appstore-native-delivery` | that "uploaded" means "installable" |
| `content-language-gate` | that "no violations found" means your scanner can see |

### `ios-package-gate`

Measured: `xcodebuild archive` printed `** ARCHIVE SUCCEEDED **` and the resulting bundle was `code object is not signed at all`. A pipeline that trusts build output will try to upload that. So this gate ignores the log and opens the package — 14 checks on the artifact: signature authority, `get-task-allow`, `beta-reports-active`, whether the embedded profile still carries `ProvisionedDevices` (i.e. it is a development profile), architecture, version fields, privacy manifest, icon, declared-vs-actual permissions, and whether `ITSAppUsesNonExemptEncryption` agrees with what the source actually imports.

Run against three different apps; rejected known-bad in three distinct ways (unsigned archive → 7 failures; signature and profile stripped → 2; undeclared permission → named the exact missing key).

One design note worth flagging, because it is the kind of thing that makes a shared gate harmful: the permission check originally came from an app whose flow asks for nothing, so it asserted *"there must be no permission strings at all."* Run against a second app it went red on a **legitimate** microphone and photo-library permission — the gate was writing one product's assumption onto another as a defect. The rule is now "permissions must match what you declared"; an undeclared one is still red, which is the real risk.

### `ios-appstore-native-delivery`

The `xcodebuild` path rather than Expo/EAS, with four traps that each cost real time:

1. Under automatic signing `CODE_SIGN_IDENTITY` **stays** `Apple Development`. Writing `Apple Distribution` yields `conflicting provisioning settings`. The distribution identity is swapped in by `exportArchive`, not by `archive` — and the `archive` output cannot be uploaded. Five attempts to find this.
2. `ARCHIVE SUCCEEDED` does not prove signing (see above).
3. `POST /v1/apps` → **403 `The resource 'apps' does not allow 'CREATE'`**. Creating the app record is a web-UI step. Until it exists, `altool` reports `Cannot determine the Apple ID from Bundle ID`, which reads like a signing failure and is routinely misdiagnosed as one.
4. JWT `exp` must be ≤ 20 minutes, or a 401 surfaces downstream as an unrelated `KeyError: 'data'`.

It keeps `"No errors uploading"`, `processingState: VALID`, and "reachable by the internal group" as **three separate claims** (installing on a device is a fourth). Bounded polling, no blind retry, never re-uploads the same binary. Tester identity is read from `/v1/users` and confirmed by reading the group back — nothing is guessed, no other user is added.

**Honest limit, stated in the SKILL.md itself:** the chain *after* `altool --upload-app` — processing poll, group creation, tester — is written and reviewed but has **never run against a real upload**, because the app record did not exist. I would rather ship that caveat than imply coverage I do not have.

### `content-language-gate`

Scans product text against forbidden-language classes from a rule file and counts originality (repeated strings are the App Review 4.3(b) template signature). Three properties make it trustworthy:

- **It self-tests every run.** Known-bad decoys go through its own patterns first; if it fails to catch them it prints `gate is BLIND` and refuses to treat a clean result as evidence. Measured reason: an earlier version matched a verb stem, mistook ordinary phrases for clinical diagnosis, and produced **8 false violations** — writing its own defect onto the product.
- **An empty scan is not a pass.** Wrong glob → `NOTHING WAS SCANNED`, exit 1. Silence is the most common way a text gate lies.
- **Fields are never merged when counting uniqueness.** Measured: a predecessor counted `text + "|" + short` as one key; because `text` always differed, repeated `short` strings were mathematically invisible — it reported `433/433 unique` while 12 strings repeated 3–4 times. 28 excess copies were hidden by the merge.

Ships a runnable synthetic example, including the two arms that prove the gate can fail.

### Shape

All three are parameterized — no bundle ids, team ids, project paths or credentials in any file. The ASC key id, `.p8` path and keychain service come from the environment with **no built-in default** (a default would also make the script silently look for the wrong key on another machine). All example content is synthetic.

Exit codes carry the real verdict, so each one works directly as a CI gate.

prs.title: Update mcp-builder skill: add a TypeScript SDK v2 guide
prs.body:
Update mcp-builder skill: add a TypeScript SDK v2 guide

The MCP TypeScript SDK v2 (`@modelcontextprotocol/server`) is now the stable `latest` release on npm. v1 (`@modelcontextprotocol/sdk`) gets only bug and security fixes. The skill's TypeScript guide covered only v1, while `SKILL.md` told the agent to fetch the `main` README, which is now the v2 README. Agents were reading v2 docs and then following a v1 guide.

## Changes

- **New `reference/node_mcp_server_v2.md`.** It follows the v1 guide section by section.
  - a v1 → v2 translation table and the codemod steps for migrating
- **`SKILL.md`:**
  - says there are two SDK versions, with a rule for choosing: new servers use v2; projects that already depend on `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` use v1 or migrate with the codemod
  - links each version's docs: v2 is the `main` README plus `ts.sdk.modelcontextprotocol.io/v2/llms.txt`, v1 is the `v1.x` README
- **`reference/node_mcp_server.md` (v1):** one note at the top pointing new servers to the v2 guide. Otherwise unchanged.

## Testing

- The guide's complete example and its 14 SDK snippets type-check under `strict` against `@modelcontextprotocol/server@2.3.1`, `node@2.1.1`, `express@2.0.2` and `zod@4.6.5`, on TypeScript 5.9.3 and 7.0.2.
- The complete example runs against a mock API with `@modelcontextprotocol/client` driving it:
  - over stdio and Streamable HTTP
  - with both 2025-era and 2026-07-28 clients
  - covering defaults, JSON/Markdown output, an empty result, schema rejection, and strict rejection of unknown keys
  - Requests with a foreign `Host` header get 403.
- I gave two fresh agents only this skill:
  - **A new MCP server:** the agent chose v2 with no v1 imports. It builds and works over stdio and HTTP.
  - **Adding tools to an existing v1 project:** the agent chose v1 because of the project's `package.json`, and stayed on v1 imports. It builds and works.

prs.title: fix(pptx): make clean.py slide resolution namespace-aware and fail closed (#1953)
prs.body:
## Summary

Addresses #1953 in `skills/pptx/scripts/clean.py`:

Previously, `clean.py` extracted slide relationship IDs from `ppt/presentation.xml` using a regex:
```python
re.findall(r'<p:sldId[^>]*r:id="([^"]+)"', pres_content)
```
If `presentation.xml` was missing, malformed, used single-quoted XML attributes (`r:id='rId1'`), or used an alternative namespace prefix (`<ppt:sldId>`), the regex returned no IDs. The safety guard then failed to trigger, causing `remove_orphaned_slides()` to delete **every** slide on disk and all associated resources (charts, drawings, media).

## Changes

1. **Robust XML Parsing**: Replaced regex extraction with `defusedxml.minidom` (already utilized throughout `clean.py`) to parse `sldId` elements and resolve `r:id` across namespaces and quotation styles.
2. **Fail-Closed Safety**:
   - Refuses to clean (`RefusedToClean`) if `ppt/presentation.xml` is missing while slides exist on disk.
   - Refuses to clean (`RefusedToClean`) if `ppt/presentation.xml` is malformed and fails to parse.
   - Refuses to clean (`RefusedToClean`) if no on-disk slides match the referenced slides list.
3. **Regression Tests**: Added `skills/pptx/tests/test_clean.py` covering missing/malformed `presentation.xml`, single-quoted attributes, alternative namespace prefixes, and mismatch detection.

Fixes #1953

prs.title: fix(skill-creator): preserve feedback through load and save failures
prs.body:
## Summary

Preserve saved evaluation notes when the initial feedback read fails, and report failed writes without showing Saved or successful completion. Retry validates the saved document before merging local edits, including deliberate blanks, then automatically saves the recovered notes. Navigation keeps an outgoing save failure visible.

Keep these behaviours in the maintained viewer template so generated pages retain them. Add 50 regression cases using Node's built-in test runner.

| Feedback state | Behaviour |
| --- | --- |
| `loading` | Display the trial and disable feedback controls until restoration finishes. |
| `known` | Queue whole-document saves and check HTTP success. |
| `unknown` | Keep local drafts, permit Retry and export only local edits without posting. |
| `local` | Export feedback without calling the feedback API. |

Done preserves completion ownership. Failed saves offer a recovery download; recovery after an unread server document explicitly excludes earlier notes. The receiver and feedback JSON format are unchanged.

## Evidence

- **Before:** With eight saved notes, a failed initial GET followed by a successful POST replaces the file with one note. The template also displays Saved and completion after a POST returns HTTP 500. The regression suite fails 45 of 50 cases on upstream `8a1541c4a3ffa5a20a5a91de0dcf3f0bab1d1ef4`.
- **After:** `node --test skills/skill-creator/eval-viewer/tests/feedback.test.mjs` passes all 50 cases with zero skips. The same checks pass against generated HTML.
- Eight synthetic request sequences through the actual receiver verify 24 accepted snapshots, preserving untouched notes and explicit blanks. Chrome 154 checks cover failed and malformed reads, a held Retry, Retry as the last action, an outgoing save failure after navigation, completion, failed writes and file mode.
- Node/Python syntax, skill metadata validation, scoped diff checks and exact patch application/reversal pass. The template matches the independently reviewed result byte for byte.

## Risk


The receiver still replaces the entire feedback document. Incorrect client state can discard notes, so writes remain blocked until restoration succeeds. Failed reads permit local editing and partial recovery; they cannot replace unread server notes.

## Unverified

Concurrent viewers, requests that never return and power loss during a write were not tested. In the unchanged generator, explicit previous context with two empty maps still looks the same as no context. Other browsers, full accessibility, mobile and hosted CI were not checked. The repository defines no build or lint command.

prs.title: skill-creator: quick_validate rejects empty name/description and checks referenced files
prs.body:
## Problem

`quick_validate.py` currently passes two damage classes that matter for skill integrity:

1. **Empty-string frontmatter values.** All format checks sit behind truthiness guards
   (`if name:` / `if description:`), so `name: ""` parses as an empty string, skips every
   check, and validates as "Skill is valid!". (Unquoted `name:` becomes `None` and is
   accidentally rejected by the type check — so the behavior differs by quoting style.)
2. **No reference-existence check.** SKILL.md may link to bundled files
   (`[guide](references/x.md)`) that don't exist on disk; nothing catches it.

## Repro (upstream main @ 8a1541c; quick_validate.py last touched in 1ed29a03)

```bash
mkdir -p /tmp/qv-demo/blank /tmp/qv-demo/dead-ref
printf -- '---\nname: ""\ndescription: ""\n---\n\n# T\n' > /tmp/qv-demo/blank/SKILL.md
printf -- '---\nname: t\ndescription: demo skill for validation.\n---\n\nSee [g](references/g.md).\n' > /tmp/qv-demo/dead-ref/SKILL.md
python3 quick_validate.py /tmp/qv-demo/blank      # before: "Skill is valid!"  after: rejects empty name
python3 quick_validate.py /tmp/qv-demo/dead-ref   # before: "Skill is valid!"  after: "Referenced file(s) not found: references/g.md"
```

## Change

- Reject empty `name`/`description` after stripping (presence of the key was already
  required; the value now must be non-empty too).
- Add a reference-existence check scoped to **markdown link targets** under
  `scripts/`, `references/`, `assets/`, skipping fenced code blocks and
  placeholder-looking paths. Inline-code mentions in prose are intentionally out of
  scope for a quick check — skill-creator's own SKILL.md uses illustrative example
  paths (e.g. `references/aws.md` in a routing pattern), and checking only link
  targets keeps false positives at zero (verified against skill-creator itself and
  several real-world skills).

## Context

Found during fault-injection experiments on skill integrity (blanking frontmatter,
deleting referenced attachments): the validator reported "Skill is valid!" for every
damaged variant. A community fork of skill-creator already ships a similar
`validate_path_references`; this brings the idea upstream in a false-positive-safe form.

prs.body:
## Summary

Addresses #1942: in `skills/skill-creator/SKILL.md`, the evaluation workflow previously assumed subagents could always be spawned unconditionally at Step 1 (`Spawn all runs (with-skill AND baseline) in the same turn`).

In harnesses like Claude Code or other environments where agent system instructions forbid unrequested subagent spawning, or in environments where subagents are not supported, this assumption caused the documented main path to fail partway through.

### Changes
1. Added an **Environment & Capability Pre-check** at the start of `## Running and evaluating test cases` to check whether subagents can be spawned autonomously.
2. In environments where spawning requires explicit user permission, prompt the user for opt-in (`"I can run N paired test subagents in parallel (with-skill vs. baseline) to evaluate this; would you like me to spawn them?"`).
3. Documented a general **Inline execution fallback** (run test cases sequentially, skip baseline comparisons, collect qualitative feedback).
4. Updated the Claude.ai section to reference this generalized inline execution fallback rather than leaving it isolated to one platform.

Closes #1942.

## Problem

The MCP evaluation guide requires questions whose answers depend on the server's tools, and the agent prompt says it must use those tools. prs.title: fix(skill-creator): do not pass negative evals on worker errors
prs.body:
## Problem

The trigger evaluator treats a failed trial as `False` (skill did not trigger). For a negative eval query, that becomes a PASS. Claude CLI failures and worker exceptions can therefore inflate specificity and let the description optimizer select a broken run. The HTML report and verbose accuracy also count failed negative trials as correct.

## Fix

Raise on a nonzero `claude -p` exit or a streamed `result` with `is_error`. Keep the existing per-query warning/continue behavior for worker exceptions, but record their count and force that query to fail. Exclude failed negative trials from the report's correct-run total and the verbose true-negative count.

## Verification

Five regressions failed before their respective fixes: nonzero CLI exit returned `False`, CLI error result returned `False`, a worker exception made a negative query pass, and both the report and verbose output counted a failed negative trial as correct. All five pass with `/opt/homebrew/bin/python3.11 -m unittest scripts.test_run_eval_errors -v` from `skills/skill-creator`.


### Review follow-up

I fixed the no-holdout report case you noted. The report normalizes only test_results=None to an empty list; numeric zero and False still fail as malformed input. The actual no-holdout history shape fails on the prior head and now renders the training score. The earlier failed-trial accounting regressions remain green. Owning suite: 7 tests pass on Python 3.13 and independently on Python 3.12.11. No model calls were made. Published follow-up `da50892789b621868883f988621283d52a89cda3`; hosted CI and maintainer review remain separate.

## Problem

`run_eval` accepts `runs_per_query=0` or a negative value. No trial is submitted, so a nonempty eval set produces `summary.total == 0` and `summary.failed == 0`. When called by the description optimization loop, this can be reported as `all_passed` even though no query was tested. The CLI exposes this through `--runs-per-query`.

## Fix

Reject nonpositive trial counts before creating the worker pool. The error is raised for both direct callers and the optimization loop.

## Verification

The new zero and negative trial regressions both failed against main and pass with this change. Ran `/opt/homebrew/bin/python3.11 -m unittest scripts.test_run_eval_options -v` from `skills/skill-creator` (2 passing tests).

Both new real-subprocess CLI cases fail against the prior head and pass here without running workers or calling a model. Owning suite: 3 tests pass on Python 3.13 and independently on Python 3.12.11. prs.title: fix(skill-creator): reject duplicate eval queries before evaluation
prs.body:
## Problem

`run_eval` groups finished trials by query text. If an eval set contains the same query twice, the two items silently collapse into one result and `summary.total` undercounts. With conflicting `should_trigger` values, the expected label depends on worker completion order. In `run_loop`, duplicates can also land on opposite sides of the train/holdout split; the result is then attributed to training, corrupting the holdout score.

## Fix

Reject duplicate query text before launching workers. The error points users to `runs_per_query` for repeated trials.

## Verification

- Added a regression that failed before this change (`ValueError` was not raised) and now passes.
- Confirmed unique queries still yield two separate results.
- Ran `/opt/homebrew/bin/python3.11 -m unittest scripts.test_run_eval -v` from `skills/skill-creator` (2 passing tests).


### Review follow-up

I addressed the CLI note in both run_eval and run_loop. A duplicate query now prints Error: Duplicate eval query and exits 1 without a traceback; direct Python callers still receive ValueError. The new real-subprocess cases fail against the prior head and pass here. They stop on validation before any worker or model call. Owning suite: 3 tests pass on Python 3.13 and independently on Python 3.12.11. No model calls were made. prs.title: fix(pptx): detect dangling third axis in 3D line charts
prs.body:
## Problem
The PPTX chart validator declares that `line3DChart` needs three axes, but its broken-reference check stopped as soon as it found two live references. A 3D line chart with a dangling third reference therefore passed the check. It also counted repeated references to the same axis separately, so `1, 2, 1` appeared to satisfy a three-axis requirement.

## Fix
Use each chart type's `AXID_MINIMUM` and count distinct resolved axis IDs. Diagnostics now report the correct minimum.

## Regression evidence
- Before: the missing-third-axis test found no problem for references `1, 2, 999`; the repeated-axis test found no problem for `1, 2, 1`.
- After: both invalid charts are reported; the three-distinct-live-axis control passes.
- `PYTHONPATH=skills/pptx/scripts python3.11 -m unittest discover -s skills/pptx/scripts/tests -p test_chart_axes.py -v` — 3 passed.
- `python3.11 -m compileall -q skills/pptx/scripts/office/helpers/pptx_chart.py` — passed.

The OOXML `CT_Line3DChart` schema specifies exactly three `axId` elements: https://c-rex.net/samples/ooxml/e1/part4/OOXML_P4_DOCX_line3DChart_topic_ID0E3EJQB.html

prs.title: fix(pptx): remove prefixed notes relations when duplicating slides
prs.body:
## Problem

`add_slide.py` documents that a duplicate must not share the source slide's speaker notes. It removes `notesSlide` relationships using a regex that only recognizes unprefixed `<Relationship>` elements. The OOXML relationship namespace can validly use a prefix such as `<rel:Relationship>`. In that case duplication retains the notes link, so the new slide points to the original slide's speaker notes.

## Change

Allow a namespace prefix on relationship element names when filtering a copied slide's `.rels` file. Other relationships remain intact.

## Regression evidence

A focused fixture uses a prefixed relationships XML with one notes link and one image link. Before this change, the copied slide still had both links and the test failed (`{'image', 'notesSlide'} != {'image'}`). After the change, both prefixed and default-namespace variants pass; the image link is preserved.

## Test plan

- `uv run --python 3.12 --with pytest pytest -q skills/pptx/tests/test_add_slide_prefixed_notes.py` — 2 passed.
- `python3.12 -m py_compile skills/pptx/scripts/add_slide.py` — passed.
- `git diff --check` — passed.

prs.title: fix(web-artifacts-builder): support current TypeScript and calendar API
prs.body:
## Problem

The documented `init-artifact.sh` workflow generates a project that does not pass its own `pnpm build` with the current Vite/TypeScript template. The script adds `baseUrl` to both tsconfig files, and TypeScript 6 exits with TS5101 because that option is deprecated. It also installs the latest `react-day-picker` (currently major 10), while the vendored `calendar.tsx` uses major 9's `ClassNames` API; once TS5101 is removed, the calendar fails with TS2353 (`table` is not a valid key).

## Fix

Keep the `@/*` path mappings without `baseUrl` (supported by current TypeScript), and constrain `react-day-picker` to major 9, which matches the vendored calendar component. This does not touch `react-resizable-panels`; open PR #1894 handles that separate major-version mismatch.

## Verification

Ran the unmodified initializer with Node 24, pnpm 11, current create-vite/TypeScript in a disposable project. `pnpm exec tsc -b` failed first at TS5101. Removing `baseUrl` exposed the calendar TS2353 error; installing `react-day-picker@9` removed calendar errors, leaving only the resizable errors covered by #1894. Ran this branch's initializer fresh and applied #1894's intended `react-resizable-panels@^3` pin locally: `pnpm build` passed, including TypeScript and Vite. The fixture test verifies the generated tsconfigs and installed day-picker major; both checks fail on `main` and pass here. `bash -n` and `git diff --check` pass.

The generated build still requires #1894 (or its equivalent) until that PR merges. This PR does not duplicate its resizable change.


### Review follow-up: alias resolution

I verified the reviewer’s Parcel concern with a real project using `tsconfig.json` paths `@/* -> ./src/*` and **no `baseUrl`**. On Node 24.19.0, pnpm 11.25.0, and Parcel 2.16.4, the repository's `bundle-artifact.sh` installed its resolver stack, built successfully, and inlined the bundle. An import of `@/lib` resolved to `src/lib.ts`; both the emitted JavaScript and `bundle.html` contain the expected `ALIAS_RESOLVED` marker. Thus the current Parcel fallback resolves the alias with the TypeScript 6-compatible config.

issues.title: Security: Community skills distributed under anthropic/ namespace enable trust boundary abuse
issues.body:
## Summary

Community-made skills are being distributed under the `anthropic/` namespace, impersonating official Anthropic skills. This creates a trust boundary vulnerability where users may grant elevated permissions to community skills they believe are official.

## Discovery

During a comprehensive security audit of 580+ installed Claude Code skills, we found 6 skills placed under `~/.claude/skills/anthropic/`:

| Skill | author field | allowed-tools |
|-------|-------------|---------------|
| anthropic-expert (root) | not set | Read, Grep, Glob |
| claude-code | not set | Read, Grep, Glob |
| claude-command-builder | not set | Read, Write, Edit, Grep, Glob, **Bash** |
| claude-mcp-expert | **raintree** | Read, Write, Edit, Grep, Glob, **Bash** |
| claude-hook-builder | not set | Read, Write, Edit, Grep, Glob, **Bash** |
| claude-settings-expert | not set | Read, Write, Edit, Grep, Glob |
| claude-skill-builder | **raintree** | Read, Write, Edit, Grep, Glob, **Bash** |

**None of these exist in the official `anthropics/skills` repository.** Two skills explicitly list `author: raintree`, confirming they are community-made.

## Security Concern

### Trust Boundary Abuse

1. Users see `anthropic/` in the skill path and assume official Anthropic provenance
2. This lowers their guard when approving operations — especially Bash execution and settings.json modifications
3. `claude-hook-builder` can write PostToolUse hooks to `settings.json`, enabling arbitrary command execution after every tool use
4. `claude-settings-expert` can directly edit `settings.json` and documents `bypassPermissions` (as a warning, but the JSON structure is shown)

### Attack Scenario

```
User installs "anthropic/" skills from a community collection
  → Trusts them as official due to namespace
  → Approves Bash operations without scrutiny
  → claude-hook-builder writes a PostToolUse hook
  → All subsequent tool executions trigger arbitrary commands
```

## Suggested Mitigations

1. **Reserved namespace**: Prevent community skills from using `anthropic/` as a directory name in skill registries
2. **Namespace verification**: Add a verification mechanism (e.g., signed manifests) for official Anthropic skills
3. **Documentation**: Warn users in the skills documentation that directory names do not imply official provenance

## Note

The skills themselves do not appear to contain actively malicious code. The `claude-hook-builder` skill includes appropriate "USE AT YOUR OWN RISK" warnings. The concern is purely about the trust boundary created by the `anthropic/` namespace impersonation.

issues.title: run_eval.py: claude -p never triggers skills/commands (0% trigger rate across all queries)
issues.body:
## Bug Description

`run_eval.py` creates a command file in `.claude/commands/` with the skill description in YAML frontmatter, then runs `claude -p` with test queries to check if Claude invokes the `Skill` or `Read` tool for that command. In practice, **no query ever triggers the skill** — all should-trigger queries get 0/3 trigger rate, including an explicit "run /lucas:memory-layer please".

## Reproduction

Tested with 8 different skills (144 total queries across all eval sets). Every should-trigger query scored 0/3 triggers. Every should-not-trigger query also scored 0/3 (correctly, but vacuously).

Diagnostic test with maximally obvious trigger:
```json
[{"query": "I need to use the lucas memory layer skill right now, run /lucas:memory-layer please", "should_trigger": true}]
```
Result: 0/3 triggers.

## Environment
- Claude Code v2.1.71
- macOS Darwin 25.3.0
- Model: claude-opus-4-6
- Ran from external terminal (no active Claude Code session)

## Analysis

The issue appears to be that `claude -p` does not auto-trigger commands placed in `.claude/commands/` the same way an interactive Claude Code session triggers skills from `~/.claude/skills/`. Possible causes:

1. **Commands vs Skills**: Commands in `.claude/commands/` may not appear in Claude's `available_skills` list the same way skills do, or may only be invocable via explicit `/command-name` syntax
2. **`claude -p` mode**: The `-p` (pipe/prompt) mode may not load commands/skills at all, or may not present them to the model
3. **Simple query threshold**: Claude may not consult skills for queries it can handle directly — but even explicit "run this skill" failed, ruling this out as the sole cause

## Expected Behavior

At minimum, an explicit request like "run /skill-name please" should trigger the command (rate > 0/3). Description-matched queries should trigger at a reasonable rate.

## Suggested Fix

- Verify that `claude -p` actually loads and presents `.claude/commands/` files to the model
- Consider placing test skills in `~/.claude/skills/` instead of `.claude/commands/` if skills and commands are triggered differently
- Add a `--debug` flag to `run_eval.py` that dumps what Claude actually sees (system prompt, available skills list) to verify the command file is being presented

issues.title: Proposing a second skill: compact-memory (symbolic notation for compact agent state)
issues.body:
Following up on my earlier question about whether external skill contributions are welcome (#1328) with a second concrete one, since these are independently useful.

This skill is compact-memory. A long-running agent spends a lot of context on its own notes and persistent memory, written in prose. Prose is redundant and it drifts: the agent paraphrases an earlier note or quietly softens a rule when it reads it back. The skill has the agent write its internal state in a small fixed symbolic notation instead, one fact per line with a consistent operator set. The result is smaller and reads back with one unambiguous meaning, which is what makes the compression safe rather than lossy.

It is self-contained: a single SKILL.md with the notation and the write discipline, no dependencies, and I would license it Apache-2.0 to match the repo. It pairs with the critical-qa skill from #1328 and three others I have packaged together (cheapest-tier routing, pre-ship web verification, claim verification) if a small bundle is more useful than single skills.

Same question stands: is a PR with a skills/<name>/SKILL.md folder following ./template the path you prefer, or an issue first? Happy to do whichever fits your review flow.

issues.title: skill-creator should be updated to best practice
issues.body:
## Summary

The skill-creator skill reads more like developer documentation than an operational skill. It explains concepts to humans rather than instructing Claude on execution. The verbose, educational tone significantly undermines token efficiency. Its very name also violates guidelines.

---

## Critical Issues

### 1. Too verbose

The skill is 356 lines—approaching the 500-line ceiling intended for *maximum* complexity. A meta-skill about creating skills shouldn't consume this much context. Most content belongs in `references/` for progressive disclosure.

### 2. Educational Tone vs. Imperative Instructions

**Problem:** Written *about* skills rather than *to* Claude.

| Current (explanatory) | Should be (imperative) |
|----------------------|------------------------|
| "Skills are modular, self-contained packages that extend Claude's capabilities..." | *(Omit—Claude knows what skills are)* |
| "Think of them as 'onboarding guides' for specific domains" | *(Omit—metaphor adds no execution value)* |
| "The context window is a public good" | "Minimize token usage; challenge each line's necessity" |

### 3. Frontmatter Weaknesses

**Name:** `skill-creator` violates the gerund convention from creating-skills.md. Should be `creating-skills`.

**Description:** 
> "Guide for creating effective skills. This skill should be used when..."

- Weak opener ("Guide for" is passive/documentary)
- First-person phrasing ("This skill should be used")
- Missing keyword density for activation

**Better:**
> "Create and iterate on Agent Skills with proper structure, frontmatter, and progressive disclosure. Use when building new skills, refactoring existing skills, or validating skill structure against the specification."

### 4. Negative Framing

The "What to Not Include" section violates positive directive framing:

> "Do NOT create extraneous documentation... README.md, INSTALLATION_GUIDE.md..."

**Should be:** "Include only files directly required for skill execution: SKILL.md plus scripts/, references/, or assets/ as needed."

### 5. Procedural Over Strategic

Step-by-step enumeration (Step 1, Step 2...) contradicts "strategic over procedural" principle. Claude can infer workflow from goals.

**Current:**
> "Step 3: Initializing the Skill... always run the init_skill.py script"

**Better:** Describe the goal (valid skill structure) and let Claude determine approach, or reference a script without mandating its use.

### 6. Base Behavior Distrust

Extensive explanation of concepts Claude already understands:
- What progressive disclosure is
- That context windows have limits  
- What "frontmatter" means
- File organization basics

This wastes tokens re-teaching the reader.

### 7. Script Dependencies Unclear

References `init_skill.py` and `package_skill.py` but the skill structure doesn't show bundled scripts. Are these expected to exist? If so, they should be in `scripts/` and the skill should verify their presence.

---

## Structural Recommendations

```
creating-skills/
├── SKILL.md              # Core workflow only (~150 lines)
└── references/
    ├── anatomy.md        # Detailed structure explanation
    ├── workflows.md      # (already referenced but not shown)
    ├── output-patterns.md # (already referenced)
    └── examples.md       # Concrete skill examples
```

Move the entire "About Skills" and "Anatomy of a Skill" sections to `references/anatomy.md`. Keep SKILL.md focused on decision framework and execution patterns.

---

## Line-by-Line Samples

| Line | Issue |
|------|-------|
| "Think of them as 'onboarding guides'" | Metaphor adds no execution value |
| "The context window is a public good" | Philosophical framing; replace with directive |
| "Default assumption: Claude is already very smart" | Meta-commentary; just write concisely |
| "To avoid overwhelming users, avoid asking too many questions" | This is base behavior—omit |
| "To turn concrete examples into an effective skill, analyze each example by:" | Procedural scaffolding Claude doesn't need |

---

## What It Does Well

- Progressive disclosure concept is correctly emphasized
- Bundled resource categories (scripts/references/assets) are clearly distinguished
- Includes concrete examples of skill contents
- Links to workflow and output-pattern references
- "Iterate based on real usage" is good strategic guidance

---

## Verdict

**Useful content, poor execution.** The information is largely correct but delivered in a way that violates the very principles it teaches. A skill about creating lean, imperative skills should itself be lean and imperative.

Estimated reduction potential: 60-70% of current content could be moved to references or eliminated.

issues.title: Skill proposal: agent-governance — safety patterns for AI agent systems
issues.body:
## Proposal: Agent Governance Skill

### Summary

A skill that teaches Claude governance patterns for AI agent systems — policy enforcement, threat detection, trust scoring, and audit trails. Currently the skills collection covers creative, technical, and enterprise workflows, but nothing focused on **agent safety and governance**.

### Use Case

When users are building AI agents (using Claude Code, ADK, PydanticAI, CrewAI, OpenAI Agents, etc.), this skill would activate to guide them toward safe patterns:

- Defining governance policies (tool allowlists/blocklists, content filters, rate limits)
- Adding threat detection (data exfiltration, prompt injection, privilege escalation)
- Implementing trust scoring for multi-agent delegation
- Building append-only audit trails for compliance
- Policy composition (org → team → agent layering)

### Proposed Skill

```markdown
---
name: agent-governance
description: |
  Patterns and techniques for adding governance, safety, and trust controls
  to AI agent systems. Use this skill when building agents that call external
  tools, implementing policy-based access controls, adding threat detection,
  creating trust scoring for multi-agent workflows, or building audit trails.
---

# Agent Governance Patterns

[6 patterns: Governance Policy, Policy Composition, Semantic Intent Classification,
Tool-Level Governance Decorator, Trust Scoring, Audit Trail]

[Framework integration: PydanticAI, CrewAI, OpenAI Agents, Google ADK, LangChain]
```

We've already built this as a [Copilot skill](https://github.com/imran-siddique/awesome-ai-governance/tree/main/awesome-copilot-contributions/skills/agent-governance) (merged as [PR #755](https://github.com/github/awesome-copilot/pull/755) in github/awesome-copilot) and can adapt it to the Agent Skills format.

### Context

We maintain [Agent-OS](https://github.com/imran-siddique/agent-os) and [AgentMesh Integrations](https://github.com/imran-siddique/agentmesh-integrations) — governance frameworks with integrations for PydanticAI (57 tests), CrewAI, OpenAI Agents, and Google ADK. Also proposed governance patterns for [Google ADK](https://github.com/google/adk-python/issues/4543), [Genkit](https://github.com/firebase/genkit/issues/4771), and [A2A protocol](https://github.com/a2aproject/A2A/issues/1501).

```
algorithmic-art, brand-guidelines, canvas-design, doc-coauthoring, docx,
frontend-design, internal-comms, mcp-builder, pdf, pptx, skill-creator,
slack-gif-creator, theme-factory, web-artifacts-builder, webapp-testing, xlsx

=== example-skills ===
(identical list)
```

Both use the same commit hash in the cache (`69c0b1a06741`).

## Impact

- **~50k wasted tokens** on duplicate skill definitions
- Skills like `pptx` (6.3k tokens) appear twice in `/context`
- Reduces available context for actual work

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Install Claude Code
2. Run: `claude plugin install document-skills@anthropic-agent-skills`
3. Run: `claude plugin install example-skills@anthropic-agent-skills`
4. Run `/context` in Claude Code
5. Observe duplicate skills in the "Plugin" section

## Environment

- Claude Code **v2.0.76**
- macOS 15.6.1
- Both plugins installed at user scope

## Suggested Fix

The plugin packaging should respect the intended separation, or the marketplace should only expose one unified plugin that contains all skills without duplication.

## Workaround

Uninstall one of the duplicate plugins:
```bash
claude plugin uninstall example-skills@anthropic-agent-skills
```

issues.title: [Proposal] Reasoning Quality Gate Pipeline: Pre-task Calibration → Adversarial Review → Delivery Verification
issues.body:
# [Proposal] Reasoning Quality Gate Pipeline: Pre-task Calibration → Adversarial Review → Delivery Verification

## Summary

A three-gate pipeline covering AI output quality across the full session lifecycle. Each gate targets a failure mode the others can't catch. Two of the three gates have been independently adopted, production-hardened, and merged in leading Claude Code ecosystem repositories, with formal attribution for the original design.

## Problem

Existing quality tools (lint, typecheck, test, security scan) verify **code artifacts**. They don't verify **reasoning quality** — whether the agent's thinking process itself was sound. In Claude Code sessions, three failure modes routinely slip through:

| Failure | When | Why existing tools miss it |
|---------|------|---------------------------|
| Agent edits files before confirming the approach is correct — writes 200 lines, then user realizes the direction was wrong | Before first keystroke | No pre-edit checkpoint exists |
| Single-pass code review misses blind spots — the same model reviewing its own output inherits the same blind spots | During implementation | Reviewer and author share reasoning gaps |
| Agent declares "done" via Stop but one or more claimed outputs were never written to disk, or requirements were silently dropped | After delivery | Stop hook has no output verification layer |

These aren't hypothetical — they're patterns extracted from real Claude Code sessions. Each gate was added when a failure mode was observed that existing checks couldn't catch.

## Three Gates

```
Session Start → ① Pre-task Calibration (PreToolUse hook, exit 2)
                    ↓ pass
                Task execution
                    ↓
                ② Adversarial Review (on-demand, multi-round)
                    ↓ pass
                ③ Delivery Verification (Stop hook, exit 2)
                    ↓ pass
                Delivery
```

### ① Pre-task Calibration

Before any Edit/Write/high-risk Bash: three mandatory questions. Any fail → PreToolUse hook exit 2, tool call blocked.

- Q1: Concept review passed? (did I validate the approach with an adversarial check before acting?)
- Q2: Inputs consistent? (do file paths, constants, and assumptions match actual code, not documentation memory?)
- Q3: Post-completion verification planned? (will I verify output, not just claim completion?)

**Mechanism**: Establishes a mandatory pre-action checkpoint via structured prompting, forcing the agent to verify feasibility and plan verification before executing any high-risk tool call. It reduces impulsive, unplanned edits by adding a consistent decision checkpoint at the only moment when prevention is cheaper than correction — before the first keystroke.

### ② Adversarial Review

**Fixed pool**: 9 sourced personas with verifiable philosophies (e.g., Rich Hickey on simplicity vs. complexity, John Carmack on edge-case testing, Don Norman on cognitive load). Each persona is grounded in documented principles with explicit confidence ratings — no fabricated quotes, no invented authorities.

**Random pool**: web-search to supplement unknown perspectives from domains outside the fixed pool's coverage, preventing echo-chamber effects.

**Mechanism**: Manager persona classifies task → selects panel → multi-round cross-review → ≥2 reviewers independently flagging same issue → auto-escalate to CRITICAL → anti-fabrication discipline (every attribution carries a confidence level; unverifiable claims are rejected rather than embellished).

### ③ Delivery Verification

**Step 0 (mechanical)**: File read-back verification — use file-read tool to confirm every claimed output file actually exists on disk with non-trivial content. This is the one verification an agent cannot fabricate: tool return values can report success without writing content, but a read-back confirms or refutes the claim deterministically.

**Steps 1-4 (reasoning, damage-severity order)**:
1. **Honesty** — is the agent being honest about what wasn't done? If failing, the remaining three dimensions audit fiction.
2. **Completeness** — did every request get addressed, or were requirements silently dropped?
3. **Consistency** — did the output contradict itself or the governing rules?
4. **Groundedness** — are claims supported by evidence, or just asserted?

Fail → Stop hook exit 2, delivery blocked. Lexicographic rule: never fix Groundedness while Honesty is failing — auditing fiction wastes effort and masks the root problem.

## Cross-gate Design Principles

1. **Mechanical where possible.** Gates ① and ③ use hook exit codes (PreToolUse + Stop). Gate ② uses a tier-classification script for review depth signals. Deterministic checks beat aspirational prompts — file timestamps, exit codes, and read-back verification don't drift.
2. **Damage-severity ordering.** Honesty before Completeness before Consistency before Groundedness. The order is not arbitrary — it reflects the cost of missing each dimension.
3. **Independent, composable.** Each gate works standalone. Combined they form defense in depth — a failure that slips past one gate is caught by another operating at a different lifecycle point with different detection mechanisms.

## Independent Validation

Two of the three gates have been independently adopted, production-hardened, and merged in leading Claude Code ecosystem repositories, with formal attribution for the original design.

### Gate ② Adversarial Review — merged with Co-authored-by attribution

- Original design proposal: `alirezarezvani/claude-skills#866`
- Maintainer-refined implementation merged to dev branch: `alirezarezvani/claude-skills#867` (2026-07-01)
- Maintainer explicit confirmation: *"core idea is genuinely valuable and filled a real gap next to adversarial-reviewer and code-reviewer"*
- **Co-authored-by attribution** added to the final merge commit per community contribution convention

### Gate ③ Delivery Verification — merged after full maintainer approval

- Original approved draft: `affaan-m/ECC#2365` (full maintainer approval from daltino)
- Final merged version: `affaan-m/ECC#2378` (2026-06-30, merged by affaan-m)
- Maintainer review: *"useful delivery-gate skill that complements the existing verification-loop by focusing on thinking quality"*

### Gate ① Pre-task Calibration — validated in production workflow

- 50+ real-world coding sessions in personal Claude Code workflow
- Not yet submitted to any public repository; included here as the upstream component completing the full pipeline

### Industry pattern alignment

The four verification dimensions (honesty, completeness, consistency, groundedness) emerged independently from real session failures — each dimension was added when a specific failure mode was observed that existing checks could not catch.

## What's Different From Existing Skills

Existing skills verify code artifacts (build, lint, typecheck, security). This pipeline verifies the **reasoning process** that produced those artifacts — before, during, and after execution. The three-gate structure was not designed upfront: each gate was added when a specific Claude Code failure mode was observed that existing gates could not catch. The result is a pipeline where blind spots are cross-covered by independent detection mechanisms at different lifecycle points.

## Request

This is a **design proposal**, not a code submission. I'm sharing the full architecture because:

- Two components have been independently production-hardened and merged with formal attribution
- The complete three-gate pipeline has been refined across 50+ real-world sessions
- The design patterns (mechanical read-back, damage-priority ordering, adversarial persona pools) are generalizable beyond any single implementation

My core contribution is the pipeline architecture and design patterns. I'm happy to help draft initial skill implementations, but I fully defer to repo maintainers on code structure, naming conventions, and integration standards to ensure consistency with the codebase.

If the team chooses to implement any part of this design internally, I ask that standard open source contribution conventions be followed for original design attribution, consistent with how prior community adoptions of these components have been handled.

## References

- Gate ② (merged, Co-authored-by): `alirezarezvani/claude-skills#866` → `#867`
- Gate ③ (merged, approved): `affaan-m/ECC#2365` → `#2378`
- Gate ③ enhanced discussion: `anthropics/skills#1367` (self-audit skill, OPEN)

issues.title: docx: merge_runs.py drops run-local namespace declarations and writes invalid XML
issues.body:
`skills/docx/scripts/merge_runs.py` removes namespace declarations on a source run when merging it into the preceding run. If a retained child uses that namespace prefix, the script reports success but writes XML with an unbound prefix. The direct `.docx` mode overwrites the input archive with the same invalid document part.

Reproduced at `dbd4588f9e1033efb41dad4bef2f7947c8993d44` on Python 3.14.7, defusedxml 0.7.1 and lxml 6.1.3, with dependencies resolved offline.

### Reproduction

Run from the repository root with defusedxml installed:

```python
import subprocess
import sys
import tempfile
from pathlib import Path
from xml.etree import ElementTree as ET

w = "http://schemas.openxmlformats.org/wordprocessingml/2006/main"
with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as tmp:
    root = Path(tmp)
    (root / "word").mkdir()
    doc = root / "word/document.xml"
    doc.write_text(f'''<w:document xmlns:w="{w}">
      <w:body><w:p>
        <w:r><w:t>Hello</w:t></w:r>
        <w:r xmlns:q="{w}"><q:tab/><w:t>world</w:t></w:r>
      </w:p></w:body>
    </w:document>''', encoding="utf-8")
    ET.parse(doc)  # Input is well-formed.
    subprocess.run([
        sys.executable, "skills/docx/scripts/merge_runs.py", str(root)
    ], check=True)
    print(doc.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
    ET.parse(doc)  # ParseError: unbound prefix
```

The command exits 0 and prints `Merged 1 runs`. The output contains `<q:tab/>`, but its `xmlns:q` declaration is gone.

### Expected behavior and validation

Merging these runs should preserve the tab and namespace binding, leaving a parseable document. Namespace declarations are valid on the run itself; moving the declaration to `w:document` is a workaround, and that control still produces valid XML after merging.

I also validated the input against the repository's `wml.xsd` with lxml: it passes. Both unpacked-directory and direct `.docx` modes reproduce the unbound-prefix failure; both corresponding controls with `xmlns:q` on the document root pass schema validation after merging. The archive fixture included `[Content_Types].xml` and `_rels/.rels` pointing to `word/document.xml`.

The loss occurs when `_merge_run_content` moves child elements into the target run and `_merge_runs_in` removes the source run without retaining its namespace declarations. Preserving the effective bindings on moved children, including conflicting prefix bindings, or declining such merges would avoid writing invalid XML.

This is a bug report rather than a patch because the DOCX skill's license restricts derivative works. The existing comment-part namespace reports (#1821/#1824) concern a different script and do not cover this run-merging failure.

issues.title: create_gradient_background never produces its documented bottom_color (interpolation ratio off by one)
issues.body:
## Summary

`create_gradient_background()` in `skills/slack-gif-creator/core/frame_composer.py`
never produces the color of its own `bottom_color` argument. The interpolation
parameter is `y / height` instead of `y / (height - 1)`, so the last row of the
image is sampled at `(height - 1) / height` and the ramp stops short of the
documented endpoint. The top edge is exact (`y = 0` → `ratio = 0.0`), so the two
endpoints of the same documented range are not treated the same way.

```python
# skills/slack-gif-creator/core/frame_composer.py:124-129 (main)
    for y in range(height):
        # Interpolate color
        ratio = y / height
        r = int(r1 * (1 - ratio) + r2 * ratio)
```

The docstring is the spec (`frame_composer.py:111-112`):

```
        top_color: RGB color at top
        bottom_color: RGB color at bottom
```

and `SKILL.md` exports the function for exactly this purpose — `SKILL.md:155`
(`create_gradient_background,  # Vertical gradient`) and `SKILL.md:91`
("Use gradients for backgrounds") — so an agent following the skill passes a
`bottom_color` it will not get.

## Reproduction

Every number below was produced by the scripts in this report against the file
bytes of `origin/main` (`git show origin/main:skills/slack-gif-creator/core/frame_composer.py`,
sha1 `7ec2269efc333bd181b8f97a1e27bacc4004f139` after newline normalisation), imported
from a scratch tree — not from a working copy.

`bottom_color` appears in the returned image **0 times**, while `top_color`
appears across the whole first row. The shortfall on the bottom row is
`(bottom - top) / height`:

| case | height | top | requested bottom | actual bottom row | error | pixels == bottom_color |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| emoji square | 96 | `(0,0,0)` | `(255,0,0)` | `(252,0,0)` | 3 | **0** |
| emoji square | 128 | `(0,0,0)` | `(255,0,0)` | `(253,0,0)` | 2 | **0** |
| builder default | 480 | `(0,0,0)` | `(255,255,255)` | `(254,254,254)` | 1 | **0** |
| tall | 1080 | `(30,60,90)` | `(200,160,120)` | `(199,159,119)` | 1 | **0** |
| reversed ramp | 120 | `(255,255,255)` | `(10,20,30)` | `(12,21,31)` | 2 | **0** |
| thin bar | 10 | `(0,0,0)` | `(255,255,255)` | `(229,229,229)` | 26 | **0** |
| thin bar | 4 | `(0,255,0)` | `(255,0,0)` | `(191,63,0)` | 64 | **0** |
| thin bar | 3 | `(0,0,0)` | `(255,0,0)` | `(170,0,0)` | 85 | **0** |
| thin bar | 2 | `(0,0,0)` | `(255,0,0)` | `(127,0,0)` | 128 | **0** |

A 2-row ramp returns its midpoint as the bottom row: the gradient covers half of
its intended range. Sweeping every height from 2 to 199 with one fixed pair of
colors: **198 of 198 heights have a bottom row that is not `bottom_color`**.

Randomised, 4000 triples (`h` in 2..300, any 8-bit colors, 612,454 rows
compared):

```
pre   first row != top_color: 0   last row != bottom_color: 3702
post  first row != top_color: 0   last row != bottom_color: 0
```

The 298 cases where `main` happens to land on the endpoint are not a counter-
example to the above: all 298 have every channel descending (`bottom <= top`), a
span smaller than the height (largest `span / height` = 0.99) and a height of at
least 43, so `int()` floors a value that is within one unit of the target. In none
of them does an ascending channel reach its endpoint.

## Suggested fix

One line, so that the parameter spans the full range and the last row samples at
`1.0`. The `height > 1` guard keeps the existing single-row behaviour (`height=1`
today returns one row of `top_color`) instead of turning it into a
`ZeroDivisionError`:

```python
-        ratio = y / height
+        ratio = y / (height - 1) if height > 1 else 0.0
```

After the fix both endpoints are exact for any input, by construction: `y = 0`
gives `int(c1 * 1.0 + c2 * 0.0) == c1` and `y = height - 1` gives
`ratio == 1.0` exactly (equal integers), hence `int(c1 * 0.0 + c2 * 1.0) == c2`.

## What the fix changes elsewhere (measured)

* The first row is unchanged in all 4000 random cases.
* 49.5% of rows (303,398 / 612,454) get a different color, because the ramp is
  re-parameterised; 278,727 of those change by exactly 1 unit out of 255. The
  largest change is 121 — a 2-to-4-row ramp, i.e. precisely the case that was
  wrong.
* In every case where a channel actually changes (`top[c] != bottom[c]`) no row
  leaves `[min(top[c], bottom[c]), max(top[c], bottom[c])]` and no channel
  reverses direction, before or after the fix. The only out-of-range values found
  anywhere are on channels where `top[c] == bottom[c]`: 188 in `main` and 207 with
  this fix, out of 1,224,908 channel values compared — that is the separate
  rounding defect described next, unchanged by this diff.
* `height` 0, 1 and 2 do not raise in either tree, and `height=1` still returns one
  row of `top_color`.

## A separate defect in the same expression, not fixed here

`int()` floors a float round-trip, so when a channel does not change
(`top_color[c] == bottom_color[c]`) some rows come out one unit *below* the
requested value. Measured over all 256 colors × heights 2..130 (256 × 8,514 =
2,179,584 rows sampled): 244 of the 256 colors have at least one wrong row, with
41,147 wrong rows in `main` and 40,522 with the endpoint fix — so this change
neither intends nor achieves fixing that. Worst color: `c = 31`, 362 wrong rows out
of the 8,514 rows sampled for it. It is
a real banding source for flat fills and deserves its own decision (rounding mode
vs. exact flat case), so I am leaving it out of the diff rather than smuggling a
rounding change in with the endpoint fix.

## Through the shipped pipeline

`GIFBuilder.save()` re-quantises to a global palette, which loses the endpoint
regardless of this bug. Building the same 480x480 `(0,0,0) → (255,0,0)` ramp
through the skill's own `core/gif_builder.py` on both trees and reading the saved
GIF back:

```
pre : unit bottom row (254, 0, 0)  -> saved GIF bottom row (246, 0, 0)  (128 colours)
post: unit bottom row (255, 0, 0)  -> saved GIF bottom row (247, 0, 0)  (128 colours)
```

`bottom_color` is absent from the saved GIF in both cases, so I am not claiming a
visible change in a quantised full-frame background. The observable effect is on
the image the function returns — which is its documented contract, what callers
composite, and what the small/short cases above get wrong by tens of units.

## Verification environment

Python 3.14 venv, Pillow 12.3.0, numpy 2.5.3, imageio 2.37.4. The repository has
no test suite for this skill (`git ls-tree -r --name-only origin/main` contains no
tests under `skills/slack-gif-creator/`), so the evidence above is the scripts in
the linked PR. No LibreOffice or Microsoft Office on this machine, so nothing here
is a rendered confirmation.

issues.title: `claude-api` skill eagerly injects ~156k tokens, exhausting the context window in a single tool call
issues.body:
# `claude-api` skill eagerly injects ~156k tokens, exhausting the context window in a single tool call

## Environment

| | |
|---|---|
| Claude Code | 2.1.220 |
| Skill | `claude-api` (bundled at `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Temp\claude\bundled-skills\2.1.220\<hash>\claude-api`; also published via `anthropic-agent-skills` → `github.com/anthropics/skills`) |
| Model | `claude-opus-5` (default context) |
| OS | Windows 11 (10.0.22631), Git Bash |
| Node | v24.14.0 |

## Summary

Invoking `Skill(claude-api)` injects a single message of **624,401 characters (~156k tokens)** — the concatenation of `SKILL.md` plus **31 reference documents**. On a default-context model this consumes the entire window, and the very next API call fails with `Prompt is too long`. The session is unrecoverable.

This is not a slow degradation. It is one tool call from a fresh session to a dead session.

## Reproduction

1. Start a new session on `claude-opus-5` (default context).
2. Prompt with a request to edit a Markdown file that mentions model names in prose, e.g.:

   > Opus 5 is now available and is more capable than Fable 5. Please update the model list in our global CLAUDE.md accordingly.

3. The model reads `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` (~1 KB), then invokes `Skill(claude-api)` per the skill's trigger.
4. Next assistant turn: `Prompt is too long`.

The task is editing a Markdown table in a config file. No code, no API calls, no SDK usage anywhere in scope.

*(The prompt above is minimized from the one that produced the transcript below; it retains the tokens that match the trigger — `Opus`, `Fable`, `CLAUDE.md`.)*

### Transcript evidence

| Entry | Type | Size |
|---|---|---|
| 6 | user prompt | 683 B |
| 13 | `Read` of a ~1 KB Markdown file | ~1 KB |
| 14 | `tool_use` / `Skill` | 1.2 KB |
| **17** | **skill payload** | **624,401 chars (~156k tokens)** |
| 19 | assistant | `Prompt is too long` |

## Expected vs. actual

**Expected:** the skill loads its entry document and reads references on demand, as the progressive-disclosure model for skills implies.

**Actual:** 32 documents arrive at once, before the model knows which — if any — are relevant.

## Analysis

### 1. Over half the payload is provably irrelevant to any given task

Composition of the 624,401 characters:

| Segment | Chars | Share |
|---|---|---|
| `shared/model-migration.md` | 143,685 | 23% |
| Managed Agents suite (14 files) | 202,069 | 32% |
| `SKILL.md` | 68,375 | 11% |
| Everything else (17 files) | 210,272 | 34% |

**`shared/model-migration.md` is the single largest file at 23% of the payload — and `SKILL.md`'s own subcommand table says to load it conditionally:**

> | `migrate` | … **Read `shared/model-migration.md` immediately** … |

It is gated behind an explicit subcommand, then loaded eagerly regardless. The Managed Agents suite (another 32%) is likewise a distinct feature area that a config-file edit never touches. **55% of the payload is two on-demand feature areas.**

Language detection does work — only TypeScript variants were included, not all nine languages. The eager loading of `shared/` defeats the savings.

### 2. No lighter invocation exists

The skill exposes exactly one subcommand, `migrate`. It cannot reduce the payload, because the dispatch instruction operates on already-loaded text:

> If the User Request at the bottom of this prompt is a bare subcommand string (no prose), **search every Subcommands table in this document** …

The document must be fully injected before the subcommand is read. There is no argument that loads less.

### 3. The trigger is far too broad for the payload size

From the skill description:

> TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`) …

Any prompt containing the bare string "Opus", "Sonnet", or "Claude" matches — including editing a file *named* `CLAUDE.md`. Coupled with a 156k-token payload and language that explicitly preempts the model's judgement (*"don't skip because it looks like a one-liner"*), the failure mode is systematic rather than incidental.

### 4. The payload was stale for the task that summoned it

The bundled content is stamped `## Current Models (cached: 2026-06-24)` and describes **Fable 5** as *"most capable widely released model"*. It contains no knowledge of Opus 5 — the exact fact being added to the file. The skill exhausted the session to supply information it did not have.

## Suggested fixes

Roughly in order of impact:

1. **Make `shared/` progressive.** Ship `SKILL.md` with an index of references and let the model `Read` what it needs. This alone cuts ~89% of the payload.
2. **Honour the existing conditional gates.** `model-migration.md` and the Managed Agents suite are already documented as on-demand; load them that way.
3. **Narrow the trigger.** Require an API/SDK signal (an `anthropic` import, an API call site, a model-id string in code) rather than any mention of a model name in prose. Editing a `.md` file should not match.
4. **Soften the anti-judgement language.** *"Don't skip because it looks like a one-liner"* suppresses exactly the check that would have avoided this.
5. **Budget-aware loading.** A skill about to consume ~78% of a 200k window should degrade to its index rather than fail the session.

## Impact

Any user on a default-context model who mentions a Claude model name loses their session. It is most likely to fire on trivial tasks — config edits, doc updates, casual questions about model choice — where the cost is least justified and the user has least warning.

**Workaround:** `"permissions": { "deny": ["Skill(claude-api)"] }` in `settings.json`, or run in a 1M-context session.

issues.title: skill-creator: eval-viewer escapeHtml is not attribute-safe and is applied inconsistently (display-path XSS)
issues.body:
### Summary

The skill-creator eval-viewer (`skills/skill-creator/eval-viewer/viewer.html`)
assembles HTML by string concatenation and assigns it with `innerHTML` in
`renderGrades` and `renderBenchmark`, relying on a helper `escapeHtml()` at each
interpolation point. Two gaps let attacker-influenced data reach the DOM as
markup:

1. **`escapeHtml()` is not attribute-safe.** It is implemented with the
   `textContent` → `innerHTML` round-trip, which escapes `<`, `>`, and `&` but
   **not** `"` or `'`. It is nonetheless used inside an HTML **attribute** — the
   per-assertion table renders grader evidence into a `title="..."` tooltip
   (`renderBenchmark`, the `<span ... title="Run N: <evidence>">` line). Evidence
   containing a double quote breaks out of the attribute and can attach an event
   handler.

2. **Several externally-sourced strings are interpolated raw**, with no
   `escapeHtml()` at all: the config label in the per-eval breakdown rows (while
   the *same* value is escaped in the table header), and `metadata.timestamp`,
   `metadata.evals_run`, `metadata.runs_per_configuration`, and the `delta.*`
   cells.

### Why this is reachable

`EMBEDDED_DATA` (from `benchmark.json` / `grading.json`) carries data that is
user-authored (assertion text, eval and skill names) or that quotes the output
of the skill under test (grader "evidence"). None of that is trusted markup.

### Reproduction

1. In a grading result, set an assertion's `evidence` to:

   ```
   x" onmouseover="alert(document.domain)
   ```

2. Generate the review and open the **Benchmark** tab.
3. Hover the ✓/✗ badge for that assertion in the per-assertion table. The
   `title="Run 1: x" onmouseover="alert(document.domain)">` markup closes the
   attribute early and the injected `onmouseover` handler fires.

### Fix

- Rewrite `escapeHtml()` to escape `&`, `<`, `>`, `"`, and `'` explicitly, so it
  is safe in both element-text and attribute contexts.
- Route the remaining raw externally-sourced string interpolations through
  `escapeHtml()`, leaving only locally-computed numbers interpolated directly.

The escaped forms render identically for normal data, so there is no visible
change.

### Scope / related

- This is the **display path**. The **embed path** — `generate_review.py`
  injecting `EMBEDDED_DATA` into the inline `<script>` without escaping `</`,
  which lets a `</script>` in skill output break out of the script element — is
  the separate issue #1075.
- The xlsx preview (`XLSX.utils.sheet_to_html` → `innerHTML`) relies on SheetJS's
  own cell-text escaping and is out of scope here.

issues.title: mcp-builder: evaluation.py scores 0/N against any real MCP server (TextContent not JSON serializable, swallowed into fabricated tool errors)
issues.body:
## Summary

`skills/mcp-builder/scripts/evaluation.py` (the Phase-4 evaluation harness) silently fabricates a tool-execution error for **every tool call against every real MCP server**, so the driven agent sees nothing but errors and the evaluation scores 0/N. The failure is invisible unless you dig into what the model was actually shown.

## Root cause

`connections.py:70` returns `result.content` from `call_tool()` — which for a real MCP server is `list[mcp.types.TextContent]` (pydantic objects). `evaluation.py:117` then does:

```python
tool_response = json.dumps(tool_result) if isinstance(tool_result, (dict, list)) else str(tool_result)
```

Since the value is a `list`, it hits `json.dumps()`, which raises `TypeError: Object of type TextContent is not JSON serializable` on **every single call**. The surrounding `try/except` converts that into a fabricated `"Error executing tool ..."` message fed back to the model, which then (reasonably) answers NOT_FOUND / gives up on every task.

One-line repro against any live MCP server:

```python
import json
result_content = await session.call_tool(name, args)  # list[TextContent]
json.dumps(result_content)  # TypeError — this is what evaluation.py does on every call
```

## Fix

Serialize the content blocks' text instead of json.dumps-ing pydantic objects, e.g.:

```python
def _serialize_tool_result(tool_result):
    if isinstance(tool_result, list):
        return "\n".join(
            block.text for block in tool_result if hasattr(block, "text")
        )
    return json.dumps(tool_result) if isinstance(tool_result, (dict, list)) else str(tool_result)
```

We patched a local copy this way and the same 11-task suite went from 0/11 (all fabricated errors) to 11/11 with real tool traffic.

## Secondary issue (same script)

The hardcoded default model is retired: `evaluation.py:223` / `:324` default to `claude-3-7-sonnet-20250219`, which returns `404 not_found_error` — so a stock run dies before the serialization bug is even reachable. Suggest defaulting to a current alias or requiring `-m`.

Found while using the skill exactly as documented (Phase-4 evaluation of a streamable-HTTP MCP server, `-t http`).

issues.title: skill-creator: silent benchmark failures (layout mismatch, inverted delta), broken trigger evals on Windows, and skill shadowing in trigger evals
issues.body:
Six reproducible issues in `skills/skill-creator`, found while auditing and testing the skill end-to-end. Roughly in order of impact:

## 1. SKILL.md directory layout is silently incompatible with aggregate_benchmark.py

SKILL.md instructs subagents to save to `<workspace>/iteration-<N>/eval-<ID>/<config>/outputs/` and to put `grading.json` "in each run directory" — a flat layout with no `run-N` level. `aggregate_benchmark.py` however skips every config dir without `run-*` subdirectories (`if not list(config_dir.glob("run-*")): continue`) and only reads `eval-*/<config>/run-*/grading.json`.

**Repro:** build a fixture in the exact SKILL.md layout, run `python -m scripts.aggregate_benchmark <dir>`. Result: `benchmark.json` with `runs: []`, summary prints only `Delta: +0.00`, exit code 0. Anyone following SKILL.md literally gets an empty benchmark with no error, and the iteration decision is made on "0% pass rate" noise. (The eval viewer, by contrast, handles the flat layout fine.)

**Suggested fix:** treat a config dir containing `grading.json` or `outputs/` but no `run-*` as a single run (`run_number = 1`), and exit non-zero when zero runs were found instead of writing an empty benchmark.

## 2. Delta sign flips in the improve flow (old_skill baseline)

SKILL.md's improve flow uses `old_skill/` as baseline next to `with_skill/`. `aggregate_benchmark.py` discovers configs alphabetically (`sorted(eval_dir.iterdir())`) and computes `delta = configs[0] - configs[1]`. Since `old_skill` sorts before `with_skill`, the baseline becomes primary.

**Repro:** with_skill pass rate 1.0, old_skill 0.0 → output `Delta: -1.00`. A clear improvement reads as a regression in benchmark.json, benchmark.md and the console summary. (The standard flow is unaffected only by the accident that `with_` sorts before `without_`.)

**Suggested fix:** fixed priority (`with_skill`/`new_skill` primary; `without_skill`/`old_skill` baseline) instead of discovery order. Also: SKILL.md line "Put each with_skill version before its baseline counterpart" is not actionable (the script decides), and schemas.md only allows `with_skill|without_skill` for `configuration` while SKILL.md mandates `old_skill` — worth reconciling.

## 3. eval_name is documented but never propagated

schemas.md documents `runs[].eval_name` in benchmark.json and viewer.html displays it as the eval heading, but `aggregate_benchmark.py` reads only `eval_id` from `eval_metadata.json`. The Benchmark tab therefore always shows "Eval 0" even though SKILL.md explicitly asks authors to give evals descriptive names.

**Suggested fix:** read `eval_name` from `eval_metadata.json` and include it in each runs[] entry.

## 4. run_eval.py: select.select() on pipes crashes every worker on Windows — and the failure is silent

`run_single_query` polls the `claude -p` subprocess with `select.select([process.stdout], ...)`. On Windows, `select()` only supports sockets; the call raises `OSError: [WinError 10093]` immediately. The parent catches the exception per query and records `False` ("not triggered"). Net effect on Windows: every should-trigger query scores 0, every should-not-trigger query "passes", exit code 0, and `run_loop.py` optimizes the description against garbage — the only hint is a stderr warning per run.

**Suggested fix:** replace select with a platform-neutral reader thread (blocking `read1()` into a `queue.Queue`, main loop polls with timeout) — patch available; happy to open a PR. Alternatively, abort the eval on such errors instead of recording `False`.

## 5. Trigger evals: an installed copy of the skill shadows the synthetic test skill

`run_eval.py` creates a synthetic command (`<name>-skill-<uuid>`) carrying the candidate description and counts a trigger only when that name is invoked. But if the skill under test is also installed in user scope (`~/.claude/skills/<name>` — the normal case when improving one's own installed skill), the real skill appears in the subprocess's skills list and wins: captured stream-json shows the model invoking `Skill: {"skill": "<name>"}` (the real one), which the eval counts as "not triggered". All positive queries then read as false negatives and the optimization loop measures nothing.

**Suggested fix:** at minimum warn when `~/.claude/skills/<name>` exists and advise temporarily moving it; better, fail fast. (Detecting the real-skill invocation and counting it as a trigger would be wrong — it fires on the installed description, not the candidate.)

## 6. No encoding="utf-8" anywhere — cp1252 pitfalls for non-ASCII skills on Windows

None of the `read_text()`/`write_text()`/`open()` calls in scripts/ and eval-viewer/ pass an encoding. On Windows (default cp1252, UTF-8 mode off) this means: UTF-8 SKILL.md files with umlauts are silently read as mojibake (`für` → `fÃ¼r`) and fed into trigger tests; emoji in SKILL.md raise `UnicodeDecodeError`; the HTML report write in `run_loop.py` crashes with `UnicodeEncodeError` on the ✓/✗ characters after the (expensive) eval iterations have already run; `package_skill.py`'s emoji prints crash under piped stdout. Workaround: `PYTHONUTF8=1`. Fix: pass `encoding="utf-8"` throughout (and consider `sys.stdout.reconfigure(errors="replace")` for the emoji prints).

---

Happy to provide the working patches for 1-5 as PRs (they are running locally: flat-layout support + loud zero-run failure, fixed delta priority, eval_name pass-through, thread-based reader, shadowing warning).

issues.title: web-artifacts-builder: bundle/init scripts fail on pnpm ≥10.1 (ERR_PNPM_IGNORED_BUILDS); stale favicon strip; fonts not inlined
issues.body: ## Summary On a current toolchain, `web-artifacts-builder`'s `scripts/init-artifact.sh` + `scripts/bundle-artifact.sh` don't produce a working self-contained bundle. There are three independent problems; **#1 is a hard blocker**. All are reproducible, and suggested fixes are included — happy to open a PR if useful. ## Environment - pnpm 11.9.0 (applies to pnpm **≥ 10.1**) - Node 26.x - Parcel 2.16.4 (auto-installed by `bundle-artifact.sh`) - recent `create-vite`, macOS ## 1. Blocker — pnpm ≥ 10.1 hard-errors on ignored build scripts, aborting the flow `pnpm add -D parcel …` (in `bundle-artifact.sh`) exits non-zero with `ERR_PNPM_IGNORED_BUILDS`, because pnpm ≥ 10.1 blocks dependency build scripts (`@parcel/watcher`, `@swc/core`, `lmdb`, `msgpackr-extract`) by default. `pnpm exec parcel …` independently re-trips the same error via its pre-exec deps-status check. With `set -e`, the script aborts before Parcel ever runs. `pnpm approve-builds` is an interactive TUI (not scriptable in a non-interactive build), and the relevant settings aren't `.npmrc`-settable. **Repro:** ```sh bash scripts/init-artifact.sh demo cd demo bash ../scripts/bundle-artifact.sh # → ERR_PNPM_IGNORED_BUILDS; build aborts before Parcel runs ``` **Suggested fix:** have `init-artifact.sh` (and/or `bundle-artifact.sh`) emit a project `pnpm-workspace.yaml`: ```yaml strictDepBuilds: false verifyDepsBeforeRun: false ``` This lets the stock flow run unmodified. The build scripts still **don't run** (prebuilt binaries are used), so it doesn't broaden the install surface. Equivalent CLI form: `--config.strict-dep-builds=false` on `pnpm add` and `--config.verify-deps-before-run=false` on `pnpm exec`. ## 2. Stale favicon cleanup → Parcel build failure on newer create-vite `init-artifact.sh` cleans the scaffold with a `sed` that only removes the old `vite.svg` icon link: ```sh sed -i '' '/` instead. Parcel doesn't honor Vite's `public/` convention, so the `/favicon.svg` reference fails to resolve (`Failed to resolve '/favicon.svg'`) and the build errors. **Suggested fix:** strip any icon link rather than only `vite.svg`: ```sh sed -i '' '/`, `

newItems.content: Frontier Red Team Claude reveals ECDSA curve origins Oct 16, 2026 “It’s just timestamps”: the decades-old mystery of the origins of one of the most popular cryptographic standards has been explained. We pursued this long-standing open question of the cryptographic community to settle concerns about ECDSA, which is one of our most widely used cryptographic standards. Readers should take this as a fun closing chapter and the end of years of speculation. There is no action to be taken or things to do differently. Most researchers trusted the curves already. Enjoy. ECDSA is the most widely used elliptic curve cryptography standard. It was adopted by NIST in 2000 as part of the FIPS 186-2 Digital Signature Standard which lists a set of standard elliptic curves of varying sizes and security levels. For curves over prime and binary fields, the specifications published a “seed” parameter whose hash value is used to define the coefficient b of the curve. The provenance of these seeds has been a long-standing question, as they were provided by the NSA with no explanation or justification. As an example, the NIST P-256 curve seed was SEED = C49D3608 86E70493 6A6678E1 139D26B7 819F7E90 with no information on where it came from. Neal Koblitz and Alfred Menezes wrote an excellent summary on this controversy, “ A Riddle Wrapped in an Enigma ”, which discusses the history and concerns around the seed values. newItems.title: Designing more efficient quantum circuits with Claude
newItems.content: Science Designing more efficient quantum circuits with Claude Oct 16, 2026 Quantum computers will need carefully designed circuits to run useful algorithms on limited hardware. We gave Claude plain-language specifications for eight such circuits, drawn from chemistry, optimization, physics simulation, and number theory, along with an automated evaluator that checks and scores each design. Working largely on its own, Claude found designs that improve on the best published circuits, in some cases by an order of magnitude or more. Such improvements substantially reduce the quantum resources that useful applications require, so practical quantum computers could arrive sooner than previously anticipated. This work was led by Andi Gu as part of Anthropic’s STEM Fellows Program, with mentorship from Alek Kemeny, a quantum physicist at Anthropic, in collaboration with Susanne Yelin (Harvard University) and Mikhail Lukin (Harvard University and QuEra Computing). Read the full paper on arXiv .
